descs.en: She married the arms dealer to protect her father. He has never stopped wondering whether she married him for love.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Elowen arranges flowers in the Walled City. Her father moves cargo for Zhao Zhendong, the arms dealer the whole city is afraid of. When three of Zhao’s containers are seized and her father takes the blame, Elowen walks into Zhao’s office at the Iron Docks and asks him to marry her.

She brings a contract. Three pages, in her own handwriting. Separate rooms. Her own shop. You don’t touch me unless I ask. He signs it without a word.

He knows why she wants him, and it isn’t love. He would burn the city down for her anyway. What he can’t do is ask the one question that matters: did she ever choose him?

Marriage of convenience · Morally grey hero · He falls first · Complete in four volumes, plus ten side stories

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

This is a dark romance. The love story is tender; the world around it isn’t. It includes:

• The arms trade, including weapons sold to militias that use child soldiers

• Torture and killing by the hero, on the page

• Unwanted touching at a dinner table

• Arson and serious burns

• A shooting at the shop with a child present

• A gunshot wound treated at home without anaesthetic

• Child abuse in a character’s past, described briefly, and a prison riot

• Grief for a mother who died giving birth

• Love scenes between the married couple, on the page

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
After The Softest Kind of Love I wanted to write the other kind: a love that’s quiet because it’s so big, between two people who aren’t soft at all.

Zhao is not a good man, and this book doesn’t pretend he is. Elowen knows exactly what he does. What she doesn’t know, for a long time, is what to do about the most frightening man in the city sleeping outside her door so she’ll never have to wonder where he is.

The flower-shop details are real: the four o’clock market, stems cut on the slant, a cooler kept just above freezing. Thank you for reading.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Elowen’s — Elowen’s flower shop in the Walled City. She painted the sign herself at nineteen.
The Walled City — The old quarter where the Lin family lives and the shop stands. Narrow streets, stairs, umbrellas.
The Iron Docks — The port where Zhao Zhendong does business, and where Lin Jian’s three containers were seized.
The house on the hill — Zhao’s house. Too many locks, two nameless dogs, and one door with no key for her.
The armory — The locked room under the house. A code for if she needs to hide; later, a key for if she just wants to come in.
The contract — Their marriage agreement. Page two, line six: he doesn’t touch her unless she asks.
Block C — The youth detention wing where Zhao met Chen Si at fifteen. He carries the scar of its winter riot.
Middlemist’s Red — A camellia thought to survive in only two places in the world. Everyone says there might be a third.
The paper twins — The Lin family’s buried secret about Raiden and Evangeline.
The Red Notice — The international alert issued with Zhao’s face on it.
The Velde deal — The biggest arms deal Zhao was ever offered, for a highland militia that uses child soldiers. He cancels it.

chapters.title: The Arms Dealer Who Bought Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: It’s raining, it’s nearly closing time, and the man her father works for buys every flower in the shop so he can wait there for her father’s call.
chapters.content:
The man who came into Elowen’s flower shop at seven o’clock on a wet Monday evening in March did not look like someone who had come to buy flowers.

He looked like someone who had come to collect a debt.

The brass bell over the door rang. Elowen looked up from the roses on her bench with “good evening” already halfway out, and then she saw the two men standing under the noodle shop awning across the street, not eating noodles. And the man who had come in without them.

He was tall, in a long black coat over a navy suit, collar open, no tie. His black hair was swept up and back, except for one strand the rain had knocked loose across his forehead. A silver watch. Heavy rings on long fingers. One hand in his coat pocket, the other at his side, and he wasn’t doing anything at all.

That, somehow, was worse.

“Good evening,” she said carefully.

His eyes settled on her. Narrow, heavy-lidded, in no hurry.

“Good evening.”

Low voice. Even. Perfectly polite.

Elowen put her knife down.

“Are you looking for something?”

“Flowers.”

Well, he’d come to the right place. She tried to ignore the cold feeling creeping up the back of her neck.

“Of course. What’s the occasion?”

“Does it matter?”

“It helps me suggest the right arrangement.”

He looked at the roses in front of her, then at the tulips by the window.

“Everything.”

She blinked. “Sorry?”

“I’ll take everything you have.”

For a second she wondered if he was joking. His face suggested he had never told a joke in his life.

“Everything in the shop?”

“Yes.”

“That’s a lot of flowers, sir.”

“I can see that.”

Elowen swallowed. “Are you opening a hotel?”

“No.”

“A restaurant?”

“No.”

“A wedding, then?”

He looked at her.

“Do I look like I’m getting married?”

She regretted asking immediately.

“No, sir.”

One corner of his mouth lifted. Lazy. Not quite a smile.

“Good. Then we understand each other.”

He took out his wallet.

“Name your price.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter past seven, Elowen had learned three things.

First, his name was Zhao Zhendong.

Second, he could pay for her entire stock without blinking. He hadn’t even let her finish the sum.

Third, he wasn’t leaving.

His men carried her flowers out to the cars at the kerb, bucket by bucket. He had taken the chair by the window, where he could see the door and the street at the same time, and he sat there with his coat open. He didn’t look at his phone. He didn’t ask for anything. He just watched.

She knew the name. Everyone in her father’s house knew it, even though nobody said it at dinner. Lin Jian had moved cargo for Zhao Zhendong for six years: containers, warehouses, customs forms that said whatever everyone needed them to say. Her father called it shipping. Elowen was twenty-four and not stupid. She knew what came through the Iron Docks in boxes nobody opened.

She also knew her father hadn’t been to his office in six days. He rang her every night at eight from somewhere he wouldn’t name, and every night she pretended not to hear how tired he sounded.

She picked up the next rose. Dry cut, on an angle, with the knife. Into cold water. Next one.

“Why a knife?”

She jumped. He hadn’t moved. He was looking at her hands.

“Scissors crush the stem. It can’t drink properly.”

He thought about that. “Like a wound. A clean one heals.”

Her knife stopped. Then it went on.

“You’re cutting them too short.”

She looked down. He was right. She’d taken half the stem off the last three, because she’d been watching him instead of the roses.

“Oh.” She moved her hand back. “Thank you.”

He leaned back. “You’re welcome.”

Silence. Then, as if he were asking the time:

“Lin Jian is your father.”

Her hand stopped.

“Yes.”

“How long have you had this shop?”

“Five years.”

“On your own?”

“Yes.”

He nodded, as if ticking something off.

“Do you know my father?” she asked.

“Very well.”

Something in the way he said it made her grip the knife tighter.

“Then you must be one of his colleagues,” she said, with the smile she kept for difficult brides.

“Something like that.”

He didn’t explain. Elowen, who could feel she’d asked one question too many, went back to her roses.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past seven, Mrs. Poon hurried in under her umbrella.

“Oh, thank goodness you’re still open. I’ve come for my mother’s tulips.”

Elowen looked at the empty buckets by the window, and her heart sank.

“Mrs. Poon, I’m so sorry. I’ve sold everything.”

“Everything?”

Elowen’s eyes went to the chair by the window. Mrs. Poon’s followed. She took in the coat, the rings, the men at the door, and her umbrella dripped slowly onto the floor.

“But it’s her birthday tomorrow,” she said, in a much smaller voice.

“How many did you order?” Zhao asked.

“Twelve. Pink.”

He turned his head a little toward the door. “Bring twelve pink tulips back in.”

One of his men went straight out into the rain.

“Mr. Zhao, you don’t have to—“

“She ordered them before I came.”

“But you’ve already bought them.”

“I remember.”

He said it so flatly that she had nothing to say back. A minute later Mrs. Poon left with her tulips in paper, thanking him three times. He didn’t answer once.

“That was kind of you,” Elowen said when the door closed.

He met her eyes. “Was it?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’re welcome.”

He turned back to the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven forty-two, his phone rang.

“Speak.”

Elowen wiped a counter that was already clean and kept her eyes down.

“Who signed the release?” A pause. His fingers tapped once on the arm of the chair. “Lin Jian.”

Her hand stopped on the cloth.

“I’ve been trying to reach him for six days.” Another pause. “Then keep looking.”

He ended the call. When she looked up, he was already looking at her.

“Does your father tell you where he goes?”

“Sometimes. He travels for work.”

“Does he answer when you call?”

“Usually.”

He nodded slowly, the way you nod at a lie you’ve decided to keep for later.

“Is something wrong?”

“Ask your father.”

“Did he do something?”

He looked at her for a while.

“Three containers of mine were seized at the Iron Docks. Your father handled their clearance. The containers are gone, the paperwork is gone, and, rather inconveniently, so is your father.”

The colour left her face. “My father wouldn’t steal from you.”

“I haven’t said he did.”

“Then—“

“I’d like to give him two weeks to explain.” He straightened his cuff. “First he has to pick up a phone.”

She understood the words. More to the point, she understood what came after two weeks.

“Does he call you every evening?”

“Almost every evening.”

“What time?”

She hesitated. Then, because there was no point: “Eight.”

He already knew. She could see it on him. He’d only wanted to see whether she’d lie.

He glanced at his watch.

“How considerate.”

He got up and came to the counter. She hadn’t realised how tall he was until he was standing on the other side of it, close enough that she could smell sandalwood and wet wool and, under it, something sharp and oily she didn’t want to name. She took half a step back without meaning to. His eyes followed the movement.

“Relax.”

“Sorry.”

“Don’t apologise.”

He looked at the clock over the counter, then at her phone beside the till.

“Does he call this number?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

The little brass clock struck eight, and the phone lit up.

Baba

Relief went through her so fast it was almost embarrassing.

“Baba!”

“Little flower.” Her father’s voice, tired and warm. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet, I was just—“

“Why not? Don’t tell me it’s only eight. You’ve been on your feet all day.”

“Then come and bring me dinner.”

“Next time. I’ll make it up to you.”

A hand appeared on the counter beside hers, palm up. Silver rings. Waiting.

She stopped talking. She looked at the hand, then at his face. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to.

“Elowen?” her father said. “Are you there?”

“Give me the phone, Miss Lin.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to speak to your father.”

Quiet, unhurried, and not a question.

“Baba,” she whispered, “someone wants to—“

“Elowen.” Her father’s voice changed. “Who’s there?”

Zhao took the phone. His fingers closed over hers on it before she let go, warm skin and cold rings, and she felt it all the way up her arm, which was a completely ridiculous thing to feel right now.

“Good evening, Lin Jian.”

The silence on the line went on and on.

“…Mr. Zhao.”

“Six days.”

“I can explain.”

“I’m sure you can.”

“Please, sir. A little more time—“

“Don’t ask me for time while I’m standing in your daughter’s shop.”

Elowen went completely still.

“Two weeks,” Zhao said. “You find out who sold my route, or you come and tell me why you can’t.”

“Yes, sir.” Then, rough: “Leave my daughter out of this.”

For the first time that evening, his face changed. Only a narrowing of the eyes.

“Then you should have answered your phone.”

He hung up and put the phone down in front of her. She looked at it as if it belonged to somebody else.

“Where is my father?”

“I was hoping you’d tell me.”

“I don’t know!” It came out too loud. She brought it down. “I really don’t. He hasn’t told me anything.”

She looked frightened. He’d expected that. If he was honest, he’d counted on it a little.

He had spent six days trying every way there was to reach Lin Jian. Locked office. A driver who knew nothing. A phone that was always off. But the man had one habit he couldn’t break: a call at eight, every night, to his eldest daughter. Zhao’s people had known that for a week. They knew where she lived and what time she locked up. He hadn’t come here for flowers.

“Mr. Zhao,” she said. “Please don’t hurt my father.”

The rain was loud against the glass.

“Then tell him to stop making me look for him.”

He put on his gloves. At the door, he stopped.

“One of my men will be outside tomorrow night. If your father wants me, he can talk to him.”

“And if he doesn’t?”

“He’ll still be outside.” He opened the door. “Next time, I’d rather not have to take your phone.”

The bell rang, and he walked out into the rain.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near midnight, in the back of his car, Zhao read the messages as they came in.

Bao: Shop’s locked. Miss Lin got home fine. She checked the side door twice.

Bao: Same tomorrow?

Zhao: Every night. Till she locks up.

He put the phone away.

On the seat beside him lay a small blue floret that had fallen off one of the delphiniums his men had carried out. Smaller than his thumbnail. Ridiculous, really. He picked it up and turned it between two fingers.

He hadn’t bought every flower in her shop because he liked flowers, or because he had anywhere to put them. He’d needed a reason to stay until eight.

He opened his wallet and slid the floret in behind his identity card, flat, where it would stay dry.

“Drive.”

Behind them, the little shop went dark in the rain.

chapters.title: Her Father Owes Three Containers
chapters.desc: Her father has lost three containers that weren’t carrying farm machinery, and he has two weeks. Elowen takes the key to his files and finds one letter.
chapters.content:
The first thing Elowen did the next morning was lie to her father. She told him she’d slept well.

The second thing was ask him if he was in trouble.

Lin Jian nearly dropped his teacup.

He had come home at midnight, for the first time in six days, smelling of the cigarettes he’d sworn on Mama’s photo he had given up. Nobody had asked where he’d been. Now it was breakfast, or what passed for it. Ah Sim had made congee and steamed buns and four little side dishes, and nobody was eating much. Raiden was scrolling on his tablet. Eliana sat curled up on her chair in one of Raiden’s hoodies, peeling an orange and listening to everything. Evangeline poured tea for everyone and said nothing, which for Evangeline was normal. Elara was away at university and knew none of this, and Elowen envied her.

Her father put his cup down very carefully.

“Why would you ask that?”

“Because Mr. Zhao was in my shop last night. You heard him.”

Raiden’s thumb stopped on the screen. “He was in the shop?”

“He bought everything.”

“Everything?” said Eliana.

“Every flower.”

Raiden gave a short laugh. “Well. That’s one way to make an entrance.”

“Raiden,” said Elowen.

“What? I’m only saying.”

“He asked about you, Baba,” she said. “He said three containers were missing. And he said two weeks.”

Lin Jian shut his eyes. There it was.

“Baba. What’s happening?”

He didn’t speak for a few seconds. Then he pushed his bowl away and stood up.

“Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The study smelled of old paper and tobacco. Her father shut the door and stood by the desk looking at its drawers, as if he couldn’t decide where to start. He was a big man, broad and grey, and this morning he looked as if someone had let half the air out of him.

“Sit down, little flower.”

She sat. He didn’t.

“Those three containers were supposed to be agricultural machinery.”

“Supposed to be?”

“They were declared as machinery. Tractor parts. The forms were done, the bookings were made, everything set to go through the Iron Docks.”

“And they weren’t tractor parts.”

“Some of it was.” He rubbed his face. “Under the tractor parts was something else. Don’t ask me what. You know what he sells.”

She did. She’d grown up in this house. You didn’t open the long boxes that sat in the garage overnight, and you didn’t ask why some of Baba’s visitors had accents from places you couldn’t find on a map.

“You did the clearance.”

“That’s my job. A container needs a port, a ship, a warehouse, a driver who doesn’t ask questions, and forms that say what everyone needs them to say. I know which forms go where. I know which customs officers like which whisky at New Year.” His mouth twisted. “Twenty years.”

“And customs took them.”

“All three. One after another, over eleven days.”

“How much?”

He didn’t answer.

“Baba. How much?”

“Enough to buy this house three times over.”

Elowen sat back. The Lin house wasn’t small. It was old and tall, all stairs, behind a red door with a brass fish for a knocker, and it was every year her father had worked since before she was born.

Three of it.

“How did customs know?”

“That’s what I’ve been trying to find out. Somebody tipped them off. They walked straight to those three. Not the ones before, not the ones after.” He sat down at last, heavily. “After the first, I thought it was a mistake in the paperwork. After the second, I knew it wasn’t. After the third, I knew someone was doing it on purpose. And all three went through my desk. So who does Zhao look at?”

“You didn’t tell him.”

“I tried to fix it first.”

“Baba, he’s Zhao Zhendong.”

“I know exactly who he is.”

He had never spoken to her that sharply. Then he sagged.

“That’s why I wanted it fixed before he found out. I’ve seen what he does to people who lose his things. I watched him make a customs officer eat the form he’d signed. Chew it and swallow it.”

Her chest went tight. “Is he going to hurt you?”

Her father looked at her for a long moment.

“I don’t know.”

That frightened her more than any other answer could have.

“Then let me help. I can go through your files, I can—“

“No.” He was on his feet again. “You stay out of this. You go to your shop and sell your flowers, and if that man comes in again, you give him whatever he wants and you smile. Promise me.”

She looked past him at the two locked cabinets in the back corner of the room.

She didn’t promise.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came back to the dining room, Raiden had given up pretending to eat. He turned the tablet round to face her.

“Traffic cameras round the shop. Eliana got me in. Don’t ask.”

“Don’t ask,” Eliana agreed, and ate a piece of orange.

A black sedan sat across the street from Elowen’s shop. Raiden swiped. The same car, another night, a little further down. Swipe. Again.

“Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Last night.” He looked up. “They were watching you before he ever walked in. He didn’t come for flowers, Jie.”

“I’d worked that out.”

“They’re not exactly subtle. He parks where he can see the front and the side door. Your side door, which you never lock.”

“I lock it.”

“You lock it sometimes.”

Eliana held out a piece of orange to her without looking up. “Did he scare you?”

Elowen thought of the hand on the counter, palm up. Of her father’s voice changing the second he heard who it was.

“A little.”

Raiden’s face went hard, which on Raiden was rare enough to notice. He spent most of his life playing the cheerful, slightly useless son, and he did it so well that half of Baba’s associates thought he was simple.

“Then stay away from him.”

“He’s looking for Baba. I don’t think staying away will make him stop.”

“It’s not your job.”

“I know.”

Knowing it and leaving it alone weren’t the same thing, though.

At the end of the table, Evangeline topped up Elowen’s tea before it was half empty. Their fingers touched on the pot, and she kept hers there a second longer than she needed to. From Evangeline, that was a whole speech.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon, Uncle Mok drove her father to the warehouse to see Old Lau, and the house went quiet.

The key to the study cabinets lived behind the clock on the bookshelf. It had lived there since Elowen was fifteen. Her father thought nobody knew.

She sat on the study floor with her back against the cabinet and went through all of it: invoices, shipping manifests, customs declarations, half of it in the shorthand her father used for anything he didn’t want to write plainly. Most of it was dull. Some of it she didn’t understand. But she could read dates, and she could read what happened first and what happened next. She had kept the household accounts since she was twelve.

The first container was seized on the seventeenth of February. The second on the twenty-second. The third on the twenty-eighth.

She laid the papers out in order on the rug. That was when she noticed the phone log.

A short call, under two minutes, the evening before the first seizure. The number was saved under one letter.

K.

She went to the second file. There it was again. The third. Again. Each time, less than a day before customs opened the box.

She checked the dates. Then she checked them again, because she didn’t like what they said.

Her father’s notes in the margins didn’t help.

Ask K about the new route.

Wait for K’s confirmation.

Do not move without K.

Folded between two manifests was a sheet with no letterhead and no signature. Only three lines.

The third container was never supposed to reach the Iron Docks.

You were told to wait.

You should have listened.

She read it three times. It wasn’t dated. It had been folded small, pocket-small, by someone in a hurry. She turned it over. Nothing. But when she tilted it toward the window, the light caught a faint dent where someone had pressed hard with a pen on the sheet above it.

One letter. K.

Her fingers had gone cold.

She photographed every page that mattered, put everything back exactly as she’d found it, locked the cabinet, and returned the key to its place behind the clock.

Whoever K was, they’d been there from the start. And they had made very sure her father would think it was his own fault.

She opened the shop at three.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan came in off his scooter at five with his helmet under his arm, nineteen and permanently starving. He had delivered for her for two years, and he talked about the motorbike he was saving for roughly every ninety seconds.

“Miss Lin. There’s a car outside.”

“There are lots of cars outside.”

“This one was there last night as well. Black. Nobody gets out.” He dropped his voice. “Is someone after you? Do you owe money? Because I’ve got savings.”

“You’ve got motorbike savings.”

“I’ve got savings. The motorbike can wait.” He thought about it. “A bit. A month, maybe.”

She almost laughed. It got stuck somewhere on the way up, because he meant it, and because a boy with motorbike savings had just offered more than anyone else had all week.

“Nobody’s after me. Take the wreath to the Chungs, and don’t go up the hill road on that thing. It’s wet.”

“It’s electric, Miss Lin. It does thirty.”

“Then you’ll crash slowly. Go.”

He went. He came back a minute later for the wreath, which he’d forgotten, and grinned at her from the doorway.

“If it is a gangster, tell him I do deliveries.”

“Xiao Pan!”

Gone, before she could tell him to wear his helmet. She stood behind the counter with her hand flat on the photographs in her phone, and looked at the car across the street until the light went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven, the black sedan pulled up across the street.

Elowen saw it while she was wrapping the last bouquet of the day. The man in the driver’s seat was one of the two from under the noodle shop awning last night: big and calm, with a tired, patient face.

She looked at him through the glass. He looked back. Neither of them moved.

She thought about pulling the blind down.

She put the kettle on instead.

At twenty past seven he got out and came in, leaving the other man in the car.

“Good evening, Miss Lin.”

“Good evening.”

She put a cup of jasmine tea on the counter. He looked at it with honest surprise.

“That’s for you.”

“For me?”

“Unless your boss drinks tea through you.”

He didn’t seem sure whether he was allowed to smile. She poured a second cup for herself.

“Please.”

He picked it up as if it might go off. “Thank you.”

“What’s your name?”

He hesitated. “Bao.”

“Does Mr. Zhao always make you sit outside in the rain, Bao?”

“It’s the job, Miss Lin.”

“Sounds miserable.”

“It’s fine.”

She drank her tea. “How long have you worked for him?”

“Six years.”

“Does he always send someone to watch the people he’s looking for?”

“Only when he needs to find them.”

There was no point pretending she didn’t understand that. She put her cup down.

“Would you take him a message?”

Bao’s shoulders changed. “What message?”

Elowen looked at the rain on the window. Then back at him.

“Tell Mr. Zhao I know he’s looking for my father.”

He waited. “And?”

She picked her cup up again.

“Tell him I’m coming.”

Bao stared at her. “Miss Lin, I don’t think—“

“You’re his messenger, aren’t you?”

He shut his mouth.

“Then please deliver it.” She gave him the smile she kept for customers. “Thanks for keeping me company.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes after eight, Zhao Zhendong was at his desk at the Docks with a shipping report he’d read four times without taking any of it in when Bao rang.

“She gave me tea, sir.”

Zhao looked up. “Tea.”

“Jasmine.”

“And?”

“She said to tell you she knows you’re looking for her father.” A pause. “And she says she’s coming.”

For a moment Zhao said nothing. He looked at the clock.

For six nights, Lin Jian had rung his daughter at eight from wherever he was hiding. Tonight her father was home, and she had used the hour to send a message to the man who wanted him.

“Did she look frightened?”

“Not really, sir.”

“Did she ask you anything?”

“My name. And how long I’ve worked for you.”

His fingers tapped once on the desk. “And you told her.”

“Six years.”

The corner of his mouth lifted. “Then you told her too much.”

“Sorry, sir.”

“Did she drink the tea?”

“She had a cup with me.”

“Good.”

He put the phone down and looked at the rain on the window. Lin Jian had a daughter who poured tea for the man sent to watch her. Who was polite to dangerous men, and who had apparently decided she was done being frightened quietly.

He picked up the phone again and rang the front desk.

“Keep the meeting room ready from tomorrow.”

“Yes, sir. Who are we expecting?”

His eyes went to the wallet on the desk, where a small blue floret was pressed flat behind his identity card.

“Miss Lin. And put fresh flowers in there.”

For the first time in six days, Zhao Zhendong was looking forward to a meeting.

chapters.title: The Florist Who Read His Shipping Routes
chapters.desc: She takes two buses to the Iron Docks to tell Zhao who sold his route. The man she means is sitting on the desk the whole time.
chapters.content:
Two days later, on Thursday morning, Elowen took two buses to the Iron Docks.

The first was packed, the second smelled of diesel, and by the time she got off at Northgate the hem of her skirt had picked up some mud. She’d thought about a taxi. Then she remembered that Zhao Zhendong had bought her whole shop without asking the price, and decided she wasn’t spending money to impress him.

She wasn’t going there to impress him anyway. She was going to tell him something he apparently hadn’t worked out for himself.

She hadn’t told her father. He’d only have locked the study, and her in it.

The Northgate building stood behind a security gate above the docks. Cranes swung containers over the water, trucks crawled through the loading bays, and men in orange vests shouted at each other between warehouses. It was not a place built with florists in mind. Elowen held her handbag tighter.

A guard stopped her at the gate. “Name?”

“Elowen Lin. I’m here to see Mr. Zhao.”

“Appointment?”

“No.”

He was opening his mouth to send her away when his earpiece crackled. He straightened.

“Miss Lin. Follow me, please.”

So he’d been expecting her. Of course he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

His office was on the top floor. A woman in a dark suit met her at the lift and offered to take her coat. Elowen kept it. She was nervous enough without having to get her things back from strangers.

The office door stood half open. Zhao was behind the desk in a beige suit, collar open, that one strand of hair down over his forehead again.

A heavier man in his forties sat on the corner of the desk with a coffee, as if he owned the desk and possibly the building. Good watch, soft face, the kind of easy smile waiters trusted.

“You’re late with those numbers,” he was saying.

“You’re early,” said Zhao. Then he saw her in the doorway, and he stood.

“Miss Lin.”

The man on the desk turned. His eyes went over her once, the handbag, the muddy hem, the folder.

“You came,” said Zhao.

“Good morning, Mr. Zhao.”

His eyes dropped to her shoes. “You took the bus.”

She blinked. “Yes.”

“Two buses.”

“How do you know that?”

He didn’t answer. The man on the desk laughed.

“Don’t bother. He probably knows what you had for breakfast too. Lin Jian’s daughter, is it? I’m Kang. I run his routes.”

Kang.

Her heart hit her ribs once, hard. Her face didn’t move. Twenty-four years in her father’s house had to be good for something.

“Mr. Kang,” she said politely.

“Little sister.” He lifted his coffee to her. “Your father talks about you.”

“Mr. Zhao,” she said, “could I speak to you privately?”

Kang laughed. “Anything you say to him, you can say to me. I’ve been with him since he was carrying boxes.”

Zhao looked at her. Then at Kang.

“Kang stays. He’s been with me eight years. There’s nothing in this office he isn’t entitled to hear.”

Kang smiled at her. Elowen felt it on the back of her neck.

She couldn’t say why without saying everything. So she sat down, put the folder on her knees, and decided she would simply not look at the corner of that desk for as long as this took.

A secretary brought in a tray and set jasmine tea in front of her.

She looked at the cup. “Thank you.”

Zhao sat down across from her. “Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She paused. “Breakfast.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He waited.

“…A bun.”

“What kind?”

“Does that matter?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then why ask?”

Kang snorted into his coffee.

“Bao,” said Zhao.

The door opened, and there was Bao. He gave her a very small nod, as if they’d shared a secret over tea, which to be fair they had.

“Get Miss Lin something to eat. Egg tarts, from the bakery on the ferry road.”

“Mr. Zhao, I really don’t need—“

“Bao.”

“Yes, sir.”

Bao went. Elowen stared at the closed door. She had come about three missing containers, and somehow she was being ordered pastry.

She drank some tea. It was very good, which was annoying.

“Does your father know you’re here?” Zhao asked.

“No.”

“Does he know you’ve been through his files?”

“No.”

He looked at her a moment longer than he needed to. “Good. What did you find?”

She laid three pages on the desk.

“The first container was seized on the seventeenth of February. The second on the twenty-second. The third on the twenty-eighth.”

“Those dates are already in my records.”

“I know. But the evening before each one, the same person rang my father. Every time.” She kept her eyes on Zhao. “He saved the number under one letter. He wrote himself notes about waiting for that person’s confirmation before he moved anything. And there’s this.”

She put the photocopy on the desk.

The third container was never supposed to reach the Iron Docks.

You were told to wait.

You should have listened.

Zhao read it. Nothing moved on his face.

“Where was this?”

“In his files. No signature. Just a letter pressed through from the sheet above.”

She didn’t say which letter. She didn’t look at the corner of the desk.

“And after every seizure,” she went on, “the Qiu brothers rang the same buyer. It’s in my father’s notes. Within a week, every time.”

“Why would it be the Qius?”

“They want the contracts you have. They had every reason to want your containers opened. But they couldn’t have known which three to point customs at, unless someone inside your company told them.”

Kang laughed.

“Oh, this is wonderful.” He picked up the photocopy and dropped it again. “A mystery letter, a few phone calls and a theory about the Qiu brothers. That’s your evidence?”

“I didn’t say it was proof.”

“Then what are you doing here?”

“Showing Mr. Zhao what I found.”

“Little girl, do you know how long I’ve run these routes? Eight years. Since before you finished school. You walk in with three bits of paper and think you understand how we work?” He shook his head. “Your father loses three containers, and his daughter comes in here to lecture us. Go back to your flower shop, Miss Lin.”

Her fingers tightened on her skirt. She’d spent two days on papers she barely understood, trying to find something that would keep her father alive. She hadn’t come here to be laughed at.

She still didn’t look at him.

Zhao picked up his phone and pressed a name.

“Si. Three route changes.” He read the dates off her page, the day before each seizure. “Whose code approved them. And one man’s phone records, both his numbers. Now.”

He hung up and put the phone face down. “It takes about half an hour. Drink your tea, Miss Lin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the longest half hour of her life.

Kang stayed on the desk. After a while he started talking again, easy and friendly: the weather, diesel prices, a place in the old town that did a duck he’d die for.

“You like duck, Miss Lin?”

“No.”

“Everybody likes duck.”

“Then I’m not everybody.”

“Shy. Lin Jian’s girls are all shy, I hear. The quiet one especially, what’s her name, the twin—“

Zhao looked up from his binder.

Kang shut his mouth.

The phone buzzed. Zhao turned it over and read the screen. He read it again. Then he put it down, very gently.

“Kang.”

“Yes?”

“The first container’s route was changed the day before customs opened it. Who approved it?”

“Operations, I think.”

“The second?”

“Same thing, probably.”

“And the third?”

“I don’t remember every adjustment.”

“All three went through on your code.” Zhao didn’t raise his voice. “And the number that rang Lin Jian the night before each one is a phone registered to you.”

Kang’s smile slipped. “Someone could have used my login. Come on. Eight years. You know me.”

“I do.”

“Then you know I’d never—“

Zhao moved.

It was so fast Elowen barely saw it. One second Kang was sitting on the desk. The next, Zhao had his wrist and had slammed his hand flat on the polished wood.

There was a sharp crack. Kang screamed.

Elowen flinched so hard her chair scraped. “Mr. Zhao!”

He didn’t look at her. “Bao. Take Miss Lin downstairs.”

Bao was back. She hadn’t heard him come in. He had a paper bag in one hand, and he put the other on her elbow, not rough but very firm, and turned her to the door.

“Eight years,” she heard Zhao say behind her, quietly. “Eight years at my table.”

She was three steps down the stairwell when she heard the second crack. After it, the screaming had no words in it at all.

Bao kept walking. His hand stayed steady on her elbow all the way down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Zhao let go.

Kang folded over his hand on the carpet, white to the lips. Two of the warehouse men had come up and stood by the door.

“His phone, his laptop, his office machine,” Zhao said. “Everything he’s touched in a month. Then take him to the doctor on Salt Street. The one who doesn’t write things down.”

“Please. I can explain—“

“You’ve had eight years to explain.”

They took him out by the back stairs.

Zhao looked at the desk. A red smear where Kang’s hand had been. Her tea, half drunk, beside it. She had sat there for half an hour knowing exactly who it was and hadn’t looked at him once.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down twenty minutes later.

She was standing in the side yard by the door, holding the paper bag Bao had pushed into her hands. He’d washed. His sleeves were dry. There was a small dark spot on one cuff.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Look at me.”

She looked up. His face told her nothing.

“Did he touch you?”

“No.”

“Did he threaten you?”

“Not exactly.”

“He won’t bother you again.”

She didn’t ask what that meant. She was fairly sure she didn’t want to know.

“Kang’s been selling my routes to the Qius,” he said, as if he were reading out the weather. “Your father’s debt is closed. He’ll have it in writing today.”

The breath went out of her. “All of it?”

“All of it.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t.” He studied her. “You found in two days what my people missed for a month. I want you to read my routes. I’ll pay you more than your shop makes in a year. Every month.”

“No.”

“You haven’t heard the number.”

“I sell flowers, Mr. Zhao.”

He nodded slowly, as if that were an answer he respected.

“Then listen. Your father’s safe from me. He isn’t safe from anyone else. The Qius have his whole network now, every warehouse, every driver, every officer he pays. And Kang had friends here. They’ll remember who pointed at him.”

“Then protect him.”

“I don’t protect the people I pay. I pay them to take the risk. Your father knows that.”

“Then who do you protect?”

Wind came in off the water. Somewhere behind the warehouses, a crane groaned. He took his time.

“What’s mine.”

His eyes dropped to her mouth, once, and came back up. Fast enough that she could tell herself she’d imagined it. She hadn’t. Heat climbed her throat, and she hated it, because twenty minutes ago she’d heard what those hands could do, and her body clearly didn’t care.

“Please don’t hurt my father,” she said.

“Your father isn’t the one I’m angry with.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao walked her to the gate.

“Does Mr. Zhao always do this?”

“Do what, Miss Lin?”

She held up the bag. Two egg tarts, still warm, the paper gone see-through at the corners.

“Order food for people who come to see him.”

Bao thought about it. “No.”

“Oh.”

“Usually he tells them to leave.”

She laughed. She hadn’t expected to. It was the first time since she’d walked into the building.

At the bus stop she ate the first tart standing up, because it turned out she was starving. When her bus came, a black car with tinted windows pulled away from the kerb across the road and followed it all the way back to the Walled City. She couldn’t see who was driving. She knew whose car it was.

Upstairs, Zhao stood at the window until the bus turned the corner. Then he rang Chen Si back.

“It was Kang.”

“I saw the records.” Chen Si’s voice was always smooth. It went smoother when he was curious. “There’s more. Three payments from a shell company that leads back to the Qius, the first two days before the first seizure. And Lin Jian held the third container, the way he was told to. Kang released it himself, under Lin Jian’s name. Then he sent him that note so he’d think it was his own fault and run.”

Zhao looked at the harbour.

“Close Lin Jian’s debt. All of it. He gets it in writing today, and he comes in on Monday. He doesn’t need to hide anymore.”

“Done. Who found it?”

“His daughter.”

“The florist?” A pause. “She found in two days what your floor missed for a month. What’s she like?”

Zhao looked at the half-drunk tea on his desk.

“She didn’t look at him once, Si. The whole half hour.”

“Zhendong,” said Chen Si. “Are you smiling? I can hear it.”

Zhao hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after noon, Elowen’s phone rang on the bus. Unknown number.

“Miss Lin.”

She knew the voice at once.

“Your father will have the letter this afternoon. He can stop jumping every time his phone rings.”

She closed her eyes. “Thank you, Mr. Zhao.”

He didn’t say anything to that. Then:

“Have you eaten?”

She looked at the paper bag on her knees, one tart left. “Yes.”

“Good. Go home, Miss Lin.”

The line went dead.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Zhao found a small slip of paper on the carpet that had fallen out of her folder. A bus ticket. Two transfers, her shop to the Iron Docks.

He looked at it for longer than a bus ticket deserved, then put it beside his phone instead of in the bin. He had expected Lin Jian’s daughter to come and beg. She had brought him the name of a traitor and hadn’t asked him for one single thing.

He pressed the intercom.

“Send fresh jasmine tea to Miss Lin’s shop in the morning. And flowers.”

He found he didn’t like the idea of her shop sitting empty.

chapters.title: A Proposal Made Like a Business Deal
chapters.desc: Old Lau ends up in hospital and her father hires a gun he can’t pay for. So Elowen writes three pages of terms and asks Zhao to marry her.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re negotiating my whole life. It seemed fair.”
chapters.content:
The envelope came at six that same evening, by courier, addressed to Lin Jian in square black handwriting.

Her father opened it standing at the dining table while Elowen laid out bowls. She saw his hands start to shake halfway down the page. By the end he’d sat down without seeming to notice the chair.

Inside was one typed page from a law firm, and clipped to it a card with four words in the same square hand.

Your daughter found it.

He read the card twice. Then he looked at her.

“You went there.”

She put the last bowl down. “Yes.”

“To the Docks.”

“Yes.”

“Alone?”

“I took the bus.”

“The bus.” He laughed, an awful cracked sound, and put his hand over his eyes. “You took the bus to Zhao Zhendong.”

“Baba—“

“You promised me.”

“I didn’t, actually.”

Wrong thing to say. He dropped his hand, and she saw how frightened he was, and how angry, and how hard he was trying to be one and not the other in front of her. Then he folded. Not loudly. Her father didn’t do anything loudly. He just put his face in his hands at the table and cried without a sound.

Elowen went to the stove and fussed with the kettle with her back to him, so he could have that.

When she brought the tea, he’d stopped. Red eyes. Hands flat on the table.

“Who was it?”

“Kang.”

He flinched as if she’d hit him. “Kang rang me himself, every time. He always asked after you children.”

“He won’t be asking anymore.”

She didn’t tell him about the crack, or the stairs, or the second sound. She told him she’d found a pattern in his papers and Mr. Zhao had checked it. All true.

Her father was a clever man under the fear. She watched him get to where she’d got to on the bus home.

“The Qius have my routes.”

“Yes.”

“And everyone at the Docks knows Lin Jian’s girl pointed at one of Zhao’s oldest men.”

“Yes.”

He stared into his tea. Neither of them said what came next. A fixer with no network had nothing left to sell, and a fixer whose daughter had cost the Qiu brothers their man inside had enemies on both sides of the water.

Well done, Elowen. Brilliant work.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight the next morning a van stopped outside the shop, and Bao carried in a red tin of jasmine tea and enough flowers to fill every bucket she owned: white peonies, garden roses, sweet peas from somewhere that definitely wasn’t the market, two armfuls of blue delphinium. No card.

It was far too much for one shop. She sold what she could and gave the rest away by the armful. Peonies for Mrs. Poon’s mother. Roses for the noodle shop across the road. Sweet peas for the girl from the bank who always looked as if she’d been crying. By closing time there was hardly anything left.

From the car across the street, Bao watched her do it. She assumed he reported it. She didn’t care.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Lau didn’t come to work on Tuesday.

On Wednesday morning, the street sweepers found him in the alley behind the fish market with both legs broken and a piece of paper in his shirt pocket.

LIN JIAN’S PEOPLE WALK SLOWLY NOW.

Old Lau had run her father’s warehouse since before Elowen was born. He was big and slow and gentle, and when she was small he used to carry her on his shoulders at the New Year market so she could see over everyone’s heads to the lion dance.

She went to the hospital that afternoon with yellow gerberas. Never chrysanthemums on a ward; every florist knew that. He was asleep, grey under the lights, plaster from his hips to his toes. His wife jumped up when Elowen came in and bowed, and bowed again, with a bag of oranges in her lap she’d forgotten to put down.

“Thank you for coming, Miss Lin. Thank you. He’ll be so happy.”

Old Lau’s eyes opened, foggy with whatever they’d given him. He found her anyway.

“Ah. Elowen. The yellow ones.”

“Don’t talk, Uncle Lau.”

“You always wanted the yellow lion.” His eyes drifted shut. “Don’t tell your father I cried. When they… don’t tell him.”

“I won’t.”

“Tell him I’ll be back Monday.”

Both legs. Plaster to the hip. Monday.

“I’ll tell him.”

Her hands were perfectly steady all the way down the corridor, past the nurses’ station, past a man asleep across three plastic chairs. They stayed steady right up until she’d locked herself in the toilet at the end of the ward. Then she held the edge of the sink and threw up, as quietly as she could, because in her father’s house you did everything so nobody heard it through a wall.

Thank you for coming, Miss Lin.

A week ago she’d been proud of herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night her father came home at two in the morning with a stranger in the car: a thin man with a gun under his jacket and eyes that kept going to the doors.

She had begged him at dinner not to do this. He’d said he wouldn’t.

“Protection,” he said now, and wouldn’t look at her.

“With what money? Nobody’s paying you. Who did you borrow from?”

“Go to bed, Elowen.”

“Baba, who?”

“I said go to bed!”

He had never once shouted at her. The man with the gun found something interesting on the ceiling. Then her father’s face crumpled, and he said sorry, and sorry again, and went into the study and shut the door.

She stood in the hall. Upstairs, light showed under Eliana’s door from her screens. Raiden’s light was on. Evangeline’s door was open a crack, the way it always was when she couldn’t sleep, so she could hear the stairs.

Five of them, and one hired stranger who would run the first time anyone shot at him.

I don’t protect the people I pay.

What’s mine.

Elowen went to her room, found her good pen, the one she kept for wedding cards, and wrote one word at the top of a clean page.

Terms.

She wrote until the birds started.

Halfway down page two her door opened without a sound. Evangeline, bare feet, old cardigan. She came and stood behind the chair and read over Elowen’s shoulder.

Elowen didn’t cover it. Ev always knew anyway.

Evangeline read the first page to the end. Her face didn’t change. Then she picked up the pencil beside the lamp and underlined one line twice.

Separate rooms.

She put the pencil down.

“Good.”

She went back to bed and left her door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning, Bao was at the gate. He didn’t ask. He took one look at her face and took her up himself.

“He’s in,” he said in the lift. “He hasn’t eaten since yesterday.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Somebody should know.”

Zhao was alone at his desk, in shirtsleeves, with a cold coffee and a binder.

Zhao didn’t get up this time. He looked at her, at the envelope in her hands, and waited.

“I’m sorry about your man,” he said. “Lau.”

Don’t, she thought. Don’t be decent. Not now.

“You said you don’t protect the people you pay,” she said, before her nerve could go. “You protect what’s yours.”

“I did.”

“Then make me yours. On paper.” She put the envelope on his desk. “If I’m your wife, my father isn’t a man you pay. He’s your father-in-law. Your men don’t touch him, and the Qiu brothers think very hard before they touch anyone with my name. Marry me, Mr. Zhao.”

For one second, Zhao Zhendong looked honestly stunned. Then it was gone, and he took the pages out of the envelope.

He didn’t answer straight away. He read every line. Three pages in neat handwriting, every clause numbered. She hadn’t come on impulse. She had worked out what she could give up and what she wouldn’t, and written it down.

On page two, a word had been crossed out so hard the pen had nearly gone through. He tilted the page to the light.

“That’s nothing,” she said. “I changed my mind about it.”

“What was it?”

“None of your business.”

He put the page down.

“May I ask you something?”

“You already have.”

His mouth moved, very slightly. “Why marriage?”

“Because protection that depends on someone’s goodwill can be taken back.”

“And you think a marriage makes it permanent?”

“No. I think it makes breaking it more complicated.”

He laughed. It was short and surprised, as if it had got out without permission.

He leaned back. “You have a very practical idea of marriage.”

“I can’t afford a romantic one.”

“Clearly.” He turned back to page one. “You want my name. My people. You want anyone who thinks your family’s an easy target to understand they’d be making themselves my problem.”

“Yes.”

“And in return?”

“I’ll be your wife in public. I’ll come to things when it’s reasonable. I won’t interfere with your business, and I won’t ask about anything you don’t want to tell me.”

“You’ve asked about my business quite a lot already.”

“That was different. Your man was selling your routes, and my father was being blamed.”

“And now?”

“Now I want my family left alone.”

No promise to love him. No promise to obey him, or to become whatever sort of wife he might want. A partnership with the edges marked.

“Why not run?” he said. “Take your family and go.”

“Where? You’d find us if you wanted to. So would the Qius. And my father would stay, because he’s too proud and too scared to leave, and the first time something went wrong at the Docks, someone would go to the house and find only him.” She held his eyes. “I don’t run, Mr. Zhao. I cut things cleanly.”

He looked at her a moment longer than he needed to.

“You’ve thought about what this gives you. Have you thought about what it gives me?”

She hesitated. “I assumed you wouldn’t say yes unless there was something in it for you.”

“Good assumption.” He put the pages down. “With Kang gone, your father knows my shipping better than anyone alive. The officers, the routes, which problems are ordinary and which ones someone arranged. And Kang wasn’t the only one who knew those routes. The Qius got their information somewhere. They may have more people inside. I want the ones who know what happened kept safe, not frightened into silence or dead before they talk.”

He didn’t say the rest. A marriage would make his protection public. Anyone who went after the Lins would be going after his household, and nobody would get to Lin Jian through his daughter or lean on her little shop where no one was watching. They were good reasons. They were more than enough.

And there was her.

“I don’t know if I can help you with your business,” she said.

“I haven’t asked you to.”

“Then what do you want from me?”

“Honesty. The sense to see when something’s wrong. And the sense to tell me, instead of quietly trying to fix it yourself.”

She looked down at the contract. “That last part might be difficult.”

“I gathered.”

“We’ve negotiated an entire marriage,” he said, “and neither of us has asked whether we like each other.”

Her cheeks went warm. “That isn’t one of the terms.”

“No.” He didn’t take his eyes off her. “Maybe it should be.”

He turned a page. “Separate rooms. Your shop stays yours, and I have no say in how you run it.”

“Yes.”

“Keep running it.”

“I intend to.”

His finger stopped on page two, line six. “And this. I don’t touch you unless you ask.”

Her face went hotter. “I thought it was important to be clear.”

“Very clear.” He looked at her over the paper. “It says you have to ask. It doesn’t say I can’t ask you.”

She stared at him.

One corner of his mouth lifted, slow.

“I’ll leave it as it is,” he said, before she’d found an answer.

Zhao picked up a pen. “One condition of my own. You don’t lie to me.”

She thought about it. “Even when the truth’s inconvenient?”

“Especially then. Lie to anyone else you like. Not to me.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t walk into danger because you think you have to carry everything on your own.”

“That sounds like two conditions.”

“Call it one.”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she reached across, took the pen out of his hand, and wrote a line under his.

You eat dinner.

He looked at it. Then at her.

“You work too much and you forget to eat. Bao says you haven’t eaten since yesterday.” She capped the pen. “If we’re married, I’m not finding out my husband lives on coffee and whatever his staff put in front of him.”

For the first time that morning, Zhao Zhendong laughed. It was brief and low, and it changed his whole face.

“You’re negotiating my meals now.”

“You’re negotiating my whole life. It seemed fair.”

He signed. Page one, page two, page three. The scratch of the pen was strangely loud.

“Tuesday,” he said.

She looked up. “What?”

“The registry. Three days from now.”

“That’s very soon.”

“Your man’s in hospital and your father has a stranger with a gun in his car. You want to wait?”

She didn’t.

“I’ll arrange the registration. Your family hears it from you before anyone hears it from me.”

He slid the contract back across the desk. Her fingers touched his on the paper. Cold. He noticed.

“One more thing, Elowen.”

It was the first time he’d said her name. She looked up.

“You don’t have to make yourself useful to me to earn this. The reasons are already there.”

She didn’t seem to know what to do with that. “Then I hope we both get what we want.”

“So do I.”

He watched her fold the pages along her own creases and put them away. At the door she turned and reminded him, very seriously, not to forget dinner.

They were good reasons. But the most interesting part of the arrangement wasn’t on any of the three pages. He’d agreed to marry a woman who had walked into his office with a contract, a list of demands, and no intention of pretending she wasn’t afraid of him.

He was already curious what she’d ask him for next.

When the door shut, he looked at the cold rice someone had left on the corner of his desk at lunch yesterday. It was disgusting. He ate all of it.

Then he rang Chen Si.

“I’m getting married on Tuesday. I need a witness.”

For once in his life, Chen Si had nothing to say. The line was completely empty.

“Si.”

“I’m here. Is she pointing a gun at you?”

“No.” Zhao looked at the empty patch of desk where her three pages had been. “Worse. She wrote a contract.”

chapters.title: Married at the Registry on a Tuesday
chapters.desc: She buys ranunculus, takes the household register and marries him at the registry on a Tuesday. The ring is two sizes too big.
chapters.content:
At seven on Tuesday morning, Elowen stood in front of her wardrobe with three dresses on the bed. Pale blue. Cream. And a dark red silk she’d bought for New Year and never worn, because it looked like something a braver woman should be wearing.

Twenty minutes on this was ridiculous. It was a registry office: a clerk, a few signatures, and a man who had already signed three pages with her.

She still wanted to look nice. Not like a bride in a magazine. Just nice.

She chose the red. Mama had been married in red.

Then she sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the household register on her dressing table. Her father’s copy. She’d taken it before dawn from the bottom drawer of his study, the one that always stuck. It had been lying beside a brown envelope with her mother’s death certificate inside.

What would Mama have said? Maybe she’d have asked why Elowen was marrying a man she barely knew. Or maybe she’d have looked at her daughter’s nervous face, fixed her hair, and told her a woman should at least eat a proper breakfast before she got married.

Elowen smiled a little, put the register in her bag, and went downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was at the table with tea and a newspaper she doubted he’d read a word of. His eyes went to the dress, then to the bag.

“Where are you going?”

She had practised this in the mirror. Every sentence went straight out of her head.

“The registry office.”

He lowered the paper. “With whom?”

“Zhao Zhendong.”

She could hear the clock in the next room.

“I’m getting married today.”

He stood up. “You’re what? You arranged this with him, and you thought you’d tell me on the morning?”

“I was going to tell you.”

“When? After you came home with his surname?” His eyes went to the bag again, and she watched him understand. “You took the household register.”

“Yes.”

He laughed, short and unbelieving, and turned away. “Your mother would never have agreed to this.”

That landed harder than the shouting.

“I don’t know what Mama would have thought,” Elowen said. “I know what I’m trying to do. Nobody gets to hurt this family to get at you.”

“And what happens to you?”

“I don’t know,” she admitted. “I’m going anyway.”

He picked up his tea. His hand wasn’t steady. “Go. Before I say something I’ll regret.”

She touched his arm on her way past. He didn’t look at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flower market was already roaring with trolleys and men shouting prices down the aisles. It smelled of wet leaves and cut stems, an ordinary Tuesday, and Elowen found that comforting.

Tuesdays were ranunculus. She chose pale pink ones that had only just started to open, their middles still tucked away.

“Little flower.”

Granny Yip sat behind her stall at the end of the row with a cigarette in the corner of her mouth, counting eucalyptus. She had sold to Mama before Elowen, and she called everyone under fifty a child.

“Why are you dressed like that?”

“Does it look strange?”

“It looks expensive.” Her sharp black eyes went over Elowen’s face. “Something’s happening today.”

Elowen hesitated. “I’m getting married.”

Granny Yip put the eucalyptus down. “Today? To that man?”

“You know about him?”

“The whole market knows about him. Old Hung at the bun stall knows about him, and Hung knows nothing about anything except buns.” She reached under the counter and brought out a little bundle in damp paper. “Here.”

Lily of the valley. Tiny white bells hanging along their stems.

“Granny, how did you get these in March?”

“I have a man.”

“What man?”

“A man! Everybody needs a man.” She pushed the bundle into Elowen’s hands. “A little flower should have flowers on her wedding day.”

Elowen’s throat went tight without warning.

“Don’t cry. Your face will run.”

“I’m not crying.”

“Then your eyes are leaking for no reason. Go on. You’re blocking my eucalyptus.”

She tied the lily of the valley in with the ranunculus with cream ribbon from her bag, right there between the buckets. It wasn’t a bridal bouquet. She’d made it herself while an old woman watched her hands, and she liked it better that way.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past nine, a black car pulled up outside the registry office.

Zhao got out first. Navy suit, white shirt open at the collar, the silver watch, the heavy rings. He looked like a man arriving for a business meeting. Chen Si got out after him with a folder.

“Do you think she’ll come?” Chen Si asked.

“She said she would. If she changes her mind, she’ll tell me.”

Chen Si studied him. “You’re taking this seriously.”

“I signed a contract.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

Zhao didn’t answer.

A taxi stopped at the kerb, and Elowen got out in dark red silk, her black hair loose down her back with a small clip above one ear. A few strands had already blown free.

Zhao looked at her once, then at the river for a second.

“Good morning,” she said.

Chen Si bowed a little. “Miss Lin. I’m the witness. Somebody has to see this with their own eyes.”

Zhao was looking at the flowers. “Ranunculus.”

“And lily of the valley. Granny Yip gave me those. She said a little flower should have flowers on her wedding day.”

“A sensible woman.”

The strand of hair had fallen over his forehead again. Before she’d thought about it, she reached up and smoothed it back.

He went completely still.

She felt it under her fingers: the most frightening man in the city had forgotten how to breathe. People stepped aside for him and kept their eyes down. She’d just fixed his hair as if she’d been doing it for years.

“It was messy,” she explained, and took her hand back.

“I see.”

The strand fell down again about a second later.

Chen Si turned away, deeply entertained.

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry was not grand: pale walls, plastic chairs, a child crying by the door. Elowen had expected nerves. She hadn’t expected to notice every ordinary thing so sharply, like the weight of the register in her bag and the smell of lily of the valley.

When the clerk called their names, Zhao held out his hand.

She looked at it. Then she put her fingers in his. His palm was warm. He didn’t grip. He only held her hand as far as the desk.

The clerk checked their papers and asked the usual questions, and Elowen heard her own voice answer from a little way off. Then the pen.

Lin Elowen. She wrote it carefully. Zhao signed underneath.

Stamp, stamp. The machine printed the date and the time into two red booklets. Nine forty-one.

“Congratulations,” said the clerk, already reaching for the next folder.

That was it. She looked at the booklet in her hands. She was married.

Zhao was looking at her.

“Mrs. Zhao,” he said, very low.

“That’s strange.”

“What is?”

“Hearing it.”

“Would you rather I called you Elowen?”

She thought about it. “Yes.”

“Then Elowen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Out on the steps, in thin spring sun, the couple ahead of them were kissing for a friend’s camera.

Zhao watched them. Then he looked at Elowen’s mouth, and she felt that look like a hand.

“Not here,” she said.

It was out before she’d thought about what it meant. He went still. Then he leaned down, close enough that his breath touched her cheek, and stopped there.

“Then where?”

Just for her. Her face went hot to the ears. He straightened without touching her. He’d heard exactly what she said, and what she hadn’t.

He took a small dark box from his jacket and opened it. A heavy band of yellow gold, plain and solid, with one small square green stone set flush in it. Heavier than anything she had ever worn.

“Your hand.”

She held out her left hand. He slid the ring on. It went over her knuckle easily, kept going, and settled halfway down her finger, nowhere near where a ring should sit.

They both looked at it. Chen Si looked at it.

“It’s too big,” Elowen said.

“Apparently.”

“By quite a lot.”

“I was given an estimate.”

“By whom?”

“Someone who claimed to know.”

Chen Si coughed. Zhao looked at him.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to.”

Elowen laughed and moved the ring to her middle finger, where it fitted, just.

“I’ll have it resized,” Zhao said.

“Not yet. I like it heavy.”

He looked at the ring on the wrong finger, and something in his face eased.

Chen Si’s phone rang. He looked at the screen and smiled. “Aurelia.” He answered. “Yes, it’s done. No, I didn’t forget.” His eyes went to Elowen, and the smile turned wicked. “Actually, she’s right here. You remember Elowen Lin?”

There was a short, total silence on the other end. Then a shriek Elowen could hear from two steps away.

Chen Si held out the phone. “She’d like a word.”

“Hello?”

“Elowen Lin.” That voice, sweet as syrup. “He told me Zhendong was marrying a florist. He didn’t tell me which florist.”

“Aurelia.”

Aurelia Song. Aurelia had held first place in their year for two years running. In their final year Elowen had taken it from her, and the student council after it, and in between they’d both wasted an embarrassing amount of energy on the same boy, a senior who preferred physics to either of them.

“Congratulations,” said Aurelia. “I’ll come and see your little shop. Soon.”

It sounded exactly like a threat. “Lovely,” said Elowen, and gave the phone back before her face could do anything.

Zhao looked between them. “Something I should know?”

“Nothing important.”

Chen Si’s smile widened. “Now I’m curious.”

“Don’t be,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch, which Chen Si claimed as a witness’s right, Bao drove her home. Zhao sat beside her in the back while the city went past. She turned the ring on her middle finger, round and round.

“It’s very heavy,” she said.

“Do you dislike it?”

“No. I like it.”

“Then keep it like that.”

“Thank you, Zhendong.”

It was the first time she’d used his name. She was busy checking the ranunculus hadn’t been crushed, and didn’t seem to notice. He turned his head and looked at her.

When the car stopped at the red door with the brass fish, she got out, then leaned back in and kissed his cheek. Quick. Gone before he could move.

His contract said he couldn’t touch her unless she asked. It said nothing at all about her.

She was up the steps before he’d breathed out. In the mirror, Bao looked very carefully at the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard her father before she reached the door.

“I don’t want to hear it.”

Then Evangeline, who spoke perhaps once a week. “She’s married, Baba.”

“I know she’s married!”

Elowen opened the door. Her father stood by the dining table. Evangeline sat at the end of it with her hands folded.

His eyes went to the red booklet in Elowen’s hand. “So it’s done.”

“Yes.”

“Did he give you money?”

“He gave me a ring.”

He let out a harsh breath. “And what do you call that? Selling yourself?”

Evangeline stood up.

For a second Elowen couldn’t find her voice. She could see what was under his anger. Fear, the kind that had been growing in him since Old Lau, since he realised the people he’d trusted were something else. He was afraid, and he was hurting her anyway.

“I didn’t sell myself,” she said. “I bought you.”

He stared at her.

“He protects this family. Your debt stays closed. I keep my shop. He doesn’t touch me unless I ask.”

“You had to put that in a contract?”

“Yes.”

“You should have let me find another way!”

“I did!” Her voice rose for the first time. “I asked you not to hire that gunman. I asked you not to make it worse, and you wouldn’t listen. They broke Old Lau’s legs to send you a message, Baba. I wasn’t going to wait for the next one.”

“I was trying to protect you.”

“I know. By doing things that put all of us in more danger.”

Evangeline came round the table and stood beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. She didn’t say anything. She didn’t have to.

Her father turned away.

“I’ll be upstairs,” Elowen said.

No one stopped her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past six Zhao came back alone, with two of his men behind him carrying flower buckets up the steps. Evangeline opened the door, looked at him, and stepped aside without a word.

He had an armful of red tulips. Her father came to the dining-room doorway and looked at them, and then at him.

“What’s this?”

“Flowers.”

“I can see that.”

“Then I think the explanation’s sufficient.”

On the stairs behind her father, Raiden made a noise and turned it into a cough.

Elowen stopped halfway down the stairs.

“Twenty red tulips,” Zhao said, looking up at her. “You gave away the ones I sent.”

The van. The peonies for Mrs. Poon, the roses for the noodle shop. “I didn’t know you were counting.”

“I’m not.”

She came down, and he put them in her arms. Fresh, still tightly closed, in cream paper.

“Is this how you’ll handle everything?” her father said.

“I brought flowers because your daughter likes them,” said Zhao. “The rest is being handled. The men who broke Old Lau’s legs are the Qius’ men, and the Qius know it was a mistake by now.” He didn’t raise his voice. “I closed your debt because you weren’t the traitor. It wasn’t a gift, and it isn’t a lever. The people who used your name won’t use your family again.”

“You expect me to trust you?”

“No. I expect you to watch what I do.”

Silence. Then Zhao looked at Elowen. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

He turned to her father. “May we stay for dinner?”

Lin Jian looked as if that was the last thing he wanted. But Raiden had come in behind him at some point, and said brightly, “Course you can, Ah Sim’s done far too much fish,” and that was that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was awful.

Her father barely spoke. Raiden talked enough for everyone (“Middle finger? Bold, Jie”). Eliana watched Zhao over her glasses like a system she was planning to break into. Evangeline passed Zhao the rice without being asked, which from Evangeline was practically a welcome.

Zhao put a piece of fish in her bowl. The belly, the best part, without a word. Her father saw. His face got harder to read.

When the plates were nearly empty, Lin Jian put down his chopsticks. “I want to talk to you.” Not to her. “Alone.”

Zhao followed him into the study.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What are you going to do with my daughter?”

“Protect her.”

“She isn’t a business asset. You don’t get to acquire her because it makes your operations easier.”

“I know.”

“Do you?” Lin Jian’s voice was rough. “She’s twenty-four. She runs a flower shop. She worries whether people have eaten. She shouldn’t have to learn to live around men who carry guns. I worked for you long enough to know there are things I’ll never be able to tell her.”

“Then don’t. She won’t be in my business unless she chooses to be. She keeps her shop, her own rooms, her own money, and she sees her family whenever she likes. I won’t ask her to be someone else to make this convenient for me.”

“And if she wants to leave?”

Zhao hadn’t expected that. He understood why it mattered.

“Then we’ll talk about it.”

“You’d let her go?”

“If that’s what she wants.”

Lin Jian looked for a lie in his face and didn’t find one. “I don’t like you.”

“You don’t have to.”

“If you hurt her—“

“I know.”

“No. You don’t.” Lin Jian’s voice dropped. “You’re used to people being afraid of you. She isn’t one of your men. She’s my daughter.”

Zhao turned at the door. “I know exactly who she is. I intend to remember it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came out first and walked past Elowen in the hall without a word. Zhao stopped beside her. “Would you like to bring the tulips home?”

“Home?”

Of course. His house. Separate rooms. She simply hadn’t seen it yet, and she had assumed married meant tonight: her things in his car and her life rearranged around his by morning.

“You don’t have to come tonight,” he said. “Not if you’re not ready.”

“Saturday,” she said. “I need to close the week at the shop. And my mother’s lemon tree won’t fit in your car.”

“Saturday.”

He said goodnight to Evangeline, who nodded once. Her father didn’t come out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the house was asleep, Elowen sat at the kitchen table and cut the tulips one by one. A knife, not scissors. On an angle. Into cold water. The lily of the valley went in a glass beside them, so small that one careless movement would break it.

Her phone buzzed. A number she didn’t have.

Unknown: Cut them?

Elowen: Who is this?

Unknown: Your husband.

She typed Zhao and deleted it. Typed Husband and deleted that so fast she nearly dropped the phone. In the end she saved the number with no name at all.

She had been married for less than a day, and she was beginning to suspect the hard part wouldn’t be living with Zhao Zhendong. It would be letting him look after her without feeling she owed him something back.

chapters.title: The House on the Hill Has Too Many Locks
chapters.desc: She moves into his concrete house with her mother’s lemon tree and names his dogs. In the basement, behind the lock she has no key for, he asks before he kisses her.
chapters.content:
On Saturday, four days after the registry, Elowen moved into her husband’s house, and the first thing she noticed about it was that it had too many locks.

The second was that it had too many windows. The third was that it had rooms enough for a large family, and felt as if only one person had ever really lived there.

The house sat on a hill above the Iron Docks: pale concrete and dark glass, long clean lines, a wide flight of steps up to the door. No fountains, no clipped hedges. Just high walls, cameras that turned to follow the van up the drive, and enough men in dark jackets to make her wonder whether she’d moved into a government building by mistake. The wind came straight off the water and smelled of salt and diesel.

A man opened the van door for her. “Good evening, Mrs. Zhao.”

She still wasn’t used to that. “Good evening.”

Zhao came down the steps. He’d come back from the Docks ahead of them and changed into a dark shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow. He looked at the boxes coming out of the back.

“Is that everything?”

“Almost. There’s one more thing.”

Two of his men were lifting a big terracotta pot out of the van between them. In it stood a small lemon tree.

Zhao looked at it. Then at her.

“That’s a tree.”

“I can see that.”

“I thought you were bringing your things.”

“It is my thing.” She folded her arms. “It’s Mama’s.”

That was all she said.

He looked at the pot again. It was worn, with a chip out of one side, and the tree wasn’t much to look at: thin branches, uneven leaves, not one lemon. But Elowen was watching the two men carry it the way people watch someone carry a sleeping child down a flight of stairs.

“Where do you want it?”

“Somewhere with morning sun. Not the hot afternoon.”

“There’s a courtyard on the east side.”

“Would it be all right there?”

“We’ll see if the light suits it.” He turned to the men. “East courtyard. Carefully.”

“I’ll unpack the rest myself,” she said.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know. I want to.”

He looked at her a moment. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found out about the locks inside twenty minutes. The front door, the side door, the garage, the garden store, the doors between the wings, several she couldn’t place. Cameras in the corridors. Sensors on the windows. A panel by the front door covered in small lights doing something she didn’t understand.

She stood in the hall and watched him lock up behind the last box. One key. Then another. Then a third.

“How many locks does one house need?”

He took a second ring of keys out of his pocket and put it on the console table. It landed with a heavy clink.

“Those are yours. Thirteen.”

“And you carry all of yours around?”

“Not usually.”

“Then why have them?”

“Because I own the locks.”

She looked at him. He looked back. Then she laughed, and the corner of his mouth moved.

“What’s funny?”

“Nothing. That’s just a very Zhao Zhendong answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The upstairs corridor was quiet, with long windows over the garden and evening light lying across the floor in pale squares. He stopped at the biggest room.

“This one’s yours.”

It was enormous. A wide bed, a sitting area by the window, a walk-in wardrobe, a little room off it that could be a study. The view went all the way down over the Docks to the water. Nothing in it was fussy, and everything looked expensive. On the bedside table stood a glass vase with nothing in it. Somebody had known there should be a vase. Nobody had known what went in it.

“This is very big.”

“You’ll have room.”

She looked down the corridor at the other doors. “Which one’s yours?”

“Downstairs. At the foot of the stairs. It’s smaller.”

“Why?”

“It’s the first door anyone reaches. If they come in.”

Oh. He was standing in the doorway with his hands in his pockets. He’d given her the room at the top and put himself between her and the front door. You didn’t say thank you for that kind of thing. She didn’t know what you said.

“It’s your house,” she said instead.

“It’s our house now.”

He said it without weight, almost carelessly. Elowen looked away first.

“Do you need help with those?”

She looked at her boxes. “Maybe the heavy ones.”

He rolled his sleeves up further. For the next half hour the most feared man on the Docks carried cardboard boxes up a staircase: clothes, books, her knives and shears, a bag of ribbon. He didn’t complain. He did stop at a box marked GLASS in her handwriting.

“What’s in this?”

“My teacups. Six.”

“You brought teacups.”

“Of course.”

He looked at the box, then at her, and put it down as if it might go off.

“You’re allowed to be surprised,” she said. “They’re very important.”

“I’ll remember.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She spent nearly fifteen minutes deciding exactly where the lemon tree should go. The courtyard had concrete walls on three sides and was open to the sky, with a strip of soil along one wall and a row of big pots somebody had filled with plants that didn’t need much love. The lemon tree looked small and lonely among them.

She crouched and pushed a finger into the soil. “It’s dry.”

“I’ll have someone bring water.”

“I can do it.”

She found a watering can by the store and filled it. The leaves shivered as the water went in, and for a minute she seemed to forget the house and the locks and the men on the wall.

“Did your mother grow it?” Zhao asked.

“She bought it when I was little. She said she wanted a lemon whenever she needed one.” She touched a leaf. “She made me lemon tea with honey when I had a cold, and made me drink it while it was hot. She kept saying one day it’d give us more lemons than we could use.”

“Has it?”

“Not yet.”

“Then it has time.”

She looked up. He wasn’t promising her anything. He was looking at the tree as if it were a living thing that deserved some time.

“If it doesn’t like it here, we’ll move it,” he said.

“You can’t keep moving a tree every time it’s unhappy.”

“I can.”

“That’s not the same.”

“I’ll take your word for it.” He was still looking at the tree. “You didn’t need my permission to bring something of yours.”

She brushed the soil off her fingers. Then she remembered. “Where are the dogs?”

✦ ✦ ✦

There were two of them in the back garden, big and dark and much more interested in Zhao than in her. One stood by the kennel, ears up. The other lay on the grass with his head on his paws, watching.

“They’re trained,” Zhao said. “They won’t come to you unless I let them.”

Elowen crouched at the gate. “Hello.”

The one by the kennel tilted his head.

“What are their names?”

“Black. And Shadow.”

She stared at him. “Did you name them?”

“Security did.”

“That’s unfortunate. They need better names.”

He looked at the dogs, then at her. “Name them, then. They’re yours if you do.”

Her face lit up. She considered the first one: broad and heavy, the kind of dog that could knock a grown man over without trying.

“Dumpling.”

Zhao turned his head slowly. “What?”

The dog came a step closer and sniffed. “Hello, Dumpling.” She looked at the other, taller one with the long serious face. “And Noodle. Because he’s long.”

The dog let out a low huff.

“See? He likes it.”

Zhao looked at two guard dogs who had spent their whole lives answering to one-word commands. “Dumpling. Noodle.”

“Do you hate them?”

“I sound like a man who’s just found out his guard dogs are named after lunch.”

She laughed so hard she had to put a hand over her mouth. He watched her for a moment, then turned to the man at the garden gate.

“Change their names on the records.”

“…Sir?”

“Dumpling. Noodle.”

“Yes, sir.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was laid at the long table, two places at one end of a table for twelve. Fish, greens, soup, rice, and soy-braised chicken wings that smelled wonderful.

Zhao put a spoonful of rice in his bowl and started eating.

“Do you always eat that little?”

“I’m not hungry.”

She didn’t argue. She put a chicken wing in his bowl.

He looked down at it. “What’s this?”
