“Dinner. You signed for it.”

She went on eating as if she hadn’t just told a man nobody told anything what to do. He picked up his chopsticks and ate the wing. Then, without a word, he pushed the whole plate of wings over to her side and didn’t take another.

She pushed it back to the middle. He pushed it back to her.

“I’m not eating all of that.”

“Then leave it.”

She left exactly half. He looked at the half, and ate it.

“From tomorrow,” she said, “we eat together. Properly. Not at opposite ends with everyone bringing things in and going away. We sit, we eat, and we talk.”

“I can’t promise to be home at the same time every night.”

“I didn’t say the same time. When you’re home, we sit down.”

He leaned back. “That I can do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After nine, looking for the laundry, she found the fourteenth lock.

It was at the end of the downstairs corridor, half hidden round a turn in the wall. A steel door with a keypad, a heavy lock and a camera over the frame. No handle on the outside. It looked like something out of a bank.

“Zhendong?”

He came down the corridor. “The laundry’s the other way.”

“What’s this?”

“Storage.”

“Your storage has a keypad and a camera.”

“Yes.”

“You have very strange storage. Can I see it?”

“No.”

It came out at once. She blinked, then nodded. “All right.”

He watched her. “You’re not curious?”

“I am. You said it’s private.” She looked at the door. “I don’t need to see everything in your house. I just need to know which doors I can open without setting off an alarm. Is this the one my thirteen keys don’t open?”

He didn’t answer, which was an answer.

“Your house really does have too many locks,” she said, and went to find the laundry.

He stood in the corridor after she’d gone and looked at the steel door for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly ten when he found her in the kitchen, putting what was left of her wedding posy into a glass. The ranunculus had opened right out in four days. The lily of the valley was still hanging on.

“You like flowers more than most people,” he said.

“Is that a complaint?”

“No. Something I’ve noticed.”

“Do you know what I’ve noticed? You don’t smile much. But you do when something’s funny.”

“Is that a problem?”

“No. I like it.”

The kitchen went quiet. Her hair had slipped out of its clip. There was a red crease on her wrist from carrying boxes. She looked tired, and comfortable. She’d stopped checking where he was every time she moved. In one afternoon she’d filled a wardrobe, watered her mother’s tree, renamed his dogs, and taken over a corner of his kitchen. Small things. The things that made a house look as if somebody lived in it.

“Come with me,” he said.

He took her back to the steel door, put in a code, turned a key, then a second lock.

The air changed on the stairs: cooler, with a faint smell of oil and metal, like a hardware shop. Concrete walls, bright lights, and along both walls, behind glass and in locked racks, guns. Rifles in rows. Pistols in drawers lined with foam. Boxes stacked to the ceiling with numbers stencilled on the sides. All of it as neat as the files in his office.

Elowen stopped on the last step. “Oh.”

“Now you know why it’s locked.”

“Is this what you sell?”

“No. What I sell never comes to this house. These are mine. For if somebody comes here.” He looked at her. “For if somebody comes here for you.”

She had known what sort of man she’d married. She’d heard the stories and seen the men on the wall. Knowing it and standing in the middle of it were not the same thing. She wasn’t frightened of him. But she understood, in a much closer way, how far his world was from hers.

“You can ask me anything,” he said.

“Do you use them?”

“Sometimes.”

She didn’t ask for details.

At the far end, behind a short passage, there was a second steel door. Inside, a small room: a chair, water, a first-aid box, a phone on its own line, a screen showing every camera in the house.

“If anyone ever comes into this house who isn’t me or Bao, you come down here. You shut this door and put in the code from the inside. Then you wait.”

“For how long?”

“For me.”

He wrote six numbers on the back of a card and held it out. Their fingers met on it, his warm from the lamp and smelling faintly of gun oil, and he didn’t let go.

They stood holding the same card under the light, close enough that she could see the pulse going in his throat. A strand of her hair had stuck to her cheek. His eyes went to it. His free hand came up and stopped a breath from her face. She tipped her head into it, just a little, and he tucked the strand behind her ear.

“Elowen. May I kiss you?”

She hadn’t expected it. Her fingers tightened on the card. “Because we’re married?”

“No.”

“Because you think you should?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because I want to.”

Her heart did something unsteady. He didn’t come any closer. He bent his head until his breath was on her mouth, and stopped there, and she could see what the stopping cost him.

“Say yes,” he said, very low. “Or go upstairs.”

She didn’t go upstairs.

“Yes.”

He kissed her carefully at first, hardly moving, as if he were testing ice before he trusted his weight to it. His hand stayed by her cheek, and she could feel it shaking. Then her fingers grabbed the front of his shirt without asking her, and he made a low sound in his chest and stopped being careful at all. Her back met the edge of the workbench. His hand slid into her hair, her mouth opened under his, and the room full of guns went somewhere very far away.

When he pulled back, it was only a few centimetres. He was breathing hard.

“That’s all,” he said, hoarse. “Tonight.”

She let go of his shirt. Her hand didn’t want to. She’d crushed the card in her other fist, so she smoothed it out against her leg to give her face something to do.

“You can ask me for another one,” he said. “Whenever you want.”

Her face went hot. “Don’t make me say things like that in the basement.”

For the first time that evening, he smiled properly, and it was teasing. “Understood.”

On the stairs he reached for her hand. He didn’t pull. He just held it, and after a moment she turned her palm and laced her fingers through his.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, she took the heavy gold ring off her middle finger and put it in its box on the bedside table, next to the vase that wasn’t empty anymore.

She had been married for four days. Tonight, for the first time, he had kissed her, because he’d asked and she’d said yes.

She touched her lips, then snatched her hand away, embarrassed, though nobody was there to see.

Outside, the cameras watched the gate, a guard’s footsteps crunched along the wall, and under the house a steel room full of guns waited for somebody who wasn’t coming tonight. In the east courtyard, a small lemon tree stood in its chipped pot in the dark.

For the first time in weeks, Elowen slept without listening for the door.

chapters.title: Breakfast With a Man Who Eats Standing Up
chapters.desc: She makes him sit down to dinner. He takes her van keys and drives her to the market at four, and she kisses him at the shop door without asking.
chapters.content:
By Sunday evening, after one full day in the house, Elowen had worked out that Zhao Zhendong had a strange relationship with dining tables.

He owned a beautiful one. Dark walnut, long enough for twelve, polished until the lights swam in it. He’d used it last night because she was there. Today she had watched him eat breakfast standing at the kitchen counter in four minutes, eat lunch in his study with a file open next to the plate, and at five o’clock eat a slice of bread while reading a report, apparently counting that as tea.

She had tried not to comment. She had failed.

So tonight she had a plan. Two places at the end of the table by the window. A jar of white flowers she’d cut from the courtyard. On the stove, lotus root soup with chicken, steamed egg, greens with garlic, and chicken braised in soy and ginger.

Her mother’s recipes. She hadn’t made them all at once in years. Mama always said a proper meal needed something warm, something green, and something that made everyone want more rice. Elowen had decided Zhao needed all three.

She was wiping the counter when he came in, jacket off, sleeves rolled, phone in hand. He stopped in the doorway.

“What are you doing?”

“Cooking.”

“I can see that.”

“That’s becoming your favourite answer.”

He looked through to the dining room. “Are we expecting someone?”

“No.”

“Then why are there two places?”

“Because we’re eating together. You agreed.”

He checked his watch. “I have a call at eight.”

“It’s quarter past seven. You have time.”

She went back to the stove as if that settled it. He put his phone down on the counter. “Do you need anything?”

“Wash your hands. You’ve been outside.”

He looked at his hands. Then, without arguing, he went to the sink. Elowen smiled into the soup. Maybe marriage wasn’t so hard. Maybe it was just a matter of teaching a man with fourteen locks how to sit on a chair.

When he came back she was carrying the soup in.

“Sit down with me.”

“You’re very determined tonight.”

“I’m your wife. I think I’m allowed to ask you to sit down for dinner.”

“Ask?”

“Tell, then.”

The corner of his mouth went up. He pulled out the chair and sat.

She served him first, a good ladle of soup with plenty of lotus root. “Careful. It’s hot.”

He drank some. Then more.

“Is it all right?”

“It’s good.”

“Just good?”

He looked at her. “Very good.”

She sat down opposite him, pleased. “It’s Mama’s.”

“Did she teach you?”

“When I was little. She said I should know a few proper dishes before I left home. By seven I could do soup, steamed egg and braised chicken. I was very proud of myself.”

“Were you any good?”

She narrowed her eyes. “I was seven.”

“I see.”

“I’ve improved.”

“I’ll take your word for it.”

He ate slowly. He didn’t look at his phone. When it buzzed, he glanced at the screen and turned it over. She noticed, said nothing, and put another piece of chicken in his bowl.

“You’re feeding me a lot.”

“You eat too little.”

“I had lunch.”

“Coffee isn’t lunch.”

He paused. “Who told you?”

“Nobody. I have eyes.”

He laughed under his breath. “I seem to have married someone very observant.”

“You should have known that before you signed.”

“I did.”

When she finished, she sat back. “See? You survived a dinner sitting down.”

“Barely.”

The lines round his eyes had eased. It wasn’t a big change. He didn’t suddenly get chatty. But he looked less like a man waiting for the next problem to walk through the door.

“Thank you,” he said. “For dinner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They washed up together. He took the bowls off her before she could argue. She was putting the leftover soup away when she wondered, out loud, who used to cook for him when he was little.

“Nobody.”

She turned round. “Nobody?”

“I was in a children’s home until I was six.” He put a plate in the rack. “Then a man took me. Old Zhao. He needed another pair of hands. He gave me his name.”

She turned off the tap. She knew almost nothing about his life before the Docks, and she’d never asked. It had seemed like one of the doors he kept shut.

“Is he—“

“Dead.”

He said it the way he said everything. She didn’t know what to do with the way he’d said it, so she didn’t do anything.

“I’m sorry.”

“Why?”

“I don’t know. I wish it had been different.”

He reached for another plate. “It was what it was.”

“Was there anyone? Anyone at all?”

He thought about it. “Chen Si. Later. We were fifteen.”

“Is he your only family?”

He stopped drying the plate. Then: “Yes.”

One word. She heard how much was in it.

“I’m glad you have him,” she said. Then, before she could stop it: “I’m glad you’re not on your own anymore.”

His face changed, a little. She heard what she’d said and went pink. “Not that you were lonely. I meant—“

“I know what you meant.” He took the damp towel out of her hands. “You don’t have to explain every kind thing you say. Go up. I’ll finish.”

“You don’t have to—“

“You cooked.”

“And you ate.”

“Exactly.”

Behind her, he put the dishes away. He’d spent most of his life treating having no family as an ordinary fact, like weather. Lately the house had started filling up with things he hadn’t expected to find in it. A jar of flowers in the kitchen. A lemon tree in the courtyard. Two ridiculous names on his dogs’ records. And a woman who seemed to think sitting down to dinner was a perfectly reasonable thing to ask of him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her alarm went at a quarter to four.

For a second she didn’t know where she was. Then she saw the strange wardrobe, the pale curtains, the vase that wasn’t empty. Right. His house. The market.

She washed her face, tied her hair back, pulled on trousers and a sweater, and took her van keys out of the bowl by the door.

The house was dark. A guard stood by the front door. She had it half open when a voice behind her said, “Where are you going?”

Zhao was at the foot of the stairs, already dressed in black, his hair untidy, looking as if he’d been awake a long time.

“The flower market.”

“Now?”

“It’s when the market is.”

“On your own?”

“I always go on my own.”

He held out his hand. “Keys.”

“My keys?”

“I’ll drive.”

“I can drive myself.”

“I know. It’s four in the morning.”

“It’s not quite four.”

He looked at her. She looked back. Then she sighed and dropped the keys in his palm.

“Fine.”

“Get a coat.”

“I’ve got a sweater.”

“It’s cold by the water. Get a coat.”

She went back up for one, mostly so she’d have something to complain about in the van.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flower market at four in the morning was a different world from the one people saw in daylight. Lorries jammed the loading bays. Sellers shouted prices over trolleys and engines. Men went past with whole sheaves of greenery on their shoulders. The air was cold and wet and smelled of leaves and soil and cut stems.

Elowen got out of the van and came alive.

“Morning, Uncle Tsui!”

“Little Elowen! You’re early!”

Zhao followed a few steps behind. He was dressed plainly, but people noticed him anyway. A seller looked twice. Two men stopped talking until he’d gone by. Elowen didn’t see any of it. She was already frowning at a bucket of roses.

“Not these.”

“What’s wrong with them?”

“Look. The outer petals are bruised, and that one’s gone soft at the neck. They’ll be dead by Wednesday.”

He looked at the rose, then at her. “All right.”

At the end of the row, Granny Yip sat behind a wall of crates in a thick cardigan with a cigarette in the corner of her mouth. Her eyes went to Zhao, then to Elowen, then back to Zhao.

“So. You brought the husband.”

“Good morning, Granny.”

Zhao gave her a polite nod. “Good morning.”

The old woman looked him up and down slowly, the way she’d look at a bunch of stock she suspected of being a day older than its label. “Hm.” She pointed her cigarette at a trolley stacked with boxes. “Eucalyptus. Twenty boxes. Bring them here.”

“Granny Yip—“

“What? He looks strong.”

Zhao looked at the boxes. Then at Granny Yip. “Where do you want them?”

“Here, of course.”

He rolled up his sleeves. The boxes were heavier than they looked. By the fifth, Elowen was hiding a smile. By the tenth, Granny Yip had decided he was useful.

“Underneath! Hold it underneath. The leaves bruise.”

He changed his grip.

“Better.”

“Granny, you don’t have to make him carry all of them.”

“Why not? He’s your husband. Marriage is helping each other.” She looked at Zhao. “Isn’t it?”

He put down another box. “Yes.”

Elowen stared at him. He looked back, perfectly calm.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Not particularly.” He picked up the next one.

“Good man,” said Granny Yip. “Come back next week.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her roses came from Uncle Pak, who’d been selling to her for two years. He knew her stem length, her colours and how she liked them wrapped.

“Twelve bundles of red, please. Twenty-five a bundle.”

“Of course. You know me.”

Zhao stood beside her holding the last box of Granny Yip’s eucalyptus. He watched Uncle Pak pull stems from the bucket and count them. He watched him bunch them loose and wrap paper round the bottom before anyone could see the heads clearly.

“Open that one,” Zhao said.

Uncle Pak paused. “What?”

“The bundle.”

“It’s twenty-five. It’s always twenty-five.”

Zhao didn’t move. Elowen untied the paper herself and counted. Twenty-two. She counted again. Twenty-two.

“A few were damaged,” Uncle Pak said quickly. “I’ll make it up next time.”

Zhao put another bundle on the counter. Elowen counted. Twenty-two. The next. Twenty-three.

“You charged me for twenty-five,” she said.

“You get good prices from me.”

“How long?” Zhao asked.

“It’s a misunderstanding.”

“How long?”

Uncle Pak looked away.

Something cold settled in Elowen’s stomach. She’d never counted. She’d trusted him because he was familiar and polite, and because she’d bought from him for so long that checking had never crossed her mind.

“Two years,” said Zhao. It wasn’t a question. The man at the next stall had been happy to tell him while she was choosing roses.

The stalls around them had gone quiet to listen.

“You’ll work out what you owe her,” Zhao said. “Every stem. Every order. Two years.”

“I don’t have that kind of money.”

“Then you shouldn’t have taken it.”

Elowen touched his sleeve. “Zhendong. Not here. I don’t want him paying me in front of everyone.”

He looked at her for a moment, then back at Uncle Pak. “A written account of every order you’ve supplied her. By tomorrow. If the numbers don’t match, we’ll have another conversation.”

Uncle Pak nodded very fast.

They walked away. Elowen didn’t say anything for a while.

“I should have checked,” she said at last.

“You trusted someone who’d given you no reason not to.” He took her notebook out of her hand and looked at the list. “Twelve bundles. We’ll get them from someone else.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past five they stopped at the soy milk stall by the gate. Before she could order, he said to the woman, “One hot, no sugar. One with a little.”

Elowen turned. “How do you know how I have it?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“Zhendong.”

“Bao watched you buy one here every morning for a week before I came into your shop.”

She stared at him. It should have frightened her. It did, a bit. It also meant that for a week before he ever walked through her door, someone had been writing down how she took her soy milk.

“That’s horrible,” she said.

“Yes.”

He handed her the cup with no sugar. She sat on a low bench by the stall. He stayed standing.

“Sit with me.”

“It’s wet.”

“Then wipe it.”

He took a tissue from the counter, wiped the bench beside her, and sat. Elowen smiled into her cup.

She went over her orders. He took two calls, kept his voice low and finished both fast. At some point her head ended up on his shoulder. She didn’t decide to put it there. Her eyes closed.

He set his cup down. He looked at her for a few seconds, then took his jacket off, laid it over her, and tucked the collar in at her neck. Her hand stayed loose on his arm.

The market went on around them: trolleys rattling past, prices shouted, a lorry reversing with its warning beep. She slept through all of it. And Zhao Zhendong, who had spent years learning to stay awake in every room he walked into, sat still on a wet bench until she woke.

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried the boxes into the shop and put them where she pointed. Then he noticed the door.

“Does that always stick?”

“Sometimes. I keep meaning to ask the landlord.”

“I’ll have someone look at it.” He checked his watch. “I have to go.”

She followed him to the door, wiping her hands on a towel. “Thank you for driving. And the eucalyptus. And breakfast.”

“Don’t use the bruised roses.”

“I know.”

He turned to go. Elowen caught the front of his shirt. “Zhendong.”

He turned back, and she went up on her toes and kissed him. Quick, warm, and completely unannounced, her fingers tight in his shirt just long enough to make sure he understood she’d meant it.

When she let go, he didn’t seem to have anything to say. Her face went hot.

“Elowen,” he said eventually. “You didn’t ask.”

Her eyes went wide. Then she understood. “I know.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “I’m not complaining.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came home that night there were two new stools at the kitchen counter. Plain wood, dark seats, one on each side.

Zhao was standing at the counter with a bowl of soup and a document. Standing, of course.

“What’s this?”

“Stools.”

“I can see that.”

“The dining room’s a long way from the kitchen every night.”

“There are only two.”

“That’s how many people live here.”

She smiled, pulled one out, sat on it, and pointed at the other. “Here.”

He looked at his papers. “I have to finish this.”

“You can finish it sitting down.”

He thought about arguing. Then he put the papers down and sat beside her.

“Good,” she said.

“Are you going to praise me every time I sit?”

“Maybe.”

“Then I may have to reconsider.”

She served him. He passed her the soy sauce. Then, without being asked, he moved the dish of chicken over to her side.

The stools weren’t expensive. The counter wasn’t beautiful, and there were still boxes upstairs waiting to be unpacked. But Zhao Zhendong sat beside his wife and ate dinner without standing up once.

chapters.title: The Other Wife Hears the News
chapters.desc: Aurelia comes to gloat that their husbands are brothers, and leaves with a commission. That night Zhao wants to know which bus the physics boy took.
chapters.content:
On Thursday, Elowen was trimming white roses when the bell over the door rang.

“Welcome. I’ll be with you in a moment.”

“Still making people wait, I see.”

The knife stopped.

A woman stood in the doorway in a pale pink cashmere coat, pearls at her throat and gold at her ears, her dark hair pushed back with a soft velvet band. Enormous sunglasses. The face of someone who had come with a purpose and meant to enjoy every second of it.

Elowen put the knife down. “Aurelia Song.”

“Chen,” Aurelia corrected cheerfully. “Aurelia Chen now.”

“Unfortunately, I can see that.”

Aurelia took off the sunglasses. Wide, sweet doe eyes, which had never once in their life been innocent. “It’s been a long time, Elowen.”

“Not long enough.”

Aurelia laughed, the same laugh from school, bright and effortless and a little too pleased with itself, and walked in looking round. “Oh, this is lovely. Very you.”

“Thank you.”

“Small, though.”

“It’s a flower shop, not an exhibition hall.”

There were people who became friends after school, and people who became strangers. And then there were people like Elowen and Aurelia, who could go years without speaking and pick the argument up exactly where the last bell had cut it off.

Aurelia put her bag on the counter. “So. You actually married him.”

“I did.”

“Zhao Zhendong. I never pictured you with someone like that.”

“Neither did I.”

“Did he sweep you off your feet?”

“No. I wrote a contract.”

Aurelia stared at her, then burst out laughing. “Oh, Elowen. You haven’t changed at all.”

“Are you going to buy something?”

“Not yet. I’m getting to the good part.” She leaned on the counter. “Your husband and mine are brothers.”

Elowen looked up. “Sorry?”

“Brothers. Not by blood. By oath, which with those two is worse. They’ve known each other since they were boys. They survived something together and decided that made them family.” She smiled. “I assumed he’d told you.”

Elowen thought of Chen Si at the registry, teasing Zhao without the slightest fear, and Zhao putting up with it. That made a great deal more sense now.

“He didn’t mention it.”

“Men.” Aurelia picked up a little vase from the counter and turned it to the light. “Anyway, it means we’ll be seeing a lot of each other. Family dinners. Birthdays, New Year, festivals, random Sundays. Every single one.”

Elowen looked at the vase. Then at Aurelia.

She thought of a lifetime of birthdays at the same table as Aurelia Song, passing the soy sauce.

“Is it too late to get divorced?”

Aurelia nearly dropped the vase.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past twelve, Aurelia had taken off her coat, accepted a cup of tea and settled on the stool behind the counter as if she’d been a regular for years. Elowen was beginning to suspect she hadn’t come for flowers at all.

“So. How’s married life?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“He eats dinner now.”

Aurelia lowered her cup. “What?”

“He used to eat standing up, or forget. Now he sits down.”

“You’ve made Zhao Zhendong sit down to dinner.”

“Whenever he’s home.”

Aurelia looked honestly impressed. “That’s more frightening than the wedding.”

“He’s not difficult.”

“Zhao Zhendong. Not difficult.”

“Not with me.”

Aurelia studied her for a moment. “Oh. You mean it.” She sipped her tea, and her face went sly. “Chen Si says you were the one who found Kang. In your father’s files.”

Elowen’s hands slowed. “He told you that?”

“He tells me most things. He’s very good with secrets. He has a gift for making things disappear. Money. Documents. Awkward questions.”

Elowen smiled sweetly. “Does that include the money he washes through your jewellery label?”

Aurelia choked on her tea. “Elowen!”

“What? You said he makes things disappear.”

Aurelia glanced at the window and back. “I’m going to tell my husband you’re spreading rumours.”

“Please do. I’d love to hear him explain his bookkeeping.”

“I came here meaning to be gracious.”

“You lasted about four minutes.”

“Three.” Aurelia laughed, then, unexpectedly, her smile went quieter. “I missed this. Arguing with you.”

Elowen looked down at the bouquet in her hands. “We were never any good at being friends.”

“We were terrible. But we were good rivals.”

She put her cup down, and for a moment the teasing went out of her face.

“Can I tell you something? Properly. Not to win.”

Elowen waited.

“The people who want to hurt men like ours don’t go away. They just get patient. And sooner or later they work out that the easiest way to a man who can’t be touched is the woman he goes home to.” Aurelia turned her ring round on her finger. “Keep a bag packed. Know two ways out of every room you sit in. Learn which of his men you’d trust with your life, and don’t tell him which. And never let anyone see you frightened in public. They remember.”

Elowen looked at her for a long moment. “Is that what you do?”

“Every day.” Aurelia smiled, and it was almost kind. “You married him to keep your family safe. I know. Chen Si told me that too. Just remember you’re one of the family now.”

“I know,” said Elowen. “That’s why I married him.”

Aurelia laughed, and the moment passed, and she was herself again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia got up at last and went to the display. “I did come for something. My label’s showing a new collection in June. I need flowers for the show.”

“What sort?”

“Elegant. White, green, a little gold. Not romantic. I want it to look expensive without looking like a wedding.”

Elowen reached for her notebook. “How many pieces?”

“Four big installations, twelve tables, and smaller things for the entrance and the cases.”

“Venue?”

“The Kingsway, the ballroom. I’ll send you the specifications.”

“Budget?”

Aurelia named a figure. Elowen looked at her, at the notebook, and at her again.

“Triple.”

“Excuse me?”

“Triple my usual event rate.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re a difficult client. You came here to gloat, you told me I’m stuck with you at every family dinner for the rest of my life, you’ve interrupted my work for an hour, and you drank my tea.”

“Forty minutes.”

“And you drank my tea.”

Aurelia stared at her, then laughed. “Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Triple. The show matters, and I want it done properly.” She picked up her bag. “This is the first time you’ve beaten me at something without either of us trying.”

“I think I’m still ahead.”

At the door Aurelia stopped. “Oh. Family dinner on Sunday. Chen Si’s bringing me. Your husband knows.”

The bell rang behind her.

Elowen stood at the counter for a minute without moving.

She was thinking about the day the final-year results went up on the board outside the staff room. Elowen’s name at the top. Aurelia’s under it, for the first time in two years. Everyone had crowded round, and Aurelia had smiled and said congratulations in a perfectly clear voice, and then disappeared.

Elowen had found her in the girls’ toilets on the third floor, behind a locked door, crying so quietly you’d only have known if you’d stopped at the sinks. Elowen hadn’t knocked. She hadn’t said anything at all. She’d pushed a packet of tissues under the door and gone back to class, and neither of them had ever mentioned it.

Second place is just the first of the losers. Aurelia’s mother had said that at a prize-giving once, loud enough for half the hall to hear.

They had never been friends. But Elowen had never once told anyone about the tissues, and she knew, without ever having asked, that Aurelia hadn’t either. Elowen looked at the empty tea cup on the stool. Then she picked up her phone.

Elowen: Your brother’s wife came to see me.

The reply came in under a minute.

Unknown: Aurelia?

Elowen: She came to gloat.

Unknown: Did it work?

Elowen: No. I charged her triple for flowers.

Unknown: Good.

Elowen: She says there’s family dinner on Sunday. And that you and Chen Si are brothers. You didn’t tell me.

Unknown: You didn’t ask.

She could almost hear Aurelia laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she took two cups of jasmine tea into the sitting room and put one beside him. He was reading something on his tablet, his jacket over the back of the sofa.

“Aurelia says you’re blood brothers.”

He put the tablet down. “By oath.”

“Since when?”

“Since we were fifteen. Before the business, before the company, before either of us had anything.” He leaned back. “We met somewhere neither of us wanted to be. He was annoying.”

“Was?”

“Is.”

She held her cup in both hands. “Where?”

He was quiet for a moment. “I’ll tell you. Not tonight.”

She didn’t push. It was one of the doors. She’d seen enough of them now to know he’d open them when he was ready.

“Does he know you think of him like that?”

“He knows.”

“Do you ever tell him?”

“No. He’d be unbearable.”

She laughed. “And now?”

He looked at her. “Now I have you.”

She went very still. He didn’t say it like a declaration. He didn’t reach for her hand. He said it the way he’d say it was raining.

She drank her tea so she wouldn’t have to say anything back yet. When she could, she said, “Aurelia told me something else. She said the people who want to hurt you will come for me, because I’m the easy way in.”

He didn’t pretend otherwise. “They’ll try.”

“And?”

“And then they won’t try anything again.”

He said it the way he’d said now I have you. She found that she believed both, and that she wasn’t as frightened by the second one as she ought to be.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, upstairs, she was taking her earrings off at the mirror while he waited in the doorway to say goodnight.

“Aurelia asked if I’d ever had a boyfriend.”

His face didn’t change. “And?”

“I said no. Which is true.” She put the earrings down. “There was someone at school, though.”

His eyes lifted. “Someone.”

“Miles Wei. He was two years above us. Aurelia and I both liked him, and we spent a whole year fighting over him.” She seemed to find it funny. “He was in the physics club. Very clever. Quiet. He always had a notebook, and he pushed his glasses up whenever he was thinking.”

Zhao’s face got harder to read with every word.

“He sounds interesting.”

“He was.”

“Did you go out with him?”

“No. Nobody did. When it got too loud between Aurelia and me, he just walked away. Then he graduated and went off to do physics somewhere, and that was that.” She caught his eye in the mirror. “We never found out which of us he liked. I don’t think it was either.”

“Which school?”

She turned round. “You know which school.”

“Say it.”

She told him.

“And his full name?”

“Miles Wei.”

“Have you seen him since?”

“No.”

“Good.”

Elowen stared at him. Then her mouth curved. “Are you jealous?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No.”

“You’re asking a lot of questions for someone who isn’t jealous.”

“I like knowing things.”

“About a boy from eight years ago?”

“Yes.”

She laughed. He came closer.

“You remember him very clearly.”

“He was my first crush.”

It was out before she’d thought about it. He stopped. Then he reached for the loose strand of hair by her cheek and tucked it behind her ear.

“Did you kiss him?”

“No.”

“Did you want to?”

“Zhendong. You’re being jealous.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You asked about his glasses.”

His eyes went to her mouth, then back up. “Elowen. May I—“

“Yes.”

She didn’t let him finish. She caught the front of his shirt and pulled, and this time nothing about it was careful. He met her halfway, one hand at her waist, her back hit the door frame, and the kiss went deep fast, all the restraint from the basement gone into something warm and possessive. Her fingers knotted in his shirt.

He drew back just far enough to look at her. Her cheeks were flushed.

“Still jealous?” she whispered.

“A little.”

“Only a little?”

He kissed her again. This time she went up on her toes to meet him, and his hand came up to hold her face, and when she moved, he moved with her.

When he finally stopped, he rested his forehead on hers. “Is that enough?”

“Maybe. You’ll have to ask again some other time.”

“I can do that.”

She let go of his shirt and smoothed the creases she’d made. At her door, she looked back.

“Zhendong? Miles had terrible handwriting.”

She shut the door on his face.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the corridor looking down at his crumpled shirt for some time. Through the door he could hear her moving about, humming something under her breath, entirely pleased with herself. A boy with bad handwriting, eight years ago, who had walked away from her. He found he disliked him intensely. Then he went downstairs to his room and sent Bao a message.

Zhao: Find the old bus routes for Lin Elowen’s secondary school. Eight years back. Archived timetables.

Bao: Understood. Is this to do with the Miles Wei inquiry?

He hadn’t told Bao about any Miles Wei inquiry. Bao, as usual, had heard anyway. Bao heard most things. It was why he’d lasted six years.

Zhao: Yes.

Bao: May I ask why, sir?

Zhao: I want to know which bus the physics boy took.

Bao didn’t ask another question.

Upstairs, Elowen had fallen asleep with her phone by her pillow, still open on an old photo Aurelia had sent that afternoon: Aurelia, Elowen and a boy with round glasses and a physics notebook, outside a classroom, all three of them impossibly young.

chapters.title: The First Dinner as His Wife
chapters.desc: Her first dinner as his wife. A broker puts his hand on her knee under the table, and her husband puts a knife through it.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I don’t know what else to do tonight.”
chapters.content:
On the first Friday in April, the earrings were waiting on her bed when Elowen came upstairs.

Two green stones in gold, soft ovals edged with tiny diamonds, catching the late light from the east windows like leaves held up to the sun. No note. There was never a note. She’d started to suspect he just hated writing cards.

The green was almost exactly the green of the stone in her ring. The ring had come back from the jeweller three days ago, the right size at last. He’d taken it himself and put it on her bedside table that evening without a word, and it lived on the proper finger now.

“Are you trying to make me look expensive?”

“Is it working?”

He was in the doorway in a black suit, tie hanging loose, one hand in his pocket.

“They’re beautiful. They match my ring.”

“I noticed.”

“You noticed the colour of my ring?”

“I bought the ring.”

“After I’d worn it on the wrong finger for two weeks.”

“I noticed then too.”

He held out the little box. “Will you wear them tonight?”

“Is that an order from my husband?”

“No. A request.”

That softened her more than she wanted it to. “Then yes.”

She fought with the clasp behind her left ear. He lifted a hand and stopped short. “May I?”

She tilted her head. He moved her hair aside, the backs of his knuckles brushed her neck, and the clasp went in. The second one was easier.

“What kind of dinner is this?”

“Business. A broker from Rotterdam called Maartens. He’s buying for a general under sanctions, through two companies that don’t exist. His end-user papers are forged.”

Her hand stopped at her ear. “You’re selling to him?”

“I’m deciding whether he’s worth the trouble.”

“And the forged papers?”

“Are the trouble.”

“Then why am I going?”

His face cooled. “Because he asked to meet my wife. I want to know why.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was the top floor of a private club above the river: dark wood, brass, low lights, and flower arrangements so tall you couldn’t see the person opposite. White orchids and pale green hydrangeas. Lovely, and much too formal. Elowen wondered whether the florist had been given too much money or too little time, then remembered where she was and stopped thinking about flowers.

Zhao’s hand rested at the small of her back as they went in. Her first dinner as his wife. Not Lin Jian’s daughter. Not the girl who’d found the traitor. Mrs. Zhao.

Maartens stood up as they reached the table. Late fifties, silver hair, a red face, and a smile that had been practised in a mirror. Expensive suit, loud watch, a handshake a beat too long.

“Mr. Zhao. At last. And this must be your beautiful wife.”

“Elowen,” said Zhao. “My wife.”

“Charmed. I’d heard you were lovely, Mrs. Zhao. The reports were accurate.”

“How lucky that your reports were reliable,” Elowen said, smiling.

A short pause. Then Maartens laughed. “A sense of humour.”

Zhao pulled out her chair. “She has several qualities.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner began pleasantly. Maartens talked about Rotterdam, shipping insurance and the nuisance of government restrictions. He praised the wine, the restaurant and Zhao’s reputation. Zhao listened without seeming particularly interested. Elowen answered when spoken to and watched. Maartens smiled a great deal, and his eyes never stopped measuring everyone at the table.

“I was surprised to hear you’d married, Mr. Zhao. You never struck me as a man with time for that.”

“It doesn’t take much time.”

“Not with your resources.” His eyes slid to her. “And you, Mrs. Zhao? Flowers, I hear. How charming. Such delicate things. Not much to do with men like us.”

“People buy flowers for all sorts of reasons,” said Elowen. “Some of them aren’t very nice.”

“Really?”

“Funerals, for example.”

Zhao’s glass stopped halfway to his mouth. Maartens laughed, less certainly. “Quite right.”

Then they got to business. Maartens laid out his papers: industrial equipment for an agricultural development company, a delivery schedule, and a certificate saying who the goods were really for. Elowen knew nothing about buying guns. She knew a great deal about paperwork, and she knew what a story looked like when someone had put it together too neatly.

“Is that the end-user certificate?”

“It is, Mrs. Zhao.”

“And the company on it is the one receiving the shipment?”

“Correct.”

“Then why is the delivery address different from the registered one?”

For the first time that evening his smile slipped. “An administrative arrangement.”

“And why does the authorisation letter name a different company from the certificate?”

The silence was small, but everybody heard it.

“These are complicated matters, Mrs. Zhao. There are often several parties.”

“I understand. The paper says one thing and the shipment goes somewhere else.”

“Your husband hasn’t explained the finer details to you.”

“Maybe he doesn’t need to.”

Maartens leaned back. “Well. Lucky, isn’t it, that the person signing the papers isn’t the person asking the questions.”

“Is that how you like to do business? Someone else signs?”

“Elowen,” said Zhao. Calm. Not a reprimand, only a reminder that they were still at dinner.

She sat back. Maartens looked relieved.

Then his hand moved under the table.

At first she thought he was reaching for his napkin. She was looking down at the company names, trying to work out which one was real, when his fingers settled on her knee.

Her whole body went still.

It wasn’t an accident. His palm lay flat on her leg just above the knee, and his thumb moved once.

Her first instinct was to pull away. Her second was to look at Zhao. She’d barely begun to turn her head when Maartens’s fingers tightened.

The fruit knife was gone from the bowl in the middle of the table.

It went through the back of Maartens’s hand and into the wood with a short, wet sound, and for a heartbeat nobody moved at all.

Then Maartens screamed. His chair shrieked back. His wine went over, red spreading across the white cloth. He grabbed at his wrist with his other hand, but the knife held him to the table.

Zhao’s hand stayed on the handle. His face hadn’t changed.

“Take your hand off my wife.”

Quiet. That made it worse.

“Get it out! Get it out!”

Zhao pulled the knife free. Maartens lurched back, clutching his hand to his chest. Zhao laid the knife down neatly beside his plate.

“Bao.”

The door opened at once.

“Get him a doctor. Then bring him back. We haven’t finished.”

Two men took Maartens out, swearing.

The room went quiet. Music, somewhere far away. Cutlery in another room. Elowen’s napkin had fallen into her lap, and her fingers were knotted in it.

Zhao turned to her. “Are you hurt?”

She shook her head.

“Did he touch you?”

“Yes.”

His jaw tightened. Only a little, but she saw it.

“Where?”

“Just there.”

“May I?”

After a moment she nodded. His hand rested over her knee, warm and careful, for a second, the way you’d check something precious hadn’t cracked. Then he took it away.

“Do you want to go home?”

She looked at the blood on the tablecloth. Then at the papers.

“No,” she said. “We haven’t finished.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Maartens came back twenty minutes later with his right hand bandaged and his face the colour of putty. Someone had explained to him that leaving before the meeting was over would cost a great deal more than staying.

“Are you comfortable?” Elowen asked.

He stared at her. “No.”

“I’m sorry to hear that.”

She pulled the papers toward her. The price was on the last page. There was a margin for risk, a margin for insurance, and a margin for the extra handling it would take to hide where the cargo was really going. And now, apparently, a margin for men who thought they could put their hands wherever they liked.

“The price goes up. Twenty per cent.”

“That’s absurd.”

“The certificate is forged. The end user isn’t the recipient. The delivery address doesn’t match, and the letter names a different company.” She tapped each one. “Your deal carries more risk than you told us.”

Maartens looked at Zhao. “You’re letting your wife negotiate?”

Zhao rested his arm along the back of her chair. “She found the problems. Discuss them with her.”

“Twenty per cent,” said Elowen. “Or we don’t go ahead.”

“You think you can simply—“

“Mr. Maartens.” Her voice was perfectly polite. “Your hand is injured. I wouldn’t make this harder than it needs to be.”

Zhao didn’t interrupt. Something moved in his face that wasn’t surprise. Pride, maybe.

Maartens signed with his left hand. The first try was crooked. The second was worse. The third was a slanted, wobbling copy of the name on his passport.

“Your wife,” he said, pushing the papers away, “is an unpleasant woman.”

Zhao stood. “Then you were lucky to meet her before she got angry. Good evening.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, the rain started again, thin silver lines down the glass. Elowen held her hands together in her lap so tightly her knuckles ached.

Her knee remembered the touch. Her ears kept replaying the sound of the knife going into the table. She’d known what kind of man he was. Knowing it wasn’t the same as watching it from an arm’s length away.

At a red light he turned his head. “Are you frightened?”

She tried to answer. Her throat closed. A small shake went through her fingers.

He didn’t reach for her. He laid his hand on the seat between them, palm up, and left it there.

She looked at it. She wanted to take it. She also wanted to ask why the look on his face afterwards had frightened her more than the blood. Neither came out.

The light changed. He left his hand where it was. He didn’t take it back when she didn’t take it, and he didn’t tell her to calm down.

A few minutes later her little finger touched his. He didn’t close his hand. She moved until her fingers rested in his palm, and only then did he turn it over and let her hold on, as tight as she wanted.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he walked her up and stopped at her door.

“Do you want me to stay?”

“I don’t know.”

“All right. I’ll be in my room.”

“You don’t have to stand guard outside my door.”

“I know.”

“Then why would you?”

He looked at her for a long moment. “Because I don’t know what else to do tonight.”

It was the most honest thing he’d said since the restaurant, and he looked as if it had cost him something to say it.

“Goodnight, Zhendong.”

“Goodnight.”

He left her door open a crack.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke after midnight and didn’t know why. Then she heard something move outside her room.

When she opened the door, Zhao was sitting on the corridor floor with his back against the wall opposite, jacket folded beside him, sleeves rolled, tie loose, reading on his phone. He looked up at once.

“What are you doing?”

“Reading.”

“On the floor.”

“Yes.”

“You said you’d be in your room.”

“This isn’t my room.”

“No,” she agreed, and leaned on the door frame. “Why?”

“I didn’t want to be far away.”

It made her chest hurt. The man who’d put a knife through a broker’s hand without changing his face was sitting on the floor outside her bedroom because he didn’t know if she wanted him close.

“Did you know he’d do that?”

“No. I thought he wanted to use you to get a better price. The questions. The way he kept looking at you.” His voice dropped. “If I’d known he’d touch you, you’d never have been at that table.”

She believed him. That was the hard part. She believed the knife hadn’t been for show. She also knew he’d do it again.

“I don’t need you to hurt people every time somebody makes me uncomfortable,” she said.

“It wasn’t about what you need. He touched my wife.”

She looked at him for a long moment. He wasn’t going to be sorry, and he wasn’t going to pretend he would be. She found she didn’t want him to.

“Then next time,” she said, “let me see it coming.”

Something in his face loosened. “I’ll try.”

“Do you want me to go?” he asked.

“No.”

She looked at his mouth, then back at his eyes. He noticed. Of course he noticed. But he didn’t move.

“Elowen,” he said quietly. “Can I?”

She could have stepped back and shut the door, and he’d have let her. Instead she crouched in front of him and kissed him.

It was softer than any of the others, and less sure. Her hand on his cheek. His at his side for a moment before it came up to her waist. He didn’t pull her closer until she leaned into him. When she did, his other hand came up against her back, careful.

When she drew away, he rested his forehead on hers.

“Are you all right?” he asked.

“Are you?”

“I’m fine.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

For a second she saw something underneath, something he hardly let anyone see. Then his hand moved slowly up her back. “I am now.”

She kissed the corner of his mouth and stood up. “Come on. I’m not inviting you to do anything scandalous. I’m asking you to stop sitting on the floor.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “Understood.”

She left the door open. He didn’t cross the threshold until she stepped aside to let him in, and then he only went as far as the armchair by the window, and sat there in the dark until she fell asleep.

chapters.title: The Night the Delivery Van Burned
chapters.desc: Someone sets fire to her van with Xiao Pan standing next to it. Zhao goes to the Qiu brothers’ warehouse and comes home with a burn she holds under the cold tap.
chapters.content:
A week later, on Friday night, a little after nine, the first thing Elowen noticed was the smell.

Not smoke. Not yet. Something sharp and chemical drifting in through the open shop door. She looked up from the invoices on the counter and frowned.

Outside, Xiao Pan was loading the last buckets into the van for a wedding first thing in the morning.

“Don’t forget the white roses!”

“I haven’t forgotten!”

“You forgot them yesterday.”

“Yesterday was different. I was hungry.”

Elowen smiled and went back to her sums. Xiao Pan had delivered for her for two years. He was nineteen, permanently starving, and could turn any instruction into a debate. His mother worked long shifts in a hotel laundry across the city. He could tie a ribbon without looking and name almost any flower in the shop from its leaves.

He went round the back of the van. A moment later she heard him swear.

Then a crash of metal, as if something had been thrown hard against the side of the van.

An orange flash lit the window.

For a second she couldn’t make sense of it. Then the sound reached her, a deep thump she felt in the counter under her hands, and the back of her van was full of fire.

“Xiao Pan!”

She was out of the door before she knew she’d moved. The rear tyre was burning. Flames ran up the side panel and licked into the open doors. A tyre burst with a crack like a gun.

Xiao Pan was on the ground by the back doors in a spill of white roses, trying to get up with his hands held to his chest.

“Don’t touch anything!”

“The roses—“

“Forget the roses!”

She got him under the arm and hauled him back just as the fire surged out of the van again. He cried out. She looked down. His palms and fingers were red and blistering. He’d reached into the van to drag the crates out when it caught. His cuffs were scorched black.

“Oh, God. Come on. Come on.”

Somebody was shouting to call the fire brigade. Somebody else was shouting to get back. Elowen hardly heard them. She got him into the shop and to the sink and turned the cold tap on full.

“Hands under. Keep them there.”

He hissed through his teeth.

“I know it hurts. Keep them there.”

“I’m sorry. I was trying to save the roses.”

“Xiao Pan, look at me. You matter more than the roses. Do you understand?”

He swallowed and nodded.

She held his wrists under the water so he couldn’t pull away. Her own hands were shaking. She made them stop.

She rang for an ambulance one-handed. Then she rang Zhao.

He answered before the second ring. “Elowen.”

“Someone’s set fire to the van. Xiao Pan was next to it. His hands are burned.”

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“You’re sure.”

“Yes. An ambulance is coming.”

“I’ll meet you at the hospital.”

Something in the background: a door, a man’s voice, fast.

“Zhendong, somebody did this on purpose.”

“I know.”

The way he said it made her look at the phone. “How do you know?”

“Stay with Xiao Pan.”

The line went dead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hospital smelled of disinfectant and wet coats. They took Xiao Pan through, and Elowen sat outside in a cardigan with a black smear down one sleeve.

She’d rung his mother. The woman had cried so hard Elowen could barely understand her. She hadn’t told her how close he’d been standing. She didn’t think she could bear to hear anyone say out loud what she was thinking.

A nurse came out. “He’s stable. It’s mostly his palms, and two fingers are worse. We’ve dressed them. The doctor will explain.”

Elowen sat down on a plastic chair that wobbled. Only then did she notice her hands. There was soot in the creases of her knuckles and a smear of Xiao Pan’s blood on her cuff, and they wouldn’t stay still.

The van had been old. She’d bought it second-hand with her own savings and fixed everything wrong with it. She could replace it. She could replace every rose in the shop.

But somebody had chosen the time. Somebody had known the van would be there, and that people would be next to it, and had been willing to set a nineteen-year-old on fire to send her husband a message.

Her phone buzzed.

Zhao: Are you with him?

Elowen: Yes. He’s stable.

Zhao: Good.

Elowen: Where are you?

No answer. She rang. It rang out.

For the first time that night, she was really frightened. Not for herself. For what he was about to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Qiu brothers’ warehouse stood behind a row of shuttered factories in the old industrial district. It wasn’t their biggest. It was where they kept things for a few days, and met people they didn’t want to be seen with, and lately where they’d been moving cargo down routes that used to be Zhao’s.

Qiu Wen was in the office upstairs. He stood when Zhao walked in.

“Zhendong. This is unexpected.”

“Is it?”

Wen glanced past him at the men in the doorway. “Perhaps we should discuss whatever’s brought you here.”

“Your people burned my wife’s van.”

Wen gave a small laugh. “Your wife’s van?”

“There was a boy standing next to it. He’s nineteen.”

The laugh went away. Zhao looked at the monitor on the desk, where a man was crossing the warehouse floor below.

“Your brother’s downstairs.”

He went down. Wen followed.

Qiu Lei was by the loading bay with four of his men. Younger than Wen, broader, and much worse at hiding his temper. He grinned when he saw Zhao.

“Look who came.”

“Did you give the order?”

Lei’s grin widened. “Maybe.”

That was enough.

The man nearest Lei went for the gun in his waistband. Zhao’s men were faster. A chair went over. Somebody hit the concrete. A shot cracked off the metal roof, then another. When it stopped, Lei’s men were face down on the floor and Lei was on his knees.

“What the hell are you doing?” Wen shouted from the stairs.

Zhao looked down at Lei. “Do you know what happened to the boy?”

Lei spat blood on the concrete. “He’s alive, isn’t he?”

For a moment, Zhao’s face was completely empty.

A rubbish drum stood by the loading bay with a fire still going low inside it, orange light crawling round its blackened rim. Zhao took Lei by both wrists and dragged him to it.

“Zhao, don’t,” said Wen.

Lei laughed, high and strained. “You think I’m scared of—“

Zhao held his hands over the fire.

Lei fought. He twisted and kicked and swore. Zhao didn’t let go. The heat came up off the drum into his face and along his own arm. The flames caught his cuff and ran up his sleeve, and he didn’t let go for that either.

“One,” he said.

He counted out loud. He didn’t hurry. Somewhere round eight, Lei stopped swearing. Somewhere round twelve, he started to beg. Wen shouted something. One of Zhao’s men stood in his way. The smell of burning skin rose over the smoke.

At twenty, Zhao let go.

Lei fell back on the concrete with his hands clutched to his chest, sobbing. Zhao beat out his sleeve with the flat of his hand and looked down at him.

“That was for the boy.”

He turned to Wen, who had gone white.

“You’ve made your point.”

“No. Your brother made his point when he put a nineteen-year-old next to a firebomb.” Zhao looked round the building. “This place is finished. Every shipment in it. Every ledger. Every account you use to move goods through this district.”

“You’ll start a war.”

“You started one.”

At the door he looked back once.

“My wife isn’t business.”

His men began to move. Papers came out of the office to be copied. The workers were sent home and the buildings either side warned. Fuel went in.

By the time his car left the district, flames were climbing the outer wall. He didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came into Xiao Pan’s room without a sound. Elowen looked up anyway.

The same black shirt he’d left the house in. No jacket. Dust on his trousers. His right sleeve was gone to the elbow, burned ragged at the edge, and the skin underneath was an angry, shining red, blistered in patches down to his wrist.

She stood up.

“How is he?” Zhao asked.

“Asleep. The doctor says it’s not as bad as it could have been.” She looked at his arm. “What happened?”

“It’ll heal.”

“That’s not an answer. Let me see.”

He held still while she took his wrist. Her face changed.

“The Qiu brothers?”

He didn’t answer, which was an answer.

“Did you hurt them?”

“Qiu Lei gave the order.”

“How badly?”

“Badly enough that he won’t forget.”

She let her breath out. She wasn’t sure what she’d expected. An apology. A denial. Something to make the world feel less terrible than it did. Instead there was just him, with a burned arm and the same calm face he’d had at dinner a week ago.

She looked at Xiao Pan’s bandaged hands on the blanket. Then at her husband’s.

“His hands,” she said. It wasn’t a question.

“Yes.”

She took his good hand. “Come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t even take her shoes off. She took him straight to the kitchen.

“Sit.”

He sat on his stool. She ran the tap until it was cool but not icy and guided his arm under it. He flinched. It was tiny. She saw it anyway.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not much.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

She stood close, one hand holding his wrist, keeping the water moving over the burn. Her hair had come out of its clip. There was soot on her cheek, and her cardigan smelled of smoke.

“Xiao Pan’s mother?” he asked.

“With him now.”

“Bao has a room for her in the hotel across the road, as long as he’s in. The hospital has my details. His bills come to me. His wages carry on.”

She looked up. “When did you arrange all that?”

“On the way to the warehouse.”

She looked back at his arm. “Twenty minutes.”

“What?”

“Cool running water for twenty minutes. That’s what the doctor said for Xiao Pan.”

“You don’t have to—“

“Twenty minutes.”

He shut his mouth.

The kitchen was quiet except for the water. He looked emptied out now, as if whatever had kept him moving all night had finally run out. She wondered how many people had ever looked at him and seen only the man who could burn down a warehouse, and how many had ever asked whether his arm hurt.

“You counted to twenty,” she said. “For his hands.”

His eyes came to hers. “Who told you?”

“Nobody. You count everything.”

He looked at her for a long time.

He reached for a strand of hair on her cheek, then stopped. She leaned into his hand. He brushed it back.

“You’re shaking,” he said.

“I was frightened. Of the fire. For Xiao Pan. Of you not answering your phone.”

“I should have answered.”

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

Zhao Zhendong didn’t apologise often. She nodded, and took it.

“Did you think about what would happen if you didn’t come back?”

His face went still. “I came back.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“I thought about you.”

“That isn’t always enough.”

“I know.”

“You’re impossible.”

“So I’m told.”

She let out a small, tired laugh, the first either of them had heard all night, and he looked at her as if he wanted to keep it.

When the twenty minutes were up, she turned off the tap, patted the good skin dry round the burn, and dressed it loosely from the first-aid box. “Don’t pop the blisters. If it gets hot or starts to smell, you go to a doctor. A real one.”

“Thank you.”

She washed her hands. When she turned back, he was still on the stool, looking at her.

He reached up with his good hand, took her face, and kissed her.

He didn’t ask. It came all at once, almost desperate in how quiet it was, his thumb rubbing at the soot on her jaw, his burned arm resting on the counter between them. For a second she was surprised. Then she kissed him back, and her fingers twisted into his shirt.

When he let go, he rested his forehead on hers. “Elowen—“

She touched his mouth with her fingertips. “You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

He didn’t say sorry. She found she didn’t want him to.

“I didn’t mind,” she said, and kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, Bao’s message was waiting.

Bao: Xiao Pan’s hospital bills are settled. His full wages continue while he recovers. His mother has a room at the hotel opposite for three weeks, and a car to take her back and forth.

She went downstairs. Zhao was at the counter reading a report left-handed, his right arm propped on a cushion.

“You paid for everything.”

“Yes.”

“His mother’s hotel too.”

“She shouldn’t have to worry where she’s sleeping while her son’s in hospital.”

“He’s going to feel terrible when he finds out.”

“Then don’t tell him.”

“He’ll find out.”

“Tell him it was a business expense.”

“He delivers flowers. He isn’t an accountant.”

He turned a page. “Then tell him it was a flower expense.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed, a surprised little laugh that made him look up, and leaned over and kissed his cheek.

He reached for his tea with his good hand. She pushed the cup nearer.

“Drink it before it gets cold.”

He looked at the cup, then at his wife. “Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

chapters.title: The Night She Asks Him to Stay
chapters.desc: A typhoon, a fever and a power cut. She asks him to stay, and in the morning she asks for more.
chapters.content:
The typhoon signal went up on a Wednesday in the middle of April, early in the season and nobody’s idea of convenient.

The rain began before noon. By three, the sky over the Walled City was the colour of wet concrete and the wind was leaning on the shop windows hard enough to make the glass hum. Elowen brought the outside buckets in, moved the big arrangements back from the door, and rang the afternoon’s customers to put off their deliveries. With Xiao Pan’s hands still bandaged and no van, there was nothing to deliver them in anyway.

By five, the street had disappeared behind the rain. By six, she had a headache. By seven, she was cold all the way through.

She was wrapping a last bouquet of white lilies when the door opened and threw a sheet of water across her floor.

Zhao stood there holding an umbrella that had clearly lost a fight. His hair was wet and his coat was dark at the shoulders. Under the sleeve, his right forearm was still bandaged.

“What are you doing here?”

“Taking my wife home.”

“I’m working.”

He looked round: buckets in, shutter half down, nobody in the street. “Are you?”

“This is the last one.”

He looked at her face. “You’re pale.”

“I’m always pale.”

“Not like this.”

He came round the counter and touched the back of his fingers to her forehead.

“That’s cold,” she complained.

“You’re burning.”

“I’m not.”

She sneezed.

Neither of them said anything. Then he took off his coat. “Sit down.”

“Zhendong, I have to—“

“Elowen.”

It wasn’t loud. It wasn’t even stern. But she knew that voice. She put the lilies down. “Fine.”

He sat her on the little sofa behind the counter and crouched in front of her with his hand on her forehead again.

“How long have you felt like this?”

“A little while.”

“How long?”

She looked at the window. “Since lunch.”

Something in his eyes went sharp. “Why didn’t you call me?”

“You were working.”

“I can work anywhere.”

He rang Bao. “Car to the side door. Someone to lock up here, and move the front display back from the glass.” He listened. “And check the drain outside. It floods.”

“You don’t need to close my shop.”

“It’s closing for the night.”

“I was going to close it anyway.”

“Then we agree.”

She stood up. The room tipped. The counter seemed to slide away from her hand.

“Elowen?”

“I’m—“

Her knees went. He caught her before she hit the floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

She remembered rain. She remembered him saying her name. She remembered being lifted, one arm under her knees and one under her back, and the cold of the street, and a car door.

When she opened her eyes again she was in bed. The room was dim. Rain rattled the windows. She was in a clean nightdress, and a cool cloth lay on her forehead.

Zhao was in the chair beside the bed with his sleeves rolled and his phone face down on the table. He looked as if he’d been there a long time.

“Did I faint?”

“Yes.”

“Oh.” She looked down at the nightdress. “Who—“

“Mrs. Chiu.” The housekeeper. “I waited outside.”

Of course he had. Page two, line six, even with her out cold. She didn’t know whether to laugh or cry, so she did neither.

“You carried me? All the way to the car?”

“Yes.”

“Did anyone see?”

“Several people.”

She shut her eyes. “How embarrassing.”

“You collapsed.”

“That doesn’t make it less embarrassing.”

“Would you rather I’d left you on the pavement?”

“No.”

“Then we’re done discussing it.”

She opened one eye. “You’re bossy when I’m sick.”

“I’m bossy when you’re not sick.”

“True.”

He held the water for her. She drank two mouthfuls with both hands round the glass.

“Have you eaten?”

“Some.”

“What’s some?”

“Half.”

“Of what?”

“A sandwich.”

“What kind?”

“Why does that matter?”

“Because I’m trying to find out whether you’ve eaten anything real.”

“Egg.”

“Half an egg sandwich.” He looked at her for a moment and stood up. “I’m making you something.”

She watched him go. She wasn’t sure whether that was reassuring or alarming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The congee was a disaster.

Zhao found this out at about a quarter to nine, when the first pot boiled over and he stood looking down at rice foaming over the sides as if it had insulted him personally. His phone was propped against the tea tin, with Chen Si on the screen.

“You’re cooking?”

“She’s sick.”

“That explains the cooking. It doesn’t explain why you think it’s a good idea.”

Zhao turned the heat down. “How do you make congee?”

“First you wash the rice.”

“I did.”

“How many times?”

“Once.”

“Wash it again.”

Zhao looked at the pot. “Too late.”

Chen Si closed his eyes. “You’re going to poison your wife.”

“She has a fever. Don’t be dramatic. How much water?”

“Depends how thick you want it.”

“How thick should it be?”

“Like congee.”

Zhao stared at the phone. Chen Si laughed and hung up.

The rice was turning into paste. He added water. Then ginger. Then salt. He found chicken in the fridge and cut it up. The pieces were uneven, and one was much bigger than the rest. He thought about taking it out and decided it would probably cook eventually.

When he carried the bowl upstairs, it was pale and lumpy and looked faintly suspicious.

Elowen looked at the bowl, then at him. “Did you make that?”

“Yes.”

“Yourself?”

“Eat it before it goes cold.”

She tasted it carefully. Her face changed. Not much. Enough.

“Is it bad?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

“I’m not.”

“Chen Si said it would be difficult.”

“Chen Si doesn’t know everything.”

The rice was too soft. The chicken was uneven. One side was all ginger and the other had no salt. But it was hot, and he’d made it. She ate every spoonful.

“Was it all right?”

“It was delicious.”

“You don’t have to lie to me because I’m your husband.”

“I know.” She reached for his hand. “It tasted like you made it for me.”

For a moment he didn’t move. Then his fingers closed round hers.

“Next time I’ll make it better.”

“Next time?”

“When you’re sick again.”

“That’s a terrible thing to look forward to.”

“I’ll practise.” He kissed her knuckles. “Sleep.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The power went at half past ten.

One second the lamp was on. The next, the room was black. Thunder rolled over the hill.

“Zhendong?”

“I’m here.”

His phone light came on. He tried the lamp, then the switch. Nothing.

“The whole house?”

“Probably the whole district. The security has its own power.”

Without the hum of the air conditioning the house was terribly quiet. Elowen pulled the blanket up. In the dark she felt small.

He brought a battery lamp from the cupboard. Its light was soft and yellow. He checked her forehead. “Still high.”

“Not as high as before.”

He took off his watch, put it on the table, and pulled the chair close.

“Are you staying?” she asked.

“Yes.”

It was the answer she wanted, and still not quite the thing she wanted to say. She put her hand out from under the blanket.

“Zhendong. Stay.”

He looked at her hand. Then her face. “I’m staying.”

He took it. She shifted toward the edge of the bed.

“Not there.”

“Where?”

“Here.” She patted the space beside her. “There’s enough room.”

He hesitated. “You need to rest.”

“I am resting.”

He looked at the bed for a long moment. Then he took his shoes off and sat on top of the covers against the headboard, and kept her hand.

Outside, the typhoon tore at the trees. Something metal clattered and rolled away down the hill.

“Tell me something,” she said. “Something I don’t know. About you.”

He was quiet for a while. Her thumb moved slowly on the side of his hand.

“Block C.”

Her eyes opened. “What’s Block C?”

“A wing of a youth detention centre up north. I was fifteen.” He looked at the black window. “Chen Si came in that autumn. His family had just been taken apart. Nobody cared about some politician’s boy, and he was too clever to be safe. He sat next to me in the laundry because I was the biggest. Then, at night, he read to me.”

“Read to you?”

“I couldn’t read. Old Zhao never sent me to school.” He said it with no shame at all. “War books. The monkey king. He read me the whole monkey king that winter.”

She held on to his hand.

“In January there was a riot. A boy called Gao had a slat off a bed frame, sharpened. He went for Chen Si. Chen Si didn’t see him.”

“And you did.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t go on. He didn’t need to.

“How bad?”

“It went in under my ribs.” He let out a small breath. “I put him down. Then I fell over. I was lucky.”

“You were fifteen.”

“I don’t remember feeling fifteen.”

She thought of a boy on a concrete floor in the middle of a riot, with nowhere to go back to, putting himself between a sharpened slat and the only person he had.

“What did Chen Si do?”

“Got us out. Through the drains. Half a kilometre of freezing water in the dark, dragging me, telling me the monkey king the whole way so I’d stay awake.” Something eased in his face. “We came up in the snow. He was crying. He kept calling me an idiot.”

“Was he wrong?”

“No.”

She laughed under her breath. “And after that you were brothers.”

“We cut our palms on a bit of glass and pressed them together. We were fifteen and sixteen. It seemed sensible.”

“It was,” she said. “I’m glad you lived.”

He looked down at their hands. “So am I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drifted in and out. Every time thunder shook the windows and woke her, he was there. Once he was reading weather updates. Once he was looking at the bandage on his arm. She reached for him, and he turned at once.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.” She moved closer to his side and looked at the little pool of lamplight. “Can I tell you something?”

“Yes.”

“My mother died after Eliana was born. I was seven. I remember the hospital. The smell. Baba walking up and down with his hands behind his back. The nurses saying Eliana was healthy and beautiful. And Mama not coming home.”

His hand tightened.

“Baba couldn’t look at Eliana. Not for a long time. So I fed her. I learned to make up the bottles. Evangeline was four and wouldn’t let go of my skirt, and Raiden wasn’t even home yet.” She swallowed. “For years I thought it was my fault. That if I’d been better, or helped more, she’d have stayed. I know it wasn’t. I’ve known for years. Knowing it and feeling it are different.”

He didn’t try to correct her. He listened.

“I used to wonder what she’d think of the shop. The flowers I picked. Whether she’d think I was stupid for marrying a man like you.”

“A man like me?”

“An arms dealer.”

“Ah.”

“She might have been a bit concerned.”

“Probably.”

She laughed, then went quiet. “That’s why I brought the lemon tree. It’s one of the only things of hers I’ve still got.”

“I’ll keep it alive.”

“You know nothing about lemon trees.”

“I’ll learn.” He brushed his thumb over her knuckles. “You’re allowed to miss her. Even when you’re happy.”

That was what undid her. Not a promise. Not everything will be all right. Just permission.

She turned her face to him. He moved the hair off her forehead. For a moment she let herself be seven again. Then she let herself be twenty-four, married and feverish, held by a man who had once been a boy with nowhere to go.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

He kissed her forehead. She slept, and this time she didn’t let go of his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the first thing she noticed was that she wasn’t cold. The second was that her head no longer felt full of wet cotton.

Grey light came through the curtains. The rain had eased. Zhao was asleep against the headboard, head tipped to one side, still holding her hand, his collar open and his shirt creased from the night. He looked younger asleep. Less severe.

She touched his cheek. He woke at once, found her face, and the tension went out of his shoulders.

He felt her forehead, then reached for the thermometer. She laughed.

“It’s down,” he said.

“You stayed all night.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t sleep.”

“I slept. At some point. Don’t interrogate me, you’re recovering.”

“Did you eat?”

“I had tea.”

“Tea isn’t food.”

“You’re ill and you’re still managing my meals.”

“Someone has to.”

He leaned down and brushed his lips against her forehead. She caught his hand before he could straighten up.

“Come here.”

He did. She lifted her head off the pillow and kissed him, warm and slow, her hand on his jaw, his stubble rough under her fingers. He kissed her back.

Then he stopped. Not suddenly. He drew back and stayed close, forehead nearly on hers.

“What?”

“You’ve still got a fever.”

“It’s gone down.”

“You’re not well.” His thumb moved on her cheek. “You might not mean it.”

She stared at him. Then she understood. He thought she was kissing him because she was feverish and grateful and soft from a long night. He was afraid she’d wake up properly and wish she hadn’t.

“I know what I’m doing,” she said.

“Then you can do it again when you’re well.”

“I want to kiss my husband. And I want you to stop looking at me like I’ll disappear if you touch me.”

“That isn’t what I think.”

“Then what?”

He was quiet. Then: “I don’t want you to feel you owe me anything.”

“I don’t. You stayed because I asked. I kissed you because I wanted to. There’s a difference.”

He kissed her forehead again. “Get better first. Then ask me.”

She sighed, very dramatically. “You’re very difficult.”

“So I’m told.”

“What if I don’t want to ask?”

“Then you don’t have to.”

She thought about that. “All right. But I’m asking for something else.”

“What?”

“Breakfast.”

He laughed quietly. “Congee?”

She remembered the bowl. The lumps, the ginger, the texture somewhere between food and wallpaper paste.

“Yes.”

“Even though it was terrible?”

“So you admit it!”

“I said it could be improved.”

She laughed, and something loosened in him. He tucked her hand back under the blanket and went to the door, and there he stopped.

“Elowen. I’m glad you asked me to stay.”

Outside, the storm was moving off. Branches lay across the courtyard. The lemon tree was still standing in its chipped pot.

She could hear him downstairs, opening cupboards, putting a pot on, looking for something. She smiled into the pillow. When she was properly well, she would ask him for another kiss. Not because she was sick, or because he’d stayed. Just because she wanted one.

chapters.title: Page Two, Line Six
chapters.desc: A week of him not touching her. Then she leaves a thermometer by his soup, says “page two, line six,” and this time nobody has a fever.
chapters.content:
Granny Yip noticed before Elowen did.

It was the Friday after the typhoon, nearly five in the morning, and the market was waking up around them. Elowen was sorting a bundle of pale pink tulips when the old woman appeared at her elbow.

“You’re distracted.”

“Good morning to you too.”

“Good morning. You’re distracted. You’ve been holding that same tulip for five minutes.”

Elowen looked down. She had. She put it in the bucket.

Granny Yip looked at the ring on her finger. “How’s your husband?”

“Fine.”

“Still eating?”

“Yes.”

“Still working too much?”

“Yes.”

“Still looking at you like somebody’ll steal you if he blinks?”

Elowen nearly dropped the next tulip. “Granny!”

“What? I’ve seen him. That man could empty this market by standing quietly at the gate. And when you walk in, he looks like he’s waiting for permission to breathe.” She watched Elowen for a moment, and her voice went gentler. “Are you happy?”

Elowen thought of the typhoon. His hand in the dark. The terrible congee. You’re allowed to miss her, even when you’re happy. Then the morning after, when he’d stopped kissing her. Not because he didn’t want to. Because he was afraid she didn’t mean it.

“Yes.”

“Good. Then whatever you’re waiting to say, don’t wait too long. Men like your husband aren’t patient.”

“He’s actually very patient.”

Granny Yip gave her a look. “Then that’s the problem.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He hadn’t touched her in eight days.

Not properly. He still held her hand when they walked. He still put his palm at her back in a crowd and tucked her hair behind her ear when it fell. But he hadn’t kissed her. He hadn’t held her. He didn’t touch her face unless she reached for him first.

At first she thought he was being careful because she’d been ill. Then the fever went. She went back to the shop and the market, ate properly, slept properly, complained that the air conditioning was too cold. He went on treating her like an invalid.

On Monday, he helped her into the car and shut the door without kissing her goodbye. On Tuesday, she stood next to him in the kitchen, close enough that their shoulders touched, and he moved away to get a cup. On Wednesday, she held his hand all evening in front of the television, and when she leaned against him, he fixed the cushion behind her back. On Thursday, she kissed his cheek. He smiled, and went back to his report.

It was getting ridiculous. She knew he wasn’t rejecting her. The problem was that he wanted her so carefully that she was beginning to feel she had to put in a written request.

Which, she supposed, was exactly what she’d once told him to make her do. She’d put it in a contract. She just hadn’t expected him to take it this seriously.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home late that night. Dinner had been kept for him, his soup still warm under its lid. He loosened his tie in the doorway.

“Have you eaten?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

“Good. Come and sit.”

He looked at the counter. Soup. Steamed fish. Rice. And, beside his bowl, a digital thermometer.

He stopped. His eyes went from the thermometer to her, and back.

She picked up her spoon. “Your soup’s getting cold.”

“Why is there a thermometer next to my dinner?”

“Just in case.”

“In case of what?”

“Fever.”

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he sat. She waited until he’d lifted the lid off his soup.

“Page two, line six.”

His hand stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

He remembered every page of it.

The first had been practical: her family, the debt, her shop. The second had been personal. Separate rooms. No forced affection. And line six: he didn’t touch her unless she explicitly asked.

He remembered line six because of the word in front of it. It had first said he would not ever touch her, and ever had been crossed out so hard the pen had nearly gone through the paper. In darker ink. A different pen from the rest of the page.

He’d asked her about it in his office, and she’d told him it was none of his business. He hadn’t asked again. He hadn’t needed to. The man he’d had sitting outside her father’s house that week had reported her lamp on all night and off at ten past four. Some time around four in the morning she’d stopped writing, picked up a different pen, and taken ever out.

He’d thought he understood. She’d left a door open. A small one. He’d taken that seriously. Too seriously, perhaps.

Then she’d kissed him with a fever, and he’d stopped, and told her to ask when she was well. He’d expected her to ask. He hadn’t expected eight days of nothing. And now she was sitting across from him looking far too pleased with herself, with a thermometer by his soup.

“You’re not sick,” he said.

“No.”

“Your fever’s gone.”

“Completely.”

“You’re sure?”

She gave him a flat look. “Would you like to take my temperature?” She glanced at the thermometer. “Or yours?”
