He sat back. Then, very quietly: “Are you asking me something?”

Her smile went. She put the spoon down.

“Yes. I’m asking you to stop treating me as if I’m going to regret wanting you.”

“Are you sure?”

“Zhendong. I’ve been sure for a week.”

He didn’t move. So she got up, came round the counter to his stool, and put her hand on his cheek.

“I’m asking you to touch me.”

He looked at her hand. A small hand, with a faint white scar at the base of her thumb from a florist’s knife. He’d watched those hands tie ribbons and carry buckets and turn the pages of her father’s shipping records. He’d watched them shake under hospital lights.

“I’m not feverish,” she said. “I’m not confused. And I’m not saying thank you for looking after me.”

“Then why?”

She leaned closer. “Because I want my husband to kiss me.”

He stood up, and nothing about it was careful.

His hands came to her waist and lifted her, and the edge of the counter met the backs of her thighs, and he kissed her the way he hadn’t let himself kiss her for eight days. She made a small sound against his mouth and pushed her fingers into his hair. He paused for half a breath, the way he always did, as if to check. This time she answered before he could ask, and pulled him back down.

“Still sure?” he said against her mouth.

“Very.”

He kissed her jaw, the side of her neck, the place under her ear that made her breath catch. Her hands went to his shoulders, then the back of his neck. A bowl rattled somewhere behind her and neither of them looked.

When he finally lifted his head, her face was hot and her mouth felt bruised.

“That took you long enough,” she said.

“Eight days.”

“Nine, if you count the morning after the typhoon.”

“I was being careful.”

“You were being unbearable.”

He rested his forehead on hers. Then, with a look she’d never seen on him before, something unsure, almost afraid, he asked, “Why did you cross it out? Ever.”

She went pink. “You noticed the ink.”

“And the time. My man outside your father’s house said your light went off at ten past four.”

Her head came up. “You had someone watching my window?”

“Yes.”

“That’s horrible.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she smoothed a crease in his collar so she wouldn’t have to look at his face.

“I crossed it out because I didn’t want it to be forever. I didn’t know you. I knew you were powerful and frightening, and I wanted you to understand I wasn’t agreeing to anything just because we were married. But I couldn’t write that I’d never want you to touch me. I just didn’t know when I would.” She looked up. “Now I’m telling you.”

He shut his eyes for a second. “Thank you for telling me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, he took his watch off and laid it on her bedside table, and for a moment neither of them moved. They’d shared a house for five weeks. They’d kissed, held hands, slept through a typhoon side by side. They had never crossed this last bit of distance.

“We don’t have to do anything tonight,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t want you to feel that because you asked me to touch you, you have to—“

“I know, Zhendong. I know I can change my mind. I know you’d stop.” She took his hand and put it at her waist, under the hem of her blouse, against her skin. “I’m not asking because I think I should. I’m asking because I want to.”

His fingers curled against her side. He kissed her slowly, as though he had all night and meant to use it.

He undid her buttons one at a time and watched her face after each one, and she let him look. When the blouse slid off her shoulders, he kissed the top of each shoulder, then her collarbone where the thin chain lay, then the place at her throat where her pulse was going far too fast. She pulled his shirt out of his trousers with hands that weren’t quite steady, got it off him, and stopped.

He had more scars than she’d expected. She’d glimpsed some of them in passing. She’d never seen them all at once, in lamplight, on a man who was standing still and letting her.

“You can look,” he said.

“I am looking.”

The first was a pale, puckered line low on his left side, under his ribs. She touched its edge with one finger.

“Block C?”

“Yes.”

She bent and kissed it. His breath went out of him and his hand went into her hair.

A small rough mark at his shoulder. “Glass,” he said, when she asked. “An argument.”

“That explains nothing.”

“It was a long time ago.”

She kissed it anyway. A thin line along his ribs. A white nick on his arm. One low on his back that she could only reach by stepping round him and laying her cheek against his skin. And one more, low on his hip above the waistband, a shiny uneven patch about the size of her palm.

“And this one?”

He went quiet.

She didn’t push. She kissed that one too, and felt him shiver.

“Why are you doing that?” His voice had gone rough.

“Because they’re part of you. And I’m not afraid to touch them.”

He caught her face in both hands and kissed her, and after that he stopped being careful at all.

She ended up on her back across the bed, her hair all over his pillow and his weight braced over her, his mouth everywhere he could reach. She’d thought he would treat her like glass. He didn’t. He touched her as if he’d been thinking about it for weeks, which, she understood with a jolt of heat, he had. He knew exactly where to put his mouth to make her arch, and exactly how long to make her wait, and he watched her face the whole time as if it were the only thing in the world worth reading. When she said his name, he stopped and looked at her. When she pulled him down again, he came.

When he finally came into her, slowly, watching her face, she wrapped her legs round him and held on, and somewhere in it she stopped thinking. There was the lamp, and the damp air through the window, and the rough slide of his palm along her thigh, and his voice saying her name into her throat as if it hurt him. Her nails in his back. His forehead pressed to hers. Her own voice saying yes, and yes, and then nothing that made any sense at all.

Afterwards, he didn’t let go. He lay with his face in her hair and one hand spread on her back, breathing slowly, and she lay on his chest listening to his heart come down.

“Does it still hurt?” she whispered, her fingers on the scar under his ribs.

“Sometimes.”

“Then tell me when it does.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at seven.

The light was the first thing. The second was his arm round her waist. He was asleep, properly asleep, hair a mess, his hand loose on her stomach.

Then she saw the clock. “Oh.”

He stirred. “What?”

“It’s seven. I’ve missed the market.”

He opened one eye. “Yes.”

“I never miss the market.”

“You have today.”

“Granny Yip will wonder where I am.”

“She can wonder.”

She laughed. “You’re a terrible influence.”

For five years she’d gone to the market almost every morning. In rain, in heat, sick, exhausted, on no sleep at all. It was how she started her days. This morning she didn’t want to get up. She wanted to stay in bed with her husband. It was so simple that it made her smile.

At twenty past seven, her phone rang.

“Where are you?” said Granny Yip.

“At home.”

“Are you sick?”

“No.”

“Is something wrong with the shop?”

“No.”

A pause. Granny Yip could hear a man’s voice in the background. “Are you with your husband?”

Elowen said nothing at all.

Granny Yip cackled. “Ah. I won’t disturb you. I’ll keep you some of the good tulips. And Elowen? Don’t come tomorrow just because you feel guilty.”

“I won’t.”

“Good girl.”

Zhao had turned on his side to watch her.

“She knows,” Elowen said.

“Knows what?”

“That I skipped the market.” She leaned on his shoulder. “She said not to come tomorrow out of guilt.”

“Then don’t.”

“You’re very pleased about this.”

“I’m pleased you’re resting.”

“I’m not resting.”

“You’re in bed.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“Then what are you doing?”

She thought about it. “Enjoying my husband.”

Something changed in his face. A smile, with something quieter under it. He put his phone down.

“Can I ask you something? Do you ever regret it?”

She blinked. “Regret what?”

“Marrying me.”

It came out evenly. Too evenly. She sat up.

“Why would I?”

He didn’t answer. She waited.

“You came to me because your father was in danger,” he said at last. “You needed protection, and I had it. You had no other reason to choose me. I’ve wondered whether you’d have married me if Lin Jian had never been threatened.”

So there it was. Not whether she loved him. Not whether she wanted him. Whether he’d ever been wanted at all.

She took his hand. “Do you remember what you asked me when I proposed?”

“Why marriage.”

“And what did I say?”

“That protection that depends on someone’s goodwill can be taken back.”

“That was the practical answer. It wasn’t the only one.” She held his eyes. “When I walked into your office, I’d read the files. I knew what you could do. But I also remembered that you listened. In the shop, even holding my phone, you still answered my questions. At the Docks, you read my papers. You took me seriously. Do you think I’d have married a man who made me feel small?”

“Maybe you thought you had no choice.”

“I had choices. I could have gone to the police. I could have hidden Baba. I could have run. I chose you.”

“And if your father had never been threatened?”

“I don’t know if we’d have met.” She brushed her thumb along his cheek. “But I’d have wanted to know you. I’d have wanted to see what you’re like when you’re not frightening everyone in the room.”

“That’s not very flattering.”

“It’s honest. I’m not going to pretend I married you for no reason. My family needed you, and that was real. It isn’t the only thing that’s real now.” She kissed him and stayed close. “I want you when there’s no danger at all. When Baba’s safe and the shop’s doing well and I need nothing from you. I want you on ordinary mornings. When you make terrible congee. When you sit at the counter pretending you aren’t waiting for me to come home.”

“I don’t pretend.”

“You absolutely do.” She smiled. “And I want you when you wake up with your hair like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you lost a fight with your pillow.”

He laughed, really laughed, and she kissed him again.

“You don’t have to keep earning your place next to me, Zhendong.”

He went very still. Then he pulled her into his arms, not carefully at all, his face in her hair and his hand spread over her back.

“All right,” he said into her hair.

He didn’t say anything else. If a smaller voice in him noticed that she’d said chose and want and never the other word, he kept that to himself, the way he kept most things.

After a while he said, “You should still eat breakfast.”

“There he is.”

“Who?”

“My husband.”

“Eggs? Toast? Tea?”

“Yes. Yes. Yes.”

She caught his hand as he got up and pulled him back for one more kiss. “That’s for breakfast.”

“And the next one?”

“For being my husband.”

For the first time in five years, she had missed the flower market. And for once, she didn’t feel she’d missed anything at all.

chapters.title: The Florist’s Husband Is Not Allowed Behind the Counter
chapters.desc: Her husband starts coming to work and her takings drop by a third. She puts up house rules. He breaks rule two in four days and gets punished in the cooler.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll keep sweeping until it does.”
chapters.content:
By the first Friday in May, Elowen had found out that being married to Zhao Zhendong came with a financial cost.

Her takings were down by a third.

She stood behind the counter with the ledger open, comparing the week with the one before. She checked the calculator. She checked the receipts. The numbers stayed insulting.

Across the shop, her husband sat in the chair by the window doing absolutely nothing. That was the problem.

He’d started coming every day. First just in the mornings, with her tea and a question about whether she’d eaten. Then he stayed for lunch. Then he discovered the chair by the window was comfortable enough to work from, and the visits stretched into whole afternoons. He never got in her way. He never complained about the cold from the storeroom. Sometimes he read things on his phone. Sometimes he talked quietly to Chen Si. Mostly he watched her.

And customers, it turned out, found a well-known arms dealer in a florist’s armchair deeply off-putting. A young man came in for roses for his girlfriend, took one look at him and walked out. A woman with a weekly standing order decided she’d collect next month. Yesterday a delivery driver saw him by the counter and forgot what he’d come in to say.

“Zhendong. Do you know my takings are down by a third?”

“Are they? Why?”

“Because people are scared of you.”

“I haven’t done anything.”

“You’re sitting there.”

He looked at the chair. “Would you like me to sit somewhere else?”

“That isn’t the point. You don’t have to speak to them. You have a face.”

The corner of his mouth lifted. “Is my face a problem?”

“Your face is a problem when it’s attached to a man who has people followed home.”

“I don’t have your customers followed home.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

He laughed quietly.

“Then stop coming every day,” she said.

The smile went. Not dramatically. He just looked at her steadily. “Do you want me to stop?”

What an irritating question. Because the answer was no. She liked seeing him. She liked knowing he was close by, that he brought her tea without asking how she took it, and that he sat quietly while she worked as if there was nowhere else on earth he needed to be. She just didn’t like losing money because her husband looked like he was choosing who to bury.

“I want you to stop frightening people.”

“I can do that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His idea of not frightening people, it turned out, wasn’t always hers.

On Monday a lorry driver parked across her loading bay. He was broad, with a cigarette behind his ear and the air of a man who took every inconvenience personally, and he’d been asked twice to move.

“I’m unloading. Ten minutes.”

“You said that a quarter of an hour ago. My delivery can’t get out.”

He looked her up and down. “You’re making a fuss over nothing. Listen, little girl—“

“She’s asked you twice,” said Zhao from the window.

The man turned. Zhao had put down his phone. His face was calm, almost bored, and the air in the shop changed so fast even Elowen felt it.

“Who are you?”

“Her husband. Move the lorry.”

“I’m doing my job.”

“So is she.” Zhao took one step forward. “Your daughter goes to Westbridge Primary. Year Two. She gets the blue school bus at quarter past three.”

The colour drained out of the man’s face. He went out without another word, and through the window Elowen watched him reverse so fast that a bucket by the door rattled.

Zhao sat down and picked up his phone.

“Zhendong. Come here.”

He came to the counter.

“Don’t do that again.”

“He was rude to you. He wouldn’t move.”

“I know. His daughter had nothing to do with it.”

“Her school was only information.”

“Information you used to frighten him.”

“He was frightened. He moved the lorry.”

“Zhendong.”

He stopped. Shouting had never bothered him; he’d had a lifetime of it. When she said his name like that, without raising her voice, he listened.

“I don’t want children in your threats. Not their schools, not their names, not where they live. If an adult’s rude to me, deal with the adult. You don’t make their children part of it.”

For a few seconds she could see the calculation going on behind his eyes. Not whether she was right. He was fitting in a rule he’d never had to keep before.

“All right. I won’t use children.”

“Even if someone’s very rude?”

“How rude are we expecting?”

“Zhendong.”

“I promise.”

He reached across the counter and stopped just short of her hand. She put her fingers in his.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Tuesday she’d decided her husband needed it in writing. Not because he couldn’t understand a request. Because he understood them perfectly and then interpreted them however suited him.

She took a sheet of cream card from under the till and wrote in big neat letters:

RULES FOR THE FLORIST’S HUSBAND

1. Do not frighten the customers.

2. Do not threaten anyone in the shop.

3. Do not discuss guns, shipping, debts or anything else unpleasant near the flowers.

4. Leave the staff alone unless it is a real emergency.

5. You are not allowed behind the counter.

She pinned it to the wall by the till.

He came in ten minutes later with two cups of tea and read it. Then read it again.

“Why am I not allowed behind the counter?”

“Because you’re not a florist.”

“I can learn.”

“You can learn to stay on the customer side.”

“Rule five is very specific.”

“It became necessary. Yesterday you walked round here without asking, picked up my scissors, and cut a ribbon.”

“It was too long.”

“It was my ribbon.”

He put her tea down. “I’ll respect the rules.”

Then, very calmly, he picked up the broom.

“What are you doing?”

“The floor’s dirty.”

“I have a cleaner.”

“She isn’t here.”

He swept. She watched a man who could silence a room full of armed men with a look push a broom under her display table, carefully round the buckets, moving his chair to get the corner behind it.

Xiao Pan came in with a crate of chrysanthemums, his hands healed to new pink skin, and stopped dead. He looked at Zhao, at the broom, at Elowen, and put the crate down very slowly.

“Boss,” he whispered. “He’s in love with you.”

Elowen nearly dropped her ribbon. “Xiao Pan!”

“What? He is.”

“Go and unpack the chrysanthemums.”

Zhao went on sweeping. He’d clearly heard every word.

“Sweeping isn’t going to bring my customers back,” she told him.

“Then I’ll keep sweeping until it does.”

She pressed her lips together.

“You’re smiling,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“You’re holding a broom.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday an old woman came in for funeral flowers. Small, silver hair in a neat bun, a green cardigan buttoned to the throat. She put a folded piece of paper on the counter as if it were an important document.

“For my own funeral, dear. Don’t look so worried, I’m not dying today. My children have terrible taste.”

“That’s very sensible,” Elowen said gently.

“White. Nothing grand. No lilies, they smell too strong. Not roses, they’re too romantic. And not chrysanthemums. Too ordinary.”

“White lisianthus, perhaps, with a little gypsophila and not too much green—“

“Delphiniums,” said Zhao from the window.

Both women turned.

“White delphiniums. They’re quieter than roses. Tall, but they don’t push.”

The old woman studied him. “You know flowers?”

“No.”

“Then why recommend them?”

He thought about it. “They’re beautiful without asking anyone to look at them.”

The old woman smiled. “I like that. Delphiniums. And put a card in. Say I was very fond of my garden, and I hope nobody throws away the old watering can.”

When she’d gone, Elowen looked at him. “White delphiniums.”

“She wanted something quiet.”

“You remembered them.” She leaned on the counter. “You remembered the blue one.”

His eyes came up to hers.

She’d found it once, the tiny floret from that first wet night, pressed flat behind his identity card. Faded, but whole.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday, four days after the rules went up, he broke rule two.

A supplier had sent the wrong grade of rose twice in a month and then tried to blame Xiao Pan. Elowen was dealing with it herself, invoice in one hand, delivery sheet in the other.

“I paid for premium. These are standard.”

“They’re all roses.”

“That isn’t how grading works.”

“You’re making trouble over flowers. Your husband should teach you how business works.”

At the window, Zhao raised his head.

“Don’t,” said Elowen.

He stood up anyway.

“You’ve been selling her standard at premium prices. I know what you paid for them. I know which warehouse you buy from and the name of the man who signs your invoices. You’ll refund her today and replace the roses. Or I’ll have a word with the people who lend you money.”

The man went the colour of putty. “Today. Yes.”

Elowen put the invoice down.

“Zhendong.” She pointed to the back of the shop. “Cooler.”

His eyebrows went up. “Now?”

“Now.”

He looked at her face and decided she meant it.

The cooler was kept at one degree, cold enough to hold flowers and miserable for anyone without a coat. Buckets of roses lined the walls. The compressor hummed. She shut the door behind them.

“You’re not allowed to threaten people in my shop.”

“He was cheating you.”

“I know. I was handling it.”

“He insulted you.”

“I know. Rule two.”

He looked at her for a moment. “You’re right.”

She’d had a whole argument ready. He’d knocked the wind out of it in two words.

“Don’t agree so fast. I’m still angry.”

“I can see that.”

“Are you sorry?”

“I’m sorry I frightened him in your shop. I’m sorry I interrupted you. And I’m sorry I made you come into the cooler.”

“That last one’s your own fault.”

“Yes.”

The cold was settling on her cheeks. His collar was crooked. Amusement was gathering at the corners of his eyes, and he didn’t reach for her. He just stood among the roses, waiting.

Her anger went soft in spite of her. She grabbed his collar.

“You’re a terrible employee.”

“I’m not your employee.”

“You’re worse. You’re my husband.”

She pulled him down and kissed him.

It wasn’t careful. She had his collar in her fist and his mouth on hers before she could think about it. He made a low sound of surprise, and his hand came up toward her waist and stopped just short. She felt the restraint. She stepped into him herself, and only then did his hand settle on her back and the other come up to her jaw, and he kissed her slowly, with the patience that always made her forget why she’d been angry.

When she pulled back, his forehead rested against hers.

“Is this the punishment?” he asked.

“That was a warning.”

“Then I’ll be careful.”

She was shivering. He took his jacket off and put it round her shoulders.

“Don’t think this means you’re forgiven.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan was waiting outside the storeroom. He looked at Elowen in Zhao’s jacket, then at Zhao’s crooked collar.

“Oh.”

“Don’t,” said Elowen.

Zhao looked at him. “How old are you?”

“Twenty next month.”

“Got a motorbike?”

“My scooter died. I’m saving.”

“There’s a woman near the Docks who builds bikes. She has a waiting list as long as your arm and she doesn’t like anybody. I’ll put your name on it.”

Xiao Pan stared at him. “How long?”

“A year, if she likes you.”

Elowen turned round. “You can’t just give people motorbikes.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s ridiculous.”

Xiao Pan raised a hand. “I’d like to respectfully disagree with the boss.”

She gave him a look. He put his hand down.

“You can’t fix every problem by buying something,” she told her husband.

“Not every problem.”

“Most problems.”

“Only the ones I can fix.”

“Thank you, sir!” said Xiao Pan.

“Don’t call him sir,” said Elowen.

“I’m not his employer,” Zhao agreed.

“Thank you, Mr. Zhao!”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, two new vans were parked outside the shop.

White, clean, much bigger than her old one, with ELOWEN’S lettered down both sides. She stood on the pavement with her keys in her hand. Zhao was leaning on the nearer one.

“What are those?”

“Vans. For the shop. The second one’s a spare.”

“The insurance was going to pay for a second-hand one.”

“Your old van was firebombed. You need something reliable.”

She walked round it. New. Not new-to-her: new, with plastic still on the seats.

“How much?”

He told her.

“Zhendong. That’s far too much.”

He handed her a folder. Registration, insurance, a service contract. She looked up slowly.

“You’ve already bought them. Without asking.”

“I knew you needed them.”

“Then I’ll pay you back. Every month.”

“No. You’re my wife.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is.”

“It isn’t. Being your wife doesn’t mean I don’t pay for my own business. My shop matters to me because I built it. I don’t want to wake up one day and find everything in it belongs to you.”

“It doesn’t. Look at the papers.”

She looked. The vans were registered to the shop. Not to him.

“You planned this.”

“I planned for them to belong to your business.” He held his hand out and waited until she gave him hers. “Pay me back if it makes you feel better. I won’t ask you for a single coin.”

She looked at the vans. Big, cooled, room enough for the installations she’d need for Aurelia’s show in June. She hated how useful they were. She hated even more that he’d thought of all of it.

“Fine. But I’m keeping the invoices. And you’re not allowed to buy a third van.”

“I don’t need a third van.”

“That sounded too easy.”

He opened the passenger door. “Do you want to see inside?”

She tried to stay stern. “Yes.”

She climbed in and looked at the storage and the cooling controls and the seats. “These are very nice.”

“I thought you’d like them.”

“You really think you can buy your way back into my good books.”

“No. I think you’re already fond of me.”

She laughed. Then she caught his hand, pulled him down, and kissed him once.

“Now move. I’m driving. You’re the passenger. Don’t frighten the pedestrians.”

“Yes, Mrs. Zhao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the next Friday, the shop had started to recover. The vans went out every morning. Granny Yip heard about them and announced that Elowen’s husband was either very generous or making up for something. Elowen said probably both.

Zhao still came. He still sat by the window. But he’d learned to take his calls outside, not to look at customers for too long, and to leave Xiao Pan alone. He kept sweeping. The rules stayed on the wall.

On Friday afternoon he came in with two cups of tea and put one by her elbow while she worked on the old woman’s white delphiniums.

“How were today’s takings?”

“Better.”

“How much better?”

“None of your business.”

“Your business is my business.”

She tapped rule five. “You’re on the right side of the counter. Stay there.”

He looked down at his feet. On the customer side. Perfectly.

A young woman came in with a photo of a bouquet on her phone. She glanced once at the man by the window. Zhao looked up, then very deliberately lowered his eyes and went back to reading. The woman relaxed.

When she’d gone, Elowen looked over. “Well done.”

“Do I get a reward?”

His eyes went to her mouth.

“Not in front of the customers.”

“I can wait.”

“I know you can.”

She went back to her stems. Behind her, her husband settled into his chair on the correct side of the counter.

For now.

chapters.title: Thorns at Six in the Morning
chapters.desc: He learns to strip roses and bleeds on two hundred of them. Chen Si comes in for anniversary flowers and finds his brother in her apron.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll do the other three hundred and ninety-something like this.”
chapters.content:
On a Monday in May, at six in the morning, Zhao Zhendong was blowing on his wife’s soy milk.

Elowen stopped halfway through tying a bundle of eucalyptus. He was standing by the stall with his coat over one arm, holding the paper cup in both hands. The steam had barely started to rise when he bent his head and blew across it. Once. Twice. Then he tried a small sip.

Her fingers went still on the twine.

“Why are you doing that?”

“It’s hot. You’ll burn your tongue.”

It was such an ordinary thing. He hadn’t asked if she wanted it cooled. He hadn’t even looked at her while he did it.

Her mother used to do that. At the soy milk stall near their old flat, Mama would hold the cup in both hands and blow across it and try it before she handed it down. Elowen hadn’t thought about that in years. Not like this.

“What’s wrong?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

He held out the cup. She took it in both hands.

“How did you know I like it cooled first?”

“You never drink it straight away. You wait.”

Of course he’d noticed. Zhao noticed everything about everyone, the kind of details that were useful in the wrong hands. Lately he’d been collecting different ones about her. How she took her tea. Which flowers she put in the kitchen. The way she rubbed her thumb along the side of her cup when she was tired.

“You’re using your powers on soy milk now.”

“Is that an improvement?”

“A big one.”

Granny Yip took one look at them going past and shook her head. “Six in the morning and you two are already stuck together.” She pointed her cigarette at the cup. “Did he cool that for you?”

Elowen didn’t answer fast enough.

“Oh, he did.” The old woman went back to her chrysanthemums, smiling to herself. “My husband used to do that. Useless man in most ways. Always remembered my soy milk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble started with four hundred roses.

A hotel wanted two hundred red and two hundred white, lower leaves and thorns stripped, ready to go to their event florist that afternoon. Simple. Tedious. Elowen had expected to finish with Xiao Pan by noon.

She hadn’t expected to find her husband in the middle of the workroom with his sleeves rolled up, looking at a rose like an unfamiliar piece of machinery.

“Why are you holding it like that?”

“How should I hold it?”

He was gripping it far too hard, his fingers right where the thorns were. She sighed and took it from him.

“Like this. Here, not there. Don’t pull against the stem or you’ll tear the skin.” She ran the stripper down in one clean stroke, turned the stem, and took the thorns off. “Try.”

He was careful. More careful than she’d expected. His hands were steady and he did exactly what she’d shown him. Unfortunately, he also had a natural habit of using force on anything that resisted.

The first rose survived. The second lost a leaf. The third left a thin red line across his finger.

She caught his wrist. “You’re bleeding.”

“It’s nothing.”

“It’s bleeding on my roses.” She looked at him pointedly. “Two hundred of them.”

“I’ll be more careful.”

“You’re not touching another rose until that’s clean.”

Xiao Pan looked up from the other table. “Shall I get the first-aid box?”

“Yes,” said Elowen.

“No,” said Zhao.

“Yes,” said Elowen, and Xiao Pan went.

At the sink she washed the tiny cut and wrapped a plaster round it. “Does it hurt?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

“A little.”

“See? You can answer properly.”

By half past eight he’d cut himself three more times. The fourth was his own fault: he got impatient with the stripper and tried to flick a thorn off with his thumb.

She looked at the fresh line of blood across his palm. Then at the three plasters already on his fingers.

“Are you starting a collection?”

“Perhaps I’m not suited to this.”

“You’re not.” She smiled sweetly. “You’re very good at other things. Making people nervous. Buying vans nobody asked for. Sitting in chairs.”

Then she relented. “Come on. I’ll show you again.”

She stood behind him, close enough that her front brushed his back, reached round, and put her hands over his.

“Hold it here. Not so tight. Turn it slowly. Now.”

He made the cut. The thorn fell.

“See? You can do it.”

He looked down at their hands. Her arms were round him and her cheek was almost on his shoulder. For a moment he didn’t move at all.

“Like this?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll do the other three hundred and ninety-something like this.”

She laughed. “I can’t stand behind you for four hundred roses. I’ve got work.”

“I’ll go slowly.”

He turned his head a little. “You’re very close.”

“You’re the one who can’t strip a rose. Pay attention.”

He did. But when he looked down again, he was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d been thinking about it all morning, every time she put another plaster on him. The scars she’d kissed one by one in lamplight, and the one he wouldn’t answer for.

At the sink after the fourth cut, she said, “There’s one you didn’t tell me about.”

He knew which one. His hands stopped under the tap.

“On your hip.”

He turned the water off and dried his hands for a long time.

“Old Zhao,” he said. “I was nine. I spilled something on his kitchen floor. He decided I needed to learn not to be careless.” He folded the towel. “He held me against the stove.”

Her stomach turned over. He saw it.

“It’s old.”

“That doesn’t make it all right.”

“No.”

He didn’t explain it away. He didn’t say Old Zhao had been drunk, or that he’d been a difficult boy, or that it had taught him something. He just stood there and let her know.

“Did anyone help you?”

“Not that time.”

She looked at him: a grown man, taller than nearly everyone, with money and power and a house full of locks. For a moment she could see a small boy in front of a stove, learning that pain was something you dealt with on your own.

She took his hand and kissed the inside of his wrist, just below the plasters.

“I don’t think about it often,” he said.

“Do you think about it when I touch it?”

He was quiet for a moment. “I’ll think about this instead.”

She kept hold of his hand a moment longer than she needed to. There was a pale little row of plasters across his fingers, and under them the old marks from things she would probably never hear about, and under all of that a boy of nine who had stood in a kitchen by himself. She couldn’t do anything about the boy. She could put plasters on the man, and make him sit down to dinner, and blow on his tea if it came to that.

From the other table, Xiao Pan cleared his throat loudly. “Boss? Are we still doing the roses? Because there’s about three hundred left.”

Elowen laughed into Zhao’s shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came in just before noon with his car keys in one hand and his phone in the other, wearing the distracted face of a man running three things at once.

“Elowen. I need anniversary flowers. For Saturday.”

“For Aurelia?”

“Unless you think I should give them to someone else.”

“What does she like?”

“Something beautiful. Something expensive. Something that makes her think I tried.”

“That last one’s the first useful thing you’ve said.”

He looked round the shop. Then he stopped.

Zhao was standing at the worktable in Elowen’s pale green apron. It was tied round his waist. There were leaves stuck to the front and a stain by the pocket. His sleeves were rolled up, there were five plasters on his fingers, and he had a white rose in his hand.

Chen Si stared. Zhao looked up. Their eyes met.

Chen Si slowly lowered his phone. “What are you wearing?”

“An apron.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why did you ask?”

Chen Si looked at Elowen. “Is this real?”

“He’s helping.”

Chen Si started to laugh. Not his usual dry little breath of a laugh. He laughed so hard he had to put his phone down on the counter.

“Choose your flowers,” said Zhao.

“You’re wearing her apron.”

“I know.”

“You’re bleeding.”

“I know.”

“Can I take a picture?”

“No,” said Zhao.

“Yes,” said Elowen, at the same time.

Chen Si already had.

His phone rang while Elowen was tying the bouquet, and he put it on speaker.

“Have you ordered my flowers?” Aurelia asked.

“I’m ordering them now. Darling, I have something to show you. Your brother-in-law is wearing an apron.”

Silence. Then: “Send me the picture.”

“No,” said Zhao.

“Already sent,” said Chen Si.

A moment later Elowen’s phone buzzed.

Aurelia: I need the apron photo from YOUR side. Immediately. I have never asked you for anything more important in my life.

Aurelia: Does it have the little pocket in front? Tell me it has the little pocket.

Elowen looked at her husband. He was staring at her phone.

“No.”

“Just one.”

“No.”

“Zhendong.”

He sighed. “One.”

It was a good picture. Him beside the worktable with a white rose, the apron tied neatly, his face completely serious, a plaster on nearly every finger and flowers all round him. She sent it.

Aurelia: I’m having this framed.

Aurelia: Chen Si has been married to me for one whole year and has never once worn an apron.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before Chen Si left, his phone rang again. He looked at the screen and his face changed, and he stepped outside to take it. When he came back he didn’t sit down.

“Zhendong. Qiu Wen’s been asking about the shop.”

Elowen’s hands stopped on the ribbon.

“Not directly. Around the freight yards. About the new vans: their plates, where they’re kept at night, who drives them. The shop’s hours. Whether you still come here every morning.”

Zhao’s face went completely still. “When?”

“Last week. Maybe before. Two transport brokers, and a man who used to work in one of the Qiu warehouses. I don’t know yet whether he’s collecting or planning.”

“Why would he want to know about my shop?” Elowen asked.

Neither of them answered straight away.

“Because he knows it matters to you,” Chen Si said.

She looked out of the window. An ordinary street. A woman with shopping bags. A cyclist at the corner. Somebody arguing with a taxi driver. It was hard to remember that an ordinary street could turn dangerous just because someone had decided it should.

“Should we stop using the vans?”

“No,” said Zhao.

“Change the routes?”

“Yes.”

“Then Xiao Pan needs to know.”

“I’ll arrange it.”

“Don’t make decisions about my shop without telling me.”

He held her eyes. “I won’t.”

Chen Si picked up the bouquet. “I’ll have someone look over the vans and find out who’s been talking.” At the door he turned. “Aurelia wants another picture. You holding a bouquet.”

“Tell her no.”

“She says she wants to see the pocket properly.”

“Chen Si.”

“Love you too, brother.”

He was gone before Zhao could answer. Zhao looked at the door, then at Elowen, who was trying very hard not to laugh, and he laughed himself.

Loud enough that Xiao Pan turned round. Not the quiet breath she was used to, not the brief smile that vanished as soon as it came. A real laugh, his head going back with it.

“You laughed,” she said.

“Did I?”

“You should do it more often.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm. “I’ll try.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes before opening, the roses were packed and gone, and Xiao Pan was outside with the buckets.

“You’re still wearing my apron,” Elowen said.

“Am I?”

“You can’t wear it home.”

“Then I’ll have to come back tomorrow.”

“You were coming back tomorrow anyway.”

He sat down on the low stool by the counter and pulled her onto his knee.

“Zhendong! We’re at work.”

“The shop isn’t open.”

“Xiao Pan could walk in.”

“He’ll knock.”

“You’ve got six plasters on.”

“Seven.” He held up his hand. She stared at the newest one.

“How?”

“A thorn.”

“Of course.”

His arm settled round her waist. He looked at her with the quiet attention that still made the rest of the room disappear.

“You’re tired,” he said.

“A little.”

“Sit down.”

“I’m sitting.”

“Good.”

His eyes went to her mouth. She leaned in before he could ask, and he met her halfway, slow and familiar, his hand firm at her waist and hers on his cheek and his shoulder, careful of his plasters. When she pulled back, he followed just far enough to kiss the corner of her mouth, and she stayed a little longer.

Outside, the first customers were gathering by the door.

“We have to open,” she said, her forehead on his.

“I know.”

He untied the apron and folded it over the stool. She held it up: green stains, leaves in the pocket, a small tear at the hem.

“You’ve ruined my apron.”

“I’ll buy you a new one.”

“No.” She folded it neatly. “This one has character now.”

The bell rang. Their first customer came in. Zhao went to his chair by the window with his plasters bright on his fingers, and Elowen went behind the counter. For a second, before she said good morning, she just looked at him: the man who could empty a room by walking into it, sitting in a flower shop with his sleeves rolled up, waiting for his wife to finish work.

chapters.title: The Rare Flower He Should Not Have Bought
chapters.desc: She reads him a paragraph about the rarest camellia in the world. Three weeks later the hill it grows on is in her name.
chapters.content:
The first time Elowen told Zhao about Middlemist’s Red, he was half asleep.

It was a Sunday evening at the end of August, warm and lazy, with the windows open and the curtains moving in the breeze. The lemon tree had put out new leaves all summer. Somewhere downstairs, Dumpling and Noodle were arguing over a rope.

She was lying across their bed with a gardening magazine open on her stomach. He was beside her with a report on his tablet. He’d learned not to interrupt her when she read. She liked to share things she found beautiful, but she liked to finish them first.

“Zhendong. Listen to this.”

He put the tablet down.

She cleared her throat with great seriousness. “’Among the rarest flowering plants in the world is Middlemist’s Red, a camellia taken from a hill garden in the East to England in 1804. Only two plants are known to survive: one in a conservatory at Chiswick, in London, and one in a garden at Waitangi, in New Zealand.’” She looked up. “Isn’t that strange? That something so beautiful can get that rare.”

He looked at the photograph. A deep rose-pink flower, its petals laid in neat overlapping rows, as if someone had folded it by hand. Not very red at all, despite the name.

She ran her fingertip round the edge of the picture. “Mama had this picture. Torn out of a gardening book and taped up by the kitchen. She said if she ever had a garden big enough, she’d want one.”

“Did she know where to find one?”

“I don’t think anybody does.” She smiled a little. “She used to say it was a shame people could lose something beautiful just because they didn’t know how to look after it.”

She read on. “’Where it first grew has never been traced, though a third plant has long been rumoured in the old tea hills of the south.’” She turned the page, then turned back. “I wonder what happened to the place it came from. I’d like to see it. A hill where they just grow, because that’s where they belong.”

“Would you want to bring one home?”

She thought about it. “No. I’d rather see it where it belongs. If it’s that rare, I’d be terrified of hurting it.”

She shut the magazine. He picked it up, looked at the picture again, and put it on his bedside table.

“Go to sleep,” he said.

“You’re the one who was nodding off.”

“I’m awake now.”

“Because of a flower?”

“Because my wife is talking.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek. “Good answer.”

By midnight she was asleep. He wasn’t.

He read the paragraph three times. The first time because he was curious. The second because he wanted to know which hills. The third time he reached for his phone.

At half past one in the morning, his lawyer answered on the fourth ring.

“Mr. Zhao?”

“There’s a tea estate in the southern hills. Wen. It has an old camellia grove on it.”

A pause. “Yes?”

“Title, boundaries, the owner, any restrictions on the grove. I want to know if it can be bought.”

“Is this for the company?”

“No. Nobody touches the staff. Nobody clears, builds or digs anything. And find a botanist to look at the plant. An independent one. Someone who doesn’t sell cuttings.”

“Yes, Mr. Zhao.”

Beside him, Elowen moved in her sleep and curled closer. He switched his phone off. He had no intention of waking her up to talk about buying land.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two other people wanted the Wen estate.

The first was a golf developer called Tse, who had spent two years trying to put a course and a clubhouse across the southern hills, with the estate sitting right in the middle of his drawings. Bao went to see him with two boxes of mooncakes from the old bakery in the eastern district, because Mid-Autumn was coming and Mr. Tse’s wife made him eat the traditional lotus-paste ones every year, and Bao knew that because Bao knew everything.

They sat in a private room over the harbour. Bao poured the tea.

“These are from the eastern district,” said Mr. Tse.

“Your wife likes them.”

Mr. Tse looked at him for a long moment. “You have a good memory.”

Bao opened a folder. “The Wen family will only sell if the estate isn’t split and the tea carries on. The hill floods every September. The road washes out. Golf greens drown.” He turned a page. “And Mr. Zhao is interested in the hill.”

He said nothing else. He didn’t need to. Mr. Tse looked at the mooncakes for a long time. He thought about his wife, and the flooded greens, and the name Zhao, which nobody in his line of work said out loud if they could help it. Then he took one, and remarked that he’d always thought the north side of the valley drained better.

The second was a villa developer called Kam, and Bao didn’t go to see him. Zhao did.

Mr. Kam’s office was down at the marina. Behind his desk hung a big framed photograph of his new yacht, white against blue water, Mr. Kam grinning on the deck. Zhao sat down without taking his coat off and looked at it.

“Nice boat.”

“Thank you. Imported.”

“I know.”

“I hear you want the Wen land kept as it is,” said Kam. “That’s an expensive preference.”

“I can afford it.”

“Then you can afford to beat my offer.”

Zhao got up, went round the desk, and took the photograph off its hook. He looked at it closely. The boat’s name was clear on the bow. So was the registration. So were the two children on deck behind their father.

He laid it face down on the desk, very gently.

Kam reached for the phone on his desk. Zhao caught his wrist before his fingers got there, turned it over, and bent it back against the edge of the desk until something in it gave with a small wet sound. Kam screamed into his own shoulder. Zhao held it there a moment longer, then let go.

“Don’t bid on the Wen estate again.”

Kam had gone grey. He was holding his wrist against his chest. “Is that a threat?”

“It’s a photograph.” Zhao went to the door. “You should keep it somewhere less public.”

He hadn’t said one word about the children. He’d promised her he wouldn’t, and he hadn’t. A wrist wasn’t a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Not quite three weeks after the magazine, on a Wednesday, the deed came by courier to the house on the hill.

Elowen was in the courtyard trimming the lemon tree when Bao brought out a thick envelope with her full name printed on the front. Lin Elowen. Not Zhao.

“Who’s it from?”

“The lawyers handling the Wen estate.”

“The what?”

Bao hesitated. “Perhaps Mr. Zhao should explain.”

She opened it. The Wen tea estate. The land, the hill, the house, the tea and the camellia grove. All of it, in her name.

She stood very still.

“Where’s my husband?”

“At the Docks.”

“Thank you.” She was already walking. “Tell the driver I’m taking the van.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked through the Northgate building with the deed under her arm. The receptionist stood up. “Mrs. Zhao—“

She didn’t stop. She knew the way.

The meeting room door was open. Zhao sat at the head of a table of men with papers. He looked up, and his face showed something that wasn’t alarm. Recognition.

“Give us the room.”

They went. Some of them went quite quickly.

She put the deed on the table. “What is this?”

“The Wen estate.”

“I can read. You bought a hill.”

“Yes.”

“A whole tea estate. In my name.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“You wanted to see the camellia.”

For a moment she couldn’t speak. It was so absurd. So completely, impossibly him. She’d read him one paragraph from a magazine and said she’d like to see where a flower grew, and he’d bought the hill.

“You can’t buy me things like this.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s an estate! Do you know what it costs? How many people work there? What it means for them, suddenly being on my land?”

“Yes.”

“Then why?”

“Because you wanted to see it.”

She let out a breath that would have been a laugh if anything had been funny. “That isn’t enough.”

“For me it was.”

He came round the table and stopped a step away. “I didn’t buy it so you’d owe me.”

“But you did buy it. And you didn’t tell me.”

“I wanted to give it to you.”

“That doesn’t make it better.”

“I know.”

She looked up sharply. “You know?”

“Yes.”

He didn’t defend himself, which made it much harder to stay angry. “I thought you’d be happy,” he said.

“I am happy. I’m also overwhelmed, and angry, and worried about everyone who lives on that hill.”

“The staff keep their jobs. The tea goes on. Nobody builds anything. A botanist is going up next month, and the grove stays protected for as long as you own it.”

“You arranged all that.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me.”

“Yes.”

“Did you buy it because I wanted the flower? Or because you wanted to give me something nobody else could?”

He was quiet. “Both. You told me your mother wanted to see it. I thought you might want to stand somewhere she only dreamed about.”

She put the deed down carefully. “I don’t want you to stop giving me things. I like the flowers. I like the tea. I even like the ridiculous earrings. But I don’t need something enormous every time I say I’d like to see something beautiful. And if you ever want to do something this big again, you ask me first.”

“I’ll ask.”

“Promise?”

“I promise.”

She took a step toward him. Then another. She put both hands on his face.

“I was angry all the way here. I had a whole speech.”

“What happened to it?”

She kissed him. His hands came to her waist only after she leaned in. He kissed her slowly, his thumb moving on her cheek, and when she pulled back she stayed close enough that their foreheads touched.

“You can’t buy me a hill.”

“I’ve already bought it.”

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed the rest of the afternoon on the sofa by the window with the estate papers.

They were thicker than the deed. A list of the workers, nineteen names with their years on the hill beside them; the oldest had been picking tea for fifty-one years. A map of the slopes, hand-drawn and photocopied, with the grove marked in red pencil. And a short typed note from the lawyer that she read twice: Mr. Wen had turned down three offers in two years, including one for twice the price, and had only agreed to sell after Mr. Zhao drove up to see him in person.

She looked up. “You went up there.”

He didn’t stop reading. “Last week.”

“On your own?”

“Bao drove.”

“What did you say to him?”

“Ask him when you meet him.”

She looked back down at the map, at the little red circle in the middle of all that tea, and didn’t say anything for a while. Then she went on reading, while he and his men went through next month’s shipments. At one point a lawyer brought something in to sign. Zhao signed it without stopping the conversation, then held his hand out across the desk without looking up.

“Your hand.”

She gave it to him. He turned it over and kissed her knuckles, and the whole room went silent. The lawyer looked very hard at his papers. Zhao let go and went back to the document in front of him.

“Go on.”

Nobody mentioned it.

At six he walked her to the van.

“Have you decided?”

“Not yet.”

“If you don’t want it, I’ll keep it.”

“For yourself?”

“For the camellia.”

She smiled despite herself. “Have you arranged for us to go and see it?”

“The tickets are booked.”

“Zhendong.”

He seemed to hear himself. “Shall I cancel them?”

“…No. When?”

“Friday next week. If you’re free.”

“You’ve already arranged everything, haven’t you.”

“Only the travel. And a room. And a driver.” He thought about it. “There’s a garden.”

She laughed. “Of course there’s a garden.” She straightened his collar. “When we get there, I want to walk up the hill. Not drive. And I want to see the camellia before anyone tells me anything about it.”

“I’ll let you look first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she took the magazine off his bedside table. It still fell open at the page.

“I wonder what Mama would say if she knew you’d bought an estate because I mentioned this,” she said.

“She might think I’m excessive.”

“She’d think you were completely ridiculous.” She leaned on his shoulder. “She’d have liked the flower, though.”

He took her hand. “Are you happy? About going?”

“Yes.”

She’d brought the photocopied map home. She unfolded it on the blanket between them and followed the path with her finger: up from the gate, past the house, along the slope to the little red circle.

“This is where it is.”

“Yes.”

“And this?” A blue line wriggling across the bottom of the hill.

“The stream. It floods in September. The road goes under for a day or two.” He watched her finger. “Mr. Wen says it always comes back.”

“You’ve learned a lot about one hill.”

“I wanted to know what I was giving you.”

She folded the map along its old creases and put it on her side of the bed, where she’d see it in the morning.

After a while she said, “Next time I read you something out of a gardening magazine, you’re not allowed to buy it.”

“Unless it’s a very good article.”

She laughed and pushed at his chest. He caught her hand, kissed her fingers, and reached for the lamp.

She was asleep before he’d put the lamp out, one hand on the folded map.

Somewhere in the southern hills, an old camellia was waiting. For once, he’d bought her something he couldn’t put in a vase and bring home. He’d bought her somewhere to go.

chapters.title: The Estate in the Rain
chapters.desc: An old tea estate, a man who won’t sell his flower, a shooting lesson on a wet terrace, and two days of rain with the road washed out.
chapters.content:
The rain started before they reached the estate.

At first it was only a fine silver mist on the car windows, and Elowen could still see the hills. Then the road began to climb between dark rows of tea and old trees, and the rain thickened until everything outside was a wash of green and grey.

She leaned closer to the glass. “Is that it?”

A low stone wall half buried in creepers, and an old wooden sign hanging from two iron chains. The letters had nearly worn away. She could just make out WEN.

“Yes.”

She smiled. Not her polite smile. He’d watched her long enough to know the difference.

“You’re pleased,” he said.

“I’ve been looking at pictures of this place for ten days.”

“You’ve looked at the same picture eleven times.”

She turned. “You counted?”

“No.”

“Then how do you know?”

“I remember.”

She turned back to the window so he wouldn’t see her face.

The driver stopped at the gate, because she’d said she wanted to walk up the hill, and he had promised. He held the umbrella over her all the way up the drive while the rain drummed on it. At the top stood the house: a dark tiled roof, a long veranda, wooden shutters weathered silver by years of wind. Tea ran down the slopes behind it in rows that followed the curve of the land. A narrow stone path led off toward a stand of taller trees.

It didn’t look like somewhere that had been bought. It looked like somewhere that had been kept.

An old man was waiting on the veranda under a black umbrella. Thin, straight-backed, his face lined by weather, his grey hair combed flat.

“Mr. Zhao. You walked up in this.”

“She wanted to.”

Mr. Wen grunted, and looked at Elowen.

“Hello, Mr. Wen. I’m Elowen.”

“Mrs. Zhao. And the new owner.” He studied her a moment longer. “Come in. It’s getting worse.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house smelled of old wood and dried tea and a fire that had been going all afternoon. Nothing in it was there to impress anybody. A row of photographs hung in the corridor; one showed the estate decades ago, when the tea was young and the hills nearly bare.

“Did your family start it?” Elowen asked.

“My grandfather kept it. Then my father. Now me.” He sounded almost offended. “You city people think an old place is only worth something once someone puts a hotel on it.”

“That’s why I bought it,” said Zhao, hanging his coat by the door.

“You bought it for the camellia.”

“I bought it to keep the land.”

“Same thing, according to you.”

“Not according to the deed.”

Mr. Wen gave a short laugh.

“Have you known each other long?” Elowen asked.

“Long enough to know he’s difficult.”

“That’s mutual,” said Zhao.

A brazier glowed in the corner of the sitting room with a kettle on it, sending up a thin thread of steam. Rain drummed on the roof.

“Your room’s ready,” Mr. Wen said. “Don’t plan on leaving tomorrow. The road down the east side’s going under already. If this keeps up, the low crossing will be gone by morning. Two days. Three, if the rain feels like being difficult.”

Elowen looked at Zhao. He looked entirely untroubled.

“Is there food?”

“Enough.”

“Then we’ll stay.”

“Good. You can help me carry tea tomorrow.”

“I didn’t come here to work.”

“Then you should have bought a hotel.”

Elowen laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Wen took them to the camellia the next morning.

The rain had eased overnight, but the sky was heavy and the ground was black with water. He led them along a narrow path behind the house with his big umbrella. Zhao held another over Elowen, his free hand at her back whenever the stones got uneven.

The grove was quieter than the rest of the hill. Tall old trees knotted together overhead. The earth smelled rich and wet. Somewhere, water dripped steadily off a leaf into a stone basin.

Mr. Wen stopped. “There.”

At first she didn’t understand what she was looking at.

A camellia stood between two older trees, its long branches held up with careful wooden props. It was taller than Zhao. Its leaves were thick and glossy and nearly black in the wet light. There were no flowers. Of course there weren’t: it was September. Instead, all along the branches, there were buds. Small, hard, green, shut tight. Hundreds of them, each one holding a flower that wouldn’t open until the end of winter.

Elowen took one step toward it. Then another. She stopped a few feet away.

In the last ten days she’d imagined this a dozen ways. Taking photographs. Asking Mr. Wen everything. Sitting with a notebook, writing down all she could learn. She hadn’t imagined crying.

The tears came quietly, without any warning at all.

Zhao moved the umbrella so that not one drop could reach her. “Is it all right?”

She nodded. She couldn’t answer. He didn’t ask her to explain. He stood beside her and held the umbrella over them both while she looked.

After a while, Mr. Wen spoke.

“When your husband first came up here, he told me you’d read about this plant. That your mother wanted to see one and never did. He said you wouldn’t want to take it home. You’d want to see where it grew.” His face softened. “He said if I had to choose between selling the camellia and selling the land, I should sell the land to someone who’d leave the flower alone.”

Elowen turned slowly. Zhao was looking at the tree, not at her.

“That’s what you told him?”

“Something like that.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“You didn’t ask.” He was quiet for a moment. “I knew you wouldn’t want it cut. So I made sure nobody would.”

She looked back at the tree. She thought of the page torn out of a book and taped up by her mother’s kitchen, and of the way Mama had talked about this flower, as if it were someone she was hoping to meet one day. She hadn’t known then that one day would never come.

She cried harder. He put his arm round her and drew her into his side and kept the umbrella over her head, and didn’t try to make her stop. Mr. Wen became very interested in a branch.

“When does it flower?” she asked at last, wiping her face.

“February. March, in a cold year.” Mr. Wen looked at the buds. “Come back then.”

“I will.”

“The botanist comes next month. He can look at the soil and the light. I won’t let anyone take a cutting to satisfy somebody’s curiosity.”

“Good,” said Elowen.

He looked at her. “You don’t want it tested? Some people would pay a great deal to prove what it is. Some would say it’s necessary.”

“Then they can test the soil. It doesn’t need to be cut open so somebody else can feel sure.”

Mr. Wen watched her for a long moment. Then he nodded, once, at Zhao.

“You chose well.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon the rain came back hard. Mr. Wen went down to see to the tea workers. Elowen was at the window with a cup of tea when Zhao held out his hand.

“Come with me.”

The terrace was wide and paved with dark stone, half sheltered by a deep wooden overhang. Beyond it, the hill dropped away into the tea. A wooden target stood at the far end, and beside it on a crate, a small tin can.

Elowen looked at the target, then at the case in his other hand.

“No.”

“You haven’t heard what I’m asking.”

“I can see the gun.”

“You live in a house with a safe room. You know the exits. You know the panel.” He opened the case on a dry table under the overhang. A small black pistol in grey foam. “If anyone ever puts one of these in your hand, I don’t want it to be the first time.”

“I don’t want to shoot anyone.”

“I know.”

She looked at it for a long time. She’d seen enough of his world to know what these were for. She also knew that refusing to learn wouldn’t make the world any safer.

“Will you be patient?”

“I’ll try. I’m told I’m a bad teacher.”

“By Chen Si?”

“Mostly.”

“If I don’t like it, we stop.”

“Of course.”

He went through the rules first, slowly. Where it points. Where your finger lives until you mean it. How to check it’s safe. He didn’t laugh when she flinched at his first shot. When he gave it to her, his face went serious.

“When you’re ready.”

It was heavier than she’d expected. He stood beside her, close but not crowding, and set her hands and her feet, and asked before he touched her wrists.

“Don’t fight the weight.”

“It’s heavier than it looks.”

“Most things are.”

“Are you talking about the gun?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t believe you.”

The first shot went wide. The second hit the frame. The third hit nothing at all. By the tenth she was frowning, and by the twentieth her arms ached. He corrected her when she asked and kept quiet when she didn’t.

“I think I’m getting worse.”

“You’re getting tired.”

“That’s a polite way of saying I’m terrible.”

“Forty-one,” he said.

“Why are you counting?”

“Because you are.”

She breathed in, raised her arms, and for once didn’t look at him. The rain went quiet round her. The tin stood small and silver at the end of the wet stone.

She fired. The tin jumped, flipped backward off the crate, and rolled away across the terrace.

She stared at it. Then she lowered the gun.

“I hit it.”

“Yes.”

“I actually hit it!”

“I saw.”

She turned to him with her face bright with disbelief, and he took the pistol out of her hands, set it down, and took her face in both of his.

He didn’t ask. He kissed her right there on the wet terrace with the rain blowing in under the overhang and the smell of gunpowder in the air, his hands warm on her cold cheeks. She grabbed his shirt and leaned into him and smiled against his mouth.

“Was that my reward?” she said, when he let her breathe.

“I hadn’t decided.”

“Decide faster next time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening the road was gone. The low crossing had flooded and part of the hill path had slid away. One of the workers came up with mud to his knees and announced that nobody was driving anywhere for at least two days.

“So we’re stuck,” said Elowen.

“Rained in,” said Mr. Wen. “Sounds nicer.”

Dinner was steamed fish, greens, rice, and a soup Mr. Wen swore was better than anything a hotel could make. Afterwards he went to check the back shutters and left them by the brazier. The lights flickered and came back.

Elowen sat on the rug by the fire with her legs folded under her, leaning against Zhao’s knee where he sat on the low sofa behind her.

“Are you disappointed? Being stuck?”

“No. I came here with you.”

She turned her cup in her hands. “Mama used to say some things are precious because they’re rare, but that isn’t why you should love them. A flower isn’t more precious because there are only two. It’s precious because it’s alive, and it grew where it could, and someone cared enough to let it keep growing.” She looked at the fire. “After she died, I kept thinking about everything she never got to do. Everywhere she never went. As if I could do all of it for her and then she wouldn’t have missed so much.”

His hand settled in her hair. “You don’t have to finish everything for her.”

“I think I’m learning that.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she said, as though it surprised her, “I’m happy.”

He looked down.

“Not just because of the flower, or being here. I’m happy. For the first time since Mama died, I can say it without feeling guilty.” She smiled up at him. “I still miss her. I always will. But being happy doesn’t mean I’ve left her behind.”

He bent and kissed her forehead. “You haven’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, Mr. Wen found Zhao alone on the veranda, smoking one of the old man’s terrible cigarettes and watching the rain.

“She’s asleep?”

“Reading.”

Mr. Wen leaned on the rail beside him. “She cried at a tree with no flowers on it. I’ve had professors up here who didn’t do that.”

“I know.”

“You don’t look like a man whose wife just cried over his present.”

Zhao looked out at the dark tea. “She married me for her father. He was in trouble, and I was the biggest gun in reach. That’s all it was.”

Mr. Wen stared at him for a long moment. Then he took the cigarette out of Zhao’s fingers and threw it into the rain.

“You’re an idiot,” he said, and went to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Zhao came upstairs, she was standing at the window in her nightdress, watching the rain run down the glass.

“Come here,” she said.

He came. She reached for his shirt, straightened a fold that didn’t need straightening, and left her fingers there.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Will you kiss me?”

“Yes.”

He bent toward her, and she put one finger on his chest.

“Not yet. I’m asking properly. I want you to kiss me, and I want you to stay with me tonight. Not because we’re stuck in an old house with a fire and nothing else to do. Because I want you.”

“That’s very specific.”

“I thought you’d like it clear.”

“I do.”

He kissed her, slowly, and when she went up on her toes for more, he drew back just far enough that she had to follow.

“Impatient,” he said.

“You’re the one making me wait.”

“I haven’t done anything yet.”

“Exactly.”

“Then let me take my time.”

He did. He took the pins out of her hair one by one and laid them on the windowsill, and pushed his fingers through it until it fell loose down her back. He kissed her temple and her closed eyelids and the corner of her jaw, and every time she reached for his mouth he moved somewhere else, until she was laughing and cross and breathless all at once. He slid one strap of her nightdress off her shoulder and kissed the skin where it had been. Then the other. He knelt in front of her on the old floorboards and kissed the inside of her wrist, the inside of her elbow, the soft skin above her knee, and looked up at her the whole time, until she had to put a hand on the window frame because her legs had stopped being reliable.

“Zhendong.”

“Yes?”

“You said you’d take your time. You didn’t say you’d take all of it.”

He laughed against her skin. Then he stood and lifted her, and the old bed creaked when he laid her on it, and the rain poured over the roof. He took the nightdress the rest of the way off her and put his mouth between her thighs and made her wait there too, until she was saying his name like a complaint, and then like a plea, and then he came up over her and into her in one slow movement and stopped making her wait at all. She held on to his shoulders and lifted her hips to meet him. The rain and the creak of the bed went on and on, and after a while she stopped hearing either.

Afterwards she lay across his chest in the dark, his heart slowing under her ear.

“Stay with me,” she murmured. “Husband.”

“Always, if you want me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke after midnight. The room was dark and the rain hadn’t stopped. She slept against him with one hand on his chest.

She’d said she was happy, for the first time since her mother died. He could still hear exactly how she’d said it: the little pause before it, and the way she’d looked at him as if she were finding out it was true while she said it.

He was glad. More than glad. Being the reason she could feel that was something he had no proper words for.

But there was another word. One he’d never asked her for.

He knew she’d chosen him. She’d chosen him when she could have walked away, and again after the debt was closed and the danger had gone quiet. She’d chosen his bed and his house and his ordinary mornings. He knew all of it. And still part of him was afraid that she’d found happiness next to him without ever falling in love with him.

He could buy her an estate. He could keep the camellia safe, mend the road and pay every worker on the hill. He could put everything he had between her and anything that might hurt her. He couldn’t buy the word he wanted, and he wouldn’t ask for it.

She moved in her sleep, closer, until her cheek was on his shoulder and her fingers curled into his shirt.

He kissed her hair and closed his eyes. She’d said happy. He would have to learn to let that be enough. For tonight, at least, he held her under the sound of the rain, and didn’t ask her for anything more.

chapters.title: Her Father Comes to Dinner
chapters.desc: Her father comes to dinner at last. Zhao cooks her mother’s fish for him, and Lin Jian tells him he was only ever the price.
chapters.epigraph: “You can say what you like about me. Not about her. Not at my table.”
chapters.content:
The glass room wasn’t there when Elowen went to bed.

It was there when she pulled the curtains back on Saturday morning: a long box of light stuck to the east side of the house, where yesterday there had been a wall, a drainpipe and a pile of builders’ sheeting she’d been told was for the gutters.

She went down in her nightdress and through the new glass passage from the kitchen. Inside there were slatted shelves at three heights, a long worktable of pale wood, a stone sink and planting beds along the low wall, gravel already raked into the bottoms. Beyond the glass stood her mother’s lemon tree in its glazed pot, with five lemons on it this year.

A card leaned against a seed tray.

For the cuttings you keep leaving on the kitchen counter.

No name. Nobody else in the house wrote like a man filling in a customs form.

“You’re up.”

Zhao was in the doorway with two mugs of tea, already dressed, navy trousers and a pale shirt open at the collar, silver watch on. One strand of black hair had come down over his forehead the way it always did before he’d been near a mirror.

“When did you build this?”

“While you were at the shop.”

“How long?”

“Three weeks. Bao told them to park on the lower road.”

The middle shelf was higher than the others because her cymbidiums didn’t fit anywhere. The drawer under it was full of twine and labels and the good secateurs she’d been meaning to buy for two years. Every single thing in the room was something she’d complained about out loud, in passing, with her mouth full, with no idea he’d been keeping a list.

She went to the sink and ran the tap. It was set a little high. Not by much. She’d have to lift a full bucket to her chest to get it under the spout. He’d stood here with the builder and held his own hands out, of course.

She turned it off and didn’t say so.

“Do you like it?”

She crossed the gravel, put her hands flat on his shirt and kissed him. Then his free hand came to her waist and stayed, and she kept kissing him until the surprise went out of him and something warmer came in.

“That’s a yes,” he said, when she let him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The argument started over breakfast, and in Elowen’s opinion it was entirely his fault.

“Bao’s seen the same white van on the lower road twice this week,” he said. “I’ve asked for two more men. And I’m moving the cases out of the basement.”

She put down the jam knife. “Moving them where?”

“The old pump house at the bottom of the garden. The basement’s too close to where you sleep.”

“It’s been too close to where I sleep since March.”

“I know. If anyone ever comes for the stock, I’d rather they came to the bottom of the hill than the bottom of the stairs.”

“So you want men carrying crates of guns past my lemon tree.”

“Twice. At night. There’s also the humidity in the old cases, and the—“

She leaned over the table and kissed him.

He stopped talking. When she sat back he had the faint, offended stillness of a man who’s been interrupted halfway through a perfectly good argument and has lost the end of it somewhere.

She picked up her toast.

“You did that to stop me.”

“Yes.”

“That isn’t a solution.”

“It worked.” She took a bite. “You tell me before anyone touches the path, and which nights. And not one crate goes past the glass room.”

He thought about it longer than he needed to. “Agreed,” he said, in the voice of a man who’d got exactly what he wanted and would like to be thanked for giving it up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The recipe box was at the back of the cupboard, where she’d put it in March and not opened it since.

The cards were soft at the corners and freckled with old oil, in her mother’s small slanted hand. Braised duck with star anise, which Elowen hadn’t eaten since she was seven. Ginger fish.

Steamed fish. Ginger, plenty. Spring onion. Light soy, little wine. Don’t overcook, it goes like cotton. Hot oil last, over the onion.

Underneath, in another pen, the ink gone brown:

Jian likes the belly. Give him the middle piece.

“Baba’s coming tonight,” she said, when Zhao came in. “He finally said yes.”

“I know. He rang Bao rather than the house.” Zhao took the card from her and read it twice, the way he read everything, and his eyes stayed on the last line. “I’ll make it.”

“You’ve never steamed a fish in your life.”

“I’ve eaten several.” He was already walking out with it.

Five minutes later she heard him in the hall, on the phone.

“Granny Yip. It’s Zhao.” A pause. “Yes, that Zhao. No, she’s fine. How long do you steam a fish?” The old woman’s voice came through the wall, rising. “About as long as my forearm.” Another pause. “A fish kind.”

Elowen went and stood in the glass room with the door shut.

By five the kitchen looked as if a small war had been fought in it and nobody had won. Spring onions in a bowl of water. A grouper scored neatly to the bone in three places. The steamer boiling hard enough to rattle its lid. And on the board, cut into fat gold coins, a whole root of ginger.

“That’s a lot of ginger,” she said.

“It says plenty.”

“Plenty for a person. Not plenty for the harbour.” She took two-thirds of it away and put it in a bowl.

He watched it go. “She should have been clearer.”

Elowen laughed, and stood behind him at the counter the way he’d once stood behind her at the shop with a rose, and put her hands over his on the knife. “Thinner. So it melts.”

He cut thinner. His rings were warm from the stove under her fingers. She showed him how to put the ginger under the fish as well as on it, how to lower the plate in without spilling the juice, how to test the thickest part with a chopstick.

“Eight minutes,” she said.

“The card doesn’t say eight.”

“The card says don’t overcook.”

At the end she heated the oil until it shimmered and gave him the pan. He poured it over the onions himself and it hit them with a sound like rain on a tin roof, and the smell came up all at once.

It was the old kitchen at home. Mama at the stove with her hair tied back. Baba coming in with his tie already loosened and stealing a piece of onion off the top.

Zhao wiped the oil off the counter and waited until she’d finished looking.

“Is that right?”

“That’s right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father arrived at half past six with a box of pears.

She had the door open before he could ring. He stood on the step in his good grey coat holding the box out in front of him.

“A man can bring fruit to his daughter’s house,” he said, before she’d said anything.

Zhao came out of the living room. He’d changed his shirt. There was a fleck of ginger on his cuff that he hadn’t noticed.

“Mr. Lin.”

“Zhao.”

They shook hands. It wasn’t warm. It wasn’t the other thing either.

Elowen took her father through the kitchen and down the passage before either of them could think of anything to say. He stopped in the doorway of the glass room and looked at the shelves, the table, the sink.

“He built this?”

“In three weeks. I didn’t even know.”

Then he looked through the glass and saw the lemon tree, and the rest of him went quiet.

He went out into the courtyard and stood under it. The garden lights had come on, and the five lemons hung yellow in the dark leaves. He touched one with the side of his finger, the way you’d touch a sleeping child.

“Five,” he said. “She only ever got two off it. She said it was sulking.”

“She’d have liked that.”

“Dinner,” said Zhao, from the passage.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were greens with garlic, braised tofu, white-cut chicken, winter melon soup, and the fish in the middle on her mother’s big oval plate, which Elowen had brought from the Lin house in March without asking anyone.

Her father saw the plate before he saw the fish.

He picked up his chopsticks, lifted the skin back off the belly, took out the middle piece and put it in Elowen’s bowl. Without looking. He’d been doing it since she was too small to find the bones.

She picked it up and put it in his.

“Mama gave it to you.”

He stared at her. Then, very deliberately, he lifted it out of his own bowl and set it in Zhao’s.

Zhao looked down at it as if somebody had handed him a live round.

“Who cooked this?” said her father.

“I did.”

“He used a whole root of ginger,” said Elowen.

“A third. She took the rest away.”

Her father ate a piece, then another.

“It’s good. She made it better.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

“Too much ginger.”

“There was going to be more.”

Her father laughed. It came out of him short and rough, as if it had been stuck somewhere for a long time. Under the table Elowen found Zhao’s knee and held on to it.

For a while it was almost easy. Her father asked whether Uncle Pak was still cheating her, and Zhao said, “No,” in a way that made her father look at him properly for the first time all evening.

Then her father put his cup down.

“You know why she married you.”

“Baba.”

He didn’t look at her. “She did it for me. Because I lost your cargo and couldn’t pay, and somebody broke Old Lau’s legs to make a point. She wrote you a contract because I’d left her nothing else.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

“You were the only man in the city who could make it stop.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying that.”

“Then tell me what you want me to say, Mr. Lin.”

Her father’s hand closed round his cup. “I want you to understand what you are. You were the price. That’s all. She paid you with her name and her house and her bed, because I failed her, and you took it.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

He said it so quietly that Elowen almost wished he’d shouted.

“I took it,” he said. “I won’t pretend I didn’t, and I’m not giving it back.” He laid his chopsticks side by side, square to the edge of the table. “But she isn’t something you owed me, and she isn’t something I bought. You can say what you like about me. Not about her. Not at my table.”

Her father stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on the front steps. The rain had stopped and the stone was still wet. Uncle Mok, waiting by the car at the bottom, became very interested in the tyres.

“Go back in, Elowen.”

“You came to my house and called my husband a price.”

“I was telling him the truth.” His voice cracked on the last word. “Wasn’t it?”

He’d carried her on his shoulders at the New Year market. He’d also shouted You sold yourself at her over Ah Sim’s fish in March and had never once said sorry.

“It was true in March,” she said.

“And now?”

She turned round. Through the dining-room window Zhao was clearing the table on his own. He’d stacked her father’s bowl on his and then stopped, and was standing with both in his hand, looking at the fish.

“Now I want to come home,” she said. “I want to argue with him about guns over toast. I want him in the corner of my shop pretending he isn’t frightening the customers. I want to be in that glass room at four in the morning with nothing wrong. Nobody threatening anyone. You fine. Nothing left to pay.” She swallowed. “I want him when there’s nothing to pay for, Baba.”

Her father looked at her face.

“You love him,” he said.

She didn’t answer. She didn’t have to.
