He breathed out as if he’d been holding it since March. Then he took her chin in his fingers for a moment, the way he had when she was small and had something on her face.

“He cooked the fish badly.”

“He did his best.”

“Too much ginger. Tell him it was good.” He let go. “And tell him not to buy any more mountains.”

He went down two steps and stopped, and said without turning round, “I’ll come again.”

She waited until the car was out of the gate before she cried, and then only a little, and only because the lemons looked so yellow under the lights.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was at the sink, washing her mother’s plate by hand. She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his back.

“He says it was good.”

“He didn’t.”

“He said too much ginger. That means good.”

He turned off the tap and stood with his wet hands on the edge of the sink. “He wasn’t wrong. About March. I’d sign it again.”

“So would I.”

His wet hand came down over both of hers and held them there. “Come upstairs.”

The bedroom was dark. She reached for the switch by the door and he caught her hand before she found it, turned her with her back to the wall, and kissed her.

It wasn’t the careful kind he’d given her in April, asking with his whole body whether she meant it. This one was slower and much more certain. His palm spread over her ribs. His thumb found the fine gold chain at her collarbone and followed it to the hollow of her throat. She came up on her toes and caught the back of his neck, and the whole evening went out of her shoulders.

“I want the light,” she said, when he let her breathe.

“Why?”

“Because I want to see you.”

He reached past her and turned it on himself.

The lamp by the bed made the room gold at the edges and left half his face in shadow. He stood still and let her undo his shirt one button at a time, watching her fingers, until she could push it off his shoulders. The scar under his collarbone. The long pale one from Block C low on his side. The burn on his hip from the stove. She’d kissed every one of them in April. She did it again now, slowly and in order, and when she got to his hip he made a sound in his throat and put his hand in her hair.

“Elowen.”

“I’m busy.”

He laughed, low and unsteady, and pulled her up, and then her dress was somewhere on the floor and the backs of her knees met the bed. He laid her down on it and braced himself over her and stopped.

He was looking at her. All of her, in the lamplight, his face very serious.

She made herself not reach for the sheet.

“Keep looking,” she whispered.

He did. He looked until she could feel it on her skin like heat off a stove, and only then did he put his mouth on her: the inside of her wrist, her elbow, her shoulder, the soft place under her jaw where her pulse was jumping. He took his time. He always took his time. She’d stopped minding in about May; tonight she minded enormously and told him so, and he said, “I know,” against her stomach and went on at exactly the same pace, the impossible man.

By the time he came back up to her she had her nails in his back and her heel hooked round his leg. He took her face in both hands, his thumbs under her ears.

“Price or not,” he said against her mouth, “you’re mine now.”

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’re mine. It’s in pencil on my copy of the contract.”

He laughed, properly, and then he stopped laughing, and she pulled him down.

The lamp stayed on. When he moved into her he did it so slowly she forgot to breathe, and she watched him the whole time: the strand of hair in his eyes, the way his jaw went tight when she said his name, the way he looked at her as though he were memorising something he’d been told he’d have to give back. She held his eyes until she couldn’t any more, until her head went back into the pillow and there was nothing in the room but his weight and his breath at her temple and her own voice saying his name as if it were the only word she had left.

Afterwards he lay with his face in her neck and didn’t move. The rain had started again. She could hear it on the glass of the new room downstairs, thinner and closer than the rain on the roof.

“You can hear it on the glass,” she said.

“I asked the builder what it would sound like.”

She turned her head. “You didn’t.”

“In the rain. I asked.”

She thought about the tap, set at the height of his hands, and decided again not to mention it.

“Baba said he’ll come again,” she said.

He lifted his head. “He said that?”

“On the steps. He didn’t turn round.”

Zhao looked at her for a moment. Then he put his face back in her neck, and his arm tightened over her waist, and he didn’t say anything at all.

chapters.title: The Shop Gets a New Floor
chapters.desc: Raiden puts a steel room under the tulips. Over the hole in her floor, Zhao tells her brother he loves her. She hears it from the doorway.
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was the tulips.

They were fine. Three buckets of them, white and apricot and a deep plum colour, stems trimmed, heads still shut tight. But they were on the wrong side of the shop. Somebody had carried them from the rear display to the front window, and the rear display table was gone altogether, and in the space where it had been two men in work boots were standing over her floor with the grave expressions of men who have found something inconvenient underneath it.

Her brother was standing between them.

Raiden had his round glasses pushed up into his hair, which was a mess even by his standards, and a roll of drawings under his arm. Elowen stood in the doorway with a bag of breakfast buns. “Why are you in my shop?”

“Good morning to you too.”

“What have you done to my tulips?”

“They’re having a holiday by the window. They’re very happy.” He unrolled the drawings across her counter and pinned the corners with her tape dispenser, her stapler, and two of her pots. “There’s a void under the back half of the floor. Old coal cellar, filled in badly sometime in the seventies. We surveyed it last week while you were at the market.”

“You surveyed my shop.”

“We surveyed the building. I’m going to dig it out, line it with steel, and put a room in it.” He tapped the paper. “Panic room. Under the tulips.”

She looked back at her brother. “Did you ask me?”

Raiden thought about lying. He’d had the same face for it since he was ten years old and had walked in through the back gate on his own, with a rucksack and mud to the knees.

“Zhendong said you’d say no,” he said. “So I came myself. Nobody says no to me. I’m adorable.”

“Raiden.”

“Fine. I should have asked.” He pushed his glasses back down on to his nose and looked at her through them, and for a second he wasn’t joking. “Somebody burned your van, El. With Xiao Pan standing next to it. I’ve been thinking about that since April.”

She put the buns down.

Drawing other people’s buildings was his job, and the plan was very neat. Steel walls behind the panelling. A ventilation unit on its own circuit. Water, a first-aid cabinet, a bench, a narrow platform to sleep on. A phone line that didn’t go through the shop’s. A second way out into the service lane behind, through a panel that opened from inside.

“Who’s paying for it?”

“Your husband. He signed it off on Thursday. He changed the door.”

“Four days?”

“Four days to dig and line, a week to fit. We’ll work afternoons. You’ll have a clear front of shop the whole time.”

“The panel can’t sit where the delivery crates go.”

“It doesn’t.”

“Xiao Pan learns how it works. Everyone who works here learns. And I want every key.”

“You’ll have every key.” He grinned at her. “That’s it? No speech?”

“I’ve already argued with one man this week about where he wants to keep his guns,” Elowen said. “I’m saving my strength.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The man from the hotel group came in at half past eleven.

He had very good teeth and introduced himself as Mr. Fok, of a development company whose hoardings were all round the old fish market. He looked round her shop like a room he meant to knock down.

“What a charming little place.”

“Thank you. Can I help you with some flowers?”

“I’m here about the building.”

Elowen wiped her hands on her apron. “Then you want my landlord.”

“I’ve been to your landlord.” Mr. Fok smiled at her. “The building changed hands in August. The new owner’s a holding company that doesn’t answer letters. We thought, since you’re the tenant, and since your husband is who he is...” He let it sit there. “We’re assembling the whole block. Boutique hotel, a little arcade of shops. We’d find you a unit in the new arcade, of course. Bigger than this. Better light.”

“I don’t want better light.”

“Perhaps you should discuss it with your husband.”

Something went tight between her shoulders. “My husband doesn’t make decisions about my shop.”

“Of course not.” He laid a card on the counter, next to her stapler. “But I suspect he makes decisions about the building.”

He went out. Elowen picked up the card and turned it over twice. Then she got out her phone.

Elowen: Did you buy my building?

The answer came in under a minute.

Unknown: Yes.

Elowen: When?

Unknown: August.

Elowen: You bought the building my shop is in two months ago and didn’t tell me.

Unknown: A hotel group had made the old owner an offer. They were going to pull the block down.

Elowen: That isn’t an answer to what I said.

There was a pause. She watched the dots appear and go away and appear again.

Unknown: I should have told you.

He hadn’t argued. That was worse, somehow. It meant he’d known all along exactly what she’d say.

Elowen: A man called Fok just came in and told me to ask my husband.

This time there was no pause at all.

Unknown: Is he still there?

Elowen: No. Don’t do anything.

He didn’t answer that one.

✦ ✦ ✦

The development company had two floors of a glass tower above the old fish market. Mr. Fok had a corner office with a model of the new block on a table by the window, little white boxes with little white trees, and where her shop stood there was a café with a striped awning.

He came back from lunch at a quarter to three and found Zhao Zhendong sitting in his chair.

Zhao didn’t get up. He had his coat on and his hands folded on the desk, and the rings on his fingers caught the light from the window. Bao stood by the door, which he’d closed.

“Mr. Zhao.” Fok’s good teeth had gone. “I didn’t know we had a meeting.”

“We don’t.”

Zhao took two things out of his inside pocket and laid them side by side on the desk. A passport, burgundy, a little bent at one corner. And a printed boarding pass for that evening’s flight, in Fok’s name.

Fok looked at the passport. Then he patted his jacket, which was a stupid thing to do, because he’d left it in the safe in his hotel room that morning, as he always did, behind a code he’d thought nobody knew.

His face changed colour slowly, from the neck up.

“About the building,” he said. “If there’s been some misunderstanding about the price—“

“No,” said Zhao.

He stood up. He walked round the desk, past the model, and on his way he reached out and picked up the little white café with the striped awning between his finger and thumb. He looked at it, and put it in his pocket, and went out. Bao followed him and shut the door quietly.

Mr. Fok was on the flight. On Thursday his company withdrew from the block, citing drainage.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited until dinner to have the argument, and by then she’d had time to make it a good one.

“I want to see the papers.”

Zhao put his chopsticks down. “Bao will bring them.”

“I want to know who owns it. Not the holding company. A name.”

“Mine.” He held her eyes. “For now.”

“What does for now mean?”

“It means I was going to put it in yours when the transfer cleared.”

“Without asking me.”

“Yes.”

“Do you hear yourself?”

“Yes.”

She leaned back in her chair. “I didn’t build that shop so that somebody could hand it to me.”

“I know.”

“I paid every month for five years. I paid through the typhoon when I had no customers. That rent is the only thing in my life nobody else has ever paid for me.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “The new owner doesn’t want rent.”

“The new owner’s going to get it.”

“Elowen—“

“No.”

“Don’t put it in my name,” she said. “Not yet. Not like that.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t tell me afterwards. Ever again. About anything that’s mine.”

Something moved in his face. “All right,” he said again, and it sounded different the second time.

On Tuesday she went to the bank on her lunch break. She opened an account in the shop’s name and called it BUILDING, all capitals, and set up a standing order for the twenty-fifth of every month, for exactly the rent she’d always paid. It would cover the roof and the drains and the insurance, and whatever was left could sit there and be hers. She didn’t tell him.

He found out on Wednesday, because Bao found out on Wednesday, because Bao found out everything.

He came into the kitchen that night with the printout in his hand and stood there reading it as if it were a ransom note.

“You opened an account.”

“Yes.”

“For the building.”

“Yes.”

“You’re paying rent to a building I own, into an account that pays for the building I own.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the printout a moment longer. Then he folded it in half, and in half again, and put it in his shirt pocket, and went and got two bowls down for the soup without another word, and she spent the rest of the evening trying not to look smug and failing completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden was right about the dust.

By Thursday the back of the shop was a hole lined with raw steel, and everything she owned had a fine grey coat on it no matter how often Xiao Pan wiped it. The contractors had gone at four. The tulips had been moved for the second time. Elowen was in the front of the shop with a bucket of white chrysanthemums for a funeral order and her phone between her ear and her shoulder, sorting out a delivery, when Zhao came in to look at the welding.

She heard Raiden say, “Your wife’s on the phone. Don’t interrupt her, she bites,” and Zhao say nothing, and then both of them go quiet at the back.

She finished the call. She was about to go back there with the measurements when she heard her brother’s voice change.

“I want the lights on their own battery,” he said. “Not just off the vent circuit. Separate.”

“It’s already separate.”

“Separate from the separate one.”

She stopped behind the chrysanthemums. Through a gap in the stock she could see them at the edge of the hole in her floor.

“Why?” said Zhao.

Raiden rocked on his heels a bit. “When I was nine,” he said, “somebody came to the farm. I don’t know who. Auntie Lan heard the cars on the track and she put me in the chest freezer in the back shed and shut the lid. It was off. It hadn’t worked for years, they kept feed in it. She put a sack of feed on top of the lid so it wouldn’t look moved.” He shrugged. “Eleven hours. I counted, mostly. I could hear them in the yard. I couldn’t see anything at all. When she let me out it was dark outside too, so it didn’t make much difference.”

Elowen had both hands round the rim of the chrysanthemum bucket.

He’d never told any of them that. He’d come home at ten with mud to the knees and made them all laugh at dinner the first night, and she’d thought for twelve years that he’d been lucky.

Zhao didn’t say anything for a while.

“The door opens from inside,” he said at last. “Without power.”

“Yes.”

“And a light that stays on. Whatever happens to the rest.”

“Yes.” Raiden pushed his glasses up. “That’s all. I just like to know there’s a light.”

“Then it stays on.”

Raiden looked at him sideways. “In March you looked at her like a contract. Now you build her steel rooms.” He waited. “Does she know?”

“Know what?”

“Zhendong. Don’t.”

Zhao was looking down into the hole. When he spoke his voice was quite level.

“I love her.”

The chrysanthemums were heavy. Elowen didn’t move.

“Have you told her?” said Raiden.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because she married me to keep your father alive.” He said it the same way he’d said the other thing, without any weight on it at all, as if it were the cost of something on an invoice. “If I say it, she’ll feel she has to answer. She’s polite. She’d say it back to be kind. I don’t want it like that.”

“She isn’t that polite.”

“She is with me.”

Raiden made an exasperated sound. “She’s my sister. I’ve known her my whole life, give or take ten years on a farm. She doesn’t say things to be kind. She says them to win.”

“You’re treating her like one of your shipments,” Raiden said. “As if you can’t sign for it till every box has been opened and counted. She’s not a contract, man.”

“I know what she is.”

“Then—“

Elowen put the chrysanthemums down on the floor, walked through the gap in the stock and across the dust, took hold of the front of her husband’s coat with both hands, and pulled him down and kissed him.

She felt him go rigid with surprise. She didn’t care. She kissed him hard, standing on her toes on the edge of the hole Raiden had dug in her floor, her fists full of his lapels, and after a second his arms came round her and his hand spread on her back and he kissed her back, as if he’d been waiting at a door and somebody had finally opened it.

“I’m right here,” said Raiden. “I’m standing right here. I can see you.”

She let go. Zhao’s eyes were on her face, very dark, searching. She looked back at him and gave him nothing at all. She straightened his coat where she’d crumpled it.

“Your measurements,” she said, and put the paper in his hand, and went back to her chrysanthemums.

Behind her she heard Raiden say, very quietly, “Well. She heard that.”

And Zhao, after a long time: “She didn’t say anything.”

“No,” said her brother. “I noticed. Good luck.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was finished on Friday. She inspected it herself, because nobody was going to tell her it was safe until she’d checked.

The floor panel lifted on a counterweight with one hand. Below it a short steep stair went down into a room the size of her old bedroom at the Lin house. Steel behind pale panels. Cool, clean, moving air. Water. A first-aid cabinet. A bench along one wall, and the narrow sleeping platform along the other. The second way out was behind a panel at the far end, and she made Raiden open it and close it and open it again, and then she did it herself. She made Xiao Pan lift the floor and use the phone, and the two women who did Saturdays as well.

Then she found the lamp.

A small brass lamp with a cloth shade, fixed over the sleeping platform, with its own switch and a little red battery light glowing underneath.

“That’s not on the plan,” she said.

“I added it.”

“Why?”

Raiden shrugged. “The ceiling lights are horrible. If you have to wait down here, you shouldn’t have to wait in that.”

She looked at him. He looked at the lamp.

“Thank you.”

“Test the exit again.”

When he’d gone up she sat under the little lamp and imagined it: the bell upstairs, something breaking, Xiao Pan next to her trying not to look frightened. She didn’t like it. She liked knowing there was a place.

She took a pen out of her apron and a blank gift card from her pocket, the kind she tied on bouquets, and wrote on it in her neat round florist’s hand.

This light stays on. I’ll come.

She tucked it into the edge of the lamp’s base, where anyone sitting under it would see it.

When she came up the stair Zhao was waiting at the top with his hand out. She took it and he pulled her up the last step.

“What did you write?”

“Nothing.”

He looked down past her into the room, where the lamp was glowing. Then back at her.

“It’s for whoever’s down there,” she said. “It’s a promise.”

He didn’t ask what it said. He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles, which were grey with dust, and didn’t seem to mind.

They locked up together at six. The floor had been relaid. The rear display was back where it belonged, and the tulips were back on it, and the panel was invisible under the table unless you knew to look. She turned the lights off one by one. At the door she stopped and looked back at her shop in the dark, five years of it, and the new thing hidden underneath.

Zhao stood behind her on the pavement with her keys in his hand, because she’d given them to him to hold and he hadn’t given them back.

“You love me,” she said, without turning round.

There was a silence so long she thought he wasn’t going to answer.

“You heard.”

“I heard.”

“You didn’t say anything.”

She turned. He was standing very still under the streetlight, waiting, the way he’d waited outside her bedroom door in April, the way he’d waited three weeks to show her a room.

She took her keys back out of his hand.

“No,” she said. “I didn’t.”

She locked the door. Then she took his arm and they walked to the car, and he let her, and he didn’t ask, and she knew exactly how much it cost him not to.

chapters.title: A Reunion Invitation With One Name on It
chapters.desc: The school turns sixty and Miles Wei is giving the speech. At two in the morning she finds her husband reading his papers.
chapters.content:
Aurelia rang on a Wednesday afternoon, while Elowen was wiring white roses for a hotel lobby and had no hands free.

She put the phone on the bench against a jar of twine and pressed the speaker with her elbow.

“Are you busy?”

“I’m working.”

“So yes. I’ll be quick. Our school is turning sixty.”

“Congratulations to it.”

“There’s a dinner on the fourteenth of December at the Harbour Hotel. Every year group. Speeches, a slideshow, old teachers who’ll tell us we haven’t changed.” A pause, so neatly judged that Elowen could hear Aurelia enjoying it. “Miles Wei is giving the address.”

A rose slipped in Elowen’s fingers. She caught it by the stem before it hit the floor.

“Miles.”

“Miles. Unless there’s another one with round glasses who carried a notebook to the canteen and wrote like a medical emergency. He’s a lecturer now. Physics, obviously. Three papers this year. They’ve put him on the invitation with a photograph.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because I’m going, and I’m not going alone with a room full of people who remember me crying in the bathroom on results day.” Aurelia’s voice went airy. “And because I’d like to see your face when you see his.”

“My face will be fine.”

“Your face was not fine at seventeen. You used to sit two rows behind him in the physics room and stare at the back of his neck as if it owed you money.”

“So did you.”

“I was assessing his posture.”

Elowen pushed the rose into the foam. “It’s a Monday.”

“I know it’s a Monday. The committee is sentimental. Bring your husband. I want to watch him at a table with our old maths teacher.” Aurelia paused. “And wear something that isn’t green. You look like a fern in green.”

She rang off before Elowen could answer.

Elowen stood there with her wire and her roses. Miles Wei, two years above them, who had sat in the back row solving things that made Mr. Hui put his chalk down. Miles, who had never once noticed that two girls were fighting a small, vicious war over him all the way through their second year, and who, when he finally did notice, had picked up his notebook and walked away and chosen physics. That was eight years ago.

She wondered what his face looked like now. Then she was annoyed with herself for wondering, and wired the next rose much too tight.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was in the study when she got home, papers on the desk, jacket over the back of the chair. She came round the desk and sat on the edge of it, on top of whatever he was reading.

He looked up. “Long day?”

“I’ve been invited to something.”

“By whom?”

“My school. It’s sixty. There’s a dinner at the Harbour Hotel on the fourteenth of December. Aurelia’s going.”

“Then go.”

“I want you to come.”

He looked at her for a moment. “As your husband?”

“As my plus one.”

“Yes.”

She’d been ready for an argument. “That was quick.”

“Why wouldn’t I?”

“There’ll be speeches about academic excellence and people asking what everyone does now. You’ll be bored.”

“I’ve been more bored.” He took his pen out from under her thigh. “Which entrance do the guests use?”

“The front one, presumably.”

“Is there a side door? Parking under the hotel? Is it the main ballroom or the one by the water?”

“Zhendong.”

“There’ll be four hundred people.”

“Are you coming to my school reunion or inspecting it?”

“Both.” He didn’t smile, but the corner of his mouth wanted to. “Bao can walk it on the Friday. Nobody will see him.”

“No frightening my old teachers.”

“I don’t frighten teachers.”

“You made a customs officer apologise to a delivery driver in front of the whole market.”

“He was rude to the driver.”

She let that go. There was one more thing, and she said it to the bookshelf behind his head, because it was easier.

“Miles Wei’s giving the speech.”

His pen stopped.

“Miles Wei,” he said.

“Yes.”

“The physics boy.”

“You remember.”

“I remember.”

Of course he did. He’d asked Bao for the old bus routes in April. She’d found out because Bao had looked guilty about it for a week.

“Does he know you’re married?” Zhao said.

“I haven’t spoken to him in eight years.”

“So no.”

“Would you like me to send him a photograph from the registry? I could have it framed.”

“No.”

She slid off the desk. He caught her wrist before she’d gone, very lightly, and looked up at her.

“You’ll tell me,” he said. “If you want to leave.”

“I’ll tell you.”

He let go. When she reached the door she looked back, and he was sitting exactly as she’d left him, the pen in his hand, not writing anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at two to cold sheets.

His side of the bed was empty and his pillow was cool. A line of light showed under the door of the study across the landing.

She pulled on her robe. The study door was open a hand’s width. He was on the old daybed under the window, the narrow one that had come with the house and that nobody ever sat on, with his back against the wall and his knees up and the reading lamp pulled round on its arm. Papers lay across his lap and on the floor. He was in a T-shirt, barefoot, his hair falling in his eyes.

She knew the name on the top sheet before she could read it.

“Good morning,” she said from the door.

He looked up. He didn’t move the papers.

“Go back to bed.”

“You first.”

She came in and took the top one off his knee. Weak gravitational lensing by low-mass haloes: a reanalysis. Then a great deal of Greek. Down the margin, in his small square hand, he’d made notes: a word underlined, a question mark, an arrow to a diagram, a line that just said why not just say this.

“You’ve read all three.”

“Two and a half.”

“You’ve made notes.”

“Some of it was badly explained.”

“Zhendong.” She held the paper up. “Are you reading my school crush’s research at two o’clock in the morning?”

He was quiet. Then: “I wanted to know what he does. In case you talk about it.”

She looked at him. He looked back, quite seriously, with his hair in his eyes and a physics paper on his bare knee.

She started laughing.

She tried to stop and it got worse. She had to sit down on the end of the daybed, which barely fitted him, and press the paper to her mouth.

“What’s funny?”

“You’ve annotated it.”

“It needed annotating.”

“You don’t care about gravitational lensing.”

“I didn’t say that.” He took the paper back from her and put it on the pile, square. “Did you like him?”

That stopped her laughing, mostly.

“I was seventeen,” she said. “He was clever and quiet and he never noticed anyone, and he had nice hands. He used to explain things to the boys in the year below without making them feel stupid. I thought that was the most attractive thing in the world. Aurelia and I fought about him for a year and he never noticed that either.”

Zhao listened. He didn’t say anything.

“I never kissed him. I never held his hand. I spoke to him properly about four times, and three of them were about homework.” She leaned forward and pushed the hair off his forehead. “And you’re sitting on a bed that doesn’t fit you, in the middle of the night, reading his footnotes, instead of in bed with your wife.”

“When you say it like that—“

“It’s terrifying, not restful.”

That got him. The corner of his mouth went. She leaned in and kissed it, and then kissed the rest of his mouth, and he made a low sound and let the papers slide off his lap on to the floor, and pulled her down on to the narrow bed with him, which was far too small for two people and which neither of them cared about for some time.

When she lifted her head, one of the papers was crumpled under her elbow. She smoothed it out. It was the last page of the third one, the references, half-empty. At the bottom, under the final reference, he’d written something in the margin and then crossed it out, not hard enough.

Does she want me there.

No question mark. He’d never been any good with question marks.

She took the pen off the lamp table and wrote underneath it, in her round florist’s hand, the same hand that went on gift cards.

You come with me. Plus one.

She gave it back to him. He read it. He didn’t say anything for a while.

“Come to bed,” she said.

He came. He left the papers on the floor. In the morning the last page of the third one was gone from the pile, and she didn’t ask where.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao came to the study on Saturday with two folders.

The first was the hotel. Floor plans, the ballroom by the water, three public entrances, a service corridor, two fire exits, the car park underneath and who ran it. Zhao read it and handed it back.

“Good.”

Bao didn’t take his hand away from the second folder.

“There’s this as well, sir.”

It was thinner. WEI, Miles. A photograph clipped to the inside cover, taken from across a street: a man in a pale blue shirt with a satchel, soft brown hair falling over thin round glasses, waiting at a bus stop and reading something folded small.

Zhao looked at it for a while without picking it up.

“I didn’t ask for this.”

“No, sir.”

He opened it.

Twenty-six. A lecturer’s post since the summer; before that two years abroad, a doctorate. Three papers this year, which he knew. A rented flat on the fourth floor of a walk-up near the university, alone. No car. He took the number fourteen bus from the stop outside the bakery at seven fifty-two every weekday and sat upstairs at the front. He bought the same coffee every morning from a cart by the physics building and didn’t drink half of it. There was nobody, as far as anyone could tell, in his life at all.

Zhao read every line. Then he read it again.

“Seven fifty-two,” he said.

“Yes, sir. Most days. It’s sometimes seven fifty-five.”

Zhao closed the folder and put it in the drawer of the desk, the one with the lock, on top of the last page of a physics paper.

“Nothing else,” he said. “Don’t follow him. Don’t get any closer.”

“No, sir.”

“And she doesn’t hear about this from you.”

Bao, who had once told Elowen about the bus routes because she’d looked at him over a cup of jasmine tea until he did, said, “No, sir,” with a great deal less confidence.

When he’d gone, Zhao sat with his hand on the locked drawer. He knew it was unreasonable. He knew exactly what kind of man had a file on a physics lecturer’s bus. He’d been that man since he was six; he’d known which bus everybody took. The difference was that he’d never once wanted to know it about someone who’d done nothing to him at all, except be seventeen at the same time as her.

He left it in the drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the dresses that afternoon.

Five of them, hanging from the rail in the dressing room in their bags, the bags unzipped a little at the top so she could see the colours. A deep red silk with a plain neck. A dark green. A black velvet with long sleeves. A champagne one. A pale blue with a drape at the shoulder.

Zhao was by the window with his phone.

“You said you didn’t know what to wear,” he said, before she could ask.

“I said I hadn’t decided.”

“So I bought you some decisions.”

“Five.”

“Aurelia said not to buy anything with lace. And not green.”

She turned round. “You asked Aurelia?”

“She sent a list.”

Elowen laughed, and went to the red one, because she’d always known it would be the red one. She took it into the bathroom and put it on.

When she came out he’d put his phone down. He looked at her and didn’t say anything at all, for long enough that she started to feel the silk on her arms.

“Too much?”

“No.”

“Too plain?”

“No.”

She went to the mirror. It was a good red, deep and warm, not the bright kind. It made her skin look like porcelain and her mouth look as if she’d meant it. The waist fitted. The hem fell just below her knee.

He came and stood behind her, and put his hands on her waist, and looked at her in the glass over her shoulder.

“Wear this one,” he said.

“Because it suits me?”

“Because I’ll be able to find you in a room of four hundred people.”

She looked at his face in the mirror. “You’re going to behave.”

“Yes.”

“You won’t glare at him.”

“I don’t glare.”

“You’re glaring now. At the mirror.” She leaned back against him. “And you won’t ask him which bus he takes.”

Something went very still behind her. In the mirror his face didn’t change at all. That was how she knew.

She turned her head and looked at him properly.

“Zhendong.”

“I won’t ask him,” he said. “I promise.”

It was a strange answer. She thought about it. Then she decided she didn’t want to know what he’d done, not tonight, in this dress, with his hands on her waist, and she let it go, which she would think about later.

“Good,” she said.

“What do I do with the other four?”

“Keep them.”

“I’ve nowhere to wear four dresses.”

“Then I’ll take you somewhere four times.”

She laughed and turned round in his hands and kissed him. When she drew back his thumb was moving on the silk at her waist, slowly, as if he were checking it was real.

That night, after she’d fallen asleep, he went down to the study and unlocked the drawer. He didn’t open the folder. He took out the last page of the third paper and folded it in four, with her handwriting on the outside, and put it in the inside pocket of the jacket he was going to wear on the fourteenth.

Then he locked the drawer again, with the folder still inside it, and went back up to bed.

chapters.title: The Arms Dealer Is Absolutely Fine About the Physics Lecturer
chapters.desc: Zhao borrows Xiao Pan’s FLOWER POWER hoodie and goes to the physics lecture in disguise. Chen Si finds him at the back.
chapters.content:
On Thursday morning Zhao Zhendong moved a meeting.

The broker was a man called Kan, who owed him for two shipments and had been owing him since August. The meeting had been at the office at the Docks at eleven. Zhao rang Bao from the car and told him it was now at twelve, in the west car park of the university, and Bao, who had worked for him for six years, said, “Yes, sir,” and didn’t ask why a broker should be seen in a university car park, because he had already looked up what was happening at the university that morning.

The public lecture in the physics building was at ten. Bending light: what gravity shows us that we can’t see. Free entry. Dr. Miles Wei.

The difficulty was the clothes.

Zhao stood in front of his wardrobe for some time. Everything in it was navy or beige or black and had been made for him. He looked, in all of it, exactly like what he was. In a room full of students he’d be noticed in three seconds, and if he was noticed somebody would say his name, and if somebody said his name it would get back to the hill house by lunch.

He needed something a person might wear.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan was in the back of the shop unpacking a crate of ceramic pots when his employer’s husband appeared in the doorway.

“Mr. Zhao.” He straightened up so fast he nearly dropped a pot. “She’s at the bank.”

“I know. I need to borrow something.”

“Of course.”

“Your sweatshirt.”

Xiao Pan looked down at himself. He was wearing his grey hoodie with the hood. It had a very large yellow flower printed across the front, and under the flower, in round white letters, it said FLOWER POWER. His aunt had bought it for him at a night market. He had worn it until the cuffs went.

He looked back up. “This one?”

“Yes.”

“Mr. Zhao, it’s a bit...”

“I can see what it is.”

“Do you want me to go and buy you one?”

“No. That one.”

Xiao Pan took it off, slowly, the way a man surrenders a weapon. Underneath he had a T-shirt with a hole in the shoulder. He held the hoodie out.

“It’s my favourite.”

“I’ll bring it back.”

“Don’t get anything on it.”

Zhao looked at the flower. He read the words. He folded it over his arm and went out through the shop without another word.

Xiao Pan stood among the pots. Then he took out his phone.

Xiao Pan: Mr. Zhao has just borrowed my FLOWER POWER hoodie

Xiao Pan: he didn’t say why

Xiao Pan: should I be worried

Elowen read it in the queue at the bank and looked at it for some time. She had a suspicion. It was a very specific suspicion and she hoped it was wrong.

Elowen: Did he say where he was going?

Xiao Pan: no. he looked very serious

Elowen: Thank you for lending it to him.

Xiao Pan: should I ask for it back

Elowen: Eventually.

✦ ✦ ✦

He parked four streets away and walked. The security car stayed at the bottom of the road. He took off his watch in the car and put it in the glovebox, and then his rings, all of them, and his hands looked strange to him without them, like somebody else’s.

The hoodie was too short in the arms. The flower covered most of his chest.

He went in by the side door of the lecture theatre and sat at the back, at the end of a row. A girl two seats along glanced at him, looked at the flower, smiled at it, and went back to her phone.

Nobody else looked at all. It was possibly the first time in years that he’d walked into a room and nobody had looked at him.

He hadn’t come because he thought Miles Wei would do anything. He had no reason to think so. He had no reason to think Elowen would be any different in a ballroom from the way she was at breakfast. He’d come because he wanted to see the man. That was the reason he’d given himself, and it wasn’t a very good one, and he was here anyway.

The lights went down a little. A man came on to the stage with a laptop and a sheaf of notes.

He was taller than he looked at a bus stop. The fringe was the same, soft and brown and a little too long, falling over the thin round frames of his glasses. Pale blue shirt, sleeves rolled to the forearm with great care, as if he’d watched someone else do it once and practised.

“Good morning,” he said. “Today I’m going to talk about light, and about how it gets lost on the way here.”

His voice wasn’t loud. It reached the back without trying.

For ten minutes Zhao understood very little. He’d read the papers, but the papers had been written for people who already knew, and the lecture wasn’t much better at first. Then a boy in the third row asked a question that was too simple for the room, and Zhao watched the lecturer stop and look at the boy and say, “Good, that’s the right place to be confused,” and go back to the beginning and draw it again, slower, with a coffee cup and a pen on the screen, the cup for a galaxy and the pen for the light going round it.

He didn’t sigh. He didn’t look at his watch. When the boy got it, Miles Wei looked pleased, as if the boy had done him a favour.

Zhao sat with his arms folded over the yellow flower.

The man was kind. That was inconvenient. It would have been much simpler if he’d been arrogant, or vain, or a little cruel to the students, or bad at it. Zhao could have disliked him without having to think about why.

“The universe,” Miles said, putting up a picture of a galaxy smeared into a ring of light round a dark middle, “is very bad at making anything easy. Which is the only reason any of us have jobs.”

The students laughed. Zhao didn’t. But he understood the joke, and he thought about it for the rest of the slide.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t know you were interested in astrophysics.”

Chen Si sat down in the empty seat beside him, in a charcoal overcoat, his hair neat as a ruled line, and crossed his legs.

Zhao didn’t turn his head. “Why are you here?”

“The foundation’s paying for a new instrument room on the fourth floor. I was meant to see the dean at eleven. He’s late.” Chen Si looked at the stage. Then he looked, for a long, silent moment, at the front of Zhao’s chest. “Is that Xiao Pan’s?”

“Yes.”

“You borrowed a sweatshirt from your wife’s delivery boy to come and look at her first crush.”

“I’m attending a lecture.”

“In disguise.”

“It’s a public lecture.”

Chen Si put two fingers over his mouth. Zhao didn’t look at him.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re going to.”

On the stage Miles had moved on to how you could weigh something you couldn’t see by the way it bent what was behind it. Chen Si watched him for a while.

“What’s he like?”

“Kind.”

Chen Si turned his head.

“Patient,” said Zhao. “He doesn’t make them feel stupid. He likes it when they understand.”

“You’ve been listening.”

“I came to a lecture.”

Chen Si laughed. He did it almost without sound, the way he did everything, but he did it for long enough that the girl two seats along looked round at them.

“Forgive me,” he said, when he could. “I’m just happy. I’ve been waiting ten years to see you meet a man you can’t do anything about.”

Zhao watched the stage. The lecturer was waiting for a girl at the front to finish a question, not interrupting, nodding at her as she went.

“She had a whole life,” Zhao said, “before I came into it.”

Chen Si stopped smiling.

“School. That man. Aurelia. Her mother at the market. Five years of that shop on her own. Whatever she was going to be.” His jaw moved. “I came in through her father’s debt. I walked in and sat in the corner of it with a gun in my coat and bought all the flowers.”

“Zhendong.”

“Sometimes I think I took the quiet one. The life she’d have had with somebody like that.” He nodded at the stage, very slightly. “Somebody who explains things with a coffee cup.”

Chen Si was quiet for a while.

“You didn’t take anything,” he said. “You arrived when it was already on fire. That isn’t the same.”

“I know.”

“She still goes to the market at four. She still runs the shop. She still tells you to eat your dinner. She shouts at you about guns.” Chen Si looked at him sideways. “She kissed you in front of her brother over a hole in her floor. Raiden told me. You can’t take a quiet life from a woman who does that. She hasn’t got one.”

Zhao didn’t answer. On the stage the lights changed, and Miles Wei put up his last slide, a ring of bent light in the dark, and thanked them for coming.

“Are you going to introduce yourself?” said Chen Si.

“No.”

“You came all this way.”

“I’ve seen what I came to see.”

They went out by the side door. Chen Si looked at the hoodie again in the daylight.

“May I say one thing?”

“No.”

“I’ve never seen you wear anything so cheerful.”

“Don’t tell her.”

“I’m absolutely going to tell her,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kan was waiting in the west car park beside his own car, smoking, as if a car park was a reasonable place to meet a man he owed money to. He saw Zhao coming and dropped the cigarette.

Then he saw the flower.

Something happened to his face that he couldn’t stop in time. It was only for a second, a twitch at the mouth, the beginning of a laugh that he swallowed. Zhao saw it. Chen Si, two steps behind, saw it, and quietly stepped back another two.

“Mr. Zhao. I was going to call you—“

“August,” said Zhao. “And September.”

“The money’s coming. There was a problem at the bank, a hold on the transfer, my partner in—“

“You told me that in October.”

“It’s true. I swear it’s true. I need two weeks.”

“Something funny, Mr. Kan?”

“No. No, Mr. Zhao.”

Zhao took him by the back of the neck, almost gently, the way you’d steer a drunk friend, and brought his face down on to the roof of his own car.

The sound was very loud in the empty car park. Kan’s legs went. Zhao held him up by the neck and the collar, so he didn’t fall, and waited until he could hear again. There was blood coming out of his nose over the white paint of the roof.

“Monday,” said Zhao. “Morning. All of it. If it isn’t there by ten I’ll stop being polite.”

Kan made a noise that meant yes.

Zhao let go and he slid down the side of the car and sat on the tarmac with both hands over his face. There was a spot of blood on the hem of the hoodie. Zhao looked at it, and frowned, and walked to the car.

Chen Si passed the man on the ground.

“Nice sweatshirt, wasn’t it?” he said pleasantly, and followed.

In the car Zhao put his rings back on one at a time, and then his watch. Chen Si watched him do it.

“You broke a man’s nose in a flower.”

“He laughed.”

“He didn’t laugh.”

“He was going to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao brought the hoodie to the shop at four, in a paper bag, washed and folded, with the little spot on the hem scrubbed nearly away. He put it on the counter beside the till as if he were handing in a weapon at a police station.

“From Mr. Zhao, madam. For Xiao Pan.”

Elowen opened the bag. A large yellow flower looked up at her.

“Bao.”

“Madam.”

“Where did he wear this?”

Bao had worked for Zhao for six years. He had stood in rooms where men were persuaded to sign things. He looked at the bag, and at her, and made the mistake of being honest.

“The physics lecture at the university, madam. At the back.”

She went very still. “Whose lecture?”

“Dr. Wei’s.”

“He moved a meeting to go?”

“He moved a meeting to the car park, madam. So he could go.”

“Did he speak to him?”

“No, madam.”

“Did Mr. Chen happen to be there?”

“Yes, madam.”

That was where her composure went.

She put both hands over her face. She tried very hard. She leaned on the counter and pressed her forehead to her wrist, and it came anyway, from somewhere low down, until she was laughing so hard she couldn’t breathe and the two women who did Saturdays came out of the back to see what was wrong. She couldn’t tell them. Every time she tried she saw him at the back of a lecture theatre with his arms folded over FLOWER POWER, frowning at a diagram of a coffee cup, and it started again, until there were tears running down her face and she had to sit on the stool.

Bao stood there through all of it, very straight, like a man waiting for a storm to finish with his house.

“Madam?”

“I’m sorry,” she gasped. “I’m sorry, Bao. Thank you. Tell Xiao Pan I’ll give it to him.”

He bowed slightly and fled.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came home a little before seven. She was waiting in the kitchen with the hoodie folded on the counter in front of her.

He stopped in the doorway when he saw it. She looked at him. He looked at the flower.

“Chen Si,” he said.

“Bao.”

He shut his eyes for a moment, briefly, as if Bao were a cost he’d always known would come due. He took his coat off and hung it up and came and stood on the other side of the counter.

“Was it a good lecture?”

“Yes.”

“Did you understand it?”

“The coffee cup.”

“And what did you think of him?”

He took a while to answer. “He’s kind,” he said. “He’s patient. He likes teaching them. He’d have been good to you.”

She’d been going to laugh at him some more. She didn’t.

“You went to see what I liked about him.”

“Yes.”

She came round the counter. She took hold of the front of his shirt, which was black and plain and smelled faintly of somebody else’s detergent where the hoodie had been, and she pulled him down and kissed him.

He made a sound low in his chest. She kissed him again, harder, until his hands came to her waist and then tightened, and then he lifted her clean off her feet and put her on the counter, next to the fruit bowl and the yellow flower, and stood between her knees.

She held his face. “I liked him when I was seventeen because he never looked at anyone. You look at me all the time. You looked at me across a shop in the rain before you knew my name.”

“I knew your name.”

“Before I knew yours, then.” She pushed his hair back off his forehead. “You don’t take things from me. I take things from you. I take your stools and your van keys and your Saturdays. I took your whole house.”

“You did.”

“So stop going to lectures.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “I didn’t enjoy it.”

“Liar.”

“I didn’t enjoy him.” His thumbs moved on her waist. “I liked the coffee cup.”

She laughed into his mouth, and he kissed her, and the hoodie slid off the counter on to the floor, and neither of them picked it up for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan got it back the next morning. Zhao gave it to him himself, folded, in front of the cooler.

Xiao Pan unfolded it and checked it all over and found nothing.

“Did you like the lecture?”

Zhao looked at him. “It was informative.”

“You can borrow it again. If you need to.”

“There won’t be a next time.”

“Right,” said Xiao Pan.

When Zhao had gone he put it on, and went and found Elowen at the bench, and held his arms out so she could see the flower.

“He said there won’t be a next time,” he said. “I think he liked it.”

Elowen, wiring a bridal posy, didn’t look up.

“So do I,” she said.

chapters.title: The Reunion, Table Nine
chapters.desc: The reunion. Aurelia fixes Miles’s bow tie, Miles asks Elowen if she’s happy, and then he walks up to the man by the wall without knowing who he is.
chapters.epigraph: “She doesn’t look like she wants to run.”
chapters.content:
The Harbour Hotel had done its ballroom in gold and ivory for the school’s sixtieth, and the school crest hung over the stage on a banner three storeys tall.

Elowen stopped just inside the doors.

She hadn’t expected to feel anything. She’d expected to be faintly bored and to make fun of the slideshow with Aurelia. Instead the crest looked back at her, the same green shield with the same lamp on it that had been sewn to her blazer pocket for six years, and for a moment she could smell floor polish and chalk and the canteen’s terrible rice, and she was seventeen and late for chemistry.

“All right?” said Zhao beside her.

“It used to look enormous.”

He looked up at the banner. “Perhaps you were smaller.”

She took his arm.

He’d worn a black suit for once, with a white shirt open at the throat because he’d refused a tie on the grounds that he wasn’t getting married. Every few minutes his right hand went to the inside of his jacket and touched something there and came away again. She’d noticed it in the car. She didn’t ask.

Table nine was by the windows, where you could see the lights on the water. Aurelia had arranged it. Aurelia had arranged, as far as Elowen could tell, about half the room.

She was standing beside it in gold, a column of it from collarbone to floor, with pearls at her throat and a black velvet band holding back her hair, and she looked like a trophy somebody had decided to give to themselves. Chen Si stood a step behind her in a dark suit and thin black gloves, holding her glass for her.

“You came,” said Aurelia, and kissed the air beside Elowen’s face. Then she stepped back and inspected her. “Red. Good. You listened.”

“He bought it.”

“I know. I sent him the list.” Aurelia looked at Zhao. “You can be taught.”

“He bought five,” said Chen Si.

Aurelia turned round. “Five?”

“Five,” said Elowen.

Aurelia looked at Zhao with something close to respect, and then at her own husband, very pointedly, and Chen Si said, “You have a wardrobe the size of a church,” and handed her back her glass.

They sat. Old teachers came by, one after another, the way old teachers do, to tell Elowen she’d always been stubborn and to tell Aurelia she’d always been loud. Mr. Hui, who had taught them both mathematics and had never once let either of them finish a sentence, stopped at their table and looked at Zhao.

“And were you one of ours?”

“No.”

“Ah. Then you missed some very important years.”

Zhao looked at Elowen. “I’ve heard about them.”

“She was a very good student,” said Mr. Hui.

“I know.”

“She was also impossible.”

“I know that too.”

“You’re supposed to defend me,” said Elowen.

“I am,” said Zhao.

Mr. Hui went away delighted. Across the table Aurelia leaned towards her husband and said, not quite quietly enough, “Yours could learn something from him,” and Chen Si said, “I defend you every day of my life, it’s simply that you never need it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles Wei arrived twenty minutes late.

Zhao had gone to the door at the far end of the ballroom to speak to Bao, who’d walked the building on Friday and had been standing in the service corridor all evening pretending to be a waiter. So he wasn’t at the table when Aurelia looked up and said, “Oh,” in a voice Elowen hadn’t heard her use since they were sixteen.

He was standing by the doors with an organiser, nodding at whatever she was telling him. Black suit, black bow tie. The same soft brown fringe falling over the same thin round glasses, though the face behind them had lost its softness and got longer and more serious. He looked exactly like himself, eight years on, and also like a stranger.

He saw them and his face lit up. He came straight over.

“Aurelia Song.”

Aurelia stood. “Still late, Miles Wei.”

“Still counting?”

“Someone has to.” She held out her hand, palm down, as if she expected it to be kissed, and he shook it instead, which was so exactly like him that Elowen laughed out loud.

He turned. “Elowen Lin.”

“Hello, Miles.”

“It’s been a long time.”

“Eight years.”

“Is it? It feels like four.” He looked at the two of them, side by side. “And you two are still friends.”

“Don’t be disgusting,” said Aurelia. “We’re rivals.”

He laughed, and shook Chen Si’s gloved hand when Aurelia introduced him, and then, a little hopelessly, put two fingers to his throat.

“Could one of you help me? It’s crooked. I’ve tried. The mirror in the gents is a disgrace.”

Aurelia stared at him. “Eight years and you still can’t tie a bow tie.”

“I can tie one. I can’t tie one straight.”

“Come here.”

She set down her glass and stepped in and took the knot in both hands and untied it, and tied it again, quickly and well, her face very close to his throat, her mouth pursed with concentration. Miles lifted his chin for her obediently.

“Stop moving,” she said.

“I’m not moving.”

“You’re breathing.”

Across the table, Chen Si watched with perfect pleasantness. His gloved fingers rested very still on the white tablecloth.

Elowen leaned over. “Are you jealous?”

“Of a physicist?”

“Of your wife’s hands on his collar.”

He looked at Aurelia’s hands. “I trust my wife completely,” he said. “I also trust her to finish soon.”

Aurelia stepped back. “There. Presentable. Don’t touch it.”

“Thank you.” Miles touched it. “I’m on in half an hour. We’ll talk after?”

“Of course,” said Elowen.

When he’d gone, Aurelia sat down and picked up her glass and found her husband looking at her.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re making the face.”

“I’m not making a face.”

She leaned close to him and said something in his ear that Elowen didn’t catch, and Chen Si’s ears went faintly pink, and he took her hand under the table and didn’t let go of it again for the rest of the night.

✦ ✦ ✦

The speech was at eight.

The lights went down. The crest disappeared and a photograph came up in its place: a galaxy, very far away, its light drawn out into a thin bright ring round a dark middle.

“Good evening,” said Miles. “They asked me to talk about the future. I’m a physicist. I’m going to talk about light instead, because that’s the only thing I know about that travels.”

He talked about how light didn’t go in straight lines, not really, not over those distances. How very heavy things bent the space around them, and the light coming past them bent too, so that something hidden behind could be seen around the edges. How you could find a thing nobody could see by looking at what it did to everything near it.

Elowen listened. She’d expected to be bored, or to be seventeen. She was neither. She just liked listening to him; she always had. He still did it the same way, looking at the room as if every single person in it might be about to understand.

She glanced at Zhao. He’d come back during the applause and sat beside her. He was listening properly, with his arms folded, the way he’d listened at the back of a lecture theatre in a borrowed sweatshirt.

Miles reached for the clicker to change slides, and it shot out of his hand.

It hit the stage with a crack that went right through the microphone, and skittered under the lectern. Four hundred people heard it. Miles looked at it for a second. Then he laughed, at himself, the same embarrassed, delighted laugh she remembered from the physics room when he got something wrong on the board.

“Even light bends,” he said, picking it up. “Apparently so do my hands.”

The ballroom laughed with him. At table nine Aurelia leaned towards Elowen.

“He’s still like that.”

“Yes,” said Elowen.

She felt Zhao look at her. She didn’t look back. She put her hand on his knee under the table and left it there until the end.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went out on to the balcony afterwards because the ballroom was hot and she wanted the air.

The hotel’s gardens went down in terraces to the water. The harbour was black and full of lights. She stood at the rail with her arms crossed and her breath going white.

“Elowen?”

Miles had come out through the glass doors behind her. He stopped at a polite distance with his hands in his pockets.

“Sorry. I’m not following you. I’m hiding from the committee.”

“Then hide.”

He came and stood at the rail too, not close. For a while they just looked at the water.

“You haven’t changed much,” he said.

“That’s not true.”

“Not your face. The thing you do with it when you already know the answer and you’re waiting to see if somebody else does.”

She laughed. “Is that what I do?”

“You did it to Mr. Hui every lesson.” He looked out at the harbour. “I heard you have a flower shop.”

“In the Walled City.”

“That’s right. I always thought you’d make something. You drew flowers in the margins of your physics.”

“I was bored.”

“You drew very good flowers, for someone who was bored.”

They talked about nothing much. Mr. Hui. The canteen rice. Who had married whom, who was in which country. She told him Aurelia had married a man who ran a great many things, and he said, “Of course she did,” and she laughed again, because it was the right answer.

Then he said, without looking at her, “Are you happy?”

It surprised her. Not because it was rude. It wasn’t. Because of the way he asked it, as if it were a question in a lecture that he actually wanted answered.

She looked through the glass doors.

Zhao was inside, against the wall by a pillar, with a glass he hadn’t drunk from. A man from the alumni committee was talking to him. He wasn’t listening to the man. He was watching the balcony door. He’d sat at the back of a lecture in a yellow flower. He’d read three papers at two in the morning and written a question in a margin and folded up her answer and put it in his jacket, and he’d touched that pocket all evening, every few minutes, like a man checking his wallet on a crowded train.

She’d known for a while. She just hadn’t had anyone ask her before.

“Yes,” she said.

Miles looked at her. Then he nodded, as if a sum had come out.

“Good,” he said. “I’m glad.”

“Are you?”

“Happy? Busy, mostly. I’ve got a lot of notebooks.” He straightened up off the rail. “I should go and be thanked by the committee. It was good to see you, Elowen. It really was.”

He went in. She stayed a minute longer with the cold on her face, and then she went in too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles saw the man by the pillar on his way across the ballroom.

He’d noticed him during the speech, at the back of his mind, the way you notice one face in a crowd that isn’t doing what the others are doing. Tall. Dark suit. No tie. Hadn’t laughed at the clicker. Now he was standing by himself, with the committee man gone, and he was watching the balcony door with an attention that Miles found, as a scientist, quite interesting.

Hotel security, probably. Or somebody’s security. This was the kind of event where certain old boys brought their own.

He went over.

“Excuse me. Are you with the hotel?”

The man turned his head and looked at him. Miles had a brief, odd feeling, standing there, like stepping out of a lift on to the wrong floor.

“No.”

“Oh. It’s just you’ve been watching that door for some time.” Miles pushed his glasses up. “If you’re worried about the woman on the balcony, she’s fine. I was just talking to her. She doesn’t look like she wants to run.”

The man said nothing for a moment.

“Good,” he said.

“She’s an old friend. From school. She’s married now, apparently, I didn’t catch to whom.” Miles held out his hand. “Miles Wei. I gave the speech.”

“I know.” The man shook it, briefly. His hand was dry and very strong and there was a heavy ring on it. “Zhao Zhendong. I’m her husband.”

“Oh,” said Miles.

He took his hand back. He looked at the balcony door, and then at the man, and did, quite quickly, what he was good at, which was work out from what was around a thing what the thing was.

“Then she really doesn’t look like she wants to run,” he said. “Congratulations.”

He went off to find the committee. Behind him Zhao stood exactly where he’d been left, and stood there, and felt the folded page in his pocket, and for the first time all night didn’t know what to do with his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him by the pillar.

“Zhendong?”

“Do you want to go?”

“Already?”

“If you like.”

She looked at his face. “Did Miles talk to you?”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

“He asked me if I was the hotel’s.” A pause. “He said you didn’t look as if you wanted to run.”

She was quiet. Then she stepped closer. “And are you jealous?”

“No.”

“Zhendong.”

“Yes,” he said, much lower. “A little.”

“How little?”

“Enough.”

He leaned down towards her. Then he stopped, a breath away from her mouth, there in the middle of the ballroom, with old teachers going past behind him, and he didn’t come any closer. She could feel him not doing it. He was waiting. Even now, even here, he was leaving the last inch to her, the way he’d left it since the night she’d written unless I ask on page two.

She caught his lapel, rose on her toes, and took it.

It wasn’t discreet. She didn’t mean it to be. Somebody behind them said, “Oh, my word,” which might have been Mr. Hui. Zhao’s hand came to the small of her back and held on, hard.

“I’m happy,” she said against his mouth. “That’s what I told him.”

“I heard.”

“You can’t have. You were inside.”

“I could see your face.” His thumb moved on her spine. “Don’t tell me I’m not jealous.”

“I’d never,” she said, and kissed him again.

Across the room, Aurelia put down her glass. “Well,” she said to her husband. “Look at that.”

Chen Si looked. “Hm.”

“Your brother has finally stopped looking like an undertaker.”

“Please don’t tell him.”

“I think,” said Aurelia, with enormous satisfaction, “that table nine has been a triumph.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left a little before eleven.

The dress had been a good choice. The shoes had not. By the time they got to the car she was walking with great dignity and very small steps, and her face had gone tight with the effort of not limping.

“Your feet hurt,” said Zhao.

“No.”

He opened the car door and waited.

“A bit.”

He went on waiting.

“A lot,” said Elowen, and got in.

He got in beside her and shut the door, and before the car had even moved he’d bent and taken her ankles and lifted her feet into his lap and pulled the shoes off. Her feet were freezing. He put his hands round them, both of them, and held them, and his palms were very warm.

She let her head fall back against the seat.

“You could have said something an hour ago.”

“I was having a nice time.”

“You were limping.”

“I was being elegant.”

He rubbed his thumb along the arch of one foot. She made a noise she wasn’t proud of. The harbour lights went by outside.

“Did you have a nice time?” she said.

“Yes.”

“Even with Miles?”

“Even with Miles.” He was looking at her feet, not at her. “If you’d wanted to take the train home,” he said, “I’d have bought the railway.”

She stared at him. Then she put her hands over her face and laughed until the seat shook.

“The railway.”

“So you could sit down.”

“Not a ticket. Not a first-class carriage.”

“There’d be other people in the carriage.”

“You can’t buy a railway because my feet hurt.”

“I could try.”

She took her hands down and looked at him. He was quite serious, as he usually was when he said the worst things, with her cold feet held in both his hands as if they were something he’d been trusted with.

She leaned over and kissed him. Her mouth tasted of the wine from dinner, and his of nothing at all, because he hadn’t touched his glass all night.

“Thank you for coming,” she said.

“Thank you for asking me.”

His right hand let go of her foot for a moment and went to the inside of his jacket, and touched the pocket, and came back. She watched it. This time she didn’t pretend she hadn’t.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Gala, Zero Ceasefire
chapters.desc: The Chen Foundation gala. Qiu Wen crushes her peony and she puts a knife to his knuckles and asks after his brother’s hands. Then Zhao dances, very badly, on purpose.
chapters.content:
The dress came on a Tuesday in a long flat box, with a smaller black case on top.

Elowen opened them on the bed. The dress was silk, a blue she’d never worn, darker than the sky and lighter than navy, the colour the harbour went for about ten minutes after the sun was gone. The case held a pair of sapphire drops and a thin bracelet of the same stones.

She knew the setting the moment she saw the clasp.

“These are Aurelia’s.”

Zhao, by the window with his phone, didn’t look up. “Yes.”

“You bought them from her.”

“From her shop. She served me herself.”

“What did she say?”

“That you’d better wear them properly. And that I should have bought the necklace.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“She said it was too expensive.” He did look up then. “After she’d shown it to me.”

Elowen laughed. “She’s impossible.”

“You’re friends.”

“That isn’t a contradiction.”

She tried it on that night. He was waiting on the landing when she came out, and he didn’t say anything for a while, which was the thing he did now instead of saying something. He took the bracelet out of the case and fastened it on her wrist himself, his big fingers very careful with the clasp. Then, halfway down the stairs, he stopped her with a hand on her arm and lifted her wrist and kissed the inside of it, just above the stones.

“Now you’re dressed,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Chen Foundation held its Spring Gala every year at the Grand Meridian, a fortnight before New Year, and every year it raised more money than the year before because Chen Si sent the invitations personally and nobody in the city had ever been brave enough to send one back.

This year the foundation had commissioned Elowen’s shop to do the flowers.

She’d built three columns of peonies for the ballroom, each one taller than Zhao, the stems packed into hidden water around branches of flowering quince. Peonies in January had meant Chile, the last of their season, flown in on Tuesday at a price she’d made the foundation’s accountant sit down to hear. They’d come in tight green balls, and she’d kept them cold and brought them up in warm water a few at a time, so that tonight they’d be at the exact moment between bud and bloom: blush and ivory and one deep raspberry pink, some still closed like fists, some just open far enough to show the crumpled silk in the middle.

The biggest column stood behind the stage. She was beside it at seven, making one last adjustment, when Aurelia came across the empty ballroom in champagne satin with pearls at her throat and a satin band in her hair.

“You’re late.”

“I’m forty minutes early.”

“Late for me.” Aurelia looked up at the column. “They’re beautiful.”

“Thank you.”

“Too much pink.”

“It’s a spring gala.”

“I know what season it is.”

“Then you know why it’s pink.”

Aurelia looked at the raspberry one. “I’d have done gold leaf on the quince.”

“I know you would. That’s why the foundation asked me.”

Chen Si, coming in behind his wife in a black dinner jacket and thin black gloves, said, “Ladies,” in the tone of a man stepping into a room where two people were already holding knives. “My wife is insulting your flowers.”

“Your wife insults everything,” said Elowen. “That’s how I know the evening’s going well.”

Aurelia gave her a look of pure delight, and then held out a hand, palm up. “Give me your phone.”

“Why?”

“Because if anything ever happens and you need my husband, I want you to be able to find him.” Aurelia took it, opened the contacts, and began to type. “And not by ringing yours, because yours will just go and do something.” Her thumbs stopped. She scrolled. She scrolled back. She looked up.

“Elowen.”

“What?”

“Who is Unknown?”

“My husband.”

Aurelia turned the screen round and held it up so Chen Si could see. Under U, between UNCLE PAK MARKET and the van insurance, there it was. Unknown. Nothing else. No surname. No photograph.

“You’ve been married to him for ten months,” said Aurelia, “and he’s still Unknown.”

“I know who it is.”

“He bought you the sapphires you’re wearing.”

“I know who bought them.”

“I have him under My Husband, with three hearts,” Aurelia said to Chen Si, as if he might not know. “And a photograph of him asleep in Positano with his mouth open.”

“I’m aware,” said Chen Si.

Aurelia saved his number under CHEN SI (FOR EMERGENCIES, NOT GOSSIP) and handed the phone back with the air of someone who’d done a great kindness and expected to be paid for it in the spring. Elowen put it away without looking at the U.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom filled from eight. Chen Si worked it the way he worked everything, without hurry, a hand on a shoulder here, three words there, always knowing where every important person in the room was standing. Aurelia stayed a step behind him and corrected his names.

Zhao arrived from the Docks at a quarter past, in navy, with his hair swept back and the one strand already falling out of it. He found Elowen by the column in the time it took him to cross the room, and put his hand on the small of her back.

“You did this?”

“Me and four people and a lorry.”

He looked up at it. “It’s beautiful.”

“Please don’t start,” said Aurelia, passing. “If you two compliment each other in front of the peonies they’ll go off.”

For a while everything was easy.

Then his hand on her back went still.

She looked where he was looking. A man had come in through the main doors in dark grey, with two other men a step behind him, and was being greeted by the foundation’s chairman like an old friend.

She’d never seen him in person. She knew the name anyway.

Qiu Wen.

Qiu Wen, whose brother Lei had had his hands held over a burning drum in April for a count of twenty because their men had thrown a bottle of petrol at her van with Xiao Pan standing next to it. Qiu Wen, who’d been asking questions about her shop in May, about the new vans, about what time she opened. Qiu Wen, who should not be here, and was, with a donor’s gold ribbon on his lapel.

“I’ll have him taken out,” Zhao said quietly.

“No.”

“Elowen.”

“It’s Chen Si’s gala. It’s a charity. I’m not having a fight under my flowers.” She put her hand over his wrist. “Find out how he got in. Don’t do anything here.”

He looked down at her. He didn’t like it. She could feel exactly how much he didn’t like it through his sleeve.

“All right,” he said, and didn’t move from her side.

Qiu Wen took his time. He shook hands, he accepted a glass, he said something that made the chairman laugh. And then he walked, quite slowly, the whole length of the ballroom, to the column of peonies behind the stage, and stopped in front of it.

“What beautiful flowers,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“Mrs. Zhao.” He inclined his head. “I’ve heard so much about your shop. Corner of Ferry Road, isn’t it? Open at seven. You do the market first. You’re always there before your boy.”

Something cold went down the back of Elowen’s neck.

He reached out and took the raspberry peony in his hand. The only one in the column. The one that was furthest open. He held its head in his palm as if he were weighing it.

“Such a soft thing to build so much around,” he said. “Peonies bruise if you hold them too hard. Did you know? You can’t see it at first. Then the next morning...”

He closed his hand.

The petals crushed between his fingers with a small damp sound. When he opened his palm the flower was a brown wet rag on the stem, and one crumpled petal fell on to the stage.

Zhao moved.

Elowen moved first. She stepped between them, took the florist’s knife out of the pocket of her dress, where she’d carried a knife at every event she’d ever done, and with her other hand she caught Qiu Wen’s wrist. She turned it palm down and laid the edge of the blade across his knuckles, flat to the bone, and pressed, just enough.

A thin bright line opened across the back of his hand.

He went perfectly still.

“How are your brother’s hands?” said Elowen.

She said it quite politely. She was surprised by how polite it came out. Her own hand wasn’t shaking at all.

For the first time, Qiu Wen’s face changed. Not much. But she saw it go.

“I cut stems for a living,” she said. “I know exactly how much pressure it takes to get through something green. Please don’t touch my work again.” She took the knife off his skin, and let go of his wrist, and wiped the blade on a napkin from the nearest table, and folded it back into her pocket. “Enjoy the evening, Mr. Qiu. Do have some of the canapés. The shrimp are very good.”

Qiu Wen looked at the line on his hand. A bead of blood was gathering at one end of it. He looked up at her, and then past her at Zhao, who was standing so close behind her that she could feel his chest against her shoulder blades.

“You’ve married a brave woman,” Qiu Wen said.

“I married her,” said Zhao. “You’re standing in front of her. I’d move.”

Qiu Wen smiled. He took a handkerchief out of his breast pocket, wrapped it round his hand without looking, and walked away towards the bar.

Only then did her hand start to shake, a little, in the folds of the silk.

Zhao took it and held it.

“You shouldn’t have done that,” he said, very low.

“I know.”

“He’ll remember it.”

“So will I.” She took the dead peony off its stem and dropped it in the pocket with the knife. Then she reached into the bucket hidden in the base of the column and brought out a spare, ivory, not quite open, and put it where the other one had been. “He knew what time I open.”

“I know.”

“Zhendong. He knew Xiao Pan comes after me.”

“I heard.” His thumb went across her knuckles, over and over. “Stay by the column. Bao’s here. I’ll be ten minutes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao had already found out. Bao always found out. By the time Zhao reached the service corridor there was a text on his phone, and a man waiting for him in a small grey room behind the kitchens where the hotel kept spare chairs.

His name was Toh. He was a deputy at the port authority. He sat on the Chen Foundation’s donor committee because the port gave the foundation money every year and liked to watch where it went, and two weeks ago he’d added a name to the donor list, late, as a personal favour. He’d been paid for the favour through a freight company he’d never heard of. He’d thought it was harmless. A name on a list, at a party.

He stood up when Zhao came in. He’d been crying, a little.

“Mr. Zhao, I didn’t know who he was.”

“Sit down.”

Toh sat. Zhao didn’t. He stood by the stack of gilt chairs and looked at him.

“You put the man whose people burned my wife’s van in a room with my wife,” he said. “For money.”

“I didn’t know.”

“You’ve worked at the port for fifteen years. You knew.”

Toh opened his mouth and shut it again.

“You’ll resign on Monday,” said Zhao. “Ill health. You’ll give Chen Si every file you’ve ever signed for money, every name and every boat, and you’ll do it before you leave. And then you’ll leave.”

“Leave?”

“The city. With your family. You can pick where. You can’t pick here.”

“Mr. Zhao, my children are in school—“

“Then you should have thought about them two weeks ago.” Zhao went to the door. “If I see you again, I won’t be the one who comes. You’ll just stop coming home one night, and your wife will spend the rest of her life wondering which night it was.”

He opened the door. Bao was outside.

“Take him out the back. Nobody sees him go.”

“Yes, sir.”

It had taken less than ten minutes. He hadn’t touched the man. He didn’t need to. Toh would be on a boat by Wednesday, and Qiu Wen, at the bar, would know by midnight that the door he’d come in by had been bricked up behind him.

He went back to the ballroom, washed his face in the gents, and was beside his wife again before the soup.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si’s speech was at nine, and it was short, because Chen Si believed that a man who needed more than four minutes to ask a room for money had already lost it. After it the band began and the floor filled.

Aurelia stood up. “Dance with me.”

“Always,” said Chen Si, and did. He danced the way he walked, precisely and without effort. Aurelia danced as if the ballroom had been built for her, which, Elowen supposed, in a sense it had.

“They look happy,” she said.

“They are.”

“Do you want to dance?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t dance.”

“Are you afraid you’re bad at it?”

He looked at her. “I’m not afraid of anything in this room.”

“Then prove it.”

She held out her hand. He looked at it for so long she thought he’d refuse. Then he took it and stood up, and let her lead him on to the floor, and put his hand on her back at a correct and rigid distance, and began to move like a man following instructions for assembling a piece of military equipment.

“Relax,” she said.

“I am relaxed.”

“You look like you’re escorting a prisoner.”

He moved his left foot. She moved her right. He went much too far, and she followed him straight into the back of the port authority’s chairman, who said, “Oh!” and moved away fast when he saw who it was.

“Zhendong.”

“I followed you.”

“You followed me into a man.”

He stepped on her shoe. She looked down at it, and then up at him, and he said, very seriously, “Your feet are very small,” and she put her forehead on his chest and laughed until she couldn’t stand up straight.

He pulled her in close while she laughed.

Then he turned her, perfectly, in time, and turned her again, and suddenly they were dancing. Properly. Easily. His hand had gone low and warm on her back and his feet knew exactly where they were going.

She lifted her head. “Oh.”

“What?”

“You can dance.”

“I never said I couldn’t.”

“You let me think it.”

“You liked teaching me.” His mouth almost moved. “You do a thing with your eyebrows.”

She stared at him. “You were doing it on purpose.”

He didn’t answer. He turned her under his arm and caught her and brought her back against him, so close she could feel his heart under the navy wool, and the music slowed down, and she gave up arguing.

Over his shoulder she saw Qiu Wen at the edge of the floor with his glass and his wrapped hand, watching them.

So did Zhao. She felt him see it. He didn’t stop dancing. He didn’t look away from the man either. He put his hand along her jaw, and bent his head, and kissed her, slowly, in the middle of the floor, for exactly as long as he wanted to, while the man who’d crushed her peony stood there and watched.

When he lifted his head, Qiu Wen had gone.

“That was for him,” she said.

“No,” said Zhao. “He just happened to be standing there.”

✦ ✦ ✦
