They left a little before midnight. Aurelia caught her in the cloakroom, flushed and pleased, holding her own shoes.

“I’ve decided the evening was a success. Your flowers were the best thing in it. I’ll deny I said that.”

“You spent all night criticising them.”

“That’s how I show love.”

Elowen laughed. “Come for New Year,” she said, before she could think about it. “At Baba’s. Eve dinner. Raiden and Evangeline will be there, and Eliana, and Ah Sim’s going to do too much food. Baba said bring whoever.”

Aurelia’s face did something unguarded. “Both of us?”

“Both of you.”

“I’ll bring dessert.”

“Don’t bring the whole shop,” said Chen Si, behind her, holding her coat.

Zhao, waiting by the door, said, “Bring her early. There’s a table to set.”

Aurelia looked at him. “He wants me to work.”

“You’re family,” said Zhao.

Aurelia didn’t say anything for a moment, which for Aurelia was a remarkable length of time. Then she turned to her husband.

“Did you hear what he called me?”

“I heard.”

“I’m bringing two desserts,” said Aurelia, and swept out.

chapters.title: The Question He Almost Asks
chapters.desc: In the car home from the gala he gets as far as her name. On their first anniversary she gives him a camellia from the hill, he gives her the key to the armory, and in the middle of the night his phone rings.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s for if you just want to come in.”
chapters.content:
In the car home from the gala she had the sapphires in her lap and a dead peony in her pocket, and her husband was quiet.

He’d been quiet since the cloakroom, and she let him. In ten months she’d learned that he went quiet when he was carrying something, and put it down in his own time or not at all.

The car went under the long bridge at the end of the waterfront. For a moment the lights went out.

“Elowen.”

“Mm?”

“Why did you—“

The lights came back. He’d stopped.

She turned her head. He was looking at the window, at his own dark reflection in it, and his hand on hers had gone completely still.

“Why did I what?”

“Nothing.”

“Zhendong.”

She knew what it was. She’d known since the mountain, since he’d lain awake beside her in the rain and thought she was asleep. She’d felt him not ask it a hundred times since, at breakfast, in the shop, with his face in her hair.

“You were going to ask why I married you,” she said.

He didn’t answer for so long that the bridge was well behind them.

“No,” he said.

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“I know.” He turned his hand over under hers. “It doesn’t matter tonight.”

She could have answered it anyway. She almost did. But he hadn’t asked, not really, and she had a feeling that if she answered a question he hadn’t asked he’d never believe a word of it.

So she traced the lines on his palm with her thumb until the car turned up the hill, and the question sat between them on the seat the whole way home, like a third passenger nobody had introduced.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of their first anniversary, Zhao Zhendong forgot it.

That was the only conclusion she could reach.

He came down at six while she was making eggs, kissed her forehead, complained that Noodle had buried one of his slippers in her parsley, looked at his phone, and went to the Docks.

Not one word.

Elowen stood by the stove with the spatula in her hand and stared at the front door.

Then she looked at the calendar on the kitchen wall, where she’d circled the seventeenth of March in red pen in January, twice, so hard it had gone through to February.

Her phone rang.

“Have you eaten?” said Granny Yip.

“I’m cooking.”

“Good. Where’s that husband of yours?”

“He’s gone to work.”

There was a pause at the other end of the line. “Today?”

“Apparently.”

“Hm,” said Granny Yip, and then, very casually, “Men with money think they can buy anything and they can’t remember a single date. My husband forgot our anniversary for forty-one years.”

Elowen put the spatula down. “Granny. Did he ask you to ring me?”

“Who?”

“Granny.”

“Eat your eggs,” said Granny Yip, and hung up.

Before she’d even put the phone down it buzzed.

Xiao Pan: Happy anniversary boss!!!

Xiao Pan: don’t let Mr. Zhao pretend he forgot. he ordered something big last week and made me swear

Xiao Pan: I’ve said nothing

Elowen: What did he order?

Xiao Pan: I know nothing

Xiao Pan: the roses are here I have to go

She stood in the kitchen and laughed out loud. He’d recruited half the market to make her think he’d forgotten.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came home at seven. She was in the glass room with her sleeves pushed up, cutting a damaged leaf off one of the camellia cuttings Mr. Wen had sent down in the autumn.

“Good evening.”

“Good evening.”

“How was the shop?”

“Busy.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

He stood in the doorway in his navy suit with his tie loose, perfectly calm, asking her nothing.

She put the secateurs down. “Have you forgotten something?”

He considered this. “Should I have brought something home?”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she picked up the flat package she’d wrapped that morning in brown paper and string and held it out.

“Happy anniversary, Zhendong.”

He took it. Something happened in his face that wasn’t calm at all.

Inside was a narrow frame of dark wood. Under the glass lay a single flower, pressed flat: five deep rose-red petals, overlapping like the scales of a fish, the colour gone a little darker than it would have been on the hill but still unmistakably itself.

A card was tucked into the corner of the frame in an old man’s careful hand. Wen Tea Estate. Fallen on the 21st of February. Not picked.

“He sent it last month,” said Elowen. “It came down on its own, in the wind, and he had the botanist press it. He said he thought we should have something from the hill that nobody had to take from it.” She watched his face. “You told me in September it only flowers in February and March. I was going to go up and see it. Then it rained for three weeks.”

He didn’t say anything for a while. He held the frame very carefully, in both hands, the way he’d held her feet in the car.

“You framed it,” he said at last.

“It deserved better than a drawer.”

“You remembered.”

“You bought me a mountain, Zhendong. I remember things.”

He put the frame down on the worktable, square to the edge, and looked at her.

“I didn’t forget,” he said.

“I know. Xiao Pan told me. Granny Yip rang me at seven.”

“I asked her to.”

“I know you did.” She stepped closer and put her hands flat on his chest. “Where is it?”

“Where is what?”

“Whatever Xiao Pan swore not to tell me about.”

He nodded at the glass. In the courtyard, beside the lemon tree, somebody had set a big ceramic vase on the gravel and filled it with white and the palest pink, sweet peas and ranunculus and lily of the valley, the whole thing taller than she was. Ranunculus and lily of the valley. What she’d carried at the registry, a year ago this morning.

“That isn’t it,” he said.

He took his hand out of his jacket pocket. There was a key in it, on a plain silver ring. Old-fashioned. Heavy. No tag.

She stared at it. “Another one?”

“The fourteenth.”

She remembered the thirteen he’d given her when she moved in, one for every lock in the house. And the one door at the bottom of the basement stairs she’d had no key for, only the code to the safe room inside it, the door to the place where he kept the things that weren’t for her.

“The armory,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You said that one wasn’t mine.”

“It wasn’t.” He put it in her palm and closed her fingers over it with his. “You’ve got a key for everything that has a reason. The gates. The shop. The plant room. The safe room has a code because you’d need it in a hurry. This one doesn’t have a reason.” He kept his hand round hers. “It’s for if you just want to come in. When I’m down there. You don’t have to knock. You don’t have to say why.”

She looked down at their hands. She could feel the key’s teeth in her palm.

“Just to come in,” she said.

“Yes.”

She didn’t say anything, because she couldn’t. She put her arms round him and her face in his shirt, and he held her in the glass room with the key between them.

✦ ✦ ✦

At dinner she served him herself, the fish and the greens and the soup, and poured his tea, and he let her.

“Jinx rang about Xiao Pan’s bike,” she said. “May. She wants to meet him first. She says if he’s an idiot she won’t build it.”

“He’s an idiot.”

“He’s a good idiot.”

“Then she’ll build it.” Afterwards she put the frame on the table on his side of the bed, and the key on hers. He took off his watch and his rings one at a time while she brushed her hair, and she watched him in the mirror.

“Do you remember the wedding?” she said.

“Yes.”

“What I wore?”

“Red. The silk you’d bought for New Year and never worn.”

“What I carried?”

“Ranunculus. Granny Yip’s lily of the valley. Cream ribbon off your own bag.”

“What time it was?”

He looked at her in the glass.

“Nine forty-one.”

She put the brush down. “You remember the minute.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He was quiet. Then he said, “In case you changed your mind.”

She turned round on the stool.

“The registration took eight minutes,” he said. “I looked at the clock on the wall when you’d signed. I thought, if she decides she doesn’t want it, if she wakes up next week and sees what she’s done, then at least I’ll know exactly how long she was mine.” He set his last ring down in the dish. “I’ve known every day since, how long. To the minute.”

She looked at him.

“I haven’t changed my mind,” she said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Mostly.” He came over and stood in front of her. “Some mornings.”

She stood up off the stool and took his hand.

“Do you know what I want,” she said, “for my anniversary?”

“Tell me.”

“You.”

“You’ve got me.”

“Not quite.”

She walked him backwards to the bed. When the backs of his knees hit it he sat, and looked up at her, and she stood between his knees and pushed her fingers into his hair and pulled his head back a little, and kissed him, slowly, from above.

“Do you remember what you promised,” she said against his mouth, “on page two?”

“That I wouldn’t touch you unless you asked.”

“Mm. I’ve been asking for a year.”

“I noticed.”

“Tonight I’m not asking.” She put her hands on his shoulders and pushed, and he went back on to the pillows and stayed there, watching her with a dark, interested stillness. She climbed over him and knelt astride his hips in her nightdress. Then she took his wrists, one in each hand, and pressed them down into the mattress on either side of his head.

He let her. He could have thrown her off with one arm. He lay there and let her, and his breathing changed.

“Tonight,” she said, “you ask.”

He looked up at her. His eyes had gone black.

She bent and kissed the corner of his mouth, and stopped. Kissed his jaw, and stopped. Put her mouth to the place under his ear where his pulse was going hard, and felt him try to turn his head after her and stopped him by leaning her weight into his wrists.

“Elowen.”

“Ask.”

“Kiss me.”

She kissed him. Once. Lightly. Took it away again.

His hands turned under hers. She held them down.

“That’s not enough,” he said, low.

“Then ask properly.”

He shut his eyes for a second. When he opened them she could see exactly what it was costing him not to simply roll her over, and she could see him decide to pay it.

“Please,” he said. “Please. Come here.”

Something in her chest went soft and fierce at the same time. She came.

She let go of his wrists then, and his hands were on her at once, her waist, her back, the back of her head, as if he’d been holding his breath for a year and had just been allowed to let it go. He kissed her the way he hadn’t let himself kiss her at the gala or the reunion or anywhere with people watching. She pushed his shirt up and he pulled it off, and her nightdress went somewhere and neither of them looked where. She kept him on his back. Every time he tried to move she put her hand flat on his chest and he stopped, and asked again, his voice going rougher each time, please, and Elowen, and please, until she stopped making him ask, and took him in, and they both stopped being able to speak in sentences at all.

She set the pace. He let her set it. His hands shook on her hips. The lamp threw their shadow huge on the wall, and the framed camellia sat on the table beside them, and outside the window the March wind moved the lemon tree against the glass.

At the end, when he was gripping her so hard she’d have marks in the morning and his head was pressed back into the pillow, she leaned down to his ear and said it.

“Yours, Zhendong.”

He made a sound she’d never heard him make. He pulled her down against his chest and held her there with both arms and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the lamp was the only light, she lay with her cheek on his chest and traced the long Block C scar low on his side with one fingertip.

“Yours,” she said again, quietly, to see what he’d do.

His hand stopped moving in her hair.

He didn’t answer. He lifted her chin and looked at her as if he were checking the date on something.

“And you’re mine?” he said.

“As long as you remember I’m also mine.”

“I remember.”

“Good.”

He kissed her forehead. She fell asleep with his heartbeat under her ear, and the last thing she thought was that he hadn’t asked her the question from the car, and that she’d have answered it tonight, every word.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning his phone rang.

He had it before the second ring. He was out of the bed and across the room before she was properly awake, standing at the window in the dark with his back to her.

“What.”

She heard Chen Si’s voice, small and tinny, saying something fast.

“Say it again.”

A pause.

“Which channel.”

Zhao turned, found the remote on the dresser, and switched on the television on the wall with the sound almost all the way down. The room filled with blue light.

A presenter. A building with flags in front of it. And along the bottom of the screen, in white capitals on red:

BREAKING · INTERPOL RED NOTICE ISSUED FOR SHIPPING MAGNATE ZHAO ZHENDONG

Elowen sat up in the bed and pulled the sheet round her.

On the screen the presenter was talking over footage of container ships. A United Nations panel of experts, the report on an arms embargo, published that evening in New York. An annex naming a network of shipping and finance companies alleged to have moved weapons into four conflict zones under embargo. A request from a member state, which the presenter didn’t name. A Red Notice, circulated by Interpol from Lyon to police forces in a hundred and ninety-odd countries: locate, and provisionally arrest, pending extradition.

Then his photograph. Not a grainy surveillance still. The good one, from a shipping awards dinner three years ago, in a beige suit with his hair swept back. Under it his name.

Zhao muted it.

“Is the notice public?” he said into the phone. His voice was perfectly level. “Not just a diffusion. The notice.”

He listened.

“Which companies.”

He listened again for longer, and his face, lit blue from the side, didn’t change at all as Chen Si read them out. Then one name made it change. Only a little.

“That company was never mine.”

Chen Si said something.

“I don’t care what the report says. Find me who signed for it. Originals, not summaries. Every authorisation.” He was walking now, the length of the room and back. “Wake the lawyers. All of them, every jurisdiction. Nobody moves anything. Nobody shreds anything. Nobody calls anyone named in that annex without a lawyer in the room. And find out who asked for the notice.”

A pause.

“I know, Si. I know.” His voice dropped. “Keep the family out of it. Hers. Yours. Keep them out.”

He ended the call. He stood in the middle of the room with the phone in his hand and his face on the silent screen behind him.

“Zhendong,” said Elowen.

He turned round.

She could see him decide. She could see the easy thing go across his face: business, go back to sleep, I’ll deal with it before breakfast. He’d been saying that sort of thing to people for twenty years. He’d been saying it to her, in other words, for ten months.

He didn’t say it. He came and sat on the edge of the bed.

“There’s a UN report,” he said. “It says companies of mine sent guns into four countries under embargo. Somebody’s asked Interpol to have me arrested if I cross a border.”

She looked at the screen. At his face. At the word NOTICE.

“Did you do it?”

She asked it quietly. It wasn’t an accusation. She just needed to know, and she wasn’t going to be frightened out of asking.

He looked at her, and didn’t look away.

“I’ve sold guns my whole life,” he said. “I’ve put them on boats with false papers. I’ve done things that wouldn’t survive daylight. You married that. You knew it.”

“I know.”

“Some of the companies in that report are mine. Some of the shipments, I know about. Some I’ve never seen.” He breathed out. “I’m not going to tell you I’m innocent before I know what they’re saying I did.”

She sat there with the sheet round her shoulders. Then she reached out and took his hand, the one without the phone in it.

“Thank you,” she said. “For not saying go back to sleep.”

His fingers closed hard round hers.

On the table beside him, in the blue light, the pressed camellia lay flat under its glass. On her side, the fourteenth key.

She got out of bed and found her clothes.

chapters.title: A Red Notice With His Face on It
chapters.desc: His phone won’t stop ringing and he’s stopped eating, so every night she takes a bowl down to the basement. Then the boy who used to sit on her wall walks into the shop as a detective and tells her which footnote to read.
chapters.content:
By the end of the first week Elowen had come to hate the sound of his phone.

It rang at breakfast, in the car, in the middle of sentences, and once in the glass room while he was looking at a new leaf on one of Mr. Wen’s cuttings. He’d listened for less than a minute and walked out with his tea still in his hand.

A buyer in Antwerp withdrew from a contract by email. A captain who’d sailed for him since before Bao was hired sent his resignation through a lawyer. Two banks froze accounts pending review. A broker who’d eaten dinner at their table in February told a newspaper he’d never met the man. His photograph was on the front of the business pages three days running.

And he’d stopped eating.

Not altogether. He drank coffee. He took two bites of whatever was put in front of him and then looked at it as if it were an appointment he didn’t have time to keep. On Tuesday his dinner went back to the kitchen untouched. On Wednesday he ate half a bowl of soup and left the rest to go cold beside a stack of shipping manifests.

He’d moved downstairs, a desk in the armory itself among the steel cabinets, three screens on it, and he sat there until two and three in the morning under the hard white light.

On Friday night, at a quarter past nine, Elowen went down the basement stairs with a bowl in her hands and the fourteenth key in her pocket.

She didn’t knock.

He didn’t look up when the door opened. “I’m working.”

“I can see that.”

“I’ll eat later.”

“You said that yesterday.” She set the bowl down on the manifests in front of him. Rice, steamed fish, greens, a little of the black bean sauce he liked. “You have a call in ten minutes. Bao told me. So you have ten minutes to eat.”

He looked at the bowl. “I had lunch.”

“What did you have?”

He didn’t answer. She pulled a stool over from the workbench and sat on it on the other side of the desk, and put the chopsticks down next to his hand, and waited.

He breathed out through his nose. It was the sound of a man discovering that an argument had been arranged in advance and that he’d lost it before he came in.

He ate. She didn’t watch him do it, because she knew he’d hate that, and she didn’t ask him anything until he’d finished.

“That’s all?” he said, when he had.

“I’m not asking you anything while you’re eating.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth. Then the phone went, and they both looked at it, and he picked it up.

“Chen Si.”

She stood. As she passed his chair he caught her hand and held her fingers for a moment without looking at her, the phone still at his ear, and then let them go.

She brought him food every night after that. She learned which calls he could put off, and that when he pressed the bridge of his nose he’d read the same page three times, and that he could listen to three lawyers arguing and sign papers at the same time and forget the tea at his elbow for two hours.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop started losing customers on Monday.

At first she blamed the rain. Then a woman came in, picked up the newspaper Xiao Pan had left folded by the till, looked at the photograph on the front, and looked at Elowen.

“Is that your husband?”

Elowen put the ribbon down. “Yes.”

“I’ll come back another time,” the woman said, and didn’t.

By lunch two standing orders had been cancelled by text. A young couple came in to talk about their wedding, saw the paper, whispered, and went out again, and the girl looked back through the glass with real pity, which was worse.

Xiao Pan was holding a bunch of white tulips very still. “Boss. Should I put the papers away?”

“No.”

“People keep looking at it.”

“They’re allowed to look.” She took the tulips from him and started trimming the stems. “Put the radio on. Something with music.”

The shop was quieter than it had been in five years. She wasn’t going to hide behind her own counter because of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday afternoon a man came in with a paper bag and looked at her for a while before he said anything.

She was cutting eucalyptus. She didn’t look up straight away. When she did, he said, “You still cut on the angle.”

The scissors stopped.

It took her a second. His face had got longer and harder, and it didn’t move very much; it never had. But he was standing the way he’d always stood, with his weight on one foot, as if he’d just climbed down off a wall and might go back up it.

“Song Wei Long.”

“Hello, Elowen.”

“You got tall.”

“That generally happens.” He put the bag on the counter. “Sesame cakes. The shop by the old school still makes them.”

She opened it. The smell came up, toasted and sweet, and she was nine years old and sitting on the wall between his house and her father’s, with her school bag beside her, refusing to go in because somebody had said something about her mother at school.

“You used to steal these out of my lunch,” he said.

“I was checking them for poison.”

“Every day.”

“You can’t be too careful.”

He didn’t smile. He’d never really smiled. But his eyes did something that she remembered.

“How’s Yu Chen?”

“Still next door. Still pretending he isn’t watching your sister’s window.” He glanced at the newspaper by the till, and then back at her, and his face settled into something more official. “I’m not here as the boy from the wall.”

He took a wallet out of his jacket and opened it just far enough. A police card. Detective Song Wei Long.

The warmth went out of her chest.

“You’re a detective.”

“Two years.”

“And you’re here about my husband.”

“Partly.” He put the wallet away. “Not officially. Can we talk somewhere?”

She took him into the office at the back and shut the door. He didn’t sit down until she told him to. He put a thick printed document on her desk among the invoices.

“It’s the report. It’s public. You can download it. I thought you might rather read it than have it read to you by a man on television.”

“Why would I read it?”

“Page sixty-one,” said Song Wei Long. “Footnote nine.”

She found it. Dense paragraphs about companies with names like laundry powders. A sentence that said the panel had been assisted by a source with direct operational knowledge of the network. And at the bottom of the page, in very small print:

9. Corporate registry filing, 2015, lists a K. Kang as beneficial owner of Halvard Freight Ltd. See annex 14 for subsequent transfers.

She read it three times.

“Kang,” she said.

“You know the name.”

“He worked for my husband for eight years. He sold my husband’s routes to the Qiu brothers. He was sitting on Zhendong’s desk the first time I walked into that office, and he called me a little girl and told me to go home to my flowers.”

“Then you know him better than the panel does.” Song Wei Long leaned forward. “That company was set up six years ago. Long before he sold the routes. Somebody planned for a very long time to make your husband’s cargo look like his own, and then gave the panel the map.”

“Is any of it true?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “Some of it, I’d guess. Your husband isn’t a florist. But some of it was put there on purpose. That footnote is the only place they slipped.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because you used to sit on that wall when something was wrong and wait for somebody to come out.” He stood. “Officially, I was never here. Don’t tell anyone I came.”

“Not even my husband?”

“Especially not your husband.”

“Why?”

“Because I’d put money on him having a file on everyone who’s ever said good morning to you.” He opened the door. “And I’d rather not be on the second page of it.”

At the front of the shop he turned back.

“Don’t believe all of that report,” he said. “But don’t decide everyone in it is innocent either. Including the ones you love.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went down to the armory that night with the report under her arm and no food at all, and he noticed.

“You haven’t brought anything.”

“Page sixty-one,” she said, and put it on the desk in front of him. “Footnote nine.”

He read it. Then he read it again, and his hand, lying flat beside the page, went completely still.

“Where did you get this?”

“Someone brought it to the shop.”

“Who?”

“An old neighbour. He’s a policeman. He said he’d never been there.”

Zhao looked up. “His name.”

“Zhendong.”

“His name, Elowen.”

“Song Wei Long. He used to live on the other side of the wall at Baba’s. He brought me sesame cakes.”

Zhao’s eyes went back to the page. “Kang,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Six years.” He was talking to the footnote. “He built it six years ago. He sat in my office for six years with that company in his pocket, and he waited.”

“Did you know?”

“No.” He pressed his thumb to the line of tiny print, as if he could hold it down. “When you came to the Docks with your dates, I knew he’d been selling to the Qius. I had Chen Si pull his phone. I’d decided before you’d finished talking what would happen to him.” He wasn’t looking at her. “He was going in the harbour that night.”

She held still.

“And then Bao took you down the stairs,” he said. “And you stopped on the landing. I heard your shoes stop. I knew you could hear the room. I knew you’d know.” He breathed out. “So I broke his fingers and took his keys and let him walk out to a doctor in Salt Street. Because you were on the stairs.”

“Zhendong.”

“He walked out and he used the time.” His voice was colder than she’d ever heard it in this house. “Somebody’s going to pay for this.”

“Who?”

He didn’t answer.

“Kang?”

“Kang. And whoever paid him.”

“You don’t know who that is yet.”

“I’ll know.”

“Then know it first.” She came round the desk. “You don’t know who changed the papers. You don’t know who asked for the notice. You know a name in a footnote. And you’re sitting down here hating yourself because you didn’t drown a man the week we met.”

His jaw moved. “I should have.”

“Would it have stopped the company existing?”

He was silent.

“I was on the stairs,” she said. “That’s all. You didn’t do it because I was there. I’m not sorry I was there.”

He looked up at her. Then he said, quite differently, “Be careful of that detective.”

“He brought me cakes.”

“He brought you a weapon and told you where to point it. Police don’t do that for nothing.” He reached for his phone. “I’ll have him checked.”

“No, you won’t.”

He looked at her hand, which had come down flat over his on the phone.

“You’ve been down here eleven nights,” she said. “You keep telling me to go upstairs as if you don’t want me here.”

“I want you here.”

“Then stop sending me away.”

She bent and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth that was almost pain. Then his hand came up into her hair and held on, and he kissed her back as if the eleven nights had been one long held breath and he’d just been allowed to let it out. She ended up half on his lap with the report crushed somewhere between them.

He stood up with her. He turned off the screens one by one with his free hand, without looking, and left the phone face down on the desk, and lifted her, one arm under her knees, and carried her out of the armory.

“You can’t just carry me away.”

“Watch me.”

He carried her up the basement stairs, and through the dark kitchen, and up the main stairs, and kicked the bedroom door shut behind them. He put her down on the bed and stood looking at her in the dark, breathing hard, not from the stairs.

“Zhendong.”

“Don’t talk.”

He came down over her and kissed her again, and there was nothing careful in it this time. He’d been careful for eleven days with lawyers and bankers and men who’d stopped saying his name. He’d run out. His hands shook on the buttons of her shirt and in the end he didn’t bother with them; she heard one go. She pulled his shirt over his head and felt how much weight he’d lost in a week, his ribs under her palms, and something fierce came up in her throat, and she held his face and made him look at her.

“I’m here,” she said.

“I know.”

“You don’t. Look.”

He looked. He looked at her as if she were the only thing in the world that hadn’t been named in an annex. Then he put his face in her neck and she felt him shaking, not from cold, and she wrapped herself round him, arms and legs, and pulled him in.

When he pushed into her it wasn’t slow, and it wasn’t gentle, and she didn’t want it to be. He held her wrists above her head with one hand for a moment and then let go of them, as if he’d frightened himself, and she grabbed his hand and put it back. The bed knocked the wall. She said his name and he said hers, again and again, into her hair, into her mouth, like a man counting things he still had. When it broke over her she bit his shoulder to stay quiet, and he made a sound she felt rather than heard, and held on to her afterwards so tightly she could barely breathe and didn’t ask him to let go.

They lay in the dark. His heart slowed down under her cheek.

“You left the phone,” she said.

“Yes.”

“It’ll be ringing.”

“Let it.”

He was asleep in minutes. She lay awake and listened to him breathe, and thought about a footnote, and about the way Song Wei Long had said the ones you love, as if it were a thing he’d already decided about her.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she went into the study for a pen and found the folder.

It was under a stack of bank letters, label up.

SONG, Wei Long.

She stood very still. Then she opened it.

His date of birth. His police number. A flat on the east side. His cousin’s name, and the house next to her father’s. Photographs: Song Wei Long going into a police station. Song Wei Long at a noodle stall. Song Wei Long outside his own front door with his keys in his hand.

At the top of the first page someone had typed: File opened 24 March 2020. Reason: contact with E. Lin.

The week after the registry. He’d sent her a message that week, she remembered now. Yu Chen says you got married. Congratulations, wall girl. She’d shown it to Zhao at breakfast and laughed.

She turned to the last page.

Three more photographs. Song Wei Long on Ferry Road with a paper bag. Song Wei Long going into her shop. Song Wei Long coming out of it, fourteen minutes later according to the timestamp in the corner, yesterday’s date.

“Good morning,” said Zhao from the door.

She didn’t turn round.

“You’ve had him followed since last March.”

He didn’t pretend not to know what she was holding.

“He sent you a message the week we married. I didn’t know him.”

“So you found out his address.”

“I found out who he was.”

“And yesterday?”

“Yesterday he went into your shop with something in his coat.”

“Cakes. And a report I could have downloaded.”

“I didn’t know that until you told me.”

She put the folder on the desk. Her hands were not quite steady.

“I know you have people round me,” she said. “I know about the cars, and the man outside the shop, and Bao. I’ve known since the first week. I’ve let it go. But this isn’t keeping me safe. This is a file on a man because he knew me before you did.”

He didn’t answer.

“You could have asked me,” she said. “In March. Who’s Song Wei Long? I’d have told you he sat on a wall and stole my lunch.”

“Would you?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the folder for a long moment.

“Then I should have asked,” he said.

It came out quietly, without any of the usual armour on it. She didn’t know what to do with it.

“Close it,” she said. “Now. While I watch.”

He picked up the phone on the desk and rang Bao, and said, “The Song file. Close it. Everyone off him today,” and put the phone down, and held the folder out to her.

She didn’t take it. She looked at him.

“I’m going to work,” she said.

She was at the shop by eight. At half past ten her phone buzzed.

Unknown: Have you eaten?

She looked at it. Then she put the phone face down on the bench, under the eucalyptus, and went to serve a customer who’d come in for a dozen white tulips and hadn’t looked at the newspaper at all.

chapters.title: The Order She Wouldn’t Fill
chapters.desc: A man with a forgettable face orders two funeral wreaths with her husband’s name on the ribbon, and she rings the detective first. Zhao walks out on her for the first time, and comes back from Chen Si’s very late with an apology.
chapters.content:
The man came in on a Wednesday, a little after ten, while she was writing out a delivery slip.

She noticed afterwards that she couldn’t describe him. Not tall, not short. Grey jacket. Clean shoes. Hair combed. A face that seemed to have been put together out of other people’s faces and then left somewhere. If she’d passed him in the market she wouldn’t have looked twice, and she supposed that was the point of him.

“Good morning,” she said. “Can I help?”

“I’d like to order two funeral wreaths.”

She reached for the order book. Wednesdays were always quiet first thing. She did the hotel orders herself on Wednesdays, and Xiao Pan didn’t come in until ten, and today he was late. “I’m sorry for your loss. When are they for?”

“The ninth.”

“Of June?”

“Of June.”

She wrote it down. “Traditional? White?”

“Chrysanthemums. Lilies. A little green.” He looked round the shop, at the buckets, the cooler, the bench where she wired things, the door to the back. “Large. Big enough to be seen from the doorway.”

“And the ribbons?”

“Zhao Zhendong,” said the man. “On both.”

Her pen stopped on the paper.

She looked up. His face hadn’t changed at all. It was pleasant and patient and slightly bored, the face of a man waiting to pay for something.

“I’m sorry?”

“Zhao Zhendong. One on each wreath. Black ribbon, gold letters.” He glanced down at her book. “Is there a problem?”

She closed it. “Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I won’t fill that order.”

“It’s only a name.”

“It isn’t.”

He seemed to think about that. Then he took a small white card out of his jacket and put it on the counter, face up, beside her hand. There was an address on it, typed, and nothing else.

“Then just the peonies,” he said. “White. For the widow.” He looked at her for a moment, almost kindly. “You’ll be here on the ninth, won’t you? It’s a Wednesday. You’re always here on Wednesdays.”

The bell rang when he went out. She watched him through the glass cross the road, turn left, and go into the crowd at the corner, and then she couldn’t find him, though she was looking straight at the place where he’d been.

Only then did she notice her hand on the order book was shaking.

She looked at the card. She didn’t touch it.

She knew what would happen if she rang her husband. She’d seen his face at the gala when Qiu Wen crushed her peony. If she rang him now, somebody would be dead by dinner, and it might be the wrong somebody, and she’d never know.

She rang Song Wei Long.

He answered on the third ring. “Song.”

“It’s Elowen. A man’s just come into the shop and ordered funeral wreaths. With my husband’s name on the ribbons. For the ninth of June.” Her voice was quite steady. She was proud of that. “And white peonies for the widow.”

There was a very short silence.

“Did he touch you?”

“No.”

“Did he leave anything?”

“A card. An address. I haven’t touched it.”

“Don’t. Put a cup over it. I’m sending someone, and I’m coming myself.” His voice didn’t soften, and she was grateful. “Elowen. Ring your husband. But ring him after you’ve had a glass of water.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drank the water. Then she rang Zhao.

“Elowen?”

“A man came into the shop,” she said, and told him. All of it. The ribbons. The ninth. The peonies. You’re always here on Wednesdays.

When she’d finished, there was no sound on the line at all. Not breathing. Not the Docks behind him. Nothing.

“Zhendong?”

“Is Bao there?”

“No.”

“Lock the door.”

“I’m not locking the door.”

“Lock it, Elowen. I’m sending Bao. I’m coming.”

“Song Wei Long’s already on his way.”

The silence came back, different.

“You rang the detective.”

“Yes.”

“Before me.”

“He can find out who that man is.”

“So can I.”

“I know you can,” she said. “That’s why I rang him first.”

He hung up.

He was there in eleven minutes, with Bao a step behind him talking into his earpiece. He came through the door without his jacket, sleeves rolled to the elbow, and crossed the shop in four strides and took her by both arms and looked at her face, all of it, as if he were checking a cargo for damage.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Did he come behind the counter?”

“No.”

“Did he say anything about the house? Your father? Your sisters?”

“No. Just Wednesdays.”

His grip on her arms tightened for a second and then let go. He looked at the cup upside down on the counter.

“Bao. Every camera on the street. Both directions. The bus. The taxis. I want where he went and who he met when he got there.”

“Yes, sir.”

Then he turned back to her. “I’m closing the shop.”

She stared at him. “No.”

“Today. Tomorrow. Until I know who he is.”

“No.”

“Elowen.”

“You’re not closing my shop because a man ordered flowers.”

“A man walked in here and told you to your face that he knows where you’ll be on the day he’s chosen to bury me.” His voice was quite quiet. “This isn’t safe any more.”

“It’s been safe for five years.”

“Until this morning.”

“You can’t shut it every time somebody threatens you. Someone threatens you every week.”

“Not in here.”

“Then let Bao look at the cameras. Let Wei Long find him. But the shop stays open.”

“Bao,” said Zhao, without looking round, “send the girls home.”

“Don’t you dare,” said Elowen.

Bao stood very still in the middle of the shop with his hand halfway to his earpiece, like a man between two oncoming cars.

“I’m not discussing it,” said Zhao.

Something in her went very cold and very calm.

“You’re not discussing it.”

“No.”

“Then get out of my shop.”

His face changed. She watched it close.

He looked at Bao. “Stay here. Inside. All day.”

“I don’t want a guard.”

“You’ve got one.”

“Zhendong—“

He walked out. She thought he would stop at the door. She thought he’d turn round and take a breath, the way he did when he’d gone too far in an argument and was deciding how to come back from it.

He didn’t. The bell rang over his head, and the black car pulled away from the kerb, and he was gone.

In fourteen months he’d never once walked out on her in the middle of a sentence.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao fetched a chair from the storeroom and put it in the corner by the shelves of wrapping paper, and sat on it with his hands on his knees and his eyes on the door.

He was a very large man in a very dark suit with an earpiece in one ear. He’d chosen the least noticeable corner of the shop and he was the most noticeable thing in it.

“Bao. You can go.”

“Mr. Zhao asked me to stay inside, madam.”

“I know what he asked.”

He looked at the floor. “I’m sorry, madam.”

She was going to argue with him. She looked at his big careful hands on his knees, and the way he’d turned the chair so that he was between the door and her, and she couldn’t.

“Then at least have some tea,” she said, and made him some.

A woman came in for a birthday bouquet, saw Bao in the corner, and remembered she had an appointment. A man came in to ask whether she still did funeral flowers, and Elowen said, “Yes,” and nearly laughed, and he looked at her face and bought nothing. Song Wei Long arrived at half past eleven, put the card in a plastic sleeve, looked at Bao, looked at her, and said only, “I’ll ring you,” and went.

Xiao Pan came in at three, late from deliveries, and stopped dead in the door.

“Boss? Why’s Bao in the corner?”

“Because my husband put him there.”

Xiao Pan looked at Bao. Bao looked at the ceiling.

“Did something happen?”

“A customer placed a very rude order.”

He looked at her for a moment. Then, without another word, he put on his apron and went and stood at the other end of the bench from her, and stayed there till six.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao wasn’t home.

His study was empty and his coat was gone from the hook. On the bedside table the framed camellia stood where it always stood, and the fourteenth key lay beside it.

She rang him at seven. He didn’t answer. She rang him at half past. She sent a message at eight.

Elowen: Are you coming home?

It stayed unread.

She ate dinner standing at the counter because she couldn’t sit at the table on her own. At ten she rang Chen Si.

“Before you ask,” said Chen Si, “yes. He’s here.”

“Is he all right?”

“Physically.”

“Can I talk to him?”

“Wait.”

She heard the phone covered, and voices, and then Chen Si came back. “He says he needs some time.”

She shut her eyes. “Did I do something wrong?”

He was quiet for a moment. “No.”

“Then why won’t he come home?”

“Because your husband,” said Chen Si, “is an idiot. I’ve known it since he was fifteen.”

She almost laughed. “Tell him I’m waiting.”

“I’ll tell him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Chens lived forty-four floors up, in a glass apartment that looked down on the harbour as if it owned it. Aurelia was on the white sofa in a silk robe with a magazine across her knees. Zhao was in the armchair opposite with a glass of water he hadn’t touched, and his phone face down on his thigh.

“Drink it,” said Chen Si.

“I’m fine.”

“You’ve said that four times.”

“Then stop asking.”

Aurelia turned a page. “What has he done?”

“He and Elowen had a fight,” said Chen Si.

“About what?”

“Someone threatened her at the shop. He told her to close it.”

Aurelia put the magazine down.

“He told his wife,” she said slowly, “to close her own shop.”

“Yes.”

“And then?”

“She told him to get out of it,” said Chen Si. “So he did. And then he came here and has been sitting in that chair for three hours.”

Aurelia looked at Zhao.

“Are you a caveman?”

“I don’t need your opinion.”

“Clearly. If you’d ever needed anyone’s opinion you’d be at home.” She leaned forward. “Did you ask her what she wanted to do?”

“I told her what was necessary.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He didn’t answer.

“Did you ask her?”

“No.”

Aurelia sat back. “Then you’re an idiot.”

Chen Si, at the window, took a sip of his own water and said, without turning round, “Should’ve bought a bird.”

Zhao looked at him. “What?”

“If you wanted something you could keep in a cage and cover with a cloth when it frightened you.” Chen Si turned. “You should have bought a bird. You married a florist.”

“Exactly,” said Aurelia, pointing at her husband with the magazine.

Zhao looked from one of them to the other.

“She rang the police before she rang me,” he said.

It came out of him lower than anything else he’d said all evening. Aurelia heard it, and stopped being amused.

“Of course she did,” she said. “Because she knew what you’d do.”

He was silent.

“She’s at home,” said Aurelia, “on her own, in that big concrete house, thinking you’ve left her because she was frightened and did something sensible. She rang Si an hour ago and asked him whether she’d done something wrong.” She picked the magazine up again and didn’t look at it. “Go home, Zhendong.”

Chen Si came and stood beside the armchair.

“She asked me to tell you,” he said, “that she’s waiting.”

Zhao turned his phone over. Seven missed calls. One message, unopened.

He stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to midnight Elowen was sitting on the stairs.

She’d tried going to bed. She’d brushed her teeth and put on her nightdress and turned off the lamp and lain there listening to the house, the hum of the security system, the dogs shifting in the courtyard. Then she’d got up again and come down and sat on the fourth stair from the bottom in the dark, with her arms round her knees, looking at the front door.

She’d stopped ringing him. She wasn’t going to beg. She wasn’t going to sleep either.

At ten to twelve the front door opened.

He stopped when he saw her. He closed the door very quietly behind him and stood in the hall with his coat on.

“You should be in bed.”

“I tried.”

He took his coat off and hung it on the hook, and then he came to the foot of the stairs and stopped on the bottom step, one below where her feet were, so that their eyes were level. He looked more tired than she’d ever seen him, even in the armory.

“I owe you an apology,” he said.

She didn’t say anything.

“I shouldn’t have told you to close the shop. I shouldn’t have put Bao in your corner like a lock on a door. And I shouldn’t have left.” He kept his hands at his sides. “I’m sorry.”

She’d heard him say a great many things in fourteen months. I know. I should have told you. You’re right. She’d never heard him say that.

“Why did you?” she said.

“Because I was frightened.”

“You didn’t look frightened.”

“I know what I looked like.” His voice was very low. “He knew your day. He’d stood where you stand. I didn’t know if he was alone or if somebody had been watching you for a month. And I thought, if I could make your world smaller, there’d be less of it for anyone to reach.” He looked at her. “And you rang the detective first, and you were right to, and I hated it.”

She looked at him for a long moment.

“You frightened me more than he did,” she said. “Not because you shouted. Because you went.”

“I know.”

“I didn’t know if you were coming back.”

“I know. I’m sorry.”

“And you can’t close the shop because you’re scared, because then you’ll close it every time.” She swallowed. “And you think that if you take the shop away I’ll be safe, as if it’s the only thing I’ve got. It isn’t. It’s mine and I love it and I won’t give it up. But it’s not the only thing I’ve got.” She looked at him. “I’ve got the lemon tree. And a glass room with the tap too high. And a stupid key that opens your armory. And you. You’re on the list, Zhendong. You’re not allowed to walk off it.”

His face moved. “The tap’s too high?”

“That’s what you heard?”

“I’ll have it moved.”

“You’ll leave it exactly where it is.”

He looked at her mouth, and then back at her eyes, and didn’t move. He never moved first.

“Oh, for God’s sake,” said Elowen. “Yes.”

She caught the front of his shirt and pulled him up the last step, and kissed him.

It wasn’t careful. It had six hours of waiting in it, and the man with the forgettable face, and the empty chair at dinner. He made a rough sound against her mouth and put his arms round her and held on, standing on the stair below with his face tipped up to hers, and she held his jaw in both hands and kissed him until she’d stopped being angry, mostly.

“Did you eat?” she said, when she let him go.

“No.”

“You were at Chen Si’s for five hours.”

“He offered.”

She stared at him. Then she took his hand and walked him down the last stair and into the kitchen, and heated the soup she’d put away for him, and stood and watched him eat every spoonful of it at the counter at midnight.

“Aurelia called you a caveman,” she said.

He stopped with the spoon halfway up. “How do you know?”

“Chen Si texted me. He also said you should have bought a bird.”

He shut his eyes. She laughed for the first time all day, a little hoarse, and leaned on the counter beside him with her shoulder against his until he’d finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song Wei Long rang at eight the next morning while Zhao was still in the shower.

“The address on the card’s a vacant shop,” he said. “Across the road from yours. Second floor. No tenant, no lease, no owner who’ll answer the phone. The window looks straight down into your counter.”

She sat on the edge of the bed with the phone very tight against her ear.

“Someone’s been up there,” said Song Wei Long. “Recently. There’s a chair at the window. And cigarette ends, a lot of them.”

“For how long?”

“We don’t know. A while.”

Zhao came out of the bathroom fastening his watch. He saw her face and stopped.

“Elowen,” said Song Wei Long. “Don’t take an order like that again. Even if he changes the name.”

“I won’t.”

She put the phone down. She told Zhao. He listened to all of it without interrupting, standing very still in the middle of the room with one hand still on his watch strap.

“I’m not going to close it,” she said.

“I know.” He finished doing up the watch. “Bao will sit outside. In the car. Where you can see him from the counter and nobody else can see him at all.”

She looked at him.

“Only if you say yes,” he said.

She thought about the chair in the window across the road, and the cigarette ends, and you’re always here on Wednesdays.

“Yes,” she said.

chapters.title: Glass
chapters.desc: Nobody says the date out loud. He buys her soy milk at the market, a little girl wants sunflowers with a yellow ribbon for her grandmother, and then a car comes down the street too slowly.
chapters.content:
Nobody said the date out loud.

Not at a quarter to four, when Elowen came down in the dark and found him already in the kitchen, dressed, with the car keys in his hand. Not in the car going down the hill, with the wipers going though it had stopped raining. Not at the market, where Granny Yip looked at Zhao, and then at Bao, who had come too and was standing two stalls back pretending to be interested in gerberas, and said nothing at all, which for Granny Yip was a speech.

The calendar on the kitchen wall had the ninth of June on it like every other day. Nobody had circled it. Nobody needed to. A man with a forgettable face had written it in her order book three weeks ago, and Song Wei Long had found the chair in the window across the road, and in three weeks nobody in the house had said the number nine.

She’d said she’d go in. He’d said he’d drive her. She’d said Bao could sit inside, today only, and he’d said, “Thank you,” as if she’d given him something. That was all either of them had said about it.

“You’re early,” said Granny Yip.

“It’s the same time as always.”

“Then I’m old.” The old woman looked past her. “You. Your wife hasn’t eaten.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

“Then what are you standing there for?”

She pushed a box of eucalyptus into his arms. He took it without a word. Then he put it down on the end of the stall and went off down the row between the buckets to the soy milk stall at the far end, and Elowen watched him go, tall in his dark coat among the trolleys, with the strand of hair already down on his forehead.

He came back with two paper cups. He’d taken the lid off hers. Before he gave it to her he bent his head and blew across the top of it, once, carefully, the way her mother had at this same stall when she was six and the cups were too hot for small hands.

She took it. She looked down into it.

He didn’t say anything. He stood beside her with his own cup and let her look.

After a while she leaned her shoulder against his arm. “Thank you.”

He put his mouth to her hair. “Drink it before it gets cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose chrysanthemums, pale roses, a bucket of lisianthus. Granny Yip put in a bundle of white sweet peas for nothing and pushed Elowen’s hand away when she reached for her purse.

“For the house,” the old woman said. “Not the shop.”

At the end of the row his phone buzzed in his coat. He looked at it, and something went across his face and away again.

“Work?” she said.

“Raiden.”

“Is he all right?”

Her brother had been in the City Hospital since Friday night, with a cracked skull and his left arm in plaster to the shoulder. A van had come round the bend on the Docks road and hit him and kept going, and nobody had got the plate. She’d sat with him on Saturday and Sunday and Monday, and he’d made jokes about his drawing hand until the nurse told him to stop.

“He’s bored,” said Zhao, and put the phone away.

He didn’t show her the message. It said: She came back last night. The girl with the jacket. Nobody knows. Please.

On Friday night, in the corridor outside the ward, while the whole Lin family stood round Raiden’s bed, Zhao had seen a biker’s jacket on the visitor’s chair, black, with oil on the cuffs, much too small for anyone in that room, and had picked it up and folded it over his arm and taken it away before Lin Jian noticed it. He’d given it back on Sunday to a young woman with grease under her nails who’d stood in the hospital car park and looked at him as if she’d fight him for it. He hadn’t asked her name. Raiden hadn’t told him.

He’d keep it. He was good at keeping things.

“Shall we go?” he said, and picked up the boxes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the shop door she stopped him.

The street was still half asleep. Bao had gone in ahead to unlock and turn on the lights. Across the road, on the second floor, the empty window was dark, with nothing behind it now. Wei Long’s people had taken the chair.

Zhao stood on the step with his arms full of eucalyptus.

She took hold of his collar with both hands and pulled him down and kissed him.

He made a muffled sound of surprise round the boxes. She kissed him anyway, standing on her toes on her own doorstep, for longer than was decent at half past six in the morning, and only let go when she’d had enough.

“For luck,” she said.

He looked down at her with an expression she didn’t have a word for. “Luck.”

“Go to work, Zhendong. Come and get me at six.”

“Six,” he said. “I’ll be early.”

He put the boxes inside the door. He looked at Bao, who nodded once from behind the counter, and at the window across the road, and at her. Then he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten the shop was busy. A hotel wanted forty table arrangements by noon, and Xiao Pan was fighting a bucket of white roses and losing.

“Not so tight,” said Elowen, reaching past him.

“If I leave gaps they’ll fall over.”

“If you don’t leave gaps they can’t breathe. Look.” She pulled two stems out and set them back a finger’s width apart. “There.”

He looked at it. “I’m starting to think flowers are worse than people.”

“They’re more honest.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

The bell went. A little girl came in holding her mother’s hand.

She was about six, with two small bunches of hair tied up in red elastic and a yellow cardigan with one button missing. She looked round the shop with the solemnity of a judge.

Elowen came round the counter and crouched down. “Hello. What are you looking for?”

“Flowers.”

“I’ve got a few of those. Who are they for?”

“My grandma. She’s coming home from the hospital.”

“Then we’d better find something good.”

“I’m Mimi,” said the girl, as if that settled it, and walked the length of the buckets with her hands behind her back, inspecting each one. She stopped in front of the sunflowers.

“These. Grandma likes yellow.”

“How many?”

Mimi thought about it seriously. “Five.”

Elowen picked five, and Mimi watched her cut the stems on the slant and strip the bottom leaves and wrap them in brown paper.

“Can I have a ribbon? Yellow. Not white. Yellow like the middle.”

“Yellow like the middle.”

Elowen cut a length and held out one end. “You hold this side.”

Together they pulled it into a bow. It came out lopsided. Mimi looked at it with enormous satisfaction.

“That’s perfect,” said Elowen.

“Grandma will like it.”

“I’m sure she will.”

Her mother paid and said, “Say thank you,” and Mimi said it, loudly, and held the sunflowers up against her chest so their faces were looking at the ceiling.

In the corner by the wrapping paper, Bao stood up.

He’d been watching the street through the front window the way he’d been watching it all morning. Now he was on his feet and moving, and Elowen didn’t understand why until she followed his eyes and saw the car.

It was dark grey with tinted glass and it was coming down the street much too slowly. Behind it a delivery van sounded its horn. The car didn’t speed up. The passenger window was coming down.

“Mrs. Zhao. Away from the glass.”

“Bao—“

“Now.”

She saw a hand.

Then the window came in.

It made a noise she would hear for the rest of her life, a crack and then a huge bright roar, and the whole front of the shop turned into light, a sheet of it, glittering, coming at her. Bao hit her before she could move. He came over the end of the counter and took her down behind it with his whole body on top of her, and something smashed into the cooler door above them, and then something else, and the sunflowers were on the floor in front of her face.

Mimi was screaming.

Over Bao’s arm Elowen saw Xiao Pan. He’d dropped the roses. He’d thrown himself across the shop at the mother and the child and taken them both down behind the big display table, and he was lying over them, his back to the street, with his arm wrapped round Mimi’s head.

“Down! Stay down! Shut your eyes, it’s all right, shut your eyes—“

Another crack. Plaster burst off the wall over the till.

Then an engine, very loud, and tyres, and the car was gone.

Nobody moved. Glass was still falling somewhere, a thin tinkling, like a wind chime.

“Don’t move,” said Bao, on top of her.

“Bao—“

“Wait.”

She could feel him breathing. She could feel something wet coming through her shirt where his arm lay across her back, and it wasn’t hers.

He lifted his head. He looked at the door, the window, the street, every corner of the room, very fast. “Xiao Pan!”

“Here!”

“Hurt?”

“I don’t know! No!”

“Keep them down!”

Elowen pushed at his arm. “Let me up.”

“Mrs. Zhao—“

“There’s a child crying. Let me up.”

He let her up. She got to her knees behind the counter. There was glass everywhere, in her hair, on the bench, in the open order book, in the water of the buckets. The front window was gone. Not cracked. Gone. The street was just there, open, a woman across the road standing with her hand over her mouth and her shopping on the pavement.

“Xiao Pan,” said Elowen. “Bring them. The back. Now.”

He looked at her over the table.

“The tulips,” she said. “Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The panic room had been Raiden’s idea, and she’d fought him for every inch of it, and now she knew every inch of it.

Xiao Pan pulled the tulips away and lifted the floor panel on its counterweight with one hand. The mother stared down the steep stair.

“What is that?”

“Somewhere safe,” said Elowen. “Please. Go down.”

Mimi was still holding the sunflowers. One stem had snapped. “My flowers.”

“Bring them.”

Xiao Pan took them down first. Elowen came after, one hand on the rail, and Bao came last with one arm held against his side, and pulled the panel shut over their heads.

The shop went away.

There was the hum of the ventilation. The little girl’s breathing, fast and hiccuping. Nothing else.

Elowen found the switch on the wall. The ceiling lights came on, hard and white, and the small brass lamp over the sleeping platform came on too, warm, with its red battery light glowing underneath it.

Tucked into the base of the lamp was a gift card in her own round handwriting.

This light stays on. I’ll come.

She looked at it for a second. Then she turned round.

“Is anyone hurt?”

The mother shook her head. There was a thin line of blood on her cheek. Mimi shook her head too, staring at everything. Xiao Pan was kneeling in front of them both, checking their hands and arms, and when he turned to reach for the first-aid cabinet Elowen saw the back of his T-shirt. It was full of glass, little bright points of it all down his spine, and spotted with blood.

“Xiao Pan. Your back.”

“It’s fine.”

“Sit down.”

“Boss—“

“Sit.”

He sat. Bao was leaning against the steel wall by the stair. Only now could she see how much blood had come through his jacket at the shoulder. A long sliver of the window was stuck in the cloth.

“It’s nothing,” said Bao.

“Sit down.”

He sat.

She opened the first-aid cabinet and got out gauze and tape and the little scissors. As she reached for them something warm ran down the side of her neck, under her ear, and into her collar.

She touched it. Her fingers came away red.

She stood still and looked at them.

“Boss!” said Xiao Pan. “Your neck—“

“I know.”

She felt for it. A cut, just below her jaw, where something had gone past her. Not deep. Long. Bleeding steadily.

Bao was on his feet. “Mrs. Zhao, let me—“

“Sit down. Look after your shoulder.”

“It’s—“

“So is this,” said Elowen, and folded a pad of gauze and pressed it against her own neck, hard.

She sat on the edge of the sleeping platform under the lamp, beside the mother. Mimi was watching her.

“Does it hurt?”

“A little.”

Mimi’s face crumpled.

“I’m all right,” said Elowen. “Look. I’m sitting up.”

Her phone was in her back pocket. The screen was cracked across one corner. It still lit.

She rang him.

He answered before it had properly rung. “Elowen.”

She shut her eyes. “Zhendong.”

“What’s happened?”

“Somebody shot at the shop. From a car. The window’s gone.”

There was less than a second of nothing.

“Are you hurt?”

“There’s glass. My neck’s cut. It’s not bad. I’m holding it.”

“Where are you?”

“In Raiden’s room. Under the tulips.”

“Who’s with you?”

“Bao. Xiao Pan. A woman and her little girl. Bao’s shoulder’s cut and Xiao Pan’s got glass all down his back. They’re not shot. Nobody’s shot.”

“Stay there.” She could hear him moving. A door. Someone shouting behind him, and his voice going away from the phone to say something short and terrible to whoever it was, and coming back. “Don’t open it. Don’t go up. Not for anyone. Not till Bao hears my voice through the floor.”

“I know.”

“The line down there’s working?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” An engine. Very loud. “I’m coming.”

“Where are you?”

“The Docks.” A pause. “Eight minutes.”

It was twenty minutes from the Docks. She knew that road.

“Don’t drive like an idiot,” she said.

He was quiet for a moment. “I won’t.”

She didn’t mean to say the next thing. It came out anyway, small, from the back of her throat.

“I’m scared.”

On the other end she heard him breathe in.

“I know,” he said. His voice had dropped right down. “I know. I’m coming.”

“There’s a little girl here. She was buying sunflowers for her grandmother.”

“Keep her by you.”

“I am.”

“Stay on the phone.”

“Zhendong?”

“I’m here.”

“Eight minutes?”

“Eight.”

“Come home,” she said, which made no sense, because she was in a steel box under her shop and he was in a car on the Docks road. He understood her anyway.

“I am,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put him on speaker and laid the phone on the platform beside her, and they all listened to the engine.

Mimi looked up at her. “Is your husband coming?”

“Yes.”

“Is he a doctor?”

“No.”

“Is he a policeman?”

“No.”

Mimi thought about this. “What is he?”

Elowen looked at the steel door at the top of the stair. On the phone the engine changed gear and somebody’s horn went and was left behind.

“He’s my husband,” she said.

That seemed to be enough. Mimi looked down at her sunflowers. One stem was broken in half and one flower had lost a fistful of petals, and the yellow ribbon had come undone and had dust on it.

“Can you fix them?”

Elowen took her hand away from her neck long enough to reach the first-aid box. There was a roll of tape in it, white, the cloth kind. She took the broken stem and bound it straight against a pencil from her apron pocket, round and round, and tied the ribbon again, lopsided, the way Mimi had made it.

“Will they still be pretty?”

Elowen looked at them. A petal missing. A tear in another. The tape bright white against the green.

“Yes,” she said. “Your grandma will still get her sunflowers.”

Above them, through the steel, she could hear nothing at all. Not the street, not the sirens that must have started by now, not the glass. Just the hum of the air and the engine on the phone and the little brass lamp over her shoulder, staying on.

She pressed the gauze back against her neck and watched the stair, and waited for his voice to come through the floor.

chapters.title: Nobody Else Touches Her
chapters.desc: He sends her sister out of the bathroom and puts the strips on her neck himself, shaking the whole time. Before dawn he tells her how long he’ll be gone, and she doesn’t say don’t.
chapters.content:
She heard him before the panel moved.

A voice through the floor, close, saying her name. Then Bao was on his feet with his bad arm held against his side, saying, “Mr. Zhao,” to the ceiling, and Mimi startled against her mother, and the floor above them lifted on its counterweight with a long scrape of metal.

Zhao came down the stair before it was fully open. He didn’t use the steps. He dropped through, landed hard on one knee on the steel floor, and came up already moving.

His coat was open. His hair had come down all over his forehead. His face had something in it she’d never seen there before, not at the gala, not on the night of the van, not at three in the morning with his name on the television. She didn’t have a word for it.

He crossed the room and took hold of her.

The gauze fell out of her hand. He pulled her into his chest with one arm locked round her waist and the other hand spread over the back of her head, holding it, and she had to take a step back to keep her balance. He didn’t say anything. He put his face in her hair and stayed there.

He was shaking.

Not the stillness he went into when he was angry. Not a tremor in the hands. All of him, from his shoulders to his knees, as if he’d been out in the cold for hours.

“I’m here,” she said into his coat.

His hand moved on her head, over her hair, down to the back of her neck, feeling for something.

“Where.”

“What?”

“Where did it cut you.”

“Here.” She touched the place under her jaw. “It’s not deep.”

He drew back far enough to look. His eyes went to the blood on her collar and stayed there. He didn’t touch it. His fingers hovered beside it and then moved over her face and her shoulders and her arms as if he expected to find something else if he kept looking.

“Bao.”

“Sir. Xiao Pan has glass in his back. The mother has a cut on her face. The girl isn’t hurt. I’ve called a doctor to the house and an ambulance here.”

“You.”

“Shoulder, sir. It’s nothing.”

Zhao looked at the sleeve of Bao’s jacket, which was black with blood to the elbow.

“It’s not nothing,” he said, and turned to Xiao Pan.

Xiao Pan was still kneeling in front of Mimi and her mother, as if he’d forgotten how to stand up. His hands had started shaking now that there was nothing for them to do.

“You covered them,” said Zhao.

Xiao Pan swallowed. “Yes, Mr. Zhao.”

“Good.”

It was one word. Xiao Pan sat up straighter under it, glass and all.

Zhao crouched in front of the little girl. She looked at him with enormous eyes over the top of her broken sunflowers.

“What’s your name?”

“Mimi.”

“Were you frightened, Mimi?”

She nodded.

“So was I.” He looked at the flowers. “Those were for your grandmother.”

“They’re broken.”

“Bao,” said Zhao, without looking round. “A car for Mimi and her mother. A doctor to see them both tonight, at home. Every bill, whatever it is, for as long as it is. And five sunflowers. The same ones.”

“With a yellow ribbon,” said Mimi.

“With a yellow ribbon.”

“Not white.”

Something went across his face. “Not white.”

She looked at him for a moment, deciding. Then she held out the one with the taped stem. “You can have this one.”

He took it from her as if it were made of glass. “Thank you.”

Elowen reached for his free hand. He turned it over and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was worse than she’d let herself imagine.

The front window was a frame of teeth. Glass lay in drifts on the floor, under the buckets, in the cooler, on the bench, a thousand bright pieces among the petals. The display table had split down the middle. The hotel’s white roses were crushed under it. A bullet had gone through the cooler door at the height of a person’s chest and left a star in the glass.

She stood in the back doorway and looked at it.

“They shot into my shop,” she said. “With a child in it.”

“Yes.”

“Did they know she’d be there?”

“No,” he said. “They knew you would.”

At the end of the counter a bucket of white peonies had been knocked over. Stock. She’d bought them on Monday, without thinking, because the hotel liked white. One lay on the floor with its stem snapped clean through and its head bruised brown on one side.

Zhao let go of her hand. He bent down and picked it up and turned it over in his fingers.

“Why that one?” she said.

He looked at it. “The order.”

She knew. Two wreaths, white, for the ninth. His name in gold. And peonies for the widow.

He put the broken flower in the inside pocket of his coat, carefully, the way he’d put away her plus-one note, the way he put away everything he meant to keep.

“Zhendong.”

“I know.”

“What are you going to do?”

He looked at her. For a moment the man standing in her ruined shop wasn’t the one who bought her soy milk. It was the one whose name was in a report in New York, and in the mouths of men who lowered their voices to say it.

“Find out who sent them,” he said.

“And then?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. She’d known what she was marrying. She didn’t ask him to promise anything, because he wouldn’t, and she wasn’t sure any more that she wanted him to.

“Take me home,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara was in the hall when they got there, with her medical-school lanyard still round her neck and a bag over her shoulder. Bao had rung her before he’d rung the ambulance.

She took one look at Elowen’s collar and said, “Bathroom. Now. Sit on the edge of the bath.”

Elowen sat. Elara knelt in front of her and peeled the gauze back.

“It’s long but it isn’t deep. It’s missed everything that matters.” Her voice was steady and practical. “I need to wash it out and check for glass, and then close it. Strips will do. I don’t want to stitch your neck if I don’t have to.”

She opened her bag and laid things out on a towel on the floor. Saline. Gauze. Tweezers. A sealed packet of thin white strips.

Zhao stood in the doorway. He hadn’t let go of Elowen’s hand until Elara made him.

Elara picked up the tweezers. Her hand shook.

It wasn’t much. Elowen had known about it for three years, since the night when Elara was eighteen and somebody who’d wanted to hurt their father had hurt her hands instead. She’d spent a year relearning to hold a pen. Nobody at the medical school knew it hadn’t gone away. Elara had told nobody but Elowen, and Elowen had told nobody at all.

Elara put the tweezers down and pressed her hand flat on her own knee, hard, and picked them up again. They still shook.

“I’ll do it,” said Zhao.

Elara looked round at him. “You?”

“Show me.”

For a second Elowen thought her sister would refuse. Elara had a temper, under all the steadiness, and she didn’t like being looked at when her hands did that. But she looked at Zhao’s face, and whatever she saw there made her move over on the bathroom floor.

“Wash your hands,” she said. “Properly. Then again.”

He did. He washed them twice, up to the wrist, and dried them on a clean towel, and knelt where she’d been kneeling.

She showed him. How to flush the cut with saline from the top down so the glass came out instead of going in. How to look along it with the light behind, for the glint. There was one tiny piece. Elara pointed. He took it out with the tweezers in one movement, his hand perfectly still now, and laid it on the towel.

“Now the strips,” said Elara. “Push the edges together. Don’t pull the skin. One in the middle first, then either side. Close, but not touching.”

He nodded.

“I’ll stay till—“

“No,” said Zhao.

Elara looked at him.

He didn’t look away from Elowen’s neck. “Thank you. I’ll do it. Go and see to Bao. He’s bleeding on my stairs and he’ll tell you it’s nothing.”

Elara looked at her sister. Elowen gave her a very small nod.

“Six,” Elara said at the door. “It’ll take six. And don’t keep touching it afterwards to see if it’s still there.”

She went out and closed the door.

He opened the packet. The first strip stuck to his finger. He took it off and started again.

“You don’t have to,” said Elowen.

“Don’t move.”

She didn’t. He leaned in until she could feel his breath on her throat. He pushed the edges of the cut together with his thumb and finger, gently, and laid the first strip across the middle. The second. The third. He did it slowly, his whole face narrowed to an inch of her skin. The fourth. The fifth. The sixth.

He sat back on his heels.

He looked at the six white strips under her jaw. Then he put the empty packet down on the towel, and his hands went into his lap, and stayed there.

She waited.

He lifted his eyes to her face, and something in his own face came apart.

A tear landed on the back of his hand. He looked at it as if he didn’t know where it had come from. Then another.

“Zhendong?”

He put the heel of his hand over his eyes.

“I should have been there.”

“You came.”

“After.” His voice had gone rough and strange. “I put Bao in the corner and drove away. I knew someone had ordered those wreaths. I knew they’d sat in that window across the road and smoked and watched you. I knew it was the ninth. And I went to the Docks.”

“Because I told you to.”

“I heard you,” he said. “On the phone. I heard you say you were scared. I was on the Docks road and I couldn’t get to you.” He slid down off his heels until he was sitting on the bathroom floor with his back against the bath, one hand gripping the edge of the cabinet as if the floor might tip. “I couldn’t get to my wife.”

She got down off the edge of the bath and knelt in front of him on the tiles.

He wasn’t hiding it. Or he was trying to and couldn’t; his face was turned towards the wall and his shoulders were shaking, and the sounds coming out of him were the worst sounds she’d ever heard a person make, because he was trying so hard to make no sound at all.

She took his face in her hands and turned it back.

“Look at me.”

He looked.

“I’m here. You’re holding my hands.” He looked down. He hadn’t known he was. “I’m sitting on our bathroom floor and I’m going to be furious about my window in the morning, and you’re going to try to buy the whole street.”

He made a noise that was almost a laugh and wasn’t.

She took a fistful of his collar and pulled him down and kissed him.

She had no other answer to what was on his face. He made a sound into her mouth and his hands came up and held her head, very carefully, his fingers well away from her neck, and he kissed her back like a man checking she was breathing.

When she let go he kept his forehead against hers.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“For what?”

“For this. For you seeing it.”

“You don’t frighten me,” she said. “The car frightened me. The glass. Bao bleeding on the floor. You don’t.” She wiped under his eye with her thumb. “Don’t hide it. Not from me.”

He turned his face and kissed the inside of her wrist, and didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when they’d both stopped shaking, he looked at her and frowned.

“There’s glass in your hair.”

She reached up. He caught her wrist.

“Don’t. You’ll cut your fingers.”

He ran the bath tap until it was warm and brought the shower head down on its hose, and made her kneel by the edge of the bath and bend her head over it, the way her mother had washed her hair when she was small. He pulled the black elastic out of the end of her plait, where it had held through everything, and slipped it over his own wrist without seeming to think about it. Then he unravelled the plait with his fingers, a little at a time, and every time he found a piece of glass he picked it out and put it on the side of the bath, until there was a small glittering heap there.

He poured water over her head, holding his other hand flat across her forehead so it didn’t run into her eyes or near her neck. He did it three times. He combed through her hair with his fingers after each time, slowly, all the way to the ends, checking.

“Is it all out?”

“Nearly.”

She stayed bent over the bath with her eyes closed and his hands in her hair, and for the first time since the window had come in, she felt her shoulders go down.

When he’d finished he wrapped her head in a towel and sat back. She looked at his wrist.

“That’s mine.”

He looked down at the black hair tie, stretched against his watch strap.

“You’ll want it back,” he said.

“Not yet.”

He didn’t take it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao came up at eleven with his shoulder stitched, grey in the face, and stood in the bedroom door.

“The car’s been found two streets away. Burned. Stolen plates. The gun’s gone. There’s a camera on the bus station that has part of the driver.” He paused. “Mimi’s grandmother has her sunflowers, madam. Five. Yellow ribbon.”

Elowen, under a blanket on the bed, closed her eyes. “Thank you, Bao.”

“And Xiao Pan, sir. They took forty-one pieces out of his back. He’s at home. His mother’s with him.”

“Pay for everything,” said Zhao. “And tell him he’s paid for the month and he’s not to come in.”

“He’ll come in, sir.”

“Then let him.”

When Bao had gone Zhao sat on the edge of the bed with his phone and didn’t read it. Every few seconds he looked up at her. She caught him at it.

“You’re staring.”

“I’m checking.”

“Checking what?”

“That you’re there.”

She put her hand out from under the blanket. He took it.

“You took the peony,” she said.

His thumb stopped on her knuckles.

“The white one. You put it in your coat.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“For the widow.” He said it very quietly. “They ordered flowers for your husband’s funeral and peonies for you to stand behind. I want to remember exactly what they ordered. When I find them I want to be holding it.”

She looked at him. She thought about telling him not to. She thought about the bullet hole in the cooler door at the height of a person’s chest.

“Come back to me,” she said instead. “Whatever you do. You have to come back.”

“I’ll come back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He got up a little before five. She felt the mattress move and opened her eyes.

He was dressed in the dark. Black trousers, black shirt, his watch on. Her hair tie still on his wrist, next to it.

“Go back to sleep.”

She pushed herself up on one elbow. “Where are you going?”

He came and sat down on the bed beside her. “To meet Chen Si.”

“How long?”

He looked at her for a moment, deciding how true to be.

“Forty-eight hours,” he said.

She was quiet.

“I need to know who sent them. Who paid. Who told them it was a Wednesday.” His voice was very even. “Bao stays here. Aurelia’s coming in the morning. I’ll ring when I can.”

“You’ll ring.”

“When I can.”

He leaned down and kissed her forehead. Then her cheek. Then, very carefully, her mouth, as if she might break.

She took hold of his shirt.

“Don’t kiss me like that. Like you’re not coming back.”

Something changed in his face.

“Then how?”

“Properly.”
