He bent his head again. This time it was slow and deep, his hand along her jaw on the side without the strips, his thumb under her ear, and she held his shirt and kissed him back until she had to breathe.

When he lifted his head she still had his collar.

She could have said don’t. It was right there in her mouth. She could have said stay, or let Wei Long do it, or let them go. She thought of Mimi’s face over the sunflowers, and the star in the cooler glass, and didn’t say any of it.

“Come back,” she said.

He looked at her for a long moment, as if he were learning her off by heart: her hair loose on the pillow, the six strips, her eyes.

“I will,” he said.

He went out. She heard the front door, and the car, and the gate.

She lay there and touched the strips on her neck, once, though Elara had told her not to. Then she turned over into the warm place where he’d been, and kept her hand on it, and didn’t sleep.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.desc: Forty-eight hours, from his side. A boy who stole a car, a driver in the harbour, a shooter on a landing, and a koi pond on the coast.
chapters.content:
Chen Si was waiting at the bottom of the drive with the engine running. He looked at the black hair tie on Zhao’s wrist before he looked at his face.

“How is she?”

“Six strips. Asleep. She wasn’t.”

“I’ve sent a glazier to the shop. And Aurelia’s packing a bag. She’ll be at the house by eight, and she says she’s staying until somebody tells her why.”

Zhao got into the car. “The car.”

“Burned out behind the bus station. Stolen on Monday from a garage on the bypass. Plates from somewhere else.” Chen Si pulled out on to the hill road. “Eliana’s had the footage since midnight.”

“Eliana’s seventeen.”

“Eighteen. And sitting her last exam next Friday. And she found the boy who stole it before the police had found the car.” Chen Si handed him his phone.

On the screen was a still from a convenience-store camera: a thin kid in a faded jacket, smoking, looking straight at the lens without knowing it. Under it a message.

Eliana: Pang Kit. 17. Works at the garage on the bypass, or did. Took the van Monday night, told his friends in a group chat he’d been paid for it. He wasn’t the driver. He sold it to a man who paid cash at the old bus station. Driver’s somebody else. Tell Zhendong he isn’t to touch the boy, he’s an idiot, he’s not the one.

Under that, a second message, sent a minute later:

Eliana: Tell El I’m fine. Tell her I’m revising.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found Pang Kit in a gaming café on the east side at nine in the morning, with a headset on and a can of something orange, and he ran the moment he saw Bao in the doorway and got as far as the fire door before two of Bao’s men closed it in front of him.

Zhao sat down on a plastic stool opposite him in the back room.

“You stole a van.”

“I don’t know—“

Zhao put a photograph on the table between them. The front of her shop. The empty window, the glass on the pavement, a smear of something dark on the step.

The boy looked at it and went the colour of paper.

“I didn’t do that. I swear. I just took it. A man paid me. I didn’t know.”

“What man?”

“Grey jacket. I don’t know his name. You couldn’t remember his face if you tried.”

Zhao looked at him for a long moment, and the boy started to cry.

“Give him to Song Wei Long,” Zhao said, standing up. “Let him tell it to the police.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The driver was a man called Little Fu, who wasn’t little. One of Bao’s men had him on a camera at the north pier the afternoon before, standing with a man in a grey jacket. By two o’clock that afternoon they had him at the north pier again.

The tide was low.

Fu saw Zhao coming along the pier and took a step backwards, and looked over his shoulder at the road, where Bao was standing, and then at the water, and understood there was nowhere useful to go.

“Mr. Zhao. I don’t know anything.”

“That’s a pity,” said Zhao.

He took Fu by the front of his jacket and walked him down the steps into the sea.

Fu’s shout went under with him. Zhao held him by the collar under the surface with one hand, knee-deep himself, his trousers soaked black, and counted. Not long. Long enough. He brought him up.

Fu came up choking, grabbing at Zhao’s wrist with both hands.

“Who paid you?”

“I don’t—“

Zhao put him under again.

When he came up the second time he was retching sea water, his eyes huge.

“Yim!” he got out. “Yim set it up! The grey jacket! Yim!”

“Who paid Yim?”

“Qiu! Qiu Wen! It was Qiu Wen’s job!”

“Who else.”

“I don’t—“

Zhao’s hand tightened on his collar and Fu screamed it before he went under.

“The Dutchman! A Dutchman! Yim said the Dutchman was paying for the hand! For his hand! He said that’s what it was for!”

Zhao held him there. Maartens. Maartens at the dinner table in April, with his hand on her knee under the cloth, and then the fruit knife, and the blood on the white linen, and the contract signed with his left hand while Elowen raised the price by a fifth.

For the hand.

“Get him out,” he said.

Bao came down and hauled Fu up the steps and dumped him on the concrete, coughing.

“Keep him breathing. I want all of it on tape.”

Zhao came up the steps with the sea running out of his clothes and picked his phone up off the bollard.

“Si. Maartens.”

“Where?”

“Find out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yim was in a flat above a shuttered restaurant near the old bus station, and he started talking before the door was all the way open.

He had a face you couldn’t keep hold of. He sat at his own kitchen table with his hands flat on the oilcloth and told them everything as fast as he could, the way a man empties his pockets.

Qiu Wen had wanted it done since the gala. Since the florist cut his hand in front of half the city and made him look small. Yim had found the van and the boy and the driver. He’d found the shooter, a man called Tian, who did this sort of thing for whoever paid. He’d placed the order for the wreaths, as a message.

“A message to whom?”

“To you, Mr. Zhao. Of course to you.”

Zhao took the order slip out of his coat. He’d got it from Song Wei Long that morning, in a plastic sleeve. Her handwriting. 9 June. Two wreaths. White. And under it, in Yim’s, the ribbon text he’d made her write.

“Not to my wife,” said Zhao.

Yim looked at the slip and didn’t answer.

“How did Qiu Wen know she was alone on Wednesdays?”

“I don’t know. He had it from somewhere. Not from me.” Yim licked his lips. “He said it came from the fixer’s people. That’s all he said. The fixer’s people. He laughed when he said it.”

The fixer. There was one man in the Walled City who’d been called that for twenty years. He moved cargo. He bought customs officers whisky at New Year. He sat at the head of a table every Sunday and passed the fish.

Zhao put the slip away very carefully.

“Which hand did you write it with?”

Yim stared at him.

Zhao took Yim’s right wrist off the oilcloth and laid the hand flat, palm down, on the table, and held it there. Yim understood half a second before it happened. He started to say something. Zhao picked up the heavy iron pan from the stove behind him and brought it down.

The sound filled the little kitchen. Yim screamed and kept screaming. Zhao held the wrist down and waited until he’d stopped.

“You’re going to live,” said Zhao. “You’re going to leave this city by Monday. You’re going to cross the road every time you pass a flower shop, for the rest of your life, in every city you ever go to. If I ever hear that you’ve walked past one on the same side of the street, I’ll know, and I’ll come and do the other hand.”

Yim nodded with his face on the table, sobbing.

Zhao let go and put the pan back on the stove.

In the stairwell Chen Si said, without looking at him, “You know that wasn’t mercy.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight that evening Aurelia rang Chen Si, and Chen Si put her on speaker in the car without asking.

“She’s eaten,” said Aurelia. “Half a bowl of noodles and a pear. She’s wearing your brother’s jumper, the grey one with the hole in the elbow. She wouldn’t let me throw it in the wash. The glazier’s measured. She told him she wants to choose the glass herself and he went quite pale.”

“Is she asleep?” said Zhao.

There was a short silence.

“Oh, it’s you.” Aurelia’s voice changed. “No. She’s on the sofa. She’s watching a gardening programme with the sound off. She hasn’t turned a page of the magazine on her knee in an hour.” Another pause. “She asked me if I thought they’d come back. I said I thought you were making sure they couldn’t. She said that wasn’t the same as an answer.”

Zhao looked out of the window at the dark harbour.

“It isn’t,” said Aurelia. “Come home, Zhendong.”

“Forty-eight hours.”

“I heard. She told me. She said it like it was a ticket with a date on it.” Aurelia breathed out. “I’m staying till you’re back. Si, I’ve taken your blue pyjamas. Don’t ask for them.”

She rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tian Haoyu had been careful for nine years and made one mistake, which was to go back for his cigarettes.

Bao’s men had the building on the south side by eleven, a six-storey block of rented rooms. Tian’s door was open when they reached it. A chair lay on its side. The window was up. In an ashtray on the sill a cigarette was still burning down.

Above them, a door banged.

Zhao went up the stairwell. It was narrow, concrete, painted the grey of old porridge, lit by one tube on each landing. He could hear running feet above him, and then they stopped.

On the half-landing between the third floor and the fourth, Tian turned round with a gun in his hand.

Zhao saw the arm come up. He fired twice.

The first one hit Tian in the chest and the second in the chest again, a hand’s width lower, and the noise in the stairwell was enormous. Tian went back into the wall and slid down it and sat. His gun went down the stairs, step by step, and stopped at Zhao’s feet.

Zhao picked it up and put it in his pocket, and went up the last steps and crouched in front of him.

Tian was looking at him with a kind of surprise. There was a lot of blood.

“Who gave you her picture?”

“Yim.”

“Why her?”

Tian’s mouth moved. “Wanted you to see.” His breath was going short and wet. “That they could. Reach her. Anywhere. Wanted you—“

He stopped.

Zhao stayed crouched there. Then he reached into the dead man’s jacket and found it.

A photograph, folded once. Elowen on the step of her shop in the morning, with an armful of white delphiniums, looking off to the side at somebody out of the frame and laughing. Somebody had drawn a circle round her face in red marker, carefully, twice round. On the back, in the same marker:

WIFE. CONFIRM.

He put it in his breast pocket, behind the snapped white peony, and stood up.

“Bao. Have it cleaned up.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go home. He went to the office at the Docks, where the night shift was pretending not to see him, and sat down at the desk in the dark, and opened the security app on his phone.

The house came up in a grid of little lit squares. The gate. The courtyard. The kitchen. The stairs. The living room.

She was on the sofa in his grey jumper, with her knees drawn up. Aurelia had fallen asleep against the other arm with her mouth open, one hand trailing off the cushion. The television was still on with the sound off. Elowen had her phone in her hand. She was looking at it.

She didn’t ring him.

He watched her put it face down on the cushion. He watched her get up and pull the blanket over Aurelia’s shoulder and go into the kitchen, and he switched to the kitchen and watched her pour a glass of water and drink half of it standing at the sink, with her other hand pressed flat on the counter.

He knew what he was doing. The cameras were for the walls and the men who might come over them. She’d never said he could sit in an office at midnight and watch her drink a glass of water.

He kept watching.

She went back to the living room. On the way she stopped in the doorway, and lifted her head, and looked up at the corner of the ceiling. Not quite at the camera. Near it. As if she’d heard something.

Then she sat down again beside Aurelia and pulled her knees up.

He sat in the dark with her face on the screen until she’d fallen asleep, and for a while after.

His phone buzzed in his hand at ten past one. It made him jump, which nothing had made him do in years.

Elowen: Have you eaten?

He looked at it.

Zhao: I will.

Elowen: Don’t lie to me. It’s in the contract.

He looked at that too.

Zhao: Tomorrow.

Elowen: I know.

He turned the cameras off.

✦ ✦ ✦

The coast villa was in a shell company’s name, but everybody knew whose it was. It sat above its own strip of beach behind a line of old black pines, a long low house built round a courtyard with a koi pond in the middle, lit at night by little lamps set into the stones.

He came without an invitation an hour before dawn on Saturday.

Bao went through the side gate first. A guard came round the corner at the end of the covered walk with a rifle already up. Bao shot him once, and he went down on the flagstones and didn’t move again. A second man ran for the main house shouting and Bao let him go, because the shouting was useful.

Zhao walked over the first man and into the courtyard.

Qiu Wen was standing by the pond in a dressing gown, with a gun in his hand that he hadn’t decided what to do with yet. The koi moved under the surface beside him, white and orange, very slowly. His right hand had a thin pink scar across the knuckles.

“You came,” he said.

“You sent a car to my wife’s shop.”

“I sent a message.”

“You sent a man with a photograph of her face.”

Qiu Wen started to lift the gun. Zhao was already there. He caught the wrist and turned it and the gun went into the pond with a small flat splash, and the fish scattered.

Qiu Wen hit him with his left hand, hard, in the side of the head. Zhao didn’t move.

He hit Qiu Wen once in the face. The jaw went under his fist with a sound like a branch breaking. Qiu Wen staggered back against the low stone edge of the pond with both hands over his mouth and blood coming between his fingers, trying to say something and not being able to make the shape of it.

Zhao took the photograph out of his breast pocket and held it up in front of him, the red circle facing out.

“You did this.”

Qiu Wen’s eyes went to it. Over his ruined jaw, something in them laughed.

Zhao took the snapped white peony out of the same pocket. It had gone brown and soft at the edges in two days. He held it out over the water and let it go, and it fell on the surface of the pond and turned slowly round.

“For the widow,” he said.

He took Qiu Wen by the back of the neck and the collar of the dressing gown and put his head into the pond.

Qiu Wen fought. He was a strong man. Zhao knelt on the stone edge and held him under with both hands, and the water thrashed, and koi went past in bright confused streaks, and the lamps under the surface lit everything gold and orange and red. He brought him up once. Qiu Wen dragged in a breath full of water and blood and tried to swear.

“Who gave you her Wednesdays?”

Qiu Wen laughed, a terrible wet sound through his broken jaw. “Ask your father-in-law,” he said, or something like it.

Zhao put him under again.

This time he didn’t bring him up. He knelt there with his hands on the back of Qiu Wen’s neck until the thrashing stopped, and then until a while after it had stopped, and then he let go.

The pond went still. The peony floated by the dead man’s shoulder. Slowly the koi came back.

Bao stood at the edge of the courtyard. “Sir.”

“I know.”

Zhao stood up. His sleeves were wet to the shoulder.

“Phones. Papers. Every name in this house.” He looked down at the water. “Leave him there.”

He took out his phone and photographed the pond: the body at the edge, face down, one arm in the water, the peony beside it. He sent it to a number in Rotterdam.

He wrote one word under it.

Next.

He watched the message go. He watched it change to read.

Then he went out to the car, and sat in the back, and took the photograph with the red circle out of his pocket. He wanted to tear it into pieces small enough that the red circle wasn’t a circle any more. He didn’t. It was her face. She’d have the right to see it. He put it back in his pocket.

His phone rang.

“Are you done?” said Chen Si.

“For now.”

“Maartens?”

“He’s seen it.”

Chen Si was quiet. “It’s been forty-seven hours,” he said. “Go home.”

Zhao looked at the black hair tie on his wrist, and his wet sleeve, and the sky going pale over the pines.

“Drive,” he told the driver.

chapters.title: He Came Home Washed
chapters.desc: He comes home scrubbed raw and she asks if anyone’s dead. He tells her the truth, comes apart on the kitchen floor, and agrees that her father is hers to deal with.
chapters.content:
Aurelia was at the kitchen counter at five in the morning with Chen Si’s blue pyjamas on under Elowen’s cardigan and her bags packed by the stairs.

“He’s on his way,” she said, when Elowen came down. “Si rang. Twenty minutes.”

Elowen stood in the doorway. She’d slept perhaps two hours, in his jumper, on top of the covers. Her neck pulled every time she turned her head.

“Sit down before you fall down,” said Aurelia, and pushed a cup of tea across the counter.

Elowen sat. She held the cup and didn’t drink it.

Aurelia watched her for a while. Then she said, “Did he ever tell you about January?”

“What January?”

“Last year. Before you. New Year’s Eve.” Aurelia turned her own cup round on its saucer. “Somebody put something on the rim of my champagne glass at the harbour dinner, knowing Si always drinks from mine. He nearly died. Two weeks in intensive care.” She said it the way she said everything, briskly, as if reading a bill. “Your husband sat on a plastic chair outside that door from midnight to six every single night. Fourteen nights. He didn’t go home. He didn’t sleep in a bed. The nurses had to make him go and shower. One night a man in a nurse’s coat came down the corridor with a syringe, and Zhendong took him into the stairwell, and the man didn’t come out.”

Elowen looked at her.

“I’m telling you,” said Aurelia, “because I sat beside him on one of those nights and fell asleep on his shoulder, and he didn’t move for four hours in case he woke me. And when Si was out of danger he went home and washed, for hours. Si says he came to the hospital the next day with his hands scrubbed raw.” She put her cup down. “He’ll come home washed. That’s what he does when he’s done something. Don’t let him do all the washing on his own.”

The gate buzzed.

Aurelia stood up and picked up her bags. At the door she stopped and looked back.

“And Elowen. Whatever he tells you, he’ll tell you the truth. He can’t help it with you. It’s very irritating.”

She went out. Elowen heard the two cars pass each other on the drive, and one go, and one stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in through the kitchen door.

His clothes were clean. Not the clothes he’d left in. His hair was damp and combed straight back off his face, without the strand. He smelled of soap, strong and medicinal, the green kind from the Docks washroom. His nails were clean. Everything about him was clean, and his knuckles were red raw, scrubbed open across every joint.

He looked like a man who’d stood under a tap for a very long time trying to get something off.

He stopped just inside the door when he saw her.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“Forty-eight hours.”

“Forty-seven.”

She held out her hand. He came and took it, and bent and kissed her forehead, carefully, on the side away from the strips. He didn’t let go of her hand afterwards.

She turned it over. She looked at his knuckles.

“Is anyone dead?”

She asked it quietly. She’d been practising it since three o’clock.

He could have said it’s dealt with. She watched him not say it.

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Three.”

She kept hold of his hand. “Who?”

“The man who shot at the shop. A man with a rifle at Qiu Wen’s house, who Bao shot when he came at us. And Qiu Wen.”

“You killed Qiu Wen.”

“Yes.”

“And the man with the gun.”

“Yes. On a staircase. He turned round with it.”

She breathed in, and out.

“The others?”

“The boy who stole the car’s with Wei Long. The driver’s alive. The man who came into your shop and ordered the wreaths is alive. He has one hand, now, that works.”

She didn’t ask what that meant. She thought she knew.

“Who paid for it?”

“Qiu Wen planned it. Maartens paid.” He said the name flatly. “The money came from Rotterdam through three companies. For the hand. That’s what they called it. For the hand.”

Maartens. The dinner in April. His fingers on her knee under the tablecloth, and then the fruit knife going through them into the table.

“Because of me,” she said.

“Because of me,” said Zhao. “I put the knife through it.”

He reached into his jacket. He took out a photograph, folded once, and held it, and didn’t give it to her straight away.

“I can keep this,” he said. “You don’t have to see it.”

She held out her hand.

He gave it to her.

She was on the step of the shop in the morning, holding white delphiniums, laughing at someone out of the frame. She remembered the morning. Xiao Pan had dropped a whole bucket of water down his front and she’d laughed until she had to sit down. Somebody had been across the road with a camera, and she hadn’t seen.

Around her face, in red marker, somebody had drawn a circle. Twice round, very carefully.

She turned it over. WIFE. CONFIRM.

She looked at the red circle.

She thought of Mimi with her five sunflowers, and Xiao Pan with forty-one pieces of glass in his back, and Bao’s weight coming down on her, and the star in the cooler door at the height of a heart. She thought of the man in the grey jacket saying you’re always here on Wednesdays. She thought of the man who’d drawn this circle, sitting in a window across the road with his cigarettes, waiting for a Wednesday.

And under all of it, quietly, without any pride at all, she found she was glad.

Glad they were dead. The one with the gun, and the one who’d paid him to use it. She didn’t feel sick about being glad. She’d thought she would. She just was.

She folded the photograph up and put it face down on the counter.

“Thank you for showing me,” she said.

He was watching her face. “You don’t have to forgive me for it.”

“I didn’t say I did.”

“I know.”

“I’m not going to tell you I wish they were alive,” she said. “I’m not going to lie to you either. It’s in the contract.”

Something happened in his face then, at that. Something gave.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit down so much as stop standing up.

He went down on to the kitchen floor with his back against the cupboard under the sink, and his hands came up and he looked at them, at the raw red knuckles, and they were shaking. Then all of him was shaking.

“Zhendong.”

He couldn’t answer. He tried. She watched him try. His jaw was clamped so hard she could see the muscle jump in it, and his breath was coming in short dry pulls, and he pressed his hands together between his knees as if he could hold them still by force.

She got down on the floor beside him.

She didn’t say anything. She didn’t tell him it was all right, because it wasn’t, and he’d know. She put her arm round his back and her other hand flat on his chest, over his heart, which was going far too fast, and she leaned her shoulder into his and stayed there.

He shook for a long time. The kitchen clock went round. The dogs came and lay down a little way off, both of them, with their chins on their paws, and watched him. Twenty minutes. Perhaps more. Once he made a sound against her hair that wasn’t a word, and she pressed her hand harder on his chest. Once he said her face, very low, and nothing else.

Slowly, under her palm, his heart came down.

When he could speak, he said, “I washed for an hour. At the Docks. I couldn’t get the smell of the pond off.”

“I know.”

“How do you know?”

“Aurelia told me what you do.”

He let his head go back against the cupboard. His eyes were red. He looked at her.

“She talks too much.”

“She loves you,” said Elowen. “It’s very irritating.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got the cream out of the drawer by the stove, the thick white one she used on her own hands in winter when the water at the market cracked them, and a bowl of warm water and a clean cloth, and sat him on the stool at the counter.

“Give me your hands.”

He gave them to her. She washed them first, gently, because there was still soap in the cracks, and then patted them dry. Then she warmed some cream between her own palms and took his right hand and worked it in, slowly, into every split knuckle, round each joint, down between his fingers.

He went very still. He watched her hands on his.

“Does it sting?”

“No.”

She looked up at him.

“Yes,” he said.

“Better.”

She did the left one. When she got to his wrist she found the black hair tie, still there, stretched now, the colour faded where it had been in the sea.

“You’re still wearing this.”

“Yes.”

“You went in the harbour with it.”

“Yes.”

She slid it off over his hand. He watched it go. She gathered her hair at the back of her neck, carefully, away from the strips, and tied it up with the elastic.

“I’m having it back,” she said.

“It’s yours.”

“I know it is.”

She went on rubbing the cream in long after it had all gone into his skin. Neither of them pretended she was still doing it for his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

“There’s something else,” he said.

She stopped.

“The man in the grey jacket. Yim. I asked him how Qiu Wen knew you were alone on Wednesdays.” He held her eyes. “He said Qiu Wen got it from the fixer’s people. He laughed when he said it. And at the pond, at the end, Qiu Wen told me to ask my father-in-law.”

The kitchen was very quiet.

“Baba,” she said.

“I don’t know that. I know what two men said, and one of them was trying to hurt me while he said it.” His voice was careful. “It might be someone round him. It might be someone who wanted me to think it.”

“The fixer.” She’d heard men call her father that all her life, on the phone in his study, at the New Year market, never to his face. “The fixer’s people.”

“Yes.”

She stood up and went to the window. In the courtyard the lemon tree was dark against the morning, wet from the night.

“Have you had him watched?”

“No.”

“Have you sent anyone to the house?”

“No.”

“Are you going to?”

He didn’t answer straight away. She turned round.

“Zhendong.”

“If someone in your father’s house sold your Wednesdays to a man who sent a gun,” he said, very quietly, “I want to know who. And I want them.”

“I know you do.” She came back and stood in front of him. “Page three.”

He looked up at her.

“The contract. Page three. You keep away from my family unless I ask. You protect them, you don’t own them. My father is mine.” She put her hand on his chest again, over the same place. “Mine to deal with. Not yours.”

He looked at her.

“And if he lies to you?”

“Then I’ll decide what to do.”

“And if it’s worse than lying?”

“Then I’ll still decide.” She held his eyes. “You can be there. You can’t go first. Not with him.”

He put his hand over hers on his chest and held it there.

“I won’t go first,” he said.

“Promise.”

“I won’t touch Lin Jian or anyone in that house until you’ve been. If I find anything, you hear it before I do anything about it.”

She breathed out.

He stood up off the stool. He was very close, and her hand was still on his chest under his, and he looked down at her. And then, without asking, without any of the stillness he always left at the end for her to cross, he bent his head and kissed her.

It was sudden and it was hard and it had two days in it. She made a small surprised sound and then she didn’t, and she went up on her toes and put her arms round his neck and kissed him back, the counter against her spine, his scrubbed hands spread on her back.

He pulled away. His face had changed.

“Elowen. I didn’t ask, I should have—“

She put her fingers over his mouth.

“Don’t,” she said.

He stopped.

“Don’t apologise for kissing your wife in her kitchen.” She took her fingers away. “I’d have said yes. I’d have said yes from the stairs. You’re allowed not to ask, sometimes. When you’ve been gone two days.”

He put his forehead against hers and breathed. She felt his hands, still faintly trembling, holding on to her shirt at the back.

“Tea,” she said, after a while. “And eggs. You’re eating something that isn’t coffee.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I don’t care.”

He sat back down on the stool. She put the kettle on and two eggs in a pan, and stood at the stove with her back to him, and heard him breathe out behind her, long and slow, as if he’d been holding it since Wednesday.

She brought him the eggs. He ate them. He was asleep on the sofa twenty minutes later with his head on the cushion where Aurelia had slept and Noodle across his feet, and she stood in the doorway and watched him for a while.

Then she went upstairs to find her shoes. Her father’s house was on the other side of the city, and she wasn’t going to wait for Sunday lunch to ask him anything.

chapters.title: She Goes to Her Father’s House
chapters.desc: She leaves her husband asleep with a second hair tie on his wrist and goes to the Walled City. Eliana has already found the man who sold her Wednesdays, and a message that says their father knew.
chapters.content:
He was asleep on the sofa when she came down, and she stood in the doorway for a while before she went in, because she’d never seen him sleep like that.

He slept like a guard dog, usually. One sound and his eyes were open. Now he was on his front with one arm hanging off the cushion and his face turned into the back of the sofa, his hair all over his forehead, and Noodle lying across his ankles like a sandbag. He didn’t move when she crossed the room. He didn’t move when she knelt down beside him.

His wrist was bare where her hair tie had been.

She took a second one off her own wrist, a pale brown one, old and a little stretched, and slid it very carefully over his hand.

His eyes opened.

“Where are you going?” His voice was thick.

“You’re supposed to be asleep.”

“I am.” He looked at the elastic on his wrist. Then at her shoes. “Your father.”

“Yes.”

“Take Bao.”

“I’m taking Bao.”

“Do you want me to come?”

“No.” She pushed his hair off his forehead. “I want to see him first. On my own.”

He looked at her for a long moment with his cheek on the cushion. Then he closed his fingers round hers and lifted them to his mouth.

“Back by dinner?”

“That’s what I was going to say.”

“Why two?” He meant the hair tie. “You took the other one back.”

“In case you lose this one.”

“I don’t lose things.”

“Back by dinner, husband,” she said, and kissed him, and he was asleep again before she’d got to the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bakery on the ferry road wasn’t open. The shutters were down and the queue that was usually outside by seven wasn’t there.

“That’s strange,” said Elowen.

Bao pulled in to the kerb. He got out.

“Bao. What are you doing?”

“Mr. Zhao sent a message before he slept, madam. About breakfast.”

One of the men from the second car came round with a hammer.

“Bao—“

The man hit the bakery shutter three times. The noise went up and down the empty street like gunfire, and a woman opened a window two floors up and shouted something, and then the shutter rattled and started to rise, and the baker’s face appeared underneath it, white with flour and alarm.

Elowen put her hand over her eyes.

She got out of the car. “I’m so sorry,” she said to the baker. “My husband’s very difficult.”

The baker looked at Bao, and the man with the hammer, and the black cars, and then at her.

“Yes, madam,” he said faintly.

She bought six egg tarts, the first out of the oven, and paid double, and apologised again. In the car she got out her phone.

Elowen: You had a man hammer on a bakery shutter.

Unknown: Did you get them?

Elowen: That’s not the point.

Unknown: Did you get them?

Elowen: Yes.

Unknown: Eat one before you get there.

She looked at the box on her knee. They were still hot through the cardboard. She ate one before they’d crossed the bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Lin house stood at the end of a lane in the oldest part of the Walled City, tall and narrow, three storeys of grey brick with a long veranda in front under a vine, and a wall round the garden that she’d climbed a thousand times. The house next door, on the other side of the wall, was the Wangs’. A boy’s bicycle leaned against it.

Raiden was sitting on the front step.

His left arm was in plaster from the knuckles to the shoulder. There was a neat row of black stitches running up into his hairline above his ear, and his round glasses were mended with tape at the hinge. He stood up when he saw her.

“Don’t you dare,” said Elowen.

He did anyway. She went up the path and put her arms round him, very carefully, round the plaster and the stitches, and he put his good arm round her and held on.

“You idiot,” she said into his shoulder.

“Good morning to you too.”

“You were hit by a van.”

“I noticed. I was there.”

She pulled back and looked at him. He tried to grin. It didn’t work very well.

“Do they hurt?” She touched the edge of the stitches.

“Only when you look at me like that.”

“Then I’ll stop.”

“You won’t.”

On the step beside him his phone lit up. A message. He put his hand over it and turned it face down on the brick before she could see the name.

She looked at the phone. She looked at him. He looked at the garden wall.

Neither of them said anything.

“Did you eat?” he said.

“Egg tarts. Zhendong had a man break into a bakery.”

Raiden stared at her. Then he laughed, and it hurt him, and he held his ribs with his good arm and kept laughing anyway.

“You married a lunatic.”

“I know.” She sat down on the step beside him. “Where’s Baba?”

“Office. He went at six. He hasn’t slept since Wednesday.” Raiden’s face changed. “Eliana’s in the dining room. You should see her before you see him.”

“Why?”

“Just see her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was at the dining table with her laptop and a stack of printouts and three empty cups. Her hair was twisted up in a claw clip that was losing the fight, and her round glasses were pushed up on her head, and there were revision notes for her last exam on the chair beside her that she had very obviously not looked at.

She stood up and hugged Elowen the way you’d hug something made of glass.

“I’m not going to break,” said Elowen.

“You might. You’ve got strips on your neck.” Eliana sat back down and pulled the laptop round. “I need to show you something, and I need you not to do anything about it until you’ve seen all of it.”

“Show me.”

Eliana turned the screen.

A list of payments. Small ones. Every couple of weeks since March. Never more than a few thousand at a time. Into an account in the name of a woman Elowen had never heard of.

“Feng Jun’s cousin,” said Eliana. “If she exists. The address is an empty flat. He opened the account himself, I’ve got the bank’s camera.” She tapped the screen. “And the money comes in from a freight company that’s paid the man in the grey jacket every month this year.”

Elowen looked at the name. “Feng.”

Feng Jun had stood behind her father’s chair for nine years. He drove him on the days Uncle Mok didn’t. He stood at the back of Sunday lunch with his hands folded, and passed the dishes if Ah Sim was busy, and called her Miss Lin even after she’d got married. She’d never once thought about him at all.

“He sold your Wednesdays,” said Eliana.

“How would he know my Wednesdays?”

Eliana looked at her. “Sunday lunch. Three weeks before the order. Baba asked you if you were still doing the market every morning, and you said—“

“I said not Wednesdays.” Elowen heard herself say it, at that table, over Ah Sim’s fish. “I said Wednesdays I do the hotels at the shop on my own till ten, so I don’t go to the market. Feng was at the door.”

“Feng was at the door.”

Elowen put both hands flat on the table.

“There’s more,” said Eliana. “I’m sorry. There’s worse.”

She clicked. A message, forwarded from somewhere. A screenshot of a phone.

“This went to Baba’s private number. From Feng. The second of June.” Eliana didn’t read it out. She didn’t need to.

I know you’ve asked the bank about me. You can let me go, or you can let me talk. If I go I’ll tell them about your paper twins. All of it. Where the girl came from. Why the boy was on a farm. Think about which one you want.

“The second of June,” said Elowen.

“The day after Baba asked the bank about Feng’s account. I found his search.” Eliana’s voice got very small. “He knew on the first. Eight days before the car, he knew Feng was being paid by the same people who ordered the wreaths. And he didn’t fire him. He didn’t tell Zhendong. He didn’t tell you.”

Elowen sat very still.

“Paper twins,” she said.

“I don’t know what it means.” Eliana pulled her glasses down and pushed them up again, which was what she did when she was lying, and Elowen saw her do it and let it go. “I know there are two birth records. Raiden’s and Evangeline’s. Same mother. Same day. Two different hospitals’ stamps. One of them’s from a clinic that closed the same year.”

“Evangeline,” said Elowen.

And as she said it, something came up out of the dark of her that she hadn’t known was there.

A kitchen. This kitchen, at night. She was small, small enough to be under the table. Mama at the sink with her back to her, and her shoulders going up and down. An infant on the counter in a basket, wrapped in a blanket that wasn’t any of theirs, pale silk, with a grey bird on it standing in water, and mountains behind the bird, embroidered in thread so fine it shone. And Baba’s voice, very low, from the door. And Mama saying, She isn’t even ours, Jian. She isn’t even ours.

She’d been not quite three. She’d thought she’d dreamed it.

“Elowen?”

“I remember,” said Elowen. “I thought it was a dream. There was a tiny girl in a silk blanket. With a bird. Mama was crying.” She looked at her sister. “Where’s Evangeline?”

“Kitchen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline was at the stove, making tea, with her hair tied back in its black ribbon the way she’d worn it since she was ten. She heard Elowen in the doorway and turned round, and her eyes went first to the strips on Elowen’s neck, and then to the printout in her hand, and stayed there.

She was twenty-three. She was Raiden’s twin. She’d been a quiet child and was a quiet woman, and she’d learned their mother’s recipes from Ah Sim without ever calling them her own, and she’d never once, in Elowen’s memory, raised her voice.

On the counter beside the kettle stood Mama’s flask.

Elowen hadn’t seen it in years. A small dented tin tea flask, painted green, the paint worn through to silver round the neck where a hand had held it. Mama had carried it to the market every morning, full of jasmine, and drunk from the cap between the stalls. After the funeral it had disappeared, and Elowen had thought it was lost.

“You kept it,” she said.

“Ah Sim gave it to me when I was twelve. To keep for you.” Evangeline picked it up and held it out across the kitchen. “I think you should have it now. You go to the market. She went to the market.”

Elowen took it. It was cool and light, and it fitted her hand exactly as she remembered it fitting her mother’s.

Evangeline looked at the printout again.

“Is that about me?” she said.

She asked it quite calmly. She asked it the way you’d ask whether the post had come. Her hands, though, had found the edge of the counter behind her.

Elowen could have said no. She could have said it’s about Feng, which was true. She looked at her sister’s hands on the counter.

“Yes,” she said.

Evangeline nodded slowly. She didn’t ask what it said. She didn’t look surprised. She looked, Elowen thought, like someone who’d been carrying something heavy up a long flight of stairs on her own, and had just heard footsteps behind her.

“Then you should go and ask him,” said Evangeline. “Before he decides to tell you something easier.”

“Do you know?”

Evangeline turned back to the stove and turned off the kettle.

“Ask him first,” she said. “Then come and ask me. I’ll tell you whatever he doesn’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden was still on the step. He’d turned the phone back over and was looking at a message on it, and he put it away again when she came out, a fraction too quickly.

She sat down beside him with the flask in her lap.

“You knew,” she said. “About the papers.”

He didn’t pretend he didn’t know what she meant.

“I knew there was something. I’ve known since I came home. Ten years on a farm because I was delicate.” He held up his plaster. “Look at me. I’m not delicate. I walked forty kilometres home on my own when I was ten because I’d decided I’d waited long enough.” He looked at the wall. “You don’t hide a delicate boy on a farm. You hide a boy on a farm so that nobody counts the infants.”

She looked at him. He looked so young suddenly, with the tape on his glasses.

“Why didn’t you say?”

“Because I didn’t know what was true. And because Evangeline’s my sister, El, whatever the paper says, and I wasn’t going to be the one who took that off her.” He swallowed. “Are you going to see him?”

“Yes.”

“Now?”

“Now.”

He nodded. His phone buzzed again in his pocket. He didn’t take it out.

“Raiden.”

“Mm?”

“Whoever that is. Don’t keep them from me forever.”

He went pink to the ears. “It’s nobody.”

“I know,” said Elowen, and kissed the top of his head, carefully, on the side without the stitches, and stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she got her phone out. There were two messages.

Unknown: Are you there?

Unknown: Did you eat one?

She looked at the flask in her lap. She looked at the printout. She thought about Feng at the door of the dining room with his hands folded, listening to her say Wednesdays I’m on my own.

Elowen: Yes. I’ve seen Eliana. I’m going to Baba’s office.

There was a long pause before the answer. She could almost see him sitting up on the sofa.

Unknown: Is Feng there?

She stared at the screen. She hadn’t said the name. She hadn’t told him anything.

Elowen: How do you know about Feng?

Another pause.

Unknown: Eliana sent it to Chen Si at four this morning. I’ve known for six hours. I haven’t moved. I promised.

She read it twice. She thought of him lying on the sofa with her pale brown hair tie on his wrist, knowing, and not moving, because she’d asked him not to go first.

Elowen: Thank you.

Unknown: Bao goes in with you.

Elowen: Bao waits outside the door.

The dots appeared and went and appeared.

Unknown: Outside the door. Back by dinner.

She put the phone in her pocket and held the flask with both hands all the way to her father’s office.

chapters.title: The Man in Her Father’s Office
chapters.desc: Feng is in the outer office eating sunflower seeds. Inside, her father finally tells her what he was paid to do with an infant in a silk blanket, while her husband cuts her tulips at the wrecked shop.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you can put me to bed yourself.”
chapters.content:
Zhao woke on the sofa at ten with a dog on his feet and two hair ties on his wrist.

He looked at them before he looked at anything else. One black, the one she’d taken back and then left on the arm of the sofa for him while he slept, as if she’d changed her mind. One pale brown, stretched, slightly fluffy at the join. He didn’t remember her putting the black one back. He remembered back by dinner and the smell of her hair.

He didn’t take them off.

There was a message on his phone from Eliana, sent to Chen Si at four that morning and forwarded on, with an account number and a name. He’d read it six hours ago and hadn’t moved. He read it again now.

Feng Jun.

He got up, showered, and went to the shop.

✦ ✦ ✦

It still smelled of glass. You wouldn’t think glass had a smell, but it did once it was broken, sharp and dusty, like a struck match. The front was boarded over with ply. The cooler door had a star in it at the height of a heart.

The glazier was on a ladder with a tape measure.

“Bank glass,” said Zhao. “Laminated, the whole front, not just the window. Steel in the frame. The same as the ground floor of the port authority.”

The glazier came down a rung. “That’s a great deal of glass, sir.”

“Then it’ll be very strong.”

“It’ll look like a bank.”

“It’ll look like a flower shop,” said Zhao. “From inside a bank.”

The glazier looked at Bao. Bao looked at nothing. The glazier went back up the ladder.

Xiao Pan was at the bench in a clean T-shirt with his back held very straight, sorting what was left of Wednesday’s stock. He’d been told not to come in. He’d come in. Behind the counter three buckets of tulips stood where they’d been left on Wednesday morning, white and apricot and plum, the stems uneven, the outer petals going soft.

Zhao took off his coat. He took her stem knife out of the drawer under the till, the short curved one she kept sharp enough to shave with, and picked up a tulip.

“Mr. Zhao, I’ll do those.”

“Do the roses.”

“But I—“

“Xiao Pan.”

Xiao Pan did the roses.

Zhao held the tulip the way she’d shown him in May, with his thumb behind the stem, and drew the knife towards himself on the angle, one clean pull. He stripped the lowest leaf below where the water would come. He put it in the fresh bucket. He took another.

He wasn’t good at this. She’d told him so often. But he knew how to cut a stem now, and which way to angle it, and that tulips kept growing after you’d cut them and bent towards the light, and that you couldn’t put them in with daffodils.

Xiao Pan watched him do ten. “That’s right,” he said.

“Was there a chance it wouldn’t be?”

“No, Mr. Zhao.”

He’d done half the first bucket when the thought came. It came the way such thoughts had always come to him, quite quietly, already complete.

Lin Jian’s office was on the second floor of an old godown by the river, with a window over the water. Lin Jian stood at that window most afternoons at four, drinking tea, looking at his barges. There was a roof opposite, a warehouse, flat, with a water tank on it. From behind the tank you could see straight into that window. It was a hundred and twenty metres. It was nothing.

Lin Jian had known for eight days. He’d known Feng was being paid by the people who’d ordered wreaths with Zhao’s name on them, and he’d let Feng stand at the back of Sunday lunch and listen to his daughter say Wednesdays I’m on my own. He’d let it happen because he was frightened for himself.

Zhao had killed men for much less. He could remember most of their names.

He stood with her knife in his hand and saw it. The roof. The tank. Four o’clock. The tea. A quiet, simple thing. He’d been doing quiet simple things since he was fifteen.

The knife was quite still in his hand.

He thought of her on the stairs of the Northgate office, a year and three months ago, stopping on the landing to listen. He thought of page three, and my father is mine, and her hand flat on his chest.

He put the knife down on the counter. It made a small sound.

Bao, at the door, looked round. “Sir?”

“Nothing.”

He picked the knife up again, and the next tulip, and cut it on the angle.

✦ ✦ ✦

Feng Jun was in the outer office eating sunflower seeds.

He was sitting in the chair by the wall where visitors waited, with one leg crossed over the other and a saucer on his knee, cracking the seeds between his front teeth and dropping the shells on the saucer one by one. There was a small grey heap of them already. He looked up when Elowen came in, and smiled.

“Miss Lin.”

She’d never liked that he called her that. She’d never said so.

“Mrs. Zhao,” she said.

“Of course.” He cracked another seed. “Your father asked me to wait.”

“Then wait.”

She went past him. Bao came in behind her and stopped just inside the door, and Feng’s eyes went to Bao and stayed on him for a moment, and then went back to his seeds.

Her father was at the window.

He turned round when she shut the door. He looked dreadful. He’d shaved badly; there was a nick on his jaw. His shirt was the same one he’d worn on Wednesday. On the desk a cup of tea had gone cold with a skin on it.

He looked at the printout in her hand. Then at the green tin flask in her other hand. Something happened in his face when he saw the flask.

“Who gave you that?”

“Evangeline. Ah Sim gave it to her to keep for me.” She put it on his desk between them. “Baba. You found Feng’s account on the first of June.”

He didn’t answer.

“Eight days before somebody shot through my window, with a six-year-old girl standing in front of my sunflowers. And Feng’s still sitting outside your door eating seeds.”

“I was finding out who else—“

“Feng sent you a message on the second. Your paper twins. Eliana has it.” Her voice was quite level. She didn’t know how. “So tell me. Not Feng. Not Eliana’s screen. You.”

Her father looked at the flask.

Then he sat down behind the desk, slowly, like an old man, and opened the bottom drawer and took out a flat envelope, soft at the edges and yellow with age, and put it beside the flask.

“In the spring of ninety-eight,” he said, “I was paid to make a child disappear.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told it to the desk, mostly.

He’d been thirty-one. He’d been moving cargo for people who paid in cash and didn’t write anything down, and he’d been good at it, because he could make papers say what he wanted and make customs officers forget what they’d seen. A man had come to him from abroad. A courtier, he supposed now, though he hadn’t known the word then. There was a little girl. She’d been born two days before to a woman who wasn’t the queen, and the man she’d been born to was a king, and the king’s family wanted her not to exist.

“Did they want her dead?”

“They didn’t say dead. They said gone. They said she must never be found and never be traced, and they paid me enough for it that I understood they didn’t much mind which.” He looked up at her for the first time. “Twenty years’ money. In one case. And an infant in a silk blanket with their crest on it, because nobody had thought to take it off her.”

A grey heron in water. Mountains behind it. She’d seen it from under a kitchen table when she was three.

“You kept her.”

“I kept her.” His mouth twisted. “I’d like to tell you I kept her because she was crying and I couldn’t do it. She was crying. I told myself it was that. I also told myself that a king’s daughter alive and hidden was worth more one day than a king’s daughter in the harbour. That’s the truth too. I’m telling you both.”

Elowen stood very still.

“Your mother was nine months gone with Raiden,” said her father. “She went into labour the night I brought the girl home. I registered them together. Twins. Born the same night, in a clinic that’s a dry-cleaner’s now. One boy, one girl.”

“And Raiden?”

“The people who paid me knew my wife had just given birth. They knew to the day. If they came to look, they’d find one newborn in my house, which was what they expected, and they’d go away.” His voice cracked. “If they found two, they’d count. And they’d know.”

“So you sent him away.”

“To the White Tower farm. Your mother’s cousin. The day he was born.” He put his hand over his eyes. “Your mother held him for an hour. Then I took him to the car. And she raised a king’s daughter in his cot and never once let anyone see her cry about it, except in the kitchen at night.”

She isn’t even ours, Jian.

“Raiden was hidden,” said Elowen slowly, “so nobody counted two infants.”

“For ten years.”

“And Evangeline grew up as his twin.”

“On paper. In every way that’s ever mattered to anyone, she is his twin.” He looked at her. “She doesn’t know who her father is.”

Elowen thought of Evangeline at the stove with her hands on the counter behind her, saying ask him first.

“Are you sure?”

He didn’t answer that.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You never ask,” said Elowen.

She hadn’t known it was going to come out until it did.

“You never ask any of us anything. You decided Mama would put a stranger’s child in her own son’s cot, and she did, and you never asked her. You decided Raiden would grow up on a farm with a cousin and come home at ten and be told he’d been delicate, and you never asked him. You decided Evangeline didn’t need to know who she was. You decided I didn’t need to know I had a sister who wasn’t my sister and a brother who’d been sent away for her.” She was shouting now. She didn’t care. “You decided Feng could stay because if he went he’d talk, and you never asked whether I’d rather be shot or have the neighbours know where Evangeline came from!”

Her father flinched as if she’d hit him.

“And you came to my house,” she said, “and sat at my table and ate my mother’s fish, and told my husband he was the price I’d paid. You. The only man in this family who ever sold anybody.”

He stood up. He came round the desk, and she thought for a second he was going to shout back, the way he had in March across Ah Sim’s fish.

He didn’t. He stopped in front of her with his hands hanging down, and his face broke.

He wept the way old men weep, without any sound to begin with, and then with a terrible sound, his shoulders going. She had never in her life seen him cry. Not at the funeral. Not at the grave every February with the red egg. He stood in front of her in his office with the barges going by outside and cried like a child.

“I was frightened,” he said. “I’ve been frightened for twenty-three years. Every time somebody knocked. Every time the girl went out of the house. I thought if I told one of you, it would come apart, all of it. I thought you’d look at me and see a man who’d taken money for a child and kept the money. I thought Raiden would hate me. I thought Evangeline would leave. I thought you’d go to him on your hill and never come back to this family.” He dragged his sleeve across his face. “I found Feng’s account and I was so frightened of what he’d say that I let him stay in the room with you. I did that. Not him. Me.”

She stood there. The anger didn’t go. But under it, now, she could see him: thirty-one, in a car at night, with a crying infant in a silk blanket on the seat beside him and a case full of money, deciding.

He’d done something good. He’d done something unforgivable. They were the same night.

“And I was wrong about him,” her father said, very low. “Zhao. At your table. I said what I said. I was wrong. He sat there and let me. He’s kept every promise he made you. I’ve broken every one I ever made your mother.” He looked at her with his ruined face. “Tell him I said so. No. I’ll tell him.”

She didn’t hug him. She wasn’t ready. But she put her hand out and took his wrist, the way you’d take hold of somebody on the edge of something, and held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the outer office, Feng had finished his seeds.

He’d heard the shouting through the door. He’d heard the old man crying. He set the saucer down on the chair beside him, quite neatly, and stood up and brushed the shells off his trousers.

“He’s been in there a long time,” he said to Bao.

Bao didn’t answer.

“Does Zhao know you’re here?”

“Yes.”

“Then he knows how this ends.” Feng’s hand went inside his jacket.

Bao had been watching that hand since he came in. He crossed the room in two steps and caught the wrist before the gun was clear of the holster, and turned it, all the way round, past where a wrist goes, and Feng’s scream went up the stairwell. The gun fell on the carpet. Bao drove him face first into the wall beside the door and held him there with a forearm across the back of his neck.

“Don’t,” said Bao.

The study door opened. Elowen stood in it, her father behind her.

She looked at the gun on the carpet. She looked at Feng, with his cheek flat against the wallpaper and his hand hanging at the wrong angle.

“Were you going to shoot me?” she said. “In my father’s office?”

Feng’s eyes swivelled to her. Then past her, to Lin Jian.

“You should’ve let me go, old man,” he said, through his teeth. “You were paid to do worse than me.”

Her father went grey.

Elowen took out her phone.

Under C, between CHEMIST and COOLER REPAIRS, there was a number Aurelia had put in at the Grand Meridian in January. CHEN SI (FOR EMERGENCIES, NOT GOSSIP).

He answered on the second ring. “Elowen?”

“Feng Jun is in my father’s office,” she said. “He’s the one who sold my Wednesdays. He’s just tried to draw a gun on me and Bao’s broken his wrist. He knows things about my family that will hurt people if he says them out loud.”

There was a short pause.

“What do you want?”

“I want him gone. I want him somewhere he can’t speak to anyone. And I want nobody to die.” She looked at Feng against the wall. “Not him. Not anyone. I don’t want to hear in a month that he fell down some stairs.”

“Elowen,” said Chen Si, “do you think I’ve no imagination at all?”

“I think you and my husband have far too much.”

He laughed, once. “Fair. Don’t let Bao loosen his grip. I’m coming myself. Forty minutes.”

She rang off. Then she sent another message, to a different name.

Elowen: Feng’s here. He tried to draw a gun. Bao has him. Nobody’s hurt but Feng. Chen Si’s coming. Don’t come. Please.

The answer came at once, as if he’d been holding the phone.

Unknown: Are you hurt.

Elowen: No.

Unknown: Baba?

She looked at her father, standing in the doorway with his hand over his mouth.

Elowen: He told me everything. I’ll tell you tonight. He’s crying.

There was a long gap.

Unknown: I’m at the shop. I’ve done your tulips. On the angle.

She laughed out loud, in that room, with a man pinned to the wall. She couldn’t help it.

Elowen: I’ll inspect them. You haven’t slept properly in three days.

Unknown: Then you can put me to bed yourself.

She looked at that for a long moment, standing in her father’s outer office with Feng breathing hard against the wallpaper, and felt something in her chest, very small and stubborn, come back to life.

Elowen: Is that an order?

Unknown: No. It’s a request. Page two.

She put the phone away.

“Baba,” she said. “Sit down. We’re waiting for Chen Si.”

chapters.title: What a Daughter Owes
chapters.desc: Chen Si takes Feng away and nobody dies. At the kitchen table her father tells them all about the paper twins. Evangeline already knew.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t being protected. I was being hidden.”
chapters.content:
Chen Si came without a convoy, which was the first thing Elowen noticed. The second was that he’d brought his wife.

Aurelia got out of the car outside the godown in a cream coat with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair and her pearls on, and looked up at the old building by the river as if she’d come to collect a parcel that had been sent to the wrong address. Chen Si came round the car in a dark overcoat. It was barely six and not yet dark, and he already had his thin black gloves on.

“Where is he?”

“Outer office,” said Bao, from the top of the stairs.

“Breathing?”

“Yes, sir. His wrist isn’t.”

Chen Si nodded as if that were a perfectly reasonable thing for a wrist to be. He looked at Elowen.

“Your husband rang me,” he said. “Twice. The first time he said he wanted Feng. He said it in a way I’ve only heard him use about three men in eleven years. All three are dead.” He took off one glove, finger by finger, and put it back on again. “The second time he said, She said no. Then no. And put the phone down.”

Elowen didn’t trust herself to say anything.

“He spent twenty minutes before that telling me he was going to respect your wishes,” said Aurelia. “I told him I’d understood the first time. He told me again. I think he was telling himself.”

“Nobody dies,” said Chen Si. “I promise you that. Feng goes to Song Wei Long with his phone and his bank and everything Eliana found, and he goes in one piece, more or less.” He glanced at Bao. “Less.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. Tell your husband he owes me a dinner.”

“He owes you a dinner every week.”

“A better one.”

Aurelia took Elowen’s arm and held on to it, and the three of them went up the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Feng was back in his chair by the wall. Somebody had given him a glass of water. His right wrist was in his lap at an angle that made Elowen’s stomach turn, and he was sweating, but he looked up at Chen Si with the same faint smile he’d had for the sunflower seeds.

“Quite a party,” he said.

Chen Si pulled a chair across and sat down opposite him, knee to knee, and looked at him for a while without saying anything at all. He did it the way he did everything, very still. After a minute Feng’s smile started to go.

“You’ve been busy,” said Chen Si. “You sold her Wednesdays. You sold them twice, once to the man in the grey jacket and once to Qiu Wen directly, because you thought nobody would notice two payments. You tried to sell this family’s history to its own father. And in March of last year you went down to the warehouse by the north dock with two of Qiu Wen’s men and broke an old man’s legs with a bar.”

Elowen went very still.

“Old Lau,” said Chen Si, without looking round at her. “You held the bar. One of Qiu’s men held him down. You wrote the note yourself. Lin Jian’s people walk slowly now. Eliana found your handwriting on a betting slip from the same week.” He leaned back. “You’d stood behind Lin Jian’s chair for eight years by then. You’d eaten his rice. Old Lau used to bring you cigarettes.”

Feng looked at the floor.

“Take him down,” said Chen Si. “My car. Not Bao’s.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He rode in the back with Feng himself. Bao drove. Aurelia took Elowen in the other car, which was how Elowen came to hear about the next part only much later, and only from Aurelia, who’d had it from her husband in bed.

Halfway across the bridge, Chen Si spoke for the first time.

“The two children,” he said. “The girl and the boy. The papers.”

Feng turned his head.

“You’ll never say those words,” said Chen Si. “Not to Song Wei Long. Not to a lawyer. Not to a cellmate. Not to a priest. If they ever leave your mouth, in a cell or a courtroom or in your sleep, I’ll know by the evening.” He looked out of the window at the river. “Your cousin’s flat is empty, I’m told. I’ve had it looked at. It wouldn’t stay empty for long. And your mother still lives behind the fish market, on the third floor, and she still goes down for her bread at seven.”

Feng said nothing at all for the rest of the journey.

At the police station on the east side, Song Wei Long was waiting on the steps in a dark jacket, with two uniforms behind him. He looked at Chen Si and Chen Si looked at him, two men who’d known each other’s names for years and had never once had cause to shake hands. They didn’t now.

“Feng Jun,” said Song Wei Long. “You’re under arrest in connection with the shooting at the shop on Ferry Road on Wednesday, conspiracy to murder, and an assault in March of last year. You don’t have to say anything.”

Feng didn’t.

Song Wei Long took the folder Chen Si held out to him. He looked at it. He looked at Feng’s wrist.

“He fell,” said Chen Si.

“Did he.”

“Against a wall. Repeatedly.”

Song Wei Long looked at him for a long moment. Then he put the folder under his arm.

“There are some old papers in here,” he said. “About two children in the Lin family.”

“They’ve nothing to do with the shooting.”

“If they have, I’ll follow them.”

“If they have,” said Chen Si, “you’ll find I’ve already been there.” He turned to go. “She trusts you, Detective. She rang you before she rang him. Don’t make her sorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight that evening the five of them sat round the kitchen table in the tall house in the Walled City, and their father stood at the head of it, because he couldn’t sit down.

Ah Sim had made too much food, out of habit and grief, and nobody had touched it. Raiden had his plaster propped on a cushion. Eliana had her laptop shut in front of her with both hands flat on the lid, as if it might open on its own. Elara had come from the hospital in her clothes from the ward and sat at the end with her arms folded tight, not looking at anyone. Evangeline sat between Raiden and the window, her hair in its black ribbon, her hands round a cup of tea gone cold.

Elowen sat at the other end, with the green tin flask on the table in front of her. Zhao wasn’t there. It was a Lin table tonight. She’d told him so in the car on the way back from the station, and he’d said, Yes, very quietly, and gone home.

Her father told it all again, from the start.

He told it better the second time, or worse. The courtier. The silk blanket with the heron on it. The case of money he’d kept. The night their mother went into labour. The boy in the car, an hour old, going to the White Tower farm. The girl in the cot. The clinic that was a dry-cleaner’s now. Ten years.

Nobody interrupted him. Elara put her hand over her mouth at one point and kept it there.

When he’d finished, Raiden said, “Ten years.”

“Yes.”

“You told me I was delicate.”

“Yes.”

“You told me I’d been ill as a small child and the city air was bad for me. You told me that at the farm every New Year when you came. You told me that on the step when I walked home.” Raiden’s voice was very quiet. It was much worse than if he’d shouted. “You’ve told me my whole life I was the one who had to look after everyone. The son. Raiden, see to your sisters. And the whole time you’d posted me to a farm so nobody would notice there were two of us.”

“Raiden—“

“I wasn’t being protected,” said Raiden. “I was being hidden.”

The kitchen was silent.

Then Raiden turned in his chair, plaster and all, and put his good arm round Evangeline and pulled her against him.

She made a small sound. She held on to him. She put her face in his shoulder and her hand flat on his back over the T-shirt, and he held her so hard his knuckles went white on her arm.

“You were two days old,” he said into her hair.

“So were you.”

“You didn’t do it.”

“No,” said Evangeline. “I just lived in it. Same as you.”

Elowen looked away, at the flask, because she couldn’t look at them.

✦ ✦ ✦

“How long have you known?” Elowen said, when Raiden let go.

Everyone turned to look at her. Then at Evangeline.

Evangeline put her cold tea down.

“Since I was fifteen,” she said.

Her father’s head came up.

“I was looking for a box of Mama’s things in the attic. For a school project. There was a cloth bundle at the back under the eaves, behind the Christmas lights.” She spoke quite calmly. “It was an infant’s blanket. Silk. Very old. There was a crest worked in the corner in grey thread, a heron standing in water with mountains behind it. I’d seen the same crest once before, on an envelope in the locked drawer of your desk that you didn’t know I’d seen.” She looked at her father. “I knew then. Not the details. But I knew I hadn’t been born in this house.”

“You never said.”

“You never asked.”

She said it gently. It was the worst thing anyone had said all night.

“I was fifteen. You’d taken me from somewhere once. I didn’t know if you’d do it again if I was difficult.” She folded her hands. “So I put it back exactly where it was, and I came downstairs, and Raiden found me crying in the bathroom and I wouldn’t tell him why.”

Raiden stared at her. “That was why?”

“That was why.”

“I thought you’d failed maths.”

“I never failed maths in my life.”

Something that was almost a laugh went round the table and didn’t quite land anywhere.

“It’s still there,” said Evangeline. “The blanket. Behind the lights. I go up and look at it sometimes. That’s all.”

Her father sat down at last, heavily, at the head of the table, as if his legs had decided for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Old Lau,” said Elowen.

Her father flinched.

“Chen Si said Feng held the bar. He wrote the note himself. Did you know?”

“No. I swear to you. Not that.” His face was grey. “I thought it was the Qiu brothers. I paid Old Lau’s hospital, I paid his rent, I went to see him every week, and the whole time the man who’d done it was driving me there and waiting in the car.”

Raiden’s good hand closed into a fist on the table. “I’ll kill him.”

“No,” said Elowen.

“He broke an old man’s legs, El. He helped them shoot you.”

“He’s in a cell. Wei Long has him. Chen Si has him.” She looked at her brother. “Nobody in this family is going to kill anybody tonight. That’s mine. I decided it. I’m not having it taken back.”

Raiden looked at her for a long moment. Then his fist opened, slowly, on the tablecloth.

✦ ✦ ✦

Their father looked round at them all. His face had gone somewhere past crying.

“I can’t give any of you the years back,” he said. “I can’t make it not have happened. If you want to know anything, I’ll tell you. Whatever it is. I won’t decide for you any more what you can carry.”

Elowen looked at him across the cold food.

“Then ask us,” she said.

He looked at her.

“That’s all. Before you decide what’s good for us. Before you hide something because you think we’ll break. Ask. Ask Evangeline what she wants to do about who she is. Ask Raiden if he wants to know about the farm. Ask Eliana before you send her to a school she doesn’t want. Ask me before you let a man stand at the door while I talk about my Wednesdays.”

“I will.”

“You’ll forget.”

“Then remind me.”

“I’m not coming to Sunday lunch,” said Elowen. “Not for a while.”

That landed harder than anything else she’d said. She watched it land.

“Are you angry with me?”

“Yes.”

“Will you come back?”

“When I’m ready. I’ll ring you. I’ll come to the grave in February. I’m not leaving the family, Baba. I’m just not sitting at that table and passing you the fish until I can do it without wanting to throw it at you.”

Her father was quiet.

“All right,” he said.

It was the first time she could remember him being told no in that kitchen and not arguing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the gate. It was full dark. The Wangs’ house next door had one window lit at the top, and a boy’s shape in it, at a desk. Bao was waiting by the car at the end of the lane.

Her father stopped at the gate with his hand on it.

“Elowen.”

“Yes?”

He seemed to struggle with something. He looked at the lane, and the car, and the lit window next door. Then he looked at her.

“Are you happy?” he said. “With him?”

She stood very still with the flask in her hands.

He’d never asked. In fifteen months he’d asked whether Zhao was paying the debt, whether Zhao was keeping his word, whether Zhao had hurt her, whether she was safe up on that hill. He’d told Zhao he was the price. He’d never once asked her the only thing that mattered.

“Yes,” she said.

He nodded slowly. He looked at her face the way he’d looked at the lemon tree in October.

“Good,” he said. “Go home, then.”

She got into the car. Bao shut the door. She sat in the dark back seat holding her mother’s flask and watched her father standing at the gate in the light from the porch, and she found, when the car had pulled out of the lane, that she couldn’t tell Bao where to go.

Home was the obvious word. She opened her mouth to say it.

She thought of Zhao at the top of the stairs, waiting, with two hair ties on his wrist and his knuckles scrubbed raw, and the question in his face that he’d been carrying since September. She thought of having to tell it all again, the heron and the farm and the cot, to someone who’d look at her the way he would.

She didn’t have it in her. There was nothing left in her to tell it with.

“Mrs. Zhao?” said Bao.

“Just drive for a minute,” said Elowen, and took out her phone.

chapters.title: A Phone Call From the Top Floor
chapters.desc: She can’t go home tonight, so Aurelia takes her forty-four floors up, runs a bath and tells her about the boat. Her husband sits on the stairs till morning.
chapters.epigraph: “Tomorrow, don’t let me sleep. Page two, line six.”
chapters.content:
She wrote it four times before she sent it.

Elowen: I can’t come home tonight.

She looked at it. It looked like an ending. She deleted it.

Elowen: I need one night away. Not from you. I just can’t tell it all again tonight. I haven’t got anything left to tell it with.

She sent it before she could change it, and held the phone in both hands in the back of the car, and watched the river go by.

It took him a long time to answer. She could see him reading it. She could see him reading it again, standing in the hall at the bottom of the stairs, deciding whether away meant the house or him.

Unknown: Where?

Elowen: Aurelia’s.

Unknown: Bao takes you.

Elowen: Bao’s already driving.

Another long gap.

Unknown: Then he stays outside her door. Not inside. Outside.

She looked at that for a while. He’d learned that this year. He’d learned it on a staircase.

Elowen: Please don’t be hurt.

Unknown: I’m not hurt.

She knew he was lying. It was in the contract, and he was lying anyway, because he thought it was the kind thing.

Unknown: Take the night. I’ll be here.

She wanted to write something else. It was right there, three words, sitting at the back of her throat where it had been since the bathroom floor on Wednesday. They were too big to fit through her mouth tonight.

Elowen: Thank you.

She put the phone in her lap. “Bao,” she said. “The Chens’, please.”

“Yes, madam,” said Bao, who had known where they were going since the first message, and had already turned on to the bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia was waiting in the lobby of the tower in her pyjamas.

They were silk, the colour of milky tea, with a long robe over them and fur-lined slippers on her feet, and she’d come down forty-four floors at eleven at night in front of the night porter and two security guards and a man delivering noodles without the slightest sign of caring. Her hair was twisted up in a clip. Her face was bare. Without her pearls and her headband she looked about seventeen.

She took one look at Elowen coming through the revolving door.

“Oh, darling,” she said, and opened her arms.

That was all. She didn’t ask anything. Elowen walked into her and put her face in silk that smelled of jasmine and night cream, and Aurelia held on to her in the middle of the marble lobby with the noodle man staring, and rocked her very slightly from side to side, the way you’d rock a child.

Behind them Bao came in with the overnight bag Elowen hadn’t packed and didn’t remember anybody packing.

“You can come up,” Aurelia told him over Elowen’s head. “And sit outside my door. Si’s got a chair. He likes a man outside the door, it makes him feel at home.”

In the lift Aurelia held her hand and watched the numbers.

“I’m not going to ask you anything,” she said. “I just want you to know that I’m not asking because I’m being a saint, I’m not asking because Si’s already told me most of it. So you needn’t.”

“How much?”

“The blanket. The farm. Feng. Old Lau.” The numbers went past thirty. “I’ve also been told that you shouted at your father until he cried. Si said Bao said they could hear it in the street.”

Elowen laughed, and it came out wet. “He cried before I’d finished.”

“Good,” said Aurelia, with great satisfaction, and the lift opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bath was already running.

It was a stone bath the size of a small boat, set right against a window that went from the floor to the ceiling, so that you’d lie in the water and look straight out over the river and the lights of half the city, forty-four floors down. Aurelia had put something in it that smelled of figs. Ripe ones, split open in the sun. The foam was up to the rim.

“You said once that it smells like an expensive fruit market,” said Aurelia. “I’ve bought you the whole bottle. Don’t argue. I’ve got another.”

There were towels warming on a rail. A robe on the back of the door. A tray on the ledge with tea, and water, and a plate of cut pear.

“You did all this?”

“I’m capable of hospitality.”

“You charge triple.”

“To clients.” Aurelia sat down on the wide stone ledge at the end of the bath, tucked her feet up under her robe, and picked up a glass of water. “Get in.”

Elowen sat down on the edge of the bath.

She didn’t take her shoes off. She didn’t take anything off. She sat there in her jeans and her shirt with Mama’s green flask still in her coat pocket, looking at the foam, and couldn’t think how you began.

Aurelia didn’t tell her to. She looked out at the river.

“Did Si ever tell you why I don’t drink champagne at dinners?” she said.

Elowen shook her head.

“New Year’s Eve, before last. There was a dinner on a boat in the harbour. Forty people. All of them important, all of them pretending to like each other.” Aurelia turned her glass round in her fingers. “Somebody painted something on the rim of my glass. Not in the wine. On the glass. They knew Si always drinks out of mine. He does it to annoy me. He’s done it since the first night.” She was quite calm. “So he took my glass out of my hand at midnight and drank from it and kissed me, and twenty minutes later his hand started to shake.”

Elowen looked at her.

“I didn’t know what it was. I knew it was wrong. He kept telling me not to make a fuss in front of everyone, so I didn’t. I put my arm round him and laughed as if he were drunk, and I walked him out to the back of the boat with my face in his shoulder, so nobody would see him fall. And then he fell.” Aurelia took a sip of water. “Your husband carried him down to the launch. Down a ladder, in the dark, over his shoulder. I’ve never seen anybody move like that.”

“What was it?”

“A heart poison. From a plant, Dr. Ma said. If he’d had a full glass he’d have died on the boat. The antidote barely worked. They didn’t think he’d live through the first night.” She put the glass down. “He was in intensive care for two weeks. And there were nine men in the Syndicate who’d have been very glad to hear he wasn’t coming back, and one of them had done it.”

“What did you do?”

“I sat at his desk.” Aurelia smiled at the river. “I told them all it was food poisoning. I signed his name. I ran it, everything, every boat and every account and every man who came to the door with a question, for fourteen days, from a laptop in a hospital corridor with a gun in my handbag, because I didn’t know which one of them it was. And I was so frightened I was sick every morning in the visitors’ toilet before I went in.”

“You found him.”

“A pharmacologist painted the glass. A man at the port paid him. And the man who paid the man at the port was Sun Wei, who’d eaten at our table every Sunday for three years and brought me orchids.” Aurelia’s face didn’t change. “Your husband offered to kill him for me. He said it quite kindly. As if he were offering to carry my bags.”

“And?”

“I said no.” She looked at Elowen. “I wanted to. I wanted to more than I’ve ever wanted anything. But Si was lying in a bed with tubes in him, and I thought, if I start, then that’s who I am when he wakes up. So Zhendong drove Sun Wei to the border in the middle of the night and left him on the other side of it with nothing but his shoes. And Si woke up and I’d done the whole thing in his name and he never found a single mistake.”

Elowen was crying. She didn’t know when she’d started.

“Why are you telling me this?”

“Because you think you’re the only woman who ever married one of them and found out what it costs,” said Aurelia. “And you think you have to be very brave about it, all the time, in front of him, because he’s so frightened for you that he can’t see straight.” She leaned forward. “You don’t. You can love him and hate what comes to the door because of him. You can be furious with your father and still want him at the grave in February. You can be all of it at once, darling. You don’t have to pick.”

Elowen looked down at the foam.

Then she stood up, in her jeans and her shirt and her shoes, and stepped over the edge into the bath.
