The water came up over her knees, hot, and soaked straight through the denim, and she sat down in it with all her clothes on, foam up to her chest, and put her face in her hands and finally, finally cried.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came up from somewhere so deep she didn’t recognise it. Huge, ugly sobs, the kind that hurt her ribs and made a noise she’d have been ashamed of in front of anyone else in the world. She cried for the window and the star in the cooler door. For Mimi’s broken stem. For Xiao Pan’s back. For the red circle round her face. For her mother in a kitchen at night saying she isn’t even ours. For a boy in a car an hour old. For Evangeline at fifteen in the attic, putting the blanket back exactly where she’d found it.

Aurelia got down off the ledge and knelt on the stone floor beside the bath in her silk robe, and leaned over the rim, and put her arms round Elowen, foam and wet shirt and all, and held on.

“There,” she said, into her hair. “There. Get it out.”

“I can’t stop.”

“Then don’t.”

“My jeans.”

“I’ll buy you new jeans. I’ll buy you a hundred pairs of jeans.”

“I love him,” said Elowen, into Aurelia’s soaking sleeve. “I love him so much and I couldn’t look at him. He was so gentle. He let me go. He didn’t even ask why.”

“I know.”

“What if he thinks I’m not coming back?”

“He will think that,” said Aurelia. “He’ll sit somewhere stupid all night thinking it. It won’t kill him. And then you’ll come back.”

She held her until it stopped. It took a long time. Then she helped her out of her wet jeans and her wet shirt, because Elowen’s fingers wouldn’t work the buttons, and dropped them on the floor in a heap, and ran more hot water, and sat back down on the ledge and held Elowen’s hand over the edge of the bath while she lay in the figs with her eyes shut and the lights of the city outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si rang his brother from the study at a quarter past one.

“Feng’s in a cell,” he said. “Song charged him at midnight. Shooting, conspiracy, the old man’s legs. Nobody’s touched him. Well. Since Bao.”

“Good.”

“Your wife’s in my bath.”

There was a silence on the line.

“She cried,” said Chen Si. “A great deal. In her clothes. Aurelia’s with her. She’s safe. She’s eaten a pear. She’s going to sleep in the green room with my wife in an armchair beside her like a dragon.”

“Thank you.”

Chen Si listened to the silence. It had a shape he knew.

“Where are you?”

“At home.”

“Where at home?”

No answer.

“Zhendong. Don’t tell me the armory.”

“No.”

“Then where.”

A pause. “The stairs.”

Chen Si shut his eyes.

He could see it. He’d seen it before, outside a door in a hospital corridor at two in the morning, on a plastic chair. His brother on the third step from the bottom in the dark, with his forearms on his knees and his phone in his hand and two of his wife’s hair ties on his wrist, facing the front door. Not going up to bed because she wasn’t in it. Not going anywhere he wouldn’t hear the gate.

“She isn’t leaving you,” Chen Si said.

“I know.”

“She just couldn’t tell it again tonight.”

“I know.”

“Then go to bed.”

“I’ll go later.”

“You won’t.” Chen Si sighed. “Fine. Sit on your stairs. Nobody died, Zhendong. You said no and you meant it. That’s never once happened before in your life.”

His brother didn’t say anything to that. After a while he said, “Goodnight, Si,” and rang off.

Chen Si went down the corridor to the green room. The door was open a crack. His wife was asleep in the armchair with her bare feet tucked under her and her mouth slightly open, and Elowen was in the bed, in a pair of Aurelia’s pale green silk pyjamas with little flowers on the collar, curled on her side, awake, looking at her phone.

He didn’t go in. He told Bao, outside the door, that he could sleep in the next room. Bao said, “No, thank you, sir,” and stayed in the chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote it at twenty to two, under the covers, in the glow of the screen.

She’d been lying there for an hour thinking about him on the stairs. Aurelia had told her. She’d laughed, because it was so exactly what he’d do, and then she’d stopped laughing because she could see it: the dark hall, the dogs, the front door, his face.

She thought about page two, line six. She’d written it in March at four in the morning with a different pen, in her old room in the Walled City, with her heart going so hard she’d thought she might be sick. You don’t touch me unless I ask. She thought about the thermometer by his soup in April. About the glass room, and the lamp left on, and his wrists under her hands on their anniversary, and please.

She typed it. She looked at it. She sent it.

Elowen: Tomorrow, don’t let me sleep. Page two, line six.

It said read almost before it had finished sending.

Nothing came back. She watched the screen. She knew exactly what he was doing: reading it again, on the stairs, in the dark, not trusting it.

Unknown: Are you sure.

No question mark. He’d never been any good with question marks.

Elowen: Yes. Not tonight. Tomorrow.

Another long gap.

Unknown: Tomorrow.

She lay there holding the phone against her chest. In the armchair Aurelia made a small sound in her sleep and turned her face into the cushion.

Elowen: I want to come home.

It took him almost a minute.

Unknown: Then come home. It’ll be here. So will I.

She put the phone under the pillow, the way she had when she was fourteen, and lay with her hand over it, and somewhere a long way below the window a boat went down the river towards the sea with its lights on. She didn’t remember falling asleep. She only remembered that, for the first time since Wednesday, she didn’t dream about glass.

chapters.title: She Comes Back Through the Front Door
chapters.desc: He spends the whole night on the bottom stair with the dogs, sure she isn’t coming back. She comes home in Aurelia’s clothes, tells him everything, and he asks her to save the last thing for a boring day.
chapters.epigraph: “If you’re going to say it, say it on a boring day.”
chapters.content:
He didn’t go up to bed.

He sat on the third stair from the bottom with his forearms on his knees and his phone in his hand, facing the front door, and he stayed there.

At some point after two Dumpling came out of the living room and lay down across the bottom step against his feet with a long sigh, as if somebody had to supervise him. Half an hour later Noodle arrived with a rope toy and dropped it on his shoe.

Zhao looked at it. “No.”

Noodle sat.

“No.”

Noodle put his chin on Zhao’s knee and looked up at him with enormous patience.

Zhao picked up the rope and held one end, and Noodle took the other, and they pulled it back and forth between them in the dark, very gently. Then Noodle lay down on the step above and put his head on Zhao’s shoulder, and the three of them sat there together facing the door.

He’d told Si he was comfortable. He’d told himself that one night was one night. He sat on the stair anyway, and somewhere around four, with the house dark and the dogs breathing, he let himself think it properly, the thing he’d been not thinking since September.

She’d married him for her father. She’d said so. She’d stayed because the danger was close, and then because it was quiet, and then because he’d built her a room, and she was kind, and didn’t like to waste things. And now she’d been to the bottom of it: the blanket, the farm, the money, the man at the door with the sunflower seeds. She’d seen what her father had done for fear and what her husband had done for her, the pond and the stairwell and the red circle. She’d stood in a stranger’s bath forty-four floors up and thought about all of it.

Perhaps she’d thought: enough.

He wouldn’t have blamed her. He’d have let her go. He’d promised that on page three, in her handwriting, the night she proposed: If I want to leave, you let me. He’d signed it.

He sat with that until it was light.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven Bao let himself in with the shop report and stopped dead in the hall.

“Morning, sir.”

Zhao nodded.

Bao looked at the dogs. He looked at the cold cup of tea on the step that Zhao had made at one and not drunk. He didn’t ask anything. He’d been at the bottom of a lot of staircases with this man.

“The glass goes in on Tuesday,” he said. “The stock that could be saved is in the temporary cooler. Xiao Pan’s been in since six. He says he’s fine.” A pause. “The car’s still outside Mr. Chen’s building, sir.”

“I know.”

“Shall I make breakfast?”

“No.”

Bao went to the kitchen anyway.

At half past seven Zhao’s phone buzzed so suddenly in his hand that Dumpling lifted his head.

Aurelia: She’s awake. She’s eaten an egg. She’s borrowing my clothes. Stop staring at your phone.

He looked at it for some time.

Zhao: I’m not.

Aurelia: You’re a terrible liar. She says so. I agree.

At five past eight, Noodle stood up and walked to the front door and whined at it.

“She doesn’t come because you ask,” Zhao told him.

Noodle wagged his tail at the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came in through the front door.

Not round by the garage, not through the kitchen with Bao ringing ahead. She came up the front steps on her own and put her key in the lock and turned it, and the sound went right through the house.

Noodle got there first, skidding on the hall tiles, nearly taking her bag out of her hand. Dumpling followed with more dignity and his tail going in circles.

“Yes,” she said. “Hello. Yes. I know.”

She was in Aurelia’s clothes. A pale cream cashmere jumper with a tiny flower stitched at the hem, black trousers turned up twice at the ankle, and a pair of Aurelia’s slippers two sizes too big. Her hair was tied back with her own black hair tie. Her eyes were swollen. She looked tired to the bone.

She saw him on the stairs.

He’d stood up. He was standing on the bottom step with one hand on the banister, in yesterday’s shirt and an old charcoal sweatshirt over it with a hole in the cuff, and his hair all over his face, and two of her hair ties on his wrist, and he was looking at her as if she might not be real, and he hadn’t moved.

She put her bag down on the floor.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

He still didn’t move. He was standing at the bottom of the stairs waiting for her to cross the hall, the way he’d waited for her to cross every distance since the night it rained, because he would never in his life be the one to close a gap she might not want closed.

So she crossed it.

She walked straight into him, and he caught her. Carefully for a second, as if he thought he might have got it wrong. Then his arms locked round her and he bent his head into her hair and held on so hard she felt it in her ribs.

“You thought I wouldn’t,” she said into his sweatshirt.

He didn’t answer. She felt his breath go out of him.

“You thought I wouldn’t come back?”

“I didn’t know,” he said, into her hair.

“I said one night.”

“I know.”

“I said I wanted to come home.”

“I know.” His voice was barely there. “People say things.”

She pulled back and looked at him. Under the hair his face was grey and his eyes were red at the rims and he hadn’t shaved.

“You sat on the stairs all night.”

“The dogs came.”

“I can see the dogs came.” She put her hand on his cheek. It was rough. “I’m home, Zhendong.”

He closed his eyes. He turned his face into her palm and kept it there.

Bao came out of the kitchen with a tray, saw them, and stopped.

“Madam.”

“Good morning, Bao.”

“Good morning, madam. Tea.” He put the tray down on the hall table. He looked at Zhao. Then at her. Something was going on in his big careful face, and she watched him decide to say it anyway.

“Madam. Excuse me. I think you should know. The first month after the wedding, he didn’t sleep in his room.”

“I know about the night after the dinner,” said Elowen. “The armchair.”

“No, madam. Every night.” Bao had gone a dull red. “From the night you moved in until the end of April. He sat outside your door. On the floor, mostly. If you turned over in your sleep he was awake. If you got up for water he was back in his room before you opened the door. He used to come down to the gatehouse at six and drink two coffees standing up and go to work.”

Zhao said, very quietly, “Bao.”

“I’m going, sir.” Bao picked up nothing and went out of the front door and shut it behind him.

Elowen stood in the hall with her hand still on her husband’s face.

“Every night,” she said.

He didn’t say anything.

“For a month. On the floor. Outside my door.”

“You were new in the house,” he said. “There were men in the gatehouse you’d never met. The dogs didn’t know you.” He looked away, at the stairs. “I didn’t want you to wake up somewhere strange and think you were alone in it.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“You’d have told me to stop.”

“I’d have told you to come in.”

He looked back at her.

“Not then, maybe,” she said. “Not in March. But by April I’d have told you to come in. I did tell you to come in. I left a thermometer by your soup.”

Something happened to his mouth that was nearly a smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs.

In the bedroom she sat him down on the end of the bed and stood in front of him and told him all of it.

She told it badly, out of order. Feng in the outer office with his saucer of shells. Eliana’s screen. Sunday lunch, and her own voice saying Wednesdays I’m on my own. The first of June. Eight days. The case of money. The heron on the blanket and the mountains behind it. A king’s daughter in a cot meant for someone else. Mama in the kitchen at night. Raiden in a car an hour old. I wasn’t being protected. I was being hidden. Evangeline at fifteen in the attic, behind the Christmas lights. Feng with the bar, and Old Lau’s legs. Chen Si in the car on the bridge. Her father at the gate.

Are you happy? With him?

He listened to every word. His hand had come up and closed round her wrist, and every so often, at the bad parts, it tightened, and then it let go again.

When she’d finished, he was quiet.

“Who else knows?”

“Chen Si. Aurelia. Wei Long has the papers, but Chen Si says he’ll keep them out of it. The family.” She swallowed. “And now you.”

“Then it stops there.” He looked up at her. “I’ll never say it. Not to Si, not to anyone. Not if somebody puts a gun in my mouth. Evangeline’s name is hers. Raiden’s farm is his. Nobody in the world gets to tell their story but them.”

“And if somebody tries to sell it again?”

His face changed, very slightly.

“Then I’ll ask you what you want done,” he said. “First.”

She looked at him for a long moment.

“You know what it’s like,” she said. “Somebody writing your story for you.”

“Old Zhao wrote mine. With a stove.” He turned her wrist over and looked at it. “I’ll keep hers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“You haven’t eaten,” she said.

“I had tea.”

“You made tea at one in the morning and let it go cold on the stairs. I saw it.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I don’t care.”

He looked up at her. She was standing between his knees in Aurelia’s soft cream jumper, with her eyes swollen and her mouth set, and he looked at her the way he’d looked at her across the shop in the rain.

She took a fistful of the front of his awful sweatshirt and pulled.

He came up off the bed into it, and she kissed him.

It was warm and clumsy and she’d been waiting all night to do it. He made a low sound against her mouth. His hands came to her waist under the cashmere and she felt the cold of his rings on her skin and gasped, and he started to apologise and she bit his lip to stop him, and then he laughed, a real laugh, startled out of him, and kissed her harder.

“This is an ugly sweatshirt,” she said, against his mouth.

“It’s warm.”

“It looks like something Si would throw out of a moving car.”

“Si has no taste.”

She pulled it over his head. It caught on his ears. He swore, and she laughed, and he got one arm stuck and stood there in the middle of the bedroom with a sleeve over his face and his other arm in the air until she took pity on him. His shirt underneath had six buttons and she managed four and lost patience and he did the last two himself, badly, his hands not quite steady.

“Page two,” she reminded him.

“I know what page it is.”

“Then why are you being so slow?”

“Because last time I was fast you bit me.”

“That was the armory. That was different.”

She stepped backwards towards the bed and her heel caught the edge of the rug, and she went over, and he grabbed for her and missed and they both went down sideways on to the mattress in a heap, his elbow in the pillow and her face in his shoulder, and she was laughing so hard she couldn’t breathe.

“Elowen.”

“Sorry. Sorry. Your face.”

“What’s wrong with my face?”

“Nothing. Nothing’s wrong with it.” She took it in both hands. She stopped laughing. “Nothing at all.”

He looked down at her. Then he stopped laughing too.

He pulled Aurelia’s jumper up over her head, slowly, his knuckles grazing her ribs, her arms, the inside of her wrists, and threw it behind him without looking where it went. It hit the chair and slid off on to the floor in a soft cream heap.

“That’s not mine,” she said. “It’s Aurelia’s. It’s cashmere.”

“I know.”

“You can’t throw cashmere.”

“I just did.”

“Fold it.”

He looked at the heap on the floor. He looked at her, lying under him in the morning light with her hair coming out of its tie.

“Later,” he said.

“Zhendong.”

“Much later.”

And then he didn’t let her sleep, which was what she’d asked for, and didn’t let her think either, which she hadn’t asked for and found she wanted more. It wasn’t graceful. Her elbow knocked a cushion off. They laughed into each other’s mouths. Somewhere in the middle of it she said your rings are freezing and he took them off one by one and put them on the bedside table without stopping kissing her neck, on the side without the strips, and she said that’s very impressive and he said I’ve had practice and she hit him, and he pulled the rest of her clothes off and his own and came into her slowly, laughing, and stopped laughing, and then neither of them said anything for a long while but each other’s names. The light moved across the floor. The dogs gave up scratching at the door and went downstairs. Aurelia’s cashmere stayed exactly where it had landed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest and his fingers going through her hair, very slowly, from the scalp to the ends, checking for glass that wasn’t there any more.

“I missed you,” she said.

His hand stopped. “One night.”

“It was a long night.”

“Yes.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. The sun was on his face. He looked younger, and very tired, and so much less careful than he’d looked at the bottom of the stairs.

There was something sitting in her chest. It had been there since the bathroom floor on Wednesday. It had been there, if she was honest, since the mountain, since before the mountain, since a dusty shop and a hole in the floor and I love her said to her brother as if it were a cost on an invoice. It had nothing to do with the stairs. It was there, and true, and it had got too big to keep.

“Zhendong. I—“

He put his fingers over her mouth.

She stopped.

“Not today,” he said.

She looked at him over his fingers.

“Not after the stairs,” he said, very low. “Not after your father and the farm and the blanket. Not after I’ve been gone two days and come home washed. Not because you think I need it.” He took his fingers away and put his thumb against her bottom lip instead. “If you’re going to say it, say it on a boring day.”

“A boring day.”

“When nothing’s happened. When nobody’s been shot at and nobody’s confessed and there’s nobody in a cell. When you’ve just come in from the market with wet hands and you’re thinking about lily prices.” His eyes were very dark. “Say it then. So I know it isn’t because of anything.”

She looked at him.

“That’s very specific,” she said.

“I’ve been thinking about it.”

“Since when?”

“September,” he said. “The mountain.”

She lay back down on his chest and listened to his heart under her ear.

“All right,” she said. “A boring day.”

“Thank you.”

“It might take a while. We’re not very good at boring.”

“I’ll wait.”

“I know you will,” said Elowen. “You’re the most patient man in the world. It’s insufferable.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went down at noon. He made eggs and she made tea, and the dogs walked between them round the kitchen as if they’d arranged the whole thing personally and expected to be thanked.

Her phone buzzed on the counter.

Aurelia: My jumper is on your floor, isn’t it.

Elowen looked at the stairs.

Elowen: I’ll have it cleaned.

Aurelia: Keep it. I hope it was worth it.

Elowen went pink. Zhao, at the stove, glanced round.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“It’s never nothing.”

She didn’t answer. She opened her contacts instead and scrolled down to U, past UNCLE PAK MARKET, to the name she’d typed in fifteen months ago on the night of the registry, sitting on the edge of her old bed in the Walled City, after a text had come in from a number she didn’t have. Cut them?

Unknown.

She’d never changed it. Not after the armory, not after the van, not after the mountain. She’d told herself it was a joke. She’d told Aurelia she knew who it was.

She pressed edit. She deleted it, letter by letter. She typed.

Zhendong.

She looked at it for a moment. Then she saved it.

He’d come round the counter with the pan in his hand and was looking over her shoulder. He saw the old name go and the new one come. He didn’t say anything at all.

She turned round. He put the pan down very carefully on the counter beside her, as if it were something that might go off, and took her face in his hands, and kissed her.

The boring day took two years.

chapters.title: A Shipment With Children’s Names on It
chapters.desc: Two years on, there’s a plant room with a tap at the height of her hip and a black card she can’t give back. Then he brings home the biggest deal he’s ever been offered and asks her to read it, every page.
chapters.content:
The new potting room had a tap at exactly the height of Elowen’s hip.

She noticed it before anything else: before the slate bench, the seed trays, the door at the far end into the courtyard, or the lemon tree beyond the glass with seven lemons still on it and the first white flowers opening. She walked in, and went to the sink, and turned the tap on, and the water came out exactly where her hands already were.

She turned it off. She turned it on again.

“Is something wrong?” said Zhao from the door.

“It’s at my hip.”

“Yes.”

“Not my chest. My hip. I can put a bucket under it without lifting the bucket.”

“Yes.”

She turned round. “Did you measure me?”

“Raiden measured you.” He was leaning on the door frame with a cup of tea, in a navy jumper, his hair still wet from the shower. “You stood at the bench at Baba’s at New Year and he looked at you and wrote something down. You didn’t notice.”

“Raiden drew this?”

“He drew all of it. He said the glass room was very beautiful and built by an idiot who measured the sink for himself.” Zhao drank some tea.

The glass room was still there, joined on at the other end, with its high tap that she’d told him to leave exactly where it was, two years ago, sitting on a stair at midnight. He’d left it. He’d built her another room instead.

“He drew the second door in red,” said Zhao. “No electric lock. It opens from inside if the power goes. He wrote non-negotiable next to it and underlined it twice.”

Of course he had. A light that stayed on. A door that opened from inside.

She went across the slate floor and put her arms round his waist.

“You built me another room.”

“You needed a sink.”

“I had a sink.”

“You had a sink at the wrong height for two years and didn’t say anything.”

“I said something on the stairs.”

“You said to leave it.” He set his tea down. “So I left it.”

She laughed into his jumper. He put his hand on the back of her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

The black card was a problem from the first morning.

He put it beside her plate at breakfast the way he’d have put down the salt. Matte black. No name on it, no bank, just a small silver mark in one corner.

She looked at it. She looked at him.

“What’s this?”

“A card.”

“I can see it’s a card.”

“It’s on an account. For you.”

“I have an account. I have the shop’s account. I have savings.”

“I know.” He buttered his toast. “This is for when you need something quickly and you stand in the shop doing sums for twenty minutes before you decide you can’t.”

She opened her mouth and shut it again. Since the glass, the shop cost more. The bank glass. The insurance, which had doubled. A new cooler door with no star in it. She’d paid for every bit of it from the shop’s money and the BUILDING account, and she’d put off replacing the van’s tyres twice, and the rose bucket with the crack, and she’d thought he hadn’t noticed.

“What’s the limit?”

He told her.

She put the card down on the table as if it were hot. “No.”

“It’s a card, Elowen. Not a proposal.”

“I’ve had one of those from you.”

“You made that one.”

She looked at it. Then she picked it up and put it in the back of her purse behind the loyalty card for the bakery on the ferry road.

“I’m not using it,” she said.

“That’s up to you.”

“And I’m not buying a mountain with it.”

“I’ve never once suggested a mountain.”

Three weeks later, at half past two on a Thursday, in the middle of a wedding order for two hundred guests, the shop’s cooler made a noise like a dying lorry and stopped.

She and Xiao Pan stood in front of it. The display went to eight degrees, and then to nine.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I haven’t said anything, boss.”

“You were thinking it.”

“I was thinking about the peonies.”

The engineer came at three, looked at the compressor, and gave her a price that made her shut her eyes. She rang the supplier. She looked at the shop’s balance on her phone. She worked out how many hours the peonies had at nine degrees before the wedding was ruined.

Then she took the black card out from behind the bakery loyalty card and paid with it, and the new compressor was in by six.

She sent him a message from the counter.

Elowen: The cooler died. I’ve used your card.

Zhendong: Good.

Elowen: Don’t be smug.

Zhendong: I’m in a meeting with eleven shipping agents. I’m not smug.

Elowen: You are. I can tell from here.

He came home that night and found the card on the kitchen counter by her keys. He picked it up and turned it over, and put it down again, and didn’t say a word, and didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ledgers came home in a locked case on a Friday.

“I’d like you to read something,” he said.

She was at the potting bench with a tray of ranunculus seedlings. “Your work?”

“Three of the companies. Warehousing. Freight. The yard at the north dock.”

“You’ve got accountants.”

“I’ve got eleven. I’d like you.” He set the case down on the slate and opened it. Ledgers, expense reports, bank summaries, a tablet. “You found Uncle Pak short-counting your roses after two years. You found Kang’s dates before anyone. You’re good at finding what people have spent a long time hiding.”

She took off her gloves.

He made her tea and went up to change. When he came back down half an hour later she had the whole bench covered, ledgers open, the tablet propped against a seed tray, and a pencil behind her ear.

“Who runs the eastern warehouses?”

“Han Qiming.”

“Does he sign his own transport expenses?”

Zhao came and looked. “He shouldn’t.”

“He does. Look.” She turned the ledger round. “Three payments on the same day to three different suppliers, nearly the same amount each time. Three invoices for separate equipment. Same handwriting on all three. The serial numbers on the equipment run one after the other.” She turned a page. “And here’s the same equipment again, three months later, booked as maintenance.”

“Double.”

“More than double. The three suppliers have the same registered address. One of the directors used to drive for Han.” She tapped another sheet. “And then there’s whoever signs off Han. Mr. Kwong.”

Zhao went still behind her.

“He’s been taking the difference out through a consultancy,” said Elowen. “It has no office and no staff and has never done anything that I can find, and it’s been paid every month by two of your companies for at least two years.”

“Kwong’s been with me for twelve years.”

“Then he’s had twelve years to practise.”

He looked down at the margin, where she’d made small neat arrows and notes in her round hand. This. And this. Ask why.

“You found this in an afternoon.”

“I haven’t finished.” She took the pencil from behind her ear. “Don’t send anybody round to Mr. Kwong’s house before your auditors have the original invoices. And don’t tell Han it was me.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Zhendong.”

“I heard you.”

The audit took eleven days. Han was gone by the end of it, and Kwong resigned by letter the night before he was due to be interviewed, which didn’t stop any of the money coming back. Chen Si rang her twice in a week, the first time to ask her to explain the suppliers again, and the second time to tell her, in a voice of deep injury, that he’d found two more of his own.

“You’ve made me distrust every invoice I’ve ever signed.”

“You should have been distrusting them already.”

“I have people for this.”

“Then you need better people.”

Down the phone she heard him say to someone, “Your wife is insulting me,” and Zhao’s voice in the background, “She’s right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The offer came home on a Monday at the beginning of March.

He put it on the kitchen island after dinner. A thick folder in dark leather, with a seal across the front that had already been cut. He didn’t sit down.

“Another set of ledgers?”

“No.”

“Something to read?”

“Yes.” He pulled out the stool for her. “All of it. Every page.”

She dried her hands and opened it.

The covering letter was from a holding company in Antwerp she’d never heard of. It was polite and short. At the bottom was a signature, and the signature leaned the wrong way, backwards, cramped, the hand of a man who’d learned to write again with the one he had left.

She knew whose it was before she read the name typed underneath.

“Maartens,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Two years ago you sent him a photograph of a man in a pond.”

“Yes.”

“And now he wants to do business.”

“He wants to make peace,” said Zhao. “Or he wants me to think he does. It comes to the same.”

She turned the pages. Company names. Payment schedules. Transport routes, insurance, end-user certificates, a delivery timetable over eight months, everything clean and correct and laid out the way he’d once taught her a good contract looked. Then she came to the summary on page eleven and stopped.

“Three hundred million.”

“Yes.”

“For one deal?”

“Five deliveries.”

“To whom?”

“The certificate says a provisional regional security authority in the Velde highlands.”

“And who gets them?”

“A militia called the Highland Front, through two companies in between.”

She kept reading. The papers were very good, which frightened her more than if they’d been bad.

At the back there was an annex in a separate sleeve, with RESTRICTED printed across the top in red.

She opened it.

A risk assessment. A map. A list of armed groups. And then a report from a monitoring organisation she’d heard of on the news, forty pages, in plain grey type.

She read the first paragraph. Then she read it again.

“Zhendong.”

He didn’t move.

“Did you read this?”

“Yes.”

The Highland Front recruited children. The report said so in the first line and then spent forty pages proving it. Children taken from villages and schools and roadsides. Children carrying ammunition, children on checkpoints, children walking in front of lorries on roads that might be mined. Testimony from boys who’d got out. Testimony from a girl.

And then names.

Not numbers. Not an estimated. Names, and ages, and where each child had last been seen, and on some of them, a photograph.

She turned the pages. She couldn’t stop.

Samuel Okonjo. 11.

A thin boy with a narrow face and his hair cut very short and unevenly, as if with a knife. His shirt was much too big for him. He was standing beside a stack of green ammunition boxes that came up to his chest, looking at the camera with no expression at all. The kind of no expression a child learns when he’s found out that showing anything makes it worse.

She put her finger on the photograph.

“Eleven.”

He didn’t answer.

“There’s a girl here who’s thirteen. There’s—“ Her voice went. She turned another page and there were more. “Did Maartens know?”

“The report was sent to his office in January. His office signed for it.”

“And he still sent it to you.”

“He sent it to me with it,” said Zhao. “So I’d know he knew. So I’d know he didn’t care.”

She looked at him over the photograph of Samuel Okonjo, and saw that he wasn’t answering the other question. The one she hadn’t asked. She asked it.

“Are you thinking about it?”

He didn’t say no straight away.

That frightened her more than anything in the folder.

She could see it go across his face: the number. Three hundred million. Enough to buy back everything the Red Notice had taken. The banks, the routes, the captains who’d resigned through lawyers. The ports that had stopped answering. Enough to make him what he’d been before the report in New York, and more. It was the deal of his life. Men like Maartens offered it once.

She shut the folder.

“No,” she said.

He looked at her.

“We don’t do this. You don’t do this.”

“Tell me why.”

He asked it quite quietly, as if he really wanted to know which reason she’d give.

“Not because of the paperwork. The paperwork’s beautiful. Not because of Maartens, though I’d like to put his other hand through a table myself.” She opened the folder again, to the page, and turned it round and pushed it across the marble to him. “Because of the names.”

He looked down at the boy.

“Because of the names,” she said. “Because somebody walked into a village and took a child who’s eleven and gave him a box of bullets to carry, and every crate in this folder is more bullets for that man to give him. That’s why. Samuel Okonjo. That’s the reason. Eleven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood looking at the photograph, and the kitchen went away.

He was eleven. It was summer, the hottest he could remember, and the rolling mill on the north side of the river was paying boys by the bundle to carry offcuts from the floor to the yard because it was cheaper than buying a crane. The steel was still warm from the line. You carried it on your shoulder with a rag under it and the rag wore through by noon. Old Zhao had sent him there because the man who ran the floor owed Old Zhao money and was paying it back in boys.

They’d said Friday. He’d carried steel for six weeks for nothing, because there was nowhere else to go and nobody who’d have taken him in if he’d run. The skin on his left shoulder had come away in the third week where a bar hadn’t cooled enough. A foreman had seen him crying and laughed and told him to carry on the other side.

He’d learned a great deal that summer. He’d learned that grown men could look straight at a child in pain and see a profit. He’d learned to keep his face still. He’d spent every year since making sure nobody would ever make him carry anything for free again.

Samuel Okonjo looked up at him off the page with exactly that face.

He closed the report. He picked up the folder, all of it, the letter and the contract and the routes and the certificates and the forty grey pages, and walked across the kitchen to the bin by the back door, and stepped on the pedal, and dropped the whole thing in on top of the eggshells and the tea leaves and the paper from that morning’s bread.

He let the lid fall.

Elowen had stood up.

“It’s finished,” he said.

“Just like that?”

“Yes.”

“Three hundred million. In the bin.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him across the kitchen. “And Maartens?”

His face went quiet. She’d seen it go like that twice before. Once over a peony at a gala. Once on the bathroom floor.

“Something’s going to happen,” he said.

“Zhendong.”

“Not tonight. Not to you.” He came back to the island. “I’m not moving his cargo. I’m not lending him a single ship or a single man. I’m not letting anyone who’s ever worked for me move it for him either.” He put his hand flat on the marble beside hers. “And he’ll take that as an answer. He’s a man who takes no as a message. Something will happen.”

“You’ll tell me first.”

“I’ll tell you first.”

“Before you do anything.”

“Before I do anything.”

She looked at him.

“You were eleven,” she said. It wasn’t a question. She’d seen it on his face.

“Yes.”

“Somebody made you carry something.”

“Steel,” he said. “For six weeks. They never paid.”

She came round the island. He didn’t move. He stood there with his hand on the cold marble the way he stood at the end of every distance, and when she got close enough he leaned down, very slightly, and stopped. A breath away. Waiting, still, after three years, for her to decide.

She took hold of the front of his jumper in both fists and pulled him the rest of the way and kissed him, hard, standing against the kitchen counter with three hundred million in the bin behind her.

He made a low sound and his hands came up and held her face. She kissed him until she could feel his heart slow down against her, and then she kept her forehead against his.

“Ring Chen Si,” she said.

“Tonight?”

“Now. And find out who else has had that folder. Who else has seen those names.” She swallowed. “And find out whether anybody’s looking for him. Samuel. Whether anybody knows where he is.”

Zhao looked at the bin.

“I’ll find out,” he said.

He rang Chen Si from the hall. She heard his voice go low and short, and Chen Si’s go sharp, and then a long silence. She went back to the bin and stood looking at the lid.

Then she lifted it, and reached in past the eggshells, and found the grey report by its corner and pulled it out, and wiped the tea off the cover with her sleeve. She left the rest where it was.

She took the report upstairs and put it in the drawer of her bedside table, under her mother’s gardening book, with the boy’s photograph on top.

chapters.title: He Cancels the Deal
chapters.desc: Chen Si says there are children in all of it, Bao tells her about his little brother, and Granny Yip says soft men live longer. Then the man who runs the northern warehouses calls her husband a dog in front of her, and she turns a page.
chapters.content:
Chen Si came on Tuesday with two coffees, a folder, and an argument.

He put the coffees on Zhao’s desk, put the folder beside them, and sat down without being asked. He was in a white shirt with the sleeves turned back once, and his hands, when he folded them on his knee, didn’t move again.

“What’s that?” said Zhao.

“An alternative.”

“I didn’t ask for one.”

“You never ask for anything. That’s usually when I bring one.”

Zhao opened it. Names of intermediaries. The companies on Maartens’s shipping plan. Two pages on the Highland Front’s supply lines, how the rifles came up from the coast in vegetable trucks and went the last forty kilometres on mules. And the monitoring report from the annex, the one with the photographs, with Chen Si’s pencil in the margins.

“Three hundred million,” said Chen Si.

“I can read.”

“I know you can read. I taught you.” He picked up his coffee. “I’m reminding you that the people who offered it won’t go away because you said no. They’ll find another broker. Another route. Someone who signs whatever’s put in front of him. There are children in all of it, Zhendong. They’re in it whether we’re in it or not.”

Zhao turned a page.

“We could have gone inside,” said Chen Si. “Taken the shipment, controlled it, followed the money to the men who hand those boys the guns. You can’t stop a chain you’re not standing in.”

“We would have supplied the weapons.”

“We’d have controlled the shipment.”

Zhao looked up.

Chen Si held his eyes for a moment. Then he put his coffee down and sat back. “I’m not saying do it. I’m saying there’s a difference between refusing a sale and stopping one.”

“Then we stop it without taking the money.”

“And if we can’t?”

“Then we don’t take the money.”

“You’re making this very simple.”

“I’m making the decision simple. The rest of it you can make as hard as you like.”

Chen Si looked out of the window at the cranes for a while. “You spent ten years telling me business is knowing what people want,” he said. “Now you’re turning down the deal of your life because of a boy’s name on a page.”

“His name was on the page before I read it.”

“Samuel Okonjo.”

“Yes.”

“Eleven.”

“Yes.”

Chen Si nodded slowly, the way he did when he’d lost and was already working out what losing would cost. “I’ll tell the lawyers. And Maartens?”

“I’ll speak to him myself.”

“Don’t make it personal.”

Zhao closed the folder. “He made it personal when he put the photographs in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came up to the house that evening and found Elowen in the potting room, pinching dead leaves off a tray of seedlings with the new tap running at her hip.

“Your husband,” said Aurelia from the doorway, “is making my husband sulk.”

“What did he do?”

“He wouldn’t argue properly. Chen Si needs to be allowed to be right for at least fifteen minutes or he can’t digest his dinner.” She came in in her pink cashmere and her pearls and picked a leaf off the bench and looked at it as though it owed her money. “He complained the whole way home. Zhendong’s gone unreasonable. Zhendong’s gone soft. Then we stopped at the lights by the ferry and he went quiet and said, ‘She read the names.’ Just that. As if it explained everything.”

Elowen’s hands stopped on the tray.

“I think it does,” said Aurelia. “He wasn’t arguing for the money, you know. Not really. He’s frightened that no just leaves those boys where they are with somebody else’s rifles. He’ll help find another way. He’ll just be insufferable while he does it.” She put the leaf down. “Come for dinner Friday. I want a witness.”

“I’ll ask Zhendong.”

“Don’t ask him. Bring him.” She was already at the door. Then she turned round. “I’m glad you read them, Elowen. Somebody in that house had to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The refusal went out the next morning on the lawyers’ letterhead. Zhao’s companies would not carry, finance, insure or facilitate the shipment, directly or through anyone else. The decision was final. It said nothing about photographs, and nothing about children.

Chen Si’s people started pulling threads. Two brokers who’d already gone shopping for another carrier. A finance house with accounts that ran, three steps down, into a charitable foundation working near the Velde highlands. The foundation was real. It had put up tents for classrooms, paid for a clinic, kept a feeding programme going until the Front took the roads and closed it.

Elowen read the report twice at the kitchen table.

“They need a school,” she said.

Zhao looked up from his laptop. “They need a great deal more than a school.”

“I know. But a boy who’s in a classroom at two o’clock isn’t at a checkpoint at two o’clock.” She turned the page towards him. “They’ve got land. They’ve got teachers who already know the families. They haven’t got walls.”

“Under whose name?”

“Nobody’s. No photographs. No ribbon. No plaque.”

“Would you trust them with it?”

“I’d trust an auditor who’s never heard of us. Money released when the walls go up, not before. And they have to be able to keep going if we disappear.”

He picked up his phone to ring Chen Si. She put her hand on his wrist.

“It doesn’t pay for anything,” she said. “It isn’t for Samuel. It’s a school.”

“I know what it is.”

She let go. He rang. By the end of the week the money sat in a trust with a name that meant nothing, and a surveyor was walking the foundation’s land with a tape.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning Bao brought her tea in the kitchen and didn’t leave.

He was a big man, Bao, broad as a door, with a shaved head and a scar through one eyebrow, and he had a way of standing still that made furniture look restless. He put the cup by her elbow and stood there.

“Madam. Can I ask about the children in the report?”

She closed the folder.

“I had a brother,” he said. “Younger. He was nine when a man came through our village saying he could get boys work in the town. My parents believed him. Everyone’s parents believed him.” He looked at the tea instead of her. “I went to the bus station every day after school for a year. I was twelve. I thought if I stood in the same place long enough he’d know where to find me.”

Elowen didn’t say anything. She’d learned that much from Zhao: sometimes the kindest thing was not to fill the space.

“They caught the man years later. He’d moved children across four provinces. Some to factories. Some to people.” Bao’s fingers had curled into his palms. “Nobody could tell us where my brother went. When the boss sent me to collect that report, I saw the ages.”

She reached out and took his hand. He looked at it as if a bird had landed on him.

“That’s why I wanted to say,” he said. “So you’d know why I was glad.”

“If you ever hear anything,” said Elowen. “Anything at all. You tell me.”

He looked at her for a moment. Then he took his hand back, straightened, and was Zhao’s man again.

“Your tea’s getting cold, madam.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Yip had an opinion. Granny Yip always had an opinion. She delivered this one at the Sunday market over a bucket of yellow chrysanthemums, trimming stems with a knife older than Elowen.

“Your husband is turning down a lot of money.”

“Who told you that?”

“People talk.” Snip. “I heard he’s making trouble for a Dutchman. I heard he won’t carry for those mountain people.” Snip. “Good. Soft men live longer.”

“He isn’t soft.”

“Men who know when to put something down. Strong men think they have to answer every insult or somebody will think they’re weak. The ones who can walk away from what they don’t need to win, they get old.” She tied the bunch and pushed it at Elowen. “Tell him. Don’t tell him.”

“Which?”

“I’m an old woman. I don’t have to be helpful.” She took Elowen’s money and counted it twice. “And tell him his hair is terrible.”

Elowen laughed all the way back to the van.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting at the northern warehouses was meant to take forty minutes. It took three hours.

Elowen went because she’d done the accounts and wanted to hear what they said when someone read them aloud. She sat at the end of the long table in the office above the loading yard with a stack of ledgers and her own folder, and nobody offered her tea, which she noticed.

Mak ran the north. He’d run it since before Zhao owned it, a thick-necked man with a gold watch and a voice that made every sentence sound like an order to a forklift. He’d hated the audit. He hadn’t looked at her once.

“Twenty-three cases,” said Zhao.

“Over a year. Five sites. That’s normal loss.”

“Loss of what?”

Mak named it. Elowen turned a page.

“The north keeps this company running,” said Mak, “while everyone else sits in offices counting.” Then he did look at her, finally. “Perhaps we could do this without the florist.”

The room went quiet.

“She’s my wife,” said Zhao.

“I know who she is. Everybody knows. That’s the trouble.” Mak leaned back. “You used to decide things. Now you bring your wife to meetings and wait for her to nod. You’ve let her put a muzzle on you. You’re a muzzled dog.”

One of the managers looked at his hands. Another went very still.

Zhao didn’t move. Elowen turned another page.

“Mr. Mak,” she said. “Do you remember the inventory review last spring? Warehouse Four?”

He frowned. “That was settled.”

“You said it was settled.” She turned the ledger round and slid it down the table. “Twenty-three cases, logged as damaged and written off. The company paid for replacements. The originals were never destroyed. I’ve got the receiving slips. I’ve got the dispatch copies you changed after the quarter closed, and the handwritten tallies you forgot to change, and invoices paid to a freight company registered to your wife’s brother.” Another page. Another. “These were signed out by drivers who were off shift. I’ve been keeping these for a year.”

“You’ve been investigating me?”

“I’ve been reading the accounts. I was asked to.”

“You don’t know how this business works.”

“No,” said Elowen. “But I can count.”

Mak stood up so fast his chair hit the wall. He looked at her, and then at Zhao, and laughed, and said it again.

“Muzzled. That’s what you—“

Zhao was round the table before the word finished. He took Mak by the scruff of the neck and put his face into the ledger table. Once. The sound was like a dropped crate. When he lifted him, Mak’s nose was bleeding over the receiving slips, and Zhao held him there, bent over his own forgeries, and spoke very quietly into his ear.

“Read it.”

Mak made a noise.

“Read the line she’s pointing at.”

Elowen’s finger was still on the page. She didn’t take it away. Mak read it, thickly, through the blood. Twenty-three cases. Warehouse Four.

Zhao let go. Mak sat down on the floor against the wall with both hands over his face.

“Get out,” said Zhao, to the room, and the other managers stood up. “Not you.” That was to Mak. “You stay where you are until Bao comes.”

Then he turned round and looked at Elowen, at the end of the table with her folder open and her finger still on the line, and something went across his face that she’d never seen in a room full of his own men. He laughed. Out loud, once, as if it had been knocked out of him.

“You brought a year of it in a folder,” he said, “to a room full of men who thought you’d come to pour the tea.”

“Nobody gave me any tea.”

He came down the table, took her face in both hands, and kissed her hard. Not a careful kiss. His hand went to the back of her neck and he laughed again against her mouth, and the two managers who hadn’t made it to the door yet found the stairs very interesting. Elowen grabbed his shirt and kissed him back.

“Your meeting isn’t finished,” she said when he let her breathe.

“It is now.”

“There’s another file at home.”

He stared at her. “How many?”

“I didn’t want to carry it all in one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mak was gone from the company by four. By eight his accounts were frozen, his badges dead, and two of his men had been caught moving a car full of boxes out of his garage. At dawn the next day his wife, his wife’s brother and their children were put on the early boat to the islands with what they could carry, and told not to come back.

“You sent his family too,” said Elowen in the kitchen that night.

“Their houses were bought with my money. The brother-in-law took the invoices.” Zhao was washing his hands at the sink. There was nothing on them; he washed them anyway. “Nobody touched them.”

“And if I asked you to bring them back?”

He turned off the tap. “Are you asking?”

She thought about it, honestly, the way he’d taught her to think about prices. “No,” she said. “I don’t want you hurting people because they insulted you. But he called me the florist and he stole for a year. I’m not going to pretend the year didn’t happen.”

“It wasn’t the florist,” said Zhao. “It was the second time.”

She looked at him a moment longer. Then she handed him the towel.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one in the morning she found him in the study with a small black notebook. Three names on the open page. The manager who’d laughed. The one who’d said decorative. The one who’d said marriage had made him easier to handle.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

She sat on the edge of the desk and waited.

“They laughed,” he said.

“Because he called you a dog.”

“Yes.”

“Is that why they’re in there? Or because you think they were in on the cases?”

He was quiet long enough to answer her. “Both.”

“And Maartens is coming tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“Then get ready for Maartens,” said Elowen, and closed the notebook with one finger. “Not for three men who laughed.”

He looked at her finger on the cover.

“Come to bed,” she said. “Page two, line six.”

“You’re using the contract to get me away from my desk.”

“I’m using my husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Maartens came on Thursday without flowers or champagne or the smile he’d worn the week before, carrying a new proposal in a leather folder. Zhao didn’t open it. He put the monitoring report on the table between them.

“I thought we’d moved past that,” said Maartens.

“We haven’t.”

“Someone else will carry it.”

“Then someone else can explain why. Don’t use my routes. Don’t use my people. Don’t use my name.”

“You’ve gone sentimental.”

“Perhaps.” Zhao stood. “If you ignore a no from me, you’ll find out what it costs.”

Maartens took the report with him when he went. Zhao let him. He had another copy.

When he got home the notebook was by his phone on the counter, and Elowen was at the stove.

“Did you add anyone?”

“No.”

“Did you cross anyone out?”

“One. He wasn’t in the cases.” He came and stood behind her and looked into the pan. “Maartens thinks I’m sentimental.”

“Granny Yip thinks your hair’s terrible.”

“Granny Yip has excellent judgement.”

“I know.”

“I’ve got another report on the eastern accounts,” he said. “If you want to see—“

She turned off the gas, took him by the collar, and pulled his mouth down to hers before he could finish. He smiled against her lips. She kissed him again, harder, until he stopped smiling and put both hands on her waist and lifted her onto the counter beside the stove.

“The report,” he said.

“Tomorrow.”

He reached past her and put the black notebook in the drawer, and shut it.

chapters.title: The Buyer Does Not Take No Well
chapters.desc: A warehouse burns with a florist’s card left on the gate, and Maartens flies in to ask for a meeting at the old shipyard. She can’t tell her husband not to go, so she moves the fish to the front of the fridge.
chapters.epigraph: “Not like this. You promised me a boring one.”
chapters.content:
Old Ming did his last round of Warehouse Four at ten past four on Friday morning, with a torch in one hand and a paper bag of chestnuts in the other.

He’d done the round the same way for longer than some of the men had been alive: loading doors, office stairs, the long aisle, the side gate. He coughed at the cold end of the aisle because he always coughed there. He ate a chestnut at the side gate because the side gate was halfway. Zhao Zhendong had tried twice to retire him, and twice he’d said he’d sooner die of boredom at work than at home, and both times the boss had let him stay.

Two vans came up the service road with their lights off. He heard them before he saw them, the way you hear rain.

By the time he got back to the loading doors there were men at them, and bottles, and a smell of petrol so thick it stood in the air like fog. He shouted. He was an old man in a padded jacket with a torch, and one of them laughed at him. Then the first bottle went in through the high window and the aisle went orange from end to end.

Old Ming didn’t run away from it. He ran to the wall where the extinguishers were, because that was his job, and he had the pin out of the first one when the stacked pallets came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen was cutting pears at the kitchen counter just after six when Bao rang.

“Madam.” He never sounded formal. He sounded formal. “There’s been a fire at Warehouse Four.”

The knife stopped against the board.

“Was anyone inside?”

“The night guard.”

“Who?”

“Old Ming.”

She knew him. She’d met him twice in the north, an old man with a cough and a terrible jacket who’d called her young madam even when she’d asked him not to, and who’d given her a paper bag of roasted chestnuts because, he said, the market ones were robbery for a florist.

“Is he—“

“He didn’t make it.”

She put the knife down.

“It wasn’t an accident,” said Bao. “There were petrol cans by the loading doors. The camera on the service road has two vans.”

“Does Zhendong know?”

“He’s here.” There was a door, and a voice, and then her husband on the line.

“Stay at home.”

“Did he suffer?”

A silence. “I don’t know.”

“Can I come?”

“No.”

“Zhendong.”

“I’ll come home as soon as I can,” he said. “Elowen. Stay at home.”

She stood by the counter after he’d gone. One of the pears had rolled to the edge of the board. She picked it up and put it back and didn’t cut it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The card came with him at four o’clock, in a clear evidence bag.

It was hers. Cream, heavy, rounded corners, the little card she tucked into every delivery from the shop. Somebody had slid it under the latch of the warehouse gate where the firemen would find it, and somebody with neat handwriting had written on it in black ink.

For the widow.

“That’s mine,” said Elowen.

“I know.”

“From the shop. From the box on the counter.”

“I know.”

“They’ve been in the shop.”

“Or a delivery. Someone kept one.” He put the bag face down on the counter. “They wanted me to understand that they can reach you.”

“Maartens.”

“Yes.”

She looked at the back of the card through the plastic. Blank. Of course it was blank.

“Did Old Ming have family?”

“A wife. A grandson they’ve been raising since his daughter died.” Zhao took his coat off. His face was perfectly composed, and there was a tightness round his eyes that she’d only seen twice before. “Chen Si’s been to see them. The company will look after them.”

“He said I looked too thin.”

“He said that to everyone.”

“He was wrong about me.” She tried to smile, and couldn’t quite. “Take that out of the kitchen. Please.”

He took it. When he came back he didn’t say anything. He put his arms round her from behind and his chin on the top of her head, and they stood like that by the pears until the light went.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a young man outside the potting-room door.

“Madam. I’m Peng.”

He was perhaps twenty-four, with a straight back and a nervous face and a new suit that hadn’t decided yet whether it fitted him. He’d been on the east gate since January.

“Boss has asked me to stay with you.”

“Where?”

“Wherever you go.”

“Am I in danger, Peng?”

He hesitated, which was an answer. “I’m to report your movements.”

“To whom?”

“To Boss. Every hour.”

She looked at him. Then she sighed and said, “Come in, then,” and took him into the kitchen and made him sit down and poured him tea, and he held the cup as if it might go off.

“Did he tell you to report what I eat?”

“No, madam.”

“Who I talk to?”

“Anyone who hasn’t been cleared.”

“If I go to the toilet?”

Peng choked on the tea. She waited till he’d stopped.

“I’m joking,” she said. “Peng, I’m not under arrest. I know you’re doing your job and I won’t make it hard for you. Tell him where I am. Tell him if anyone comes near me. Don’t follow me round the shop, and don’t tell him every time I go from one room to the next.”

“Yes, madam.”

It lasted till Monday. On Monday night Zhao left his phone on the arm of the sofa when he went to take a call in the study, and it lit up, and she looked, because it was lying there face up with her name on it.

Peng: 10:00 shop. 11:00 shop, back room, alone 6 min. 12:00 ate half her lunch. 13:00 market road, spoke to Granny Yip (cleared). 14:00 shop.

A whole day of her. Every hour of it. Half her lunch.

When he came back she was holding it.

“I told him not to,” she said.

“I know.”

“And you told him to anyway.”

“Yes.”

“I’m not a shipment, Zhendong. You don’t track me.”

He sat down opposite her. He didn’t reach for the phone and he didn’t apologise. That was the worst of it; he looked at her quite steadily, the way he’d looked at Mak across the ledger table, as if there was simply no other way for this to go.

“A man wrote for the widow on your card,” he said. “Until he’s dead, Peng tells me every hour. After that you can have him back.”

She put the phone down between them on the cushion and went upstairs. It was a long time before he followed, and when he did, he stood in the bedroom doorway and didn’t come in until she held the covers back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Maartens flew in that same Monday, and didn’t ring.

He sent a man. A small, polite man in a raincoat who came to the Docks office and asked for Mr. Zhao by name and put an envelope on the desk and went away again before Bao could decide what to do with him. Inside was a single typed line.

You have refused me. Let us speak face to face. Hengli shipyard, Wednesday, midnight. No lawyers.

“Don’t go,” said Chen Si.

Elowen was by the window. She’d brought Zhao’s dinner up in a tin because he’d stopped coming home for it, and it was going cold on the side table while the three of them looked at a piece of paper.

“I’ll hear what he has to say,” said Zhao.

“He burned a warehouse with a man inside. He put your wife’s card on the gate. Now he wants you at a dead shipyard in the middle of the night, and you want to hear what he has to say.” Chen Si turned to her. “Elowen. Tell him.”

“Can you refuse?” she asked Zhao.

“Yes.”

“Will you?”

He didn’t answer.

“Please,” said Chen Si. “I know what he is. I know what Maartens is. This is the meeting he wants. We can find another way to him.”

She knew Zhao would go. She knew that if she asked him not to and he went anyway, there would be a thing between them afterwards with her name on it, and she didn’t want it. She didn’t want the other thing either.

“Zhendong,” she said. “Is this what no costs?”

Something moved in his face. “Yes.”

“Then I can’t tell you not to.” She looked at Chen Si. “I can ask. I can’t choose for him.”

Chen Si shut his eyes. He didn’t argue again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday morning she bought a grouper at the market, because she’d promised him fish on Thursday and she wanted something in the house that belonged to Thursday.

He left at a quarter to eleven that night. Dark shirt, a vest under it that he didn’t hide from her, black gloves. Two cars in the drive. Bao by the door, not looking.

She’d been trying not to cry for an hour and she’d lost.

“Don’t,” he said, and touched her face.

“I’m not.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“So are you.” She came up on her toes. She had the words ready; she’d had them ready for two years, and her mouth was already open on them when he put two gloved fingers against her lips.

“Not tonight.”

“Zhendong—“

“Not like this. You promised me a boring one.”

She stood there with his fingers on her mouth and the leather cold, and nodded, because he wouldn’t take it any other way.

“Then come home for one,” she said against them.

He took his hand away and kissed her. Long, and not desperate. He held her face as if he were learning it, and when he lifted his head he put his forehead against hers.

“Lock the door. Peng outside. Don’t go to the shop till Bao’s checked it.”

“I know.”

He looked at her for one more second. Then he went out, and the dogs stood beside her in the hall without making a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep. At midnight she went into the kitchen and opened the fridge and moved the fish to the front shelf. Then the ginger beside it. Then she took the spring onions out and put them in a bowl of water on the counter. She didn’t know why. Something in the house had to be ready for him.

At one fifty-two Chen Si texted.

Chen Si: In position. Don’t wait up.

Elowen: Is he all right?

Nothing came back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Hengli yard smelled of rust and diesel and the sea, and every light on it was dead except the one over the old loading platform, which Maartens had paid someone to switch on.

Zhao came in on foot from the east with Bao a step behind and to the left. Lok had the west gate, where the rail spur came in. Chen Si was on a roof behind them with a rifle and a radio, because Chen Si had refused to stay in the car.

Maartens was standing under the light in a good coat with two men, and he smiled when he saw Zhao, and that was how Zhao knew.

“You came,” said Maartens.

“You asked.”

“I’m going to ask once more.”

“No,” said Zhao, and on the far side of the stacks something metal fell over.

The second group came through the containers from the west, four of them, fast. Lok’s radio said one word and then Lok was shooting, and Zhao was moving before he’d decided to, behind the nearest container with his gun already up. Bao went down beside him with a grunt and kept firing from the ground. One of Maartens’s two men turned towards the noise and Zhao shot him through the chest, and the other one got off a burst that took the corner off the container a hand’s width from his face, and Zhao shot him too.

Lok came running down the rail spur towards them with his left arm hanging. He was nearly there. He was close enough for Zhao to see his face when the round from the stacks took him in the back of the neck and he went down on the rails without putting his hands out.

Zhao looked at him for half a second too long.

Something punched him low in the side, under the ribs, hard enough to turn him round. He didn’t hear it. He was looking at the platform, where Maartens was walking backwards out of the light with a pistol in his hand, towards the water.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past two the phone rang. She had it in her hand before the first ring finished.

“Elowen.” Chen Si’s voice was wrong. Too careful. Behind him there were engines and men shouting and someone calling for a medic. “Listen to me first.”

“Where is he?”

“Maartens is down. Two of his are dead. Lok’s dead.”

“Where is my husband?”

“Bao’s hit, he’s alive, he’s talking.” A breath. “Zhendong was shot. In the side. We saw him go after Maartens towards the loading platform, and then the platform went, and we lost him.”

The kitchen tilted. She put her hand flat on the counter next to the spring onions.

“Lost him.”

“The divers are coming. We’re looking.”

“Then why are you ringing me?”

He didn’t answer for so long that she thought the line had gone. Then he said, “Because I didn’t want you to hear it from anyone else,” and she understood that he’d rung her because there was nothing else he could do with his hands.

“Find him,” she said.

“I will.”

When he’d gone she stood there. She didn’t scream. She didn’t cry, either; there didn’t seem to be room in her.

She went upstairs and took his old coat out of the back of the wardrobe, the grey one with the frayed cuffs and the one wrong button he’d worn the first winter, before he’d bought six others. It smelled of cedar and his soap. She went down through the dark house with it, past Peng on the step, past the dogs, to the armory door, and let herself in with the fourteenth key.

The emergency light was on. The panel glowed. The walls were so thick that the whole hill could have fallen down outside and she wouldn’t have heard it.

She opened the case on the bottom shelf and took out the pistol he’d taught her on, at the estate in the rain, and checked it the way he’d shown her, and put it on the floor beside her. Then she sat down with her back against the steel and his coat round her shoulders and her phone on her knee.

She thought of the card she’d left in the room under the tulips at the shop. This light stays on. I’ll come.

She’d written it for someone frightened. She’d never thought it might be her.

chapters.title: Three Days
chapters.desc: Three days in the armory with his coat and a gun. Everyone who loves her comes to the steel door, and she won’t open it for any of them.
chapters.content:
At eighteen minutes past three on Thursday morning, Elowen sent her husband a message.

Elowen: Are you hurt?

One grey tick. It sat there. She sent another.

Elowen: Chen Si says they’re still looking. I know you probably haven’t got your phone. I’m going to keep writing anyway.

The armory had no windows. It had its own air and its own light, water in the cupboard, a first-aid kit the size of a suitcase, a panel that could talk to the guardhouse, and a door that would stand up to anything Elowen could imagine and several things she couldn’t. It had been built to keep people alive. Nobody had built it for sitting in.

She sat in it. His coat round her shoulders, the pistol on the floor, the phone on her knee with its single grey tick.

At six there were three taps on the steel.

“Madam. It’s Bao.”

She was at the door before she knew she’d stood up. She didn’t touch the lock.

“Have they found him?”

“Not yet.”

She put her palm flat on the metal. “Then don’t tell me he’s fine. Don’t anyone tell me he’s fine.”

He didn’t. He stood outside for a few minutes more, she could hear his weight shift, and then he went away.

At ten past seven she wrote:

Elowen: The fish is still in the fridge. I put it at the front so I wouldn’t forget.

At twenty to nine:

Elowen: It’s too late to steam it now. I’ll buy another one.

At three minutes past nine:

Elowen: Come home.

Then she scrolled up past all of them to the last ordinary conversation, the one from Tuesday, about tea. He’d asked jasmine or chrysanthemum. She’d told him to buy both because he always forgot which. He’d said he knew perfectly well. She’d sent him a photograph of both tins on the kitchen shelf, unopened, side by side.

Zhendong: You’re difficult.

Elowen: You married me.

Zhendong: Fortunately.

She read it until the words stopped meaning anything, and then somewhere after that she fell asleep with her cheek on his collar.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia arrived at eleven. Elowen knew it was her because she knocked twice and then said something extremely rude about the door.

“Elowen. I know you’re in there.”

Silence.

“If you don’t answer I’m coming in.” A pause. Then, more quietly: “I’m not coming in. I’m sitting down.”

There was the whisper of cashmere on stone. Aurelia Chen, who had once sent back a car because the seats were the wrong grey, had sat down on the armory steps.

“Chen Si hasn’t slept,” she said. “He’s rung every hospital and clinic in the city and every harbour office that might have pulled a man out of the water. He’s shouting at people who are trying to help him. That’s how I know he’s still himself.” A rustle. “Bao’s shoulder is stitched. Elara did it at the Docks office last night, he’ll moan about it for a month and then say it never happened. I brought congee. I made it. It’s terrible. It’s outside the door.”

“I can’t.”

“All right.”

She didn’t argue. She stayed. After a while she started talking about the launch she’d done the week before, and a client who’d tried to walk out wearing a display necklace because she thought it was a gift, and a supplier in Milan who addressed every email to Mr. Aurelia. Elowen didn’t answer. Aurelia went on anyway. Around four she ran out. Around five Elowen heard her change position on the step and swear under her breath at her own knees.

At six she stood up.

“Six hours,” said Elowen through the door. Her voice came out rough.

“I know. I’m not angry with you.” A hand on the steel, flat, on the other side of hers. “I won’t ask again today.”

When she was certain the steps were empty, Elowen opened the door the width of a bowl and took the congee in. It was cold. She ate three spoonfuls.

At nine that night she heard Peng on the step outside, talking to himself, and then the small tap of a phone screen. She knew what it was before she’d worked it out. Every hour, the way he’d been told. 21:00. Armory. Door shut. Sent to a phone at the bottom of the harbour.

“Peng,” she said through the door.

He jumped; she heard it. “Madam?”

“Keep sending them.”

There was a pause. Then, “Yes, madam,” in a voice that had nearly gone, and at ten she heard the tap again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday afternoon Bao came back with his arm in a sling and asked if he could come in, and she let him.

He saw the pistol on the floor and looked at it and then at her.

“I haven’t used it.”

“I know, madam.” He sat on the bench opposite, carefully, like a man who’d been told how much he was allowed to move. “I saw the boss on the platform. I want to tell you what I saw. Only what I saw.”

She held the coat closed at her throat.

“He was already hit. There was smoke. Maartens was walking back towards the water with a gun in his hand, and the boss went after him. I heard two shots. Maartens went over the edge. Then the boss was at the edge, and the railing went, and the platform under it.” He looked at his bandaged shoulder. “I was on the ground by then. I couldn’t get up.”

“Did you see him come up?”

“No.”

“Did he call out?”

“Madam.”

“Did you hear him call out, Bao?”

“No.”

She gripped the edge of the worktable. Bao started to stand.

“I should have been closer,” he said. “I was—“

“You were shot.” She turned round. “You were shot standing next to him, and you were shooting back, and you’re going to stand in front of me and say sorry for not being in two places? Don’t.”

He stood there a moment. Then he sat down again.

“Why did he go after him?”

“I think,” said Bao, “so he couldn’t come after you.”

“I didn’t want that,” she said. “I wanted him home.”

“I know, madam.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The divers found his phone late on Friday afternoon, in the mud under the old platform, several metres out. Screen smashed, case split, full of the harbour. Chen Si rang her himself.

“It wasn’t on him,” he said. “It was out in the mud.”

“So he could have thrown it.”

“Yes.”

“Or dropped it. Or someone took it off him.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t tell her to hope, and he didn’t tell her to prepare herself. She was grateful for both.

“I’m his brother,” said Chen Si. “I should have been able to bring him back.”

“Then bring him back.”

The silence on the line went on so long she thought it had dropped.

“I will,” said Chen Si.

That night she unlocked the cabinet and took down his heavy gun, the one he kept for himself, and sat at the worktable and checked that it was empty and laid out the cloth and the little tools. She’d watched him do it a hundred times, late, with his watch still on and his sleeves rolled, the lamp on his hands. She’d sat beside him reading and complained that the whole house smelled of oil. He’d said it was maintenance. She’d said it was an excuse not to come to bed. He’d smiled without looking up.

She did the barrel. The slide. The small parts he’d told her never to force. Her hands weren’t steady and she went slowly. When it was clean she put it back exactly where it lived, and then sat on the floor until it was morning, because she didn’t know what else to do with her hands either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came before it was light on Saturday. He didn’t knock.

“Jie. Don’t open it. I just want to give you something.”

A sheet of paper came under the door, folded twice. She unfolded it on the floor.

It was the house. Every floor of it, drawn in his small hard draughtsman’s hand, and over the top of it, in four colours, lines. Front gate. East service door. The potting room’s red door, which opened from inside whatever the power did. The maintenance passage behind the kitchen. The lower stairwell from the courtyard. The armory’s own way out, on its own circuit. He’d marked every emergency light.

“What is this?”

“Every way back into the house,” said Raiden through the steel. “I walked them all yesterday. They’re all clear.”

“I don’t need a way out.”

“It’s not for you.”

She put her hand over her mouth.

“I’m going to sit here a bit,” he said. “That’s all. I’m not going to ask.”

He sat there an hour. When he’d gone, someone else came down the steps, slower, and stood without speaking for long enough that she knew who it was by the breathing.

“Baba?”

“Wenwen.”

He hadn’t called her that since she was nine. She pressed her forehead to the door.

“I’m not going to tell you to come out,” said Lin Jian. “I wanted to tell you something about your husband. He’s been asking after us. For a year now. Every few weeks a message, never from him, always from Bao. Whether Eliana’s exams went well. Whether Raiden was really better after the van. Whether I was sleeping. Whether Evangeline had what she needed.” A pause. “In January he asked me how many lemons were on your mother’s tree.”

“He knows how many. It’s in his courtyard.”

“That’s what I said. He said he wanted to know if I knew.”

Her eyes filled.

“Seven,” said Lin Jian. “I told him seven. He said that was right.”

She couldn’t answer. After a while she heard him say, very quietly, “He didn’t marry you and forget the rest of us,” and then his feet going back up the steps, one at a time, like an old man’s, which she’d never once thought of him as.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon Evangeline left an orchid on the step. She didn’t knock. She said through the door, “It’s from the greenhouse at home. It needs light, so don’t forget it. Mama liked these,” and went away before Elowen could find her voice to say thank you.

It was pale pink. Three flowers open and one bud closed tight. Elowen brought it in and put it under the emergency light, which was the only light there was.

In the evening there were voices on the steps, arguing.

“The east camera isn’t useless. It’s pointed at the wrong bit of drive.”

“That’s the same as useless.”

“It isn’t.”

“Jiejie?” said Eliana. “Don’t open it. Listen. I’ve been through every camera round the harbour. Not just the yard. Service roads, the fuel station, the north quay, the fish market. There’s one on the north access road that works. It caught a car leaving after the shooting. I can’t see who’s in it, but I sent it to Chen Si.”

“Thank you.”

“I’m not finished. Xiao Pan’s been helping because he knows the delivery roads better than anyone.”

“Madam,” said Xiao Pan. “The shop’s open.”

She stared at the door.

“I came up on the red bike Jinx built me. We opened it this morning. The cooler’s working. The front’s done. I put the tulips in and the white delphiniums, the ones you ordered.” A pause. “People asked when you’re coming back. Granny Yip sent chrysanthemums and said if I didn’t put them out properly she’d come and do it herself.”

“Is the sign still up?”

“Your hours. Yes.”

She could almost smell it through the steel. Wet stems. The cold of the cooler. The old wooden counter. Her whole life was sitting there with the door unlocked.

“Thank you, Xiao Pan.”

“Just come back when you’re ready, madam.”

“And eat something,” said Eliana, and Xiao Pan laughed, the first laugh anywhere near that door in three days. When they’d gone there was a paper bag on the step with two custard buns and a carton of soy milk in it. She ate both buns.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to eleven she started writing to him again.

Elowen: I know you can’t read this.

Elowen: I’m wearing your coat. The grey one.

She stopped, because her wrist had brushed something stiff in the inside pocket.

It was folded small and the edges had gone soft. She opened it on her knee. A page of Miles Wei’s old paper, the last one, with the dense equation she’d once called showing off. In the margin, in Zhao’s careful hand, from the night before the reunion: Does she want me there. And underneath, in hers, in the pencil she’d kept by the bed:

You come with me. Plus one.

She remembered writing it. She remembered him folding the page and putting it aside and not saying anything. She’d forgotten all about it.

He’d carried it for more than two years. In the pocket of a coat he didn’t even wear.

“Oh, Zhendong,” she said, and his name broke in the middle.

Elowen: I found the page. You kept it.

Elowen: You ridiculous man.

She sat with the phone in her lap. Then she wrote the thing she’d been thinking since the stairs, and didn’t let herself delete it.

Elowen: I’m not making you wait again. Whatever day it is when you walk in. I don’t care if it’s boring.

Elowen: Come home and eat it.

One grey tick.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past three in the morning Dumpling barked.

She woke with the coat sliding off her shoulders. Then Noodle, deeper. They weren’t barking at the road, the way they did at foxes and delivery vans. They were barking at the gate, frantic, the way they barked at nothing else.

She snatched up the phone and opened the camera on the front court.
