The dogs were at the gate. Dumpling was jumping at the bars. Noodle had his whole nose pressed to the gap underneath. And beyond the gate, at the very edge of the picture where the light from the lamp gave up, something was holding on to the metal.

A hand.

She was already running.

chapters.title: He Crawled the Last Mile
chapters.desc: He crawls home up the hill with a bullet in his side. Elara brings two bags of stolen hospital supplies, and Elowen holds his face on the kitchen table for two hours.
chapters.content:
Maartens was waiting at the end of the platform with the water at his back and his pistol up.

Zhao came out of the smoke holding his side. His glove was wet to the wrist. He didn’t look at it; he knew what was on it. He’d been shot before, and the first minutes always told you the same thing, that you were fine, that it was nothing, that you could walk.

“You should have taken the deal,” said Maartens.

“You should have taken no.”

Maartens’s arm came up the last few degrees, and Zhao shot him twice. The first went into his chest and turned him half round. The second caught him as he staggered and took him backwards over the edge of the platform, and for a moment the Dutchman’s face was there above the rail, white and surprised, and then it wasn’t, and the harbour had him.

Zhao went to the edge to make sure. That was the mistake. He heard the old platform groan under him like a ship, and the rail he’d put his hand on came away in his hand, and the whole corner of it went down into the black water with him on it.

The last thing he saw was the work light over the platform, swinging. It looked like the little light in the armory.

He thought of a fish at the front of a fridge. Then the water closed over his head.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke in the dark with a smell of diesel and old rope and fish, and the floor moving.

A hold. A boat. Something rough under his cheek. A man sitting by the open hatch with a cigarette, an old man with a face like a dried river, who’d clearly decided a long time ago not to ask questions that might have answers.

“Awake,” said the man. “Good. I thought I’d got a dead one.”

His name was Kwai. He fished out of the old north quay. He’d found Zhao tangled in his net at first light with the tide going out, and had nearly put him back when he moved, and then he’d seen the hole in his side and pulled him in and called nobody. He didn’t say why. Zhao didn’t ask. He didn’t have the breath.

He couldn’t go to a hospital. He lay in the hold and worked it out as clearly as he could, which wasn’t very. A gunshot wound walked into any ward in the city and the ward rang the police. The police ran his face. His face was on a Red Notice in every country that had a police force. They’d take him from the hospital in a van, and they’d go up the hill with a warrant before anyone had told her he was alive.

He borrowed Kwai’s phone and rang Chen Si’s number, the one he knew by heart. It didn’t connect. Of course it didn’t. After a shooting every phone in the organisation went in the sea and new ones came out of a drawer. He’d written that rule himself.

He packed the wound with strips of his own shirt and Kwai’s rag and lay still.

By Friday the wound smelled wrong. Kwai smelled it too.

“You need a doctor.”

“I know.”

Kwai looked at him a long time. “Someone waiting?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop being stubborn and let me take you somewhere.”

Zhao almost laughed. He’d been told that before, in the same words, by his wife.

On Saturday he could stand for as long as it took to count to ten. That night, when the fever had come up behind his eyes like weather, he asked how far it was to the hill.

“Which hill?”

He told him the road.

Kwai shook his head. “Two kilometres. More. Uphill all the way. You’ll die on it.”

“Maybe.”

“Then why?”

“Because I said I’d be home for dinner.”

Kwai looked at him as if he’d gone mad. Perhaps he had. He climbed out of the hold anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t remember the first part. He remembered the road under his palms. Grit going into the heels of his hands. Stopping against a drainage wall because he couldn’t breathe and go forward at the same time, so he picked one. He lost a shoe somewhere. He was sick in the grass, water and blood. No car came. The city was asleep.

He’d bought warehouses, routes, ships, a whole hillside. He’d made men afraid to say no to him. He couldn’t make his own legs do what he said.

So he crawled. He thought of her in the hall with his fingers on her mouth, the words right there behind them. He’d stopped her because he’d wanted a boring day. He wondered if he’d get one. That hurt more than the hole in him.

The dogs heard him before the gate did. Dumpling first, then Noodle, so loud he couldn’t hear himself breathe. He got a hand on the bars. It slipped. He got it there again. The metal was so cold it felt wet.

“Open,” he said. He didn’t know if he’d said it out loud.

The gate moved. She was on the other side of it, in a grey coat that was his, with her hair down and her feet bare on the gravel, and for one second she looked at him as if she didn’t know him. Then she did.

“Zhendong?”

He’d imagined it the whole way up. Walking in, finding her in the kitchen, saying sorry. He hadn’t imagined not being able to stand. He took one step and his knees went, and she caught him, or tried, and they both went down together on the stones.

Her hands were on his face. She was crying. He wanted to wipe it off and his arm wouldn’t come. She bent and kissed his mouth, cracked and cold and tasting of salt and blood, and didn’t seem to care what it tasted of.

“I’m late,” he said against her cheek. “For dinner.”

She made a sound that was half a laugh. “Yes. You’re late.”

“Fish?”

“Ruined.”

“Shame,” he said, and the gravel and the dogs and her face all went out like a light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen didn’t call an ambulance. Every part of her wanted to. She sat on the gravel with his head in her lap and her hand pressed into his side, where it was hot and wet, and made herself think it through, and the answer came out the same every time: a hospital meant a report, a report meant his name, his name meant the Red Notice, and the Red Notice meant men in uniform taking him away down the hill before anyone knew whether he’d live till morning.

“Peng,” she said. He was beside her; she didn’t know when he’d come. “Ring Elara. Tell her he’s home and he’s been shot and it’s three days old. Tell her to bring everything she’d need for that, and tell her I said to take it.”

“Take it from—“

“She’ll know.”

He rang. She heard him say it all, word for word, in a steady voice that only cracked on three days.

Raiden came running down the drive in a T-shirt and bare feet. He’d stayed the night in the room over the garage, in case. He took one look and said, “Get a door. Any inside door, flat. Now,” and two of the guards ran, and came back with the storage-room door off its hinges.

They slid it under him. Raiden took the head, Peng and a guard the sides. Elowen walked beside it with one hand on his cheek all the way through the house, and they didn’t go to the bedroom or the armory. They went to the kitchen, because it had the biggest table and the most light.

The fish was still at the front of the fridge. The ginger beside it. The spring onions in their bowl on the counter, gone soft.

She looked at them once, and then she didn’t look at them again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara arrived just after four with two big bags, her long brown hair scraped back in a knot and her pearl earrings still in from whatever she’d been doing at midnight. She put the bags on the counter.

“Move the lamp. Clear the table. Towels, boiled water, every light in this room.”

They moved. She opened the bags. Saline. Dressings. Gloves. Drips. Antibiotics in boxes with the hospital’s labels on them. A whole instrument set in a blue wrap that had another department’s name stamped on the corner.

“Where did you get all that?”

“Don’t ask.”

“Elara—“

“Not tonight. Later, if you like. Not tonight.” She pulled on gloves. “Has he been awake?”

“For a minute. At the gate.”

“Did he say anything?”

“He asked about dinner.”

Elara looked at her. Then, despite everything, she let out one short breath through her nose. “Of course he did.”

She cut the shirt away and her face changed. Three days in a fish hold and a crawl up the hill had done what three days would. The wound was hot and swollen and angry and it smelled. She checked his pulse, his pressure, his breathing, and said what it was out loud in a flat voice so that Elowen would hear it as facts.

“It’s infected. It needs opening and cleaning, all the dead tissue out. Properly that’s a theatre and an anaesthetist. I can numb the edges. I can’t put him under on a kitchen table without monitoring, so it’s going to hurt him a great deal.” She looked up. “If his breathing changes, if he stops responding, if it bleeds faster than I can deal with, we stop pretending and he goes to a hospital and we live with what happens. Say yes.”

“Yes.”

“Then go to his head and hold it, and talk to him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen took his face in her hands. His skin was cold and damp. She’d seen her sister’s hands shake over a teacup two years ago, badly enough that Elara had laughed and switched to a mug. They weren’t shaking now. Elowen saw it, and put it somewhere for later, and didn’t say a word.

The first touch woke him. His whole body went tight on the table, and Raiden leaned on his shoulders.

“Zhendong. Look at me. You’re home.”

He found her. For a second he knew where he was. Then Elara went in, and a sound came out of him that Elowen had never heard from anyone.

She’d heard him angry. She’d heard him give orders in a voice that made rooms stand up, and laugh, and say her name against her neck. She’d never heard him scream. It went on. She wanted to tell Elara to stop. She wanted to throw herself across him. She knew exactly what would happen if they stopped, so she held his face and talked.

“Do you remember the first night? You came in out of the rain and bought every flower in the shop. You didn’t even want them. You sat in the chair by the window like you owned it.” His eyes were screwed shut. “I was terrified of you. Don’t look pleased.”

Something that might have been a laugh came out of him between breaths.

“You remember the registry? You called me Mrs. Zhao before the ink was dry. The ring was so big it went halfway down my finger and you said you’d have it fixed, and you did, you put it by my bed without a word.” She kissed his forehead. “You remember the dogs? You hated their names.”

His lips moved. “Didn’t.”

“You did. You stood in the hall and said Dumpling as if it were a disease.”

Elara worked. Raiden held. Peng kept the water coming and turned his face away every time it went red.

Some time after five Elowen leaned her cheek against his temple and said, “Remember the estate? The rain. Mr. Wen. You taught me to shoot.”

“Forty-one,” he said through his teeth.

She stared at him and then laughed, a wet, cracked laugh. “You remember the number?”

“You,” he said, and couldn’t finish, and didn’t need to.

“He’s answering,” said Elara, without looking up. “That’s good. Keep him with you.”

So she told him about the apron. About Chen Si laughing until he cried and Aurelia demanding the photograph from both sides. He tried to say burn it. She told him he’d looked very handsome, even in the apron, and he made a sound that was definitely a laugh, and Elara said, “Hold still, you idiot,” with real tenderness.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came in at twenty to six, soaked to the bone from a third night on the harbour. He stopped in the doorway. Then he crossed the room and put his hand on Zhao’s shoulder and couldn’t seem to take it off again.

“Brother.”

Zhao didn’t answer. He’d gone quiet a little while before.

“Do you know how long I’ve been looking for you?” said Chen Si. “Three days. Three fucking days.” He rubbed his face. “Sorry.”

“Don’t be,” said Elowen.

“I thought you were dead.” He was talking to Zhao. “You’d better wake up. I’ve got a great deal to say to you, and Aurelia’s outside with clean clothes for everyone, and Bao wants to see you, and all of it can wait, but you’d better wake up for it.”

He went and stood against the wall by the fridge and didn’t move again.

At half past six Elara finished the dressing and stripped her gloves off and stood with her bloody hands held away from herself, and looked at her sister.

“That’s what I can do here,” she said. “He needs a hospital.”

“He can’t have one.”

“I know.” Elara washed her hands at the kitchen sink, slowly, to the wrists. “Then he has me. Every day, morning and night, till he doesn’t. And you call me the minute anything changes, I don’t care what time it is.”

Zhao’s eyes opened.

He looked confused, and then he found Elowen above him, and his face went still.

“Elowen.”

“I’m here.”

He tried to lift his hand. She caught it before it could pull at anything.

“Sorry,” he said.

“For what?”

He swallowed. “Dinner.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed and cried in the same breath. “You’re apologising for dinner?”

“Late.”

“Yes. You’re very late.” She pressed his hand against her cheek. “Don’t do it again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven Raiden and Chen Si lifted the door between them and carried him up the stairs to their bedroom, slowly, a step at a time, with Elara walking beside them holding a bag of fluids up in the air and Elowen behind with her hand on his foot because she couldn’t reach anything else. They laid him in the bed. Elara hung the drip from a coat hook.

Behind them, the kitchen table was empty. Two bags on the counter, a towel that would have to be burned, the ginger, the spring onions. At the front of the fridge the fish she’d moved there three nights ago had finally gone off.

She’d throw it out later.

He’d crawled two kilometres uphill with a bullet in him because he’d said he’d be home for dinner. She sat down on the edge of the bed in his coat, still barefoot, with gravel in her soles, and held his hand while he slept.

chapters.title: “I Stained Your Life”
chapters.desc: Two days of fever. He wakes once, says sorry for everything, and falls asleep on the question he’s been carrying for three years.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not the stain, Zhendong. You’re the wall. You keep it out.”
chapters.content:
The fever didn’t break on Sunday.

Elara came at eight and at six and in between she rang every three hours, and in between that Elowen sat by the bed with two fingers on the inside of his wrist and watched the bag on the coat hook go down a drop at a time. She changed the cloth on his forehead when it went warm. She learned the names of the antibiotics and the order they went in. By the afternoon Elara had stopped explaining things and started just telling her, which Elowen understood was a promotion.

He was hot to touch all day, and far away.

At noon his mouth moved.

“Si.”

She leaned in. “Chen Si’s downstairs.”

“Si. Don’t.” His brow pulled tight. “Don’t come back for me. Go.”

She didn’t know where he was. Somewhere cold, by the sound of it.

“He’s not going anywhere,” she said. “He’s in the kitchen being rude to Peng.”

His fingers moved on the sheet. “Bao.”

“Bao’s alive. He’s stitched. He’s furious about it.”

“Lok.”

She had to choose the words. There weren’t any good ones. “Lok didn’t make it.”

His face changed. She thought he’d heard her. Then it went loose again and he said, quite clearly, in an ordinary voice, as if he were telling Bao where to park, “My wife’s at the counter,” and turned his head on the pillow towards the window, where there was no counter and no shop, only the lemon tree with its seven lemons.

“I’m here,” said Elowen. “I’m not at the counter. I’m here.”

He slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came in the afternoon with a bag of clothes, a flask of soup, and the expression of a woman who had decided that everyone in this house was going to be looked after whether they liked it or not.

“You look dreadful,” she said.

“Hello to you too.”

“I’m being kind. Have you eaten?”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I didn’t ask if you were hungry.” She poured soup into a bowl and put it into Elowen’s hands and stood over her until she’d had half of it. Then she looked at Zhao, grey against the pillow, with the drip line taped to the back of his hand, and her face did something it didn’t do in public.

“How is he?”

“Still hot.”

Aurelia touched the back of Elowen’s hand, once. Then she said, “Come here,” and pulled a comb out of her bag.

“Aurelia—“

“Your hair’s been in that knot since Wednesday. Turn round.”

Elowen turned the chair. Aurelia worked through the tangles from the ends up, surprisingly gently for someone who’d once made a hairdresser cry at a fashion week.

“Chen Si hasn’t slept,” said Elowen.

“No. He thinks if he stops moving something terrible will happen.” The comb paused. Then it went on. “He’s frightened. Don’t ask me if he thinks Zhendong will die. I don’t ask him either.”

She tied Elowen’s hair back loosely with a ribbon off the soup flask and said, “There,” and sat down on the arm of the chair, shoulder to shoulder, and didn’t leave. “Don’t make me do this every day. I have a label to run. My husband can’t do it for me, he once washed cashmere with washing-up liquid.”

Elowen laughed, a small one. Aurelia looked very satisfied with herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara’s phone kept lighting up.

She’d check the dressing and look at it. She’d change the bag and look at it. In the evening it died, and she went out onto the landing and asked Peng, of all people, if he had a charger, and Peng produced one from his jacket like a magician, and she sat on the top stair with it plugged into the wall and typed with both thumbs.

Elowen, coming out with the basin, saw the screen over her shoulder before Elara turned it away. No name on the conversation. Just a number.

Elara: Still febrile. Wound’s clean. She hasn’t left him.

Elara: Please don’t come up the road. I’ll ring you.

“Who’s that?” said Elowen.

“No one.” Elara put the phone face down on her knee.

“No one who knows what febrile means.”

“Lots of people know what febrile means.” She stood up. “I’m sorting something out. Go and sit with your husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning Bao came up with his arm strapped across his chest and stood at the foot of the bed without saying anything. He looked at the drip. He looked at the boss’s face. Then he looked at the window, the way he’d looked at it in the kitchen when he told her about the bus station.

“I went to Lok’s mother last night,” he said. “She asked me if he was brave.”

“What did you tell her?”

“Yes.”

“Was he?”

“He was running towards the boss when they shot him. With one arm.” Bao’s jaw moved. “He was twenty-six. He always ate the boss’s leftover rice at the office because he said it was a sin to waste it, and the boss always left some.”

Elowen hadn’t known that. She’d known Lok’s name and his face and the way he said madam as if it had three syllables. She hadn’t known about the rice.

“Tell me the next time you go to her,” she said. “I’ll come with you.”

Bao nodded once. At the door he stopped and said, without turning round, “He’d have liked that you asked,” and went down the stairs one at a time, holding the rail with his good hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song Wei Long came on Monday evening, just after six, on foot from the bottom of the hill.

Elowen went down to the hall to meet him. He was in a black coat with the rain on its shoulders, his black hair falling over his forehead, and he had the stillness of a man who had spent his whole working life standing in doorways deciding things. He carried a folder. He smelled of rain and of a cigarette he’d put out at the gate.

“I’m not here,” he said.

“I gathered.”

“How is he?”

“Alive. Hot. Not awake.”

He nodded as if she’d given him a list of numbers. Then he opened the folder on the hall table.

“Four men dead at the Hengli yard. Maartens, two men he’d flown in, and Lok Wing-kei, employed by a shipping company I can’t prove anything about. One wounded man, also employed by that company, treated privately for a shoulder injury he says he got falling off a ladder. Maartens’s body came up at the north quay this morning.” He turned a page. “Officially, nobody’s identified Zhao Zhendong at the scene. The footage is bad. The witnesses disagree with each other. I have nothing that puts him there.”

“But he was there.”

“Yes.” Song looked at her steadily. “There’s a Red Notice with his name on it, and a dozen agencies who’d very much like to know he’s alive. If I write down that he was at that yard, they’ll know by the morning. I need time to find out who bought the second group, and I can’t have that time if he’s in a cell.”

“Are you helping him?”

“I’m trying to stop this turning into a second disaster while he can’t stand up.” He took a photograph out of the folder. A still from a camera, very grainy. The north access road, a little after two. A car’s headlights. And at the edge of the picture, low down by the drainage wall, a dark shape that might have been anything.

“Your sister found this camera,” said Song. He put one finger on the shape. “This is the cat.”

Elowen looked at it. Then at him.

“In my report,” he said, “that’s a cat. A large one, crossing the road at fourteen minutes past two. Cats are very common round the harbour.” He closed the folder and gave it to her. “Tell him that the next time he walks out of a gun fight into the sea, I may not be able to find a cat.”

He went back out into the rain. She stood in the hall with the folder against her chest. Song hadn’t given him innocence. He’d given him time, and just now time was the only thing they needed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came up after Song had gone and sat on the far side of the bed.

“You look terrible,” he told Zhao. Zhao didn’t answer. “I had a very long list. I was going to start with idiot. Then Lok. Then Bao, then Aurelia threatening to kill me for not sleeping. Then this shirt. You owe me a shirt. This one’s ruined.”

His voice went on the last word. He stopped.

Elowen was at the window. She didn’t come over, and she didn’t say his name, because she thought he’d hate that.

“Can I ask you something?” said Chen Si after a while.

“Yes.”

“Do you love him?”

She looked at Zhao. The fever had made his skin look almost thin enough to see through. His hair was all over the pillow. She thought of him in the hall with his fingers on her mouth, and on a stool by her shop window for three years, and on the gravel at the gate on his hands.

“Yes,” she said.

Chen Si looked at her for a moment as though he’d been braced for anything else.

“Then tell him.”

“He won’t let me. He wants a boring day.”

Chen Si laughed, once, without any pleasure in it. “Of course he does. He thinks you’d say it because he’s hurt. Because you’re frightened. Because you want him to feel better.”

“I can be frightened and mean it.”

“He doesn’t know that yet. He’s never had both at once.” Chen Si looked at his brother. “He thinks he stained your life. He’s never said it. I know him. Everything that’s happened to you since that registry, he’s got it written down somewhere as his.”

“He didn’t make the world dangerous,” said Elowen. “He didn’t make my father lie to us for most of our lives. He didn’t put my card on that gate.”

“No.”

“He gave me somewhere to come home to.”

Chen Si reached across the bed and put his hand on Zhao’s arm, and left it there.

“Then I hope he wakes up in time to hear you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke just after midnight. She’d fallen asleep in the chair with one hand on the mattress, and his fingers moving against hers brought her up at once.

“Zhendong?”

His eyes were barely open. He looked at her. Then his face crumpled.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t talk.”

“Sorry,” he said again, through the oxygen. “Everything.”

“What everything?”

“The shop. Your family. The notice.” He was crying. She’d never seen it; it didn’t look like anything she’d expected, just water running sideways into his hair while his face stayed almost still. “Your life. I stained it. I thought I could keep it away from you. Every time, something else. You had a shop and your family and your flowers. You had a life before.”

She took his face in both hands.

“And I have a life now.”

“Not the one—“

“The one I picked.” She leaned close enough that he had to look at her. “You think I married you without knowing what you were? You think I didn’t read the routes?”

“Should have kept—“

“You don’t get to decide my life was better before you.” Her hands were shaking against his cheeks. “You’re not the stain, Zhendong. You’re the wall. You keep it out.”

He stared at her as if he didn’t know where to put the words.

She kissed him. Not gently. Not carefully. She kissed him with everything she’d swallowed behind the armory door for three days, both hands on his face, until he made a small hurt sound against her mouth that wasn’t about the wound. When she let him go she was crying too.

“Do you hear me?”

His mouth moved. “I’d still.”

“Still what?”

“Say yes.” A breath. “To you. Again.”

She shut her eyes. Even now. Even like this.

“I know,” she said, and kissed his cheek. He tried to smile. “Again,” he said, and she kissed it again.

Then something else came into his face, careful, as if he were lifting something heavy he’d been carrying round so long he’d stopped noticing.

“Elowen. Three years. I want to ask—why did you—“

His eyelids were coming down.

“Why did you—“

“Zhendong?”

He was asleep. The question stayed in the room, halfway out.

She put her forehead down on his hand. “Ask me when you wake up,” she said into it. “Ask me properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after two his breathing changed. She was at the edge of sleep and the change brought her up, terrified, before she understood it had gone deeper and slower, not worse. His skin under her palm was damp now instead of dry.

Elara came in from the landing in her socks with the thermometer, and read it, and read it again.

“It’s coming down.”

“Really?”

“It’s breaking.” Elara pulled the blanket up. “He’s not out of it. Don’t let me see you think he’s out of it. But that’s what we wanted.”

“Thank you,” said Elowen.

“Sleep.”

“I will.”

“You said that yesterday.”

“I meant it yesterday.”

Elara shook her head and went out. And Elowen, alone with him for the first time in four days without a number to watch, put her face down against his good shoulder and cried. Not the way she’d cried in the armory, with nobody to hear. It came up from somewhere much further down and there was no stopping it. For Old Ming. For Lok on the rails. For Bao’s shoulder, and Chen Si on the harbour in the rain, and two kilometres of road.

His hand came up, weak and clumsy, and found her hair, and stayed there.

She lifted her head. His eyes were still shut. He hadn’t woken. But his fingers were on the back of her head, the way they always were, and she lay down very carefully along the edge of the bed with her cheek on his shoulder and let them stay.

chapters.title: The Question He Never Asked
chapters.desc: Two weeks after the shipyard, on the most boring day there has ever been, he finally asks why she married him. She tells him the truth, and makes him wait for the rest.
chapters.content:
The first thing Zhao Zhendong learned about getting over a gunshot wound was that his wife had no sympathy whatsoever for his pride.

The second was that her sister had less.

“Don’t move.”

“I’m not moving.”

“You’re getting ready to.” Elara was kneeling on the bed beside him with a tray of packing and saline and a face like a ward sister’s, though she was still a student and wouldn’t sit her finals till May. “This is going to hurt.”

“I know.”

“Then stop tensing up before I’ve touched you.”

“I’m not tensing.”

She pressed the first strip of gauze into the wound and his jaw went tight enough to crack a walnut.

“Would you like me to call your wife?”

“No.”

“Would you like me to call Chen Si?”

“No.”

“Would you like to stop pretending this doesn’t hurt?”

He looked at the ceiling. Elara smiled very slightly and carried on.

He’d been interrogated in a cellar once, in his twenties. He’d been cut and burned and had bones broken, and he’d gone into a harbour with a bullet in him. None of it had involved a twenty-three-year-old in pearl earrings telling him every morning at eight to stop being difficult.

Elowen leaned in the bedroom doorway with a cup of tea. “Is he being difficult?”

“Extremely.”

“I’m shocked.”

“You’re enjoying this,” said Zhao.

“A little.” She drank her tea. “I’m with my sister.”

“Of course you are.”

Elara taped the dressing down and sat back on her heels. “Nothing heavier than a teacup. Nobody walks anywhere without someone in the room. If your temperature goes up, you ring me, not him.” She pointed at Elowen. “Her. She’ll tell me the truth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came on Wednesday with a cane.

It was a beautiful thing, black wood with a silver head shaped like a bird, the kind of object that belonged to an old general who had never once needed it. He’d found it in an antique shop behind the court buildings and paid too much for it, and he held it out across the bed with the face of a man who’d already won.

“What’s that?” said Zhao.

“A cane.”

“I can see that.”

“Then we’re getting somewhere.”

Elowen laughed from the window seat. Zhao didn’t take it.

“I don’t need it.”

“You do.”

“I can walk.”

“Then you can walk with it.”

They looked at each other. Raiden, who’d spent his first ten years on a farm being told nothing and the next fifteen being underestimated by everyone in the city, could hold a stare against a wall. Zhao had only ever lost a stare to one person in his life, and she put her cup down.

“Zhendong. Take it.”

He took it.

“Good,” said Raiden.

“Are you satisfied?”

“Very.” He watched Zhao test his weight on it, and stop when the wound pulled, and say nothing about it. “Baba says you’re to come to lunch on Sunday if you can sit in a car. Ah Sim’s making two cakes.”

“Two?”

“She says one cake isn’t enough for two birthdays.” Raiden looked at his hands. “She’s never said that before. Every year it’s been one.”

Elowen looked at him across the room. Her brother and her sister, born two days apart and given the same birthday on paper, and one cake for both of them every April since the paper was signed. “Good for Ah Sim,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Thursday after that he came to the market.

He wasn’t supposed to. Elara would have had a great deal to say. But it was four in the morning and he was dressed and standing at the bottom of the stairs with the cane when Elowen came down, and he said, “I’ll sit,” in a way that meant he’d thought about it all night.

He sat on an upturned crate at the end of Granny Yip’s row with his coat buttoned to the throat, while the trolleys went past and the hoses ran and the lights buzzed in the roof. Granny Yip came out from behind her buckets and looked at him the way she looked at a bunch of tulips somebody had kept too long.

“Too thin.”

“I’m recovering.”

“Too thin,” she said again, as if he hadn’t understood the first time, and turned to Elowen. “Feed him. Make him sleep. Men are troublesome.”

“She’s been telling me,” said Zhao.

“Then listen to her.” And she went back to her chrysanthemums.

Elowen bought yellow tulips and white lisianthus and a bucket of eucalyptus, and he stood up to take the eucalyptus and she took it off him without a word. Her hands were frozen from the buckets. She was rubbing them together at the end of the row when he held his right arm out from his side, just a little, the good side.

“What?”

“Your hands.”

“Your ribs.”

“That side’s fine.”

She looked at him. Then she undid two buttons of his coat and slid both her cold hands inside it, under his jumper, flat against his skin, on the side that didn’t have a hole in it. He drew a breath through his teeth.

“Cold?”

“Very.”

“Good,” said Elowen, and left them there.

His arm came round her back. They stood like that at the end of the row in the noise of the market, vendors shouting prices, a kettle hissing behind the stall, a man swearing at a forklift. Nobody looked twice. She put her forehead against his chest.

“You’re tired.”

He didn’t argue, which was how she knew.

When they got home he lay down on top of the covers with his coat still on and slept for four hours without moving. It was the first time he’d slept since the gate without someone waking him for a drip or a dressing or a dream. She sat in the window with a book and turned the pages very quietly.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday Peng came to the potting-room door in his new suit, which fitted him now, and stood there turning a phone over in his hands.

“Madam. Boss says I’m to go back to the east gate.”

Elowen put down the seed tray. “Since when?”

“Since this morning. He said—“ Peng looked at the phone as if it might help. “He said Maartens came up at the north quay, so you could have me back. But I’m not to go back to you. I’m to go back to the gate.” He frowned. “I don’t think he meant it the way it came out.”

“No,” said Elowen. “He never does.”

She found Zhao in the study, upright in the chair with the cane against the desk, reading a contract he’d been told not to read.

“You took Peng off me.”

“I said I would.”

“You said until he’s dead.”

“He’s dead.” Zhao turned a page. “I don’t break the ones I say out loud.”

She stood in the doorway and looked at him: thinner, grey under the eyes, his hair falling in his face because he couldn’t lift his arm high enough yet to push it back. She’d been angry with him about those messages for a whole night. She still was, a little, somewhere. She went in and pushed the strand off his forehead with one finger.

“Every hour,” she said. “Half my lunch.”

“You never finish your lunch.”

“That’s not the point.”

“No,” he agreed, and caught her finger, and kissed the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday he could walk to the bathroom on his own. Elara found out.

“You were supposed to call someone.”

“It was five metres.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“I didn’t fall.”

“That isn’t the point either.” She snapped her bag shut. “I’m beginning to think you don’t want to be well.”

“I’m beginning to think this house has conspired against me.”

“Good. Then perhaps you’ll behave.”

When she’d gone, Elowen did up his shirt for him, one button at a time. “You walked to the bathroom without telling anyone.”

“I was going to tell you afterwards.”

“That’s not how telling works.”

He caught her hand at the top button and kissed her knuckles.

“Are you trying to distract me?”

“Yes.”

“It’s working.”

At three o’clock her phone buzzed.

Xiao Pan: Nothing happened today.

Elowen: Nothing?

Xiao Pan: No glass. No men asking for wreaths. Nobody fainted. Two old ladies bought freesias and argued about their grandsons.

Xiao Pan: I’ve been sitting down for twenty minutes. I don’t know what to do with myself.

Elowen: Enjoy it.

She showed Zhao. He read it twice and gave the phone back without a word, and she watched him look out of the window at the lemon tree for some time afterwards as if somebody had told him something wonderful about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara was making tea in the kitchen on Saturday evening when her phone lit up on the counter, face up, and Elowen happened to be reaching past it for the sugar.

Unknown: Did you eat?

Elara turned it over so fast it spun.

“Who’s that?”

“Nobody.”

“Nobody who wants to know if you’ve eaten.”

“It’s a very common question.”

“Is it?”

“In medicine. All the time.”

The phone buzzed again under her palm. She looked at it, under her hand, like a card in a game. Her face went pink from the neck up.

“Oh,” said Elowen.

“There’s no oh.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You’ve got a face that says things.” Elara picked up her bag. “I have to go. I’ll do the last bag in the morning, and after that he doesn’t need me. He needs to stop walking to the bathroom.”

She was out of the door before Elowen could ask anything else, with her phone already at her ear, saying, “Yes. Yes, I ate. I’m coming down now,” to nobody at all.

Zhao was at the kitchen island on a stool. He’d watched all of it.

“Who?”

“Nobody,” said Elowen.

He looked at her. She looked at him. They both started to smile at the same time.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday he couldn’t sit in a car for an hour each way, and they both knew it, so they didn’t go to the Walled City.

Raiden sent photographs instead.

Raiden: Two cakes.

One with little yellow sugar flowers and one with a slightly drunk border of chocolate cream. Ah Sim beside them with her arms folded. Evangeline at the end of the table, very straight in pale blue with her black ribbon in her hair, looking at the second cake as if nobody had ever given her one before.

Raiden: Ah Sim says Baba can’t cut his slice till Ev’s chosen hers. Baba says he’s scared of her.

Raiden: He saved you both the corner pieces.

Elowen sent back a photograph of the steamer on the stove, because that was what she’d promised.

She’d said fish when he could sit at a table. He could sit at a table now, more or less, if the table came to him. So she made it the way the note in her mother’s handwriting said, ginger in fat gold coins, spring onion, light soy, a little wine, hot oil last over the top so that it hissed, and carried it up on a tray to the table by the bedroom window where he could see the courtyard.

He looked at it and didn’t pick up his chopsticks.

“You made it.”

“I promised.”

He picked up his chopsticks. He lifted the skin back off the belly, found the middle piece, and put it in her bowl, without looking, the way her father had done since she was too small to find the bones.

Then he took the belly for himself.

Elowen stopped with her chopsticks in the air.

“That’s Baba’s.”

“I know.”

“Nobody eats the belly but Baba. Mama wrote it down.”

“Your father isn’t here.” He took a bone out carefully. “Someone in the family has to eat it.”

She didn’t say anything. She couldn’t, quite. He ate. He said, after a while, “It’s good,” and she said, “It’s the same recipe,” and he said, “It isn’t the same,” and didn’t explain, and didn’t need to. He’d come home to eat it. That was the difference.

Afterwards the tray sat between them with the bones on it, and the courtyard went blue, and he put his chopsticks down side by side, and looked at them instead of at her.

“Elowen. Can I ask you something?”

There it was. Three years, nearly to the week. She’d known it was coming since the gala, since the car on the way home with the rain on the windows and his mouth opening on it and closing again.

“Yes.”

“Did you marry me to control your father’s boss?”

“Yes,” said Elowen.

He looked up.

“Yes,” she said again. “I walked into your office with three pages because you were the most powerful man my father had ever worked for, and if I was your wife you’d have to listen to me. I wanted my family out from under you. I wanted Baba to stop being frightened. That’s why I married you.”

He was quiet. He didn’t look hurt. He looked like a man who’d finally been handed a bill he’d been waiting for, and found it was the amount he’d thought.

“That’s the answer to the question you asked,” said Elowen.

Something moved in his face. “There’s another question.”

“Yes. You haven’t asked it.”

He didn’t move. Then, very carefully, the way he’d stand up with the cane, he said, “Why did you stay?”

“Tomorrow,” she said. “At the shop, at closing.”

“Why tomorrow?”

“Because I want to say it where I’d have said it if none of this had happened. Behind my own counter.” She looked out at the sky over the courtyard, which had gone thick and low. “And because it’s going to rain.”

“And if it doesn’t rain?”

“Then you’ll wait.”

He looked at her across the tray for a long moment. Then he reached over it, past the bones and the tea and the little dish of ginger, and put his hand round the back of her neck and drew her towards him across the table. And stopped, an inch away, and waited, the way he’d waited every time for three years, with his eyes on her mouth.

“Can I?”

She laughed in his face. “Obviously yes. You idiot.”

He kissed her over the tray. The dish of ginger went over. Neither of them picked it up.

chapters.title: The Flower in His Lapel
chapters.desc: Closing time, rain, and a camellia from the mountain in his lapel. She tells him why she stayed, and he finally says it back.
chapters.content:
The camellia came on Monday morning in a little wooden box.

It was on the counter when Elowen got back from the market, still wet from the rain, wrapped in brown paper and tied with plain string. No sender, no address, just her name in Mr. Wen’s careful old-fashioned hand. She knew what it was before she’d got the string off.

Inside, on damp tissue, lay a single red flower.

Middlemist’s Red, from the grove on the mountain. Petal over petal, the colour going deeper towards the middle the way it did in the photographs nobody believed. There were still drops of water on it. Mr. Wen would no more cut one of those than cut off his own hand, and under the tissue there was a folded note to say he hadn’t.

It came down in last night’s rain. I caught it before the boy swept the path. It would rather be with you than on the ground.

Don’t let him touch it.

Elowen laughed out loud in the empty shop. She took a photograph and sent it.

Elowen: Mr. Wen sent something.

Zhendong: Is it damaged?

Elowen: No.

Zhendong: Keep it cold.

Elowen: I know how to look after a flower.

Zhendong: I know.

Zhendong: I’m coming to the shop at closing.

She looked at the clock. Nine hours. She floated the camellia in a shallow glass dish in the cooler and didn’t tell him she’d be counting them. She suspected he knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

By closing it was pouring. It hammered the window and turned the street into a long smear of gold and grey, and the gutters ran like rivers past the step. Xiao Pan had gone at six, after checking the orders twice and telling her, very casually, that he wouldn’t be coming back for anything he’d forgotten. She suspected he’d guessed something too.

She turned the sign. She was wiping down the counter when the bell went.

He stood on the mat.

He was soaked through. His hair was flat and dark and pushed back off his forehead, apart from the one strand, which had given up entirely. His coat was black with rain. Under it his shirt was buttoned wrong, one side of the collar higher than the other, the top button through the second hole.

He stood exactly where he’d stood three years ago, on a wet Monday at seven o’clock, and looked at her across the shop.

“What happened to you?” she said.

“Rain.”

“The driver has an umbrella.”

“The driver does.”

“Then why are you wet?”

“I was in a hurry.”

She put the cloth down. “You were in a hurry to get here.”

“Yes.”

She came round the counter. “Take your coat off.”

He did. She hung it on the hook by the back door to drip and came back and looked at the buttons.

“Did you dress in the dark?”

“No.”

“Were you distracted?”

“Yes.”

“By what?”

He looked at her.

“Come here,” she said, and he stepped off the mat, and she undid his shirt from the top, button by button. It was wet through. Her knuckles brushed his chest and he stood very still and didn’t touch her.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

“Zhendong.”

“A little.”

She did them up again properly, one at a time, smoothed the collar flat, and then went to the cooler and brought out the dish. He looked at the flower and didn’t reach for it.

“Mr. Wen said you’re not allowed to touch it.”

“Wise man.”

She took a pin from the drawer and fixed the camellia to the lapel of his jacket, carefully, the stem tucked under, and stepped back. The red was very bright on the navy. He looked formal, and unusually nervous.

“Very handsome,” she said.

“Because of the flower?”

“Don’t get vain.”

“Too late,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the low bench by the worktable, where she sat to strip roses when her back hurt. The rain went on. The shop was warm and smelled of wet leaves and the cooler hummed behind its glass. He held her hand between both of his and looked at it.

“You asked me why I stayed,” said Elowen.

“Yes.”

“I didn’t decide it. I want you to know that first. I didn’t wake up one day and know. I kept doing it, without noticing, and then one day I noticed.” She turned her hand over in his. “I started looking for your car outside before I’d taken my coat off. I started keeping things to tell you. Granny Yip’s prices. A customer who wanted roses that matched her dog. I’d stand at the counter and think, I’ll tell him that tonight. I started buying things at the market and wondering if you’d like them. I stopped thinking of the house as where the agreement said I lived.”

He was holding her hand so carefully it might have been the camellia.

“I chose you when you made me angry,” she said. “Which was often.”

“Frequently.”

“Very frequently.” She leaned her shoulder on his. “I didn’t stay because I was scared to go. I didn’t stay because I owed you, or because you’d made it impossible. You never once made it impossible. You built me rooms with doors that open from the inside.” She looked at the rain. “I know what your life is. There are things in it I’ll never like and things you’ll have to answer for, and loving you doesn’t make me stop seeing them. They just don’t cancel the man who carried eucalyptus round the market for Granny Yip, and learned my mother’s fish so Baba would feel at home at our table. And came up the hill on his hands.”

She put her palm on his face.

“Zhendong. I love you.”

For a moment he didn’t move. Then something went in his face, not all at once, something small and terrible: his mouth came open and his eyes closed and his hand on hers tightened as if he’d been holding himself up by it for years and had just run out.

“Elowen.”

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“I love you.”

His breath went ragged. “Again.”

“I love you, Zhao Zhendong.”

He bowed his head. A tear ran down beside his nose and she wiped it off with her thumb.

“You said it,” he said, almost laughing.

“I did.”

“Without a fever.”

“Without a fever.”

“Without being frightened.”

“I’m frightened of plenty of things.” She held his jaw. “Not of this.”

He moved before she’d finished the sentence. He came up off the bench and took her with him, both arms round her, and hauled her up against him so hard her feet left the floor, and kissed her. He didn’t ask. He didn’t wait. It was the kiss of a man who’d been waiting so long to hear something that he’d almost decided he never would, open-mouthed and rough, one hand at her waist and the other in her hair, and she grabbed his collar and kissed him back just as hard.

There was a soft, unmistakable crunch between them.

They broke apart and looked down. The camellia was flat against his lapel. One petal had folded under the pin and another had come away and was stuck to the front of her jumper.

For a second neither of them said anything. Then she started laughing and couldn’t stop.

“Mr. Wen,” said Zhao, looking at it in real horror, “is going to be disappointed.”

“He told you not to touch it.”

“I didn’t touch it.”

“You crushed it with your chest.”

“I was busy.”

She laughed so hard she had to hold on to him. He looked at her, and then he smiled, a real one, unguarded, that made him look about twenty.

She took the pin out and laid what was left of the flower on the worktable. “It had already fallen,” she said. “He’d rather it was here than on the path.”

He was looking at her, not the flower.

“I loved you first,” he said.

She went still.

“Before the office.” He brushed her hair off her face. “Before you came in with your three pages. I don’t know when it turned into this. I knew your father. I knew he had a daughter with a flower shop on Ferry Road. I knew what time you opened and when you closed and which mornings you went to the market and that you rang him every night at eight.” He didn’t look away while he said it, and he didn’t make it sound better than it was. “I’d been past that window more times than I’ll tell you. The first time I saw you, you had a blue flower tucked behind your ear and you were cutting roses on the angle.”

“A delphinium.”

“I think so.”

“You were watching me.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. It wasn’t nothing. It sat in her chest beside everything else, a cold small stone, and she let it sit there and didn’t pretend it wasn’t. Then she thought of a man on a mat in the rain saying name your price because he had no other way of standing in a room with her, and the stone didn’t go, but it moved over.

“I bought every flower you had,” said Zhao, “because I wanted a reason to stay in the shop.”

“You bought them because you wanted Baba.”

“That too.”

“You could have rung him.”

“He wasn’t answering.”

“So you bought a flower shop.”

“I bought the flowers.” His thumb moved on her cheek. “I loved you before you knew my name. I knew it was unreasonable and I never thought you’d give it back. But you chose. That’s the part that counts.”

She kissed him. This time she held his jacket away from the pin, though there was nothing left on it to crush.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d meant to take him home. She’d meant to make him rest. Both plans went when he kissed her again and she felt him smile against her mouth.

“Your side,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’ve still got stitches.”

“I know.”

“You’re agreeing with everything.”

“I don’t want to argue tonight.” He rested his forehead on hers. “You said you love me.”

“That’s a very poor reason.”

“It’s the only one I’ve got.”

She got up and held out her hand. He took it and stood carefully, and she put him against the edge of the big worktable, where the bench was low and solid and came to his hip, and moved the buckets and the knives and the rolls of paper out of the way with her arm. He watched her do it.

“What are you doing?”

“Making room.”

“For what?”

“My husband,” said Elowen, and pushed him gently down to sit on the edge of it.

She climbed into his lap. Slowly, one knee on the bench either side of him, well away from his side, her hands on his shoulders. His breath went out of him. His hands came to her waist and stayed there, light, not pulling, the way they’d been the very first time, three years ago, as if she were something that could be taken away.

“Tell me if anything hurts,” she said.

“You first.”

“Nothing hurts.”

“Then I won’t either.”

She kissed him slowly. She undid the buttons she’d done up for him, every one, and pushed the wet shirt back off his shoulders, and ran her hands down over his chest and stopped at the edge of the dressing, flat, so he’d know she knew where it was. He shivered. It wasn’t the cold. She kissed his throat and the hollow of it and the old burn on his shoulder, and his head went back against the shelf behind him and knocked a roll of ribbon off it, and it unwound across the floor.

Neither of them went after it.

He got her jumper off over her head without letting go of her for more than a second. He touched her the way he always did when he’d been afraid, like a man reading something in the dark, with the flat of his palm, her back, her ribs, the line of her spine. She took his hand and put it where she wanted it and heard him say her name, low, like something that had been knocked out of him. The rain came down harder on the window. The lamp over the counter made everything gold. Every time he tried to take more of her weight she pressed him back down by the shoulders, and every time he let her.

“Elowen—“

“Hold still,” she said against his mouth. “I’ve got you.”

So for once he held still and let her have him. She moved over him slowly in the lamplight with the stitches between them like something they were both minding, and he watched her face the whole time as if he’d been told he’d only get to see it once. When it took him, he said it into her shoulder, over and over, I love you, I love you, and she held his head against her and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he sat on the bench with his back against the worktable and her across his lap in his half-dry shirt, and she ran her fingers through his hair while the rain wound down to a patter. The crushed camellia lay beside them on the dark wood with its petals coming loose.

“Mr. Wen will blame you,” she said.

“He can send another.”

“He won’t.”

“Then I’ll go up the mountain and apologise.”

“You’re not climbing a mountain with stitches. Write him a letter.”

“He’ll be more upset that I touched it.”

“You crushed it.”

“I didn’t touch it,” said Zhao, and kissed her shoulder.

She looked down at him. His eyes were shut. There was ribbon round his ankle.

“Zhendong. Say it again.”

He didn’t open his eyes. “I love you.”

“Again.”

He kissed her hand. “I love you, Elowen. Three years, one month and eight days.”

“You counted.”

“I always count.”

She laughed and put her forehead down on his. He’d thought, for years, that when it finally came it would be enormous, a great certainty arriving that everything he’d done to earn it had been worth something. It was raining. The shop was a mess. There was a flattened flower on the bench and a ribbon on the floor and his wife was sitting in his lap with her fingers in his hair, and he had never been so happy in his life, and he didn’t want to buy a single thing.

He only wanted to stay till morning. So they did.

chapters.title: Closing Half an Empire
chapters.desc: He starts shutting down the worst of the business, slowly. Chen Si lies for him, Elowen keeps the books, one man finds out what happens if he cheats, and Wei Long gets a list.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to be useful to get a place here.”
chapters.content:
The first list had eighty-seven names on it.

He put it on the dining table one morning in May, a month after the camellia, beside his tea and a piece of toast he wasn’t going to eat. Columns in his own small hand: companies, the men behind the companies, routes, how they paid, who the goods really went to when they’d gone past the place they said they were going. Some had a K beside them. Some had an S.

“What’s K?” said Elowen.

“Keep.”

“And S.”

“Stop.”

“You’re making a shopping list.”

“The other way round.” He turned it so she could see. “Eighty-seven live accounts. Some are clean. Some aren’t. Some are clean until you see who’s waiting at the end of the road. I’m going to close the ones I shouldn’t have opened, keep the ones that can stand on their own, and sell or bury the rest.”

“All at once?”

“Slowly. If I shut it all tomorrow, the men on those routes go to someone worse by the weekend. Some run with the money. And some work out why.” He looked at the list. “Chen Si says I’m being sentimental.”

“Are you?”

He thought about it properly. “Probably.”

She pulled out the chair next to him. “Then let’s count.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The work ate the dining room. By June there were folders on the table, folders on the sideboard and a shelf of them in the study that she’d made him label in plain words instead of his codes.

He marked the buyers. K. S. S. K. Sometimes he told her why. When he didn’t, she asked, and he told her, and she learned that a mark was hardly ever about the man. It was about where the cargo went after it left his hands, and whose fingers the money went through, and whether the business could be cut loose from the thing it was attached to without bleeding to death.

One afternoon he sat looking at a single name for ten minutes.

“What’s wrong with that one?”

“Eleven years with me. Three ports. Hundreds of people on the payroll, real ships, real cargo. And six contracts a year with something under the rice.” He rubbed his eyes. “If I stop it, people lose their jobs. If I keep it, it keeps doing what I don’t want it to.”

“Can the clean part be cut off?”

“Maybe. It’d take months.”

“Then don’t mark it today. Find out who in there could run it straight. If nobody can, you’ve got your answer.”

He put the pen down. “Unmarked.”

She was sitting on the tall stool at the end of the table with her heels hooked on the rung, and she leaned down from it in the middle of his next column and kissed him, upside down and sideways, because she’d been looking at his mouth for twenty minutes instead of the figures. He laughed into it. When she straightened up he caught her left hand, turned it over, and drew a small neat K on the back of it in his black ink.

“What’s that for?”

“Keep,” he said, and kissed the ink.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si started the story in June, at a dinner with three shipping men, very casually, the way he did everything that mattered. Zhao had been ill. Zhao was tired. Zhao was concentrating on a smaller portfolio now, preferred his evenings at home, didn’t see everybody who thought they had something to sell him. By July the harbour believed Zhao Zhendong’s health had gone, and Chen Si didn’t correct anyone.

“My husband says yours has retired,” said Aurelia at the shop, picking through the ranunculus. “He says he’s taken up gardening.”

“That part’s true.”

“Apparently half the port thinks he’s one bad afternoon from buying a fishing boat.”

“He’d frighten the fish,” said Elowen.

From the stool by the window Zhao said, “I can hear you.”

“Good,” said Aurelia. “Then you know your reputation’s being managed.”

Chen Si came in behind her with two coffees. “Improved.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Tsang had a K by his name. He’d run the north since Mak, and the routes he’d been given were supposed to be clean all the way through.

In the last week of July Elowen found forty crates of agricultural machinery on a north-warehouse statement with a domestic buyer on the invoice and a different port on the dispatch slip. She checked the payment. Then the receiving company. Then the receiving company’s directors. Then she went back to the start and did it all again.

“Zhendong. Come here, please.”

He came out of the study and read it standing up. His face didn’t change much. She’d learned to read how little.

“Forty crates. Through his own man.”

“To a buyer on your stop list. Signed out by Tsang. Nobody approved it.”

“Thank you,” he said, and gathered the pages, and she caught his wrist.

“Make sure it’s all there before you do anything. I don’t want you doing something because you’re angry. I want you to know exactly what he did.” She held on. “And the people who were meant to get the crates. You find them alive.”

He looked down at her hand. “Alive,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao found Tsang at noon the next day in an office over a freight depot, with a bag half packed. They brought him to the north warehouse, to the empty bay at the far end where the roof leaked, and sat him on a pallet, and Zhao came in at two.

He didn’t hurry. He took off his jacket and handed it to Bao and rolled his sleeves to the elbow, and Tsang started talking before he’d finished the second one. The crates were already sold. The money was owed to someone else. He’d only taken a commission. He had a daughter.

“Where did they go?” said Zhao.

Tsang told him a port. Zhao hit him.

He hit him the way he did everything, with complete attention and no wasted movement, until Tsang was on the concrete and the port had become the right port, and a ship’s name, and a man’s name on the dock, and the name of the man who’d paid that man. Bao wrote it all down. When there was nothing left in Tsang but noise, Zhao stood back and looked at his own knuckles, split across the first two, and then at Bao.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to.

Bao took his gun out, stepped round the pallet, and shot Tsang once behind the ear. The sound went up into the steel roof and came back down again in pieces. Zhao watched it the whole way, because he’d always believed a man who gave an order like that owed it his eyes.

“The ship,” he said. “Tonight.”

The crates were taken off it at two in the morning, further down the coast, by men who were paid well not to remember the night. Nobody on the ship was hurt. Nobody waiting at the other end was either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home with his right hand wrapped in a handkerchief. She saw it when he reached for his tea.

“Sit down.”

He sat. She went to the freezer and came back with a bag of peas in a tea towel and put it over his knuckles and held it there.

“That’s new,” he said.

“They’re good for it.”

“Are you going to ask?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I asked you for the people on the ship,” said Elowen. “Did you get them?”

“Yes. All of them.”

“Then hold still.”

He rested his hand on her knee under the peas. She held them there till the swelling went down. She didn’t ask about Tsang, and he didn’t tell her, and she knew perfectly well that not asking was its own kind of answer, and she held the peas anyway.

When she’d gone up, he sat with the list. Tsang’s name had a line through it. Beside it, in his own hand, a single letter.

✦ ✦ ✦

By August there were forty accounts to close and she was doing the paperwork for all of them: which could be wound up clean, which needed an outside auditor, which belonged to men who’d decided that a sick, distracted Zhao Zhendong wouldn’t notice what they did any more. They were wrong about that.

Mr. Yao, the senior accountant, had been frightened of her for over a year. In August he started knocking before he came into the dining room.

“Mrs. Zhao. The dissolution papers for the eastern companies.”

“Thank you. Put them there.”

He put them down very carefully. “Would you like me to go through the outstanding liabilities?”

“Please.”

He went through them. She asked three questions and put her finger on a figure that didn’t match the June return. Mr. Yao stopped. He looked at it. He looked at it again.

“I’ll correct that.”

“Thank you.”

At the door he hesitated. “Mrs. Zhao. Do you intend to stay involved in the accounts?”

“I suppose it depends how many mistakes you make,” said Elowen.

Mr. Yao went quite still. “Understood,” he said, and left.

From the next room Zhao said over his newspaper, “You’ve frightened him again.”

“I asked about liabilities. That’s his job.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Song Wei Long came to the shop on a Thursday at the end of August with no pastries and a face like a shut door.

She’d been waiting for him. She’d asked him to come. She put a folder on the counter.

“Nine names,” she said. “They come up again and again in the accounts I’ve been closing. Freight companies, agricultural suppliers, payments that don’t fit the cargo. And this.” She turned a page. “A container in the north warehouse records last month. Refrigeration equipment. It weighs wrong for refrigeration equipment, and it went out with its seal changed.”

“Where is it now?”

“I don’t know.”

“Does your husband?”

“He knows I found it. He hasn’t given me anything I can give you.”

Song looked at her for a long moment with those deep-set eyes. “You know what you’re giving me.”

“Yes.”

“These are people who’ll come to your shop.”

“They’ve been to my shop,” said Elowen. “There are children in that container, Wei Long. I don’t want to know what happens to the men. I want the children found.”

He took the folder. At the door he turned. “Don’t go near any of this yourself.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“And tell your husband if he goes near my investigation, I’ll make his recovery a great deal less comfortable.”

The container turned up two nights later in a little freight yard on the coast with a new seal on it. Song rang her just before midnight.

“Nine,” he said. “Behind a false wall. All alive. Two in hospital, dehydrated. The rest are being looked after.”

She sat down on the kitchen floor with the phone.

Upstairs Zhao was awake. He’d heard her voice. “Song?”

“Nine. All alive.”

He shut his eyes. Then he held his arm out and she came and lay against him and he kissed her hair.

“You gave him the list from my accounts.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“You don’t mind?”

“Especially because it came from my accounts,” he said.

In the morning she told Bao. He was by the cars. He listened, and nodded, and asked how old they were, and when she told him he walked down to the bottom of the drive and stood with his back to the house until the dogs went down to see what he was doing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Ming’s widow lived over a grocer’s in the east of the city. Zhao went himself, and Elowen went with him.

Mrs. Ming opened the door and saw who it was and stood very still. Behind her, at a little table, a boy of twelve was doing his homework under a strip light, and on the sideboard there was a photograph of Old Ming outside Warehouse Four with a paper cup of chestnuts, smiling at whoever had held the camera.

“There’s the insurance,” said Zhao, at the table, “and there’s money from me.”

She looked at the figure. “It’s too much. He was only a night guard.”

“He was responsible for that building. He did his job.” Zhao didn’t look at the photograph. “He told me once he wanted a noodle shop. Somewhere with windows. Somewhere people came in at lunch.”

Her face crumpled and recovered. “He never stopped talking about it.”

“The money’s in an account for you and the boy. If you want the shop, the premises and the equipment will be yours. No partner. No loan.”

The boy had stopped writing. “Did you know my grandpa?”

“Yes.”

“Was he brave?”

Zhao looked at the photograph then. “He was reliable.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Brave men aren’t always reliable,” said Zhao. “Your grandfather was both.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of August, on a warm evening, she found him in the courtyard looking at the lemon tree. The branches had got heavy. A few of the new lemons were starting to turn.

“What’s wrong?”

He turned his wedding ring with his thumb. “I don’t know what I’m for.”

She sat down beside him on the step.

“For years everything had a use. Every route, every man I kept, I knew what it was for. Now I’m shutting things. People are leaving. The work’s going away.” He looked at the tree. “I don’t know what I do when it’s gone.”

She looked at him for a while. Then she stood up and held out her hand. “Come with me.”

She took him through the kitchen and the potting room to the store cupboard at the back, where she kept the spare buckets, and pointed at two big empty ones by the sink.

“Those.”

“What about them?”

“Carry them.” She put one in his hand. “Tomorrow you can help me unload the eucalyptus. Then we’ll see.”

“Elowen. I’m serious.”

“So am I. You don’t have to be useful to get a place here. You don’t have to build another empire to make up for the one you’re closing. But if you want something to do, I’ve got a shop. You can carry buckets and strip roses and sweep, and stop frightening the customers, and when you’re tired you can sit by the window and drink tea and come home for dinner.”

He looked at the bucket.

“You make it sound easy.”

“It isn’t,” she said. “We’ll learn.”

At six the next morning Xiao Pan looked up from the counter and saw the boss in the doorway with two empty buckets.

“Boss?”

“Morning.”

Xiao Pan looked at Elowen. She was doing the white roses and didn’t look up. “He’s here to work,” she said.

“Doing what?”

“Carrying buckets.”

There was a long pause. Then Xiao Pan nodded with great seriousness. “Good. We’ve got loads of buckets.”

Zhao took a stack of them into the back. Elowen followed him and took half of it off him without a word, and he let her, and kissed her over the top of the rest.

“Am I being paid?”

“Tea. Lunch. And the good stool by the window.”

“That’s my stool?”

“It is now,” said Elowen, and went back to her roses.

chapters.title: The Wedding They Eloped From
chapters.desc: Three and a half years after the registry, they have the wedding in the flower shop. Raiden walks in with a wife nobody knew about, and Baba asks about the lemon tree.
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen announced over Sunday lunch that Elowen had never had a proper wedding, with a glass of wine in one hand and no intention at all of being argued with.

“You went to a registry office on a Tuesday morning. You signed some paper. Chen Si watched. You went home.” She put the glass down. “No flowers you didn’t carry yourself. No music. Not one photograph of the two of you standing next to each other.”

“We have photographs,” said Elowen.

“Security footage doesn’t count.”

Chen Si choked on his tea. Zhao put his chopsticks down and looked across the table at his wife.

“Do you want a wedding?”

She opened her mouth to say no. She’d never wanted a big one; the registry had been quick and frightened and exactly right for what it was, and she’d never once wished it different. But she looked at him, three and a half years and one bullet later, and found there was something she’d wanted without admitting it. A day that belonged to them. Not to her father’s debt or the men leaning on her family or the agreement that had put them in the same room. Just them.

“I wouldn’t mind,” she said.

“Good,” said Aurelia. “I’ve already started.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop closed for three days and Aurelia took over the front counter with a notebook, two phones and the authority of a woman who’d run a fashion week. Elowen was allowed to choose the flowers. She wasn’t allowed to change the guest list. Zhao was told to stay out of the way, and took it badly.

“I paid for the building,” he said.

“Congratulations, you own a building,” said Aurelia. “Now move.”

Elowen wanted it to look like a flower shop, not a hotel ballroom pretending to be one. White lisianthus, pale yellow roses, sprays of gypsophila and greenery cut from the courtyard. The front display came out to make an aisle. The worktables went to the back.

Raiden turned up on Wednesday with a borrowed truck full of old timber, grey and salt-marked, with the nail holes still in it.

“Where’s that from?”

“Hengli. They’re pulling the old platform down. I asked.” He started unloading. “You need something to walk under.”

By the afternoon there was an arch at the end of the aisle, plain and solid, made of the dock where the worst week of her life had started. She hung white lisianthus off it and stood under it with her brother.

“It’ll hold,” said Raiden.

“I know,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana did the lights. She’d been planning them for weeks and wouldn’t say why: warm bulbs along every beam, hidden strips under the shelves, threads of tiny lights wound through the greenery. On Friday night she said she’d be finished by midnight.

At half past one Elowen came back for her phone and found her asleep behind the counter on a folded blanket with her claw clip coming out and her glasses pushed up on her head. There was a man’s leather jacket over her, much too big. A steel flask of milk tea stood by her hand, still warm. The ladder by the arch had been folded and leaned neatly against the wall by someone who’d held it for a long time and then slipped out before anyone came.

Elowen knew whose jacket it was. She’d seen it every winter on the boy next door to the Walled City house, leaning on the garden wall. She decided not to ask. She put the flask closer to her sister’s hand, turned off the work lights, and went home.

Elara made the cake, and wouldn’t say what it was.

“Chocolate?”

“No.”

“Vanilla?”

“No.”

“Lemon?”

Elara paused with the palette knife in the air.

“It’s lemon,” said Elowen.

“I didn’t say that.”

“You stopped moving.”

“Go away,” said Elara, pink to the ears, and turned her phone face down on the counter when it buzzed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning Evangeline came to the shop with a small pot held in both hands. She put it on the counter. A young orchid, two green leaves and a new root curling over the edge of the soil.

“Is that—“

“Mama’s. The one by the kitchen window.” Evangeline touched a leaf. “Everyone said it had died. I kept watering it. In June there was a shoot.”

Elowen picked it up. She’d been seven the last time she’d seen it flower.

“You’ve got a good life,” said Evangeline, in her quiet way, as though she were telling her the time. “I wanted it here today.”

She kissed Elowen’s cheek and went and stood at the back of the shop by the door, and didn’t move from there all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came at four, with Jinx.

She was carrying the bottom tier of Elara’s cake in a steel box she’d made specially to keep it level on the bike, and at the door, before she came in, she took a ring out of her pocket and put it on. Raiden broke the bit of string he wore round his neck and put his on too. Then he walked into the middle of thirty people, holding her hand, and stopped.

“Everyone,” he said. “This is Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

The shop went silent.

Xiao Pan said, “That’s my mechanic.”

Eliana said, “Since when?”

“Two years next Saturday.”

“Two years?”

“We were going to tell you.”

“When?”

Raiden considered. “Today, as it turns out.”

Elowen walked up to him and hit him on the arm, quite hard, and then put both arms round him. “You idiot.” Then she turned to Jinx, who had long tangled black hair and a hard beautiful stare and grease in the creases of her knuckles that no amount of washing would get out, and who was very obviously trying not to laugh. “I’m furious,” Elowen told her.

“I know. He said you would be.”

“Thank you for marrying him.”

Jinx’s stare went somewhere else for a second. “He makes very good fish,” she said.

Lin Jian had come in behind them with a box of fruit. He’d stopped on the step when he heard my wife. He looked at his son, and at the ring, and at the girl wearing it, and he put the fruit down on the step and walked out into the street.

Jinx went after him. Nobody else moved.

Through the window they saw her stand next to him on the pavement, hands in her pockets, not saying anything. After a while he looked at her properly. Then, quite suddenly, he pointed at her, and his face changed.

“Cao Tiehan’s girl,” they heard him say. “Under the bench. Fifteen years old, with a carburettor in pieces on a newspaper.”

“Twelve.”

“Twelve.” He laughed, short and surprised. “He cooks, you said? My son?”

“Better than you.”

Lin Jian laughed properly then. “Dinner,” he said. “Next week. Bring him.”

“I knew,” Zhao said quietly to Raiden, at the back by the cooler, while the shop started breathing again.

“I know you did. Since the hospital.”

“Since her jacket on the chair.” Zhao straightened his cuff. “It was your marriage.”

“Thank you.”

“Look after her.”

“I intend to.”

“I wasn’t talking to you,” said Zhao, and looked across the shop at Jinx, who’d come back in and was now standing by the door next to Evangeline. The two of them watched the street together without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Wen came down from the mountain with his grandson driving and stood under the arch for some time examining the flowers. “Not bad,” he said, and to Zhao, “You look nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“Of course not.”

Song Wei Long came in a dark suit with a small box, and stiffened when Elowen hugged him.

“I didn’t know you were coming.”

“I was invited.”

“By whom?”

He glanced towards the back. “Your husband.”

Song didn’t sit. He stood by the window most of the evening, and every so often looked up at the roof of the building across the street, where nothing could possibly be, and then looked at Evangeline by the door, and said nothing at all to anyone.

A very tall man in gold-rimmed glasses and a black turtleneck arrived alone at six and went and stood beside the cake. Nobody introduced him. He didn’t seem to expect it. He stood by the cake all evening as if somebody had asked him to guard it, and every time Elara walked past he looked at her and then at nothing.

“Oh,” said Aurelia, at Elowen’s elbow, looking at Elara’s throat. There was a thin gold chain round it, with something on it that had been tucked under her collar and had worked its way out. “Oh, indeed.”

“He’s a colleague,” said Elara, passing.

“Of course he is, darling.”

“Did everyone get married without telling me?” said Elowen, and Zhao, beside her, said, “Apparently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain stopped at half past nine. The lights weren’t on yet. The shop was full of the last grey daylight and the smell of wet roses.

Elowen wore ivory, plain, no veil. The green earrings he’d given her. Her ring, back from the jeweller three weeks ago, sitting where it should. She carried yellow roses and white lisianthus with a sprig of courtyard green, and her father walked beside her in the black suit he’d bought for Mama’s funeral and worn to every important thing since, with his grey hair cut too short and his reading glasses in his breast pocket because he’d forgotten to leave them in the car.

He was crying before they’d taken three steps. He didn’t wipe it.

Halfway down the aisle he stopped. The shop held its breath. He looked along the rest of it to where Zhao was standing under the arch, in a dark suit with no tie, and asked, very seriously, across the whole room:

“How is the lemon tree?”

Zhao’s face changed. “Nine lemons.”

Lin Jian nodded. “Good.” He looked at his daughter. “Does she like them?”

“She counts them every morning.”

“Her mother would have liked that.” And he walked her the rest of the way, and put her hand in Zhao’s, and went and sat down in the front row next to Evangeline and held her hand instead.

There was no celebrant. Aurelia had wanted one and Elowen had said no. There was no paper to sign; they’d signed it. Chen Si stood beside Zhao. Aurelia stood beside her. Granny Yip had started crying in the second row and was telling the woman next to her it was the pollen.

“When I married you,” said Elowen, “I gave you three pages of conditions. You signed every one. You gave me a house and never once asked me to give up mine. You learned to sit down for dinner. You learned to strip a rose. You learned that two guard dogs could be called Dumpling and Noodle and there was nothing you could do about it.” Laughter, all round the shop. He smiled. “You kept my mother’s tree alive. You built me a room to grow things in, and when I asked you to let me keep my life, you learned to stand next to it instead of in front of it. I didn’t know what love looked like when I married you. I knew you listened. Now I know what it looks like. It’s ordinary mornings. Your hand finding mine under the table. You coming home.” She held on to him. “I choose you. Not because I have to. Because I want every boring day there is with you.”

He took a breath and looked at her and for a second didn’t seem to have any.

“I knew how to keep things,” he said. “Money. Ships. Men who wanted to leave. I didn’t know how to ask anyone to stay without it sounding like an order. You taught me.” His thumb moved over her ring. “I loved you before you knew me. I loved you when you came into my office with your three pages, and when you told me to eat, and when you renamed my dogs. I love you now, when you don’t need anything from me.” He touched her face. “I choose you. Every day. Even the boring ones.”

“Especially the boring ones,” said Elowen.

By the switch on the wall, Eliana looked at her watch. At exactly nine forty-one she turned the lights on, and the whole shop went gold, every beam and shelf and thread of green at once, and Elowen understood all at once what her sister had been doing for weeks without saying. The minute on the registry slip. The minute they’d begun.

Zhao kissed her under it, in front of everyone, long and slow, both hands on her face. Granny Yip clapped. Xiao Pan whistled through his fingers. Chen Si cheered like a schoolboy. Aurelia cried openly into a handkerchief. Lin Jian looked down at his hands and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cake was lemon, four tiers, covered in sugar camellias so fine you could see the light through the petals. Zhao ate two pieces. Elowen accused him of eating hers. Raiden danced with Jinx. Eliana went out to the back lane for ten minutes and came back wearing the leather jacket.
