Later, Elowen found her husband by the cooler, talking to Chen Si in a low voice. She waited till Chen Si had gone, then took Zhao by the tie and pulled him through the cooler door and shut it behind them.

The cold hit them both. The motor hummed. Buckets of spare roses on every shelf.

“You didn’t tell me you knew about Raiden.”

He blinked. “That’s what this is?”

“Two years, Zhendong.”

“He asked me not to.”

“I know.”

“It was his to tell.”

She looked up at him, and in the cold and the hum she thought of Evangeline at a kitchen table in July, turning a silver ring round and round her finger, telling her she’d married a man none of them had met and asking her to tell no one. Not even Zhendong. Elowen hadn’t. It was the first thing she’d ever kept from him. She thought about that for a while. Then she straightened his tie.

“I’m glad you kept it,” she said.

“You are?”

“He deserved to say it himself.” She tugged it again. “You still could have told me you knew.”

“You’d have asked questions.”

“Lots.”

“Are you going to punish me?”

“Perhaps,” said Elowen, and pulled him down by the tie and kissed him against the shelf of white roses until there was a knock on the steel and Aurelia’s voice said, “We need the bride and groom,” and then, after a pause, “I’m counting to a hundred.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight, when most of the guests had gone and the floor was petals and the glasses were everywhere, Lin Jian went over to the very tall man who was still standing by the ruins of the cake.

“I don’t think we’ve been introduced.”

“No, sir.”

“Your name?”

The man looked at Elara, across the room with a stack of plates. Then back at her father.

“Wang Xing Yue,” he said. “Her husband.”

Lin Jian looked at him. Then he looked at his second daughter, who had dropped a plate.

“Sunday,” he said. “One o’clock. Bring him.”

Elowen, under the arch with Zhao’s arms round her from behind, felt him start to laugh into her hair, and couldn’t stop laughing either.

chapters.title: Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: Five years on, it starts to rain over the Docks and he walks out of a meeting without his umbrella. He’s on her mat at closing time, and a girl outside is looking at the tulips in the window.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d pay that every night. Just to stand on that mat again.”
chapters.content:
Five years after the first rainy night, it rained again over the Iron Docks.

It started just before six, a Sunday, when the sky over the harbour went the colour of old pewter and the windows of Zhao’s office filled up with the reflections of the crane lights. The meeting had been going for two hours. Kan had been talking for most of them.

Kan had paid late for as long as anyone could remember and haggled over every invoice. Four winters ago Zhao had broken his nose for him at a university lecture wearing somebody else’s hoodie, and Kan had paid on time for exactly six months. Now he’d heard what the whole port had heard, that Zhao Zhendong was sick and tired and shutting things down, and he’d come in with flattery and a pen and the idea that a tired man might sign anything to make the noise stop.

“The original figure is unreasonable,” he said, and pushed the contract back across the desk for the third time. “We’ve worked together for years. Surely there’s room—“

Zhao put his hand on the paper. Kan stopped.

“You’ve negotiated against a number I gave you three times,” said Zhao. “You’re not looking for room. You’re trying to make me tired.”

“I’d never—“

“Everyone says you’ve gone soft,” said Kan, and smiled, and put his own hand on the desk next to Zhao’s as if they were friends. “Everyone. Retired to the garden. Carrying buckets for your wife. I’m only trying to help you while you—“

Zhao picked up Kan’s hand by the wrist, laid it flat on the desk, and bent the first two fingers back until they went.

It made a small dry sound, like snapping a pencil. Kan screamed. Zhao held the wrist down on the wood and waited until the scream had become breathing, and then he let go and pushed the contract back across with one finger.

“Sign the terms I gave you,” he said. “Leave the room. Don’t send me another proposal until you can read.”

Kan signed with his left hand. It took him a long time. Bao held the door.

“And Kan,” said Zhao. Kan stopped in the doorway, his hand clutched to his chest. “I’ve made my business smaller. I haven’t forgotten how to read a bad deal.”

When the door had shut, Chen Si, by the window with a coffee gone cold, said, “You used to let them talk longer.”

“I used to have more businesses.”

Chen Si looked at the clock. “You’re leaving.”

“Yes.”

“It’s raining.”

“I know.”

“Bao. Give him the umbrella.”

Bao held it out. Zhao shook his head and picked up his coat.

“Zhendong. You’ve got a car. You’ve got a driver.”

“I know.”

Chen Si stared at him. Then he looked at Bao. “Let him go. Apparently we’re not allowed to come between him and the weather.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked out past the car and down the Docks road in the rain with Bao twenty metres behind him carrying an umbrella nobody was under, looking more and more unhappy about it. He didn’t hurry. He knew the shop shut at seven. He knew she’d be on the accounts at half past six, then the cooler, then the front display, and that Xiao Pan would go first if the deliveries were done. He’d spent five years learning the shape of her days.

The rain went down his collar and through his shirt. By the time he got to the corner of Ferry Road it was sticking to him.

The sign on the door still said OPEN. He went in.

She was behind the counter with an invoice. She looked up and stared at him. Then she looked out of the window at the rain, and back at him.

“Where’s your umbrella?”

“Bao has it.”

“Why?”

“I didn’t need it.”

“You’re soaked.”

“I noticed.”

She went into the back without another word. There was a drawer, a rustle. She came back out and threw a towel at his head. He caught it.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. Dry your hair.”

He dried his hair, standing on the mat, dripping on it.

“Did you walk here? From the Docks? In that?”

“Yes.”

“Are you five years old?”

“No,” said Zhao. “It’s our anniversary.”

Her face changed. She looked at the clock over the door. Seven o’clock, exactly. Five years ago it had been a Monday. Then she came round the counter.

“Of course you remembered,” she said, and took the towel off him and did his hair herself, roughly, then more gently round his ears.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d finished, he reached inside his wet coat and took out a folded piece of card, soft at the creases and gone a little yellow.

She knew it before he’d unfolded it. RULES FOR THE FLORIST’S HUSBAND. Her own big careful capitals from the first May, when he’d taken to sitting in the shop all day and frightening people.

“Why have you still got that?”

“It was in my desk.”

“Next to the shipping contracts?”

“Next to the shipping contracts.” He turned it round. Under rule five, You are not allowed behind the counter, there was a line in black ink in his small hand that she’d never seen.

Unless she says so.

And under that, in newer ink:

She always says so.

She looked at it. “You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.”

“What are you doing here, Zhendong?”

“Buying flowers,” he said.

“All of them?”

“If possible.”

“Again?”

“Again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She made him wait while she counted. All of it. The tulips in buckets by the window, the roses in the front display, the chrysanthemums on the wall, the lilies, the delphiniums, the little bunches by the till and the slightly bent stems she’d put aside to go in the bin in the morning.

“Even the bent ones?”

“Especially those.”

“You’re not allowed to watch me while I count,” she said, halfway down the wall. “I lose my place.”

“Then I’ll count.”

“You’ll get it wrong. You once called a single bucket of eucalyptus twenty boxes.”

“That was different.”

She did the sum on the back of an invoice. She finished it this time; he didn’t stop her. Then she looked at the total, and at him, and turned the paper round so he could see.

“That’s what it would have been,” she said. “That night. If you’d let me get to the end.”

He looked at the figure. Four thousand two hundred. He’d paid her three times that without letting her get past the roses.

“I’d pay that every night,” he said. “Just to stand on that mat again.”

“You don’t have to pay to stand on my mat.”

“I know.”

“You live with me. You’ve got a key.”

“Fourteen of them.”

She laughed, and he paid her, and she wrapped the flowers in paper and stacked them on the counter until there wasn’t any counter left.

There was a little noise outside. A girl of seven or so was standing at the window with her nose almost on the glass, looking at the empty bucket where the tulips had been and the tulips now on the counter. Her mother stood behind her with an umbrella, looking at the rain.

Elowen opened the door. “Do you like those?”

The girl jumped. Then nodded. “My mama likes them.”

“I used to buy them,” said the mother, a little embarrassed. “Before. We’re only looking.”

“Come in out of the rain for a minute,” said Elowen, and they did, dripping on the mat. The girl looked at the tulips wrapped on the counter as if they were jewels in a case.

Elowen didn’t say anything. She just looked at her husband.

He picked up a bunch of the yellow tulips and held them out to the girl. “For your mother.”

“Oh, no, we can’t—“

“Please,” said Zhao, quite quietly, and the mother stopped arguing.

The girl held them against her chest with both arms. “Are they the same as the ones you used to bring home?”

“Almost,” said her mother, in a voice that wasn’t quite steady.

When they’d gone out under the umbrella, Elowen turned round.

“You gave away your flowers.”

“I bought them for you. They were yours.”

She took the front of his wet shirt in both fists and pulled him down and kissed him against the counter, hard, with the wrapped flowers sliding off it on both sides and the rain on the window. He put his hands on her waist and kissed her back.

“Happy anniversary,” she said against his mouth.

“Happy anniversary.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They loaded the van together. The rain had gone to mist. He stood by the driver’s door looking back at the shop.

“What are you thinking about?”

“Five years.”

“You stood on that mat,” said Elowen. “You frightened me. You sat in that chair like you owned it. You were very rude.”

“I was.”

“You kept looking at the flowers.”

“I was looking at you.”

“You were looking at the flowers.”

“I was trying not to look at you,” said Zhao, and took her hand and lifted it to his mouth. “I remember the delphinium.”

“The one that fell?”

He reached into his coat again and took out a small flat case and opened it. Under a clear cover lay a tiny blue floret, faded at the edges, its shape still there. The one off the delphiniums his men had carried out to the cars on the first night, that had fallen on the back seat beside him.

“You kept it.”

“In my wallet first. Then this.”

“For five years.”

“It was the first thing I took from your shop.”

“You didn’t take it. It fell.”

“I know,” he said, and closed the case and put it back where it lived.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she made him take everything off in the bathroom and stand there while she towelled him dry, his hair first, then his shoulders and his back, the long Block C scar low on his side and the newer, uglier one above it from the harbour. He tried once to say he could do it himself. She looked at him and he stopped.

“You’ll catch cold.”

“I won’t.”

“You walked through the rain like a child.”

“I wanted to see you.”

She stopped with the towel on his shoulders. Then she put it down and went up on her toes and kissed his ear, which was freezing. Then the other one.

“What’s that for?”

“Warming them.”

“With your mouth?”

“It works,” said Elowen, and kissed his jaw, and the corner of his mouth.

He caught her round the waist. “Can I?”

“Yes.”

He took his time. He always did when it mattered: he kissed her as if he had all night and intended to use it, until she was the one pulling at him. He undid her dress at the back with fingers that were still cold and made her gasp, and said sorry against her shoulder, and didn’t sound sorry at all. He walked her backwards to the bed. The rain started again on the window. She lay back and pulled him down by the wet hair and he came, and kissed her throat and her collarbone and the thin gold chain there, slowly, all the way down, until she said his name in the voice that meant now and he looked up at her from the dark with that lazy half-smile that had once frightened her half to death.

“Five years,” he said.

“Stop counting.”

“Never.”

He came into her slowly, and it was slow, and then it wasn’t. She wrapped her legs round him and held on to his shoulders and he held her face in his hands the whole time, looking at her, as if he were still standing on the mat at seven o’clock in the rain and couldn’t believe she’d let him in. Afterwards he lay with his head on her chest and his arm heavy across her, and she ran her fingers through his drying hair till his breathing went long.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, with the lights off, she heard the drawer.

She opened one eye. He was propped on his elbow with the black notebook and a pen.

“Zhendong.”

He stopped.

“What are you writing?”

“The date.”

“You know the date. You know the minute we married. You know the first night. You’ve got the flower in a case.”

“Yes.”

She held out her hand. After a moment he gave it to her. She turned on the lamp.

2 March. Five years since the first night.

She came home with me.

She smiled at that. Then her eye went up the page, to the entry before it, in the same neat hand, from earlier that day.

Kan. Two fingers. Signed.

She looked at the two lines, one above the other, in the same ink. He watched her read them and didn’t try to take the book back. He didn’t explain, either. It was his notebook, and he’d never once lied to her in it.

“You don’t have to write down every time I choose you,” she said at last.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He didn’t answer. She closed the notebook and put it in the drawer and shut the drawer, and turned the lamp off, and lay down against him in the dark with her hand flat on his chest.

“I’m here,” she said. “Tomorrow I’ll be here. And the day after.”

“Good,” said Zhao, into her hair.

Outside the rain went soft over the hill. In the courtyard the lemon tree stood in the wet with more lemons on it than anyone had counted in years. In the study the old house rules lay folded in their drawer. And in a small flat case beside his wallet, a blue floret from the first night had lasted five years.

He’d bought every flower in her shop once because he hadn’t known any other way to stay in the room.

Tomorrow he’d go to the shop again anyway. If she let him, he’d carry the buckets.

chapters.title: The Arms Dealer Tries to Arrange Flowers
chapters.desc: The florist has a fever on Mother’s Day, so her husband takes her forty-three orders. He measures every bow with a ruler, and then he gets to the one that says use your judgment.
chapters.content:
Mother’s Day was the busiest day of the year at the shop on Ferry Road, and it was the morning Zhao Zhendong found out a thermometer could be a weapon.

“Thirty-eight point nine.”

Elowen blinked at him from under the duvet. He looked at the thermometer again, as though it might give a more reasonable answer if he gave it a second chance.

“That’s not so bad,” she croaked.

“Thirty-eight point nine.”

“I heard you.”

“You’re not going to the shop.”

“There are forty-three orders, Zhendong. Some of them are complicated. Xiao Pan can’t do them on his own.”

“I’ve rung him.”

She tried to sit up. He put his hand on her shoulder and pressed her back down into the pillow, very gently and completely immovably.

“I’m the florist,” she said.

“Today I’m the florist.”

She looked at him. She looked at the thermometer. “You can’t arrange flowers.”

“I can follow instructions.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I’ll learn.” He pulled the duvet up to her chin, put a glass of water by the bed, and kissed her hot forehead. “Sleep. Forty-three. I’ve got them.”

He was gone before she could argue. She lay listening to the front door, and then reached for her phone.

Elowen: Don’t let him use the good scissors.

Xiao Pan: Too late, madam.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past eight he was behind the counter in her pale green apron with his sleeves rolled up, his hair combed, and a steel ruler beside the order book.

Xiao Pan stared at the ruler. “What’s that for?”

“Consistency.”

“Of the flowers?”

“The bows.”

He read the first order twice, chose the ribbon, measured eleven centimetres, cut it and tied it. The second bow: eleven centimetres. The third. By order seven Xiao Pan had stopped asking. By order twelve he’d started moving the ruler a little further away every time the boss looked down, and every time the boss found it without looking up and moved it back.

Order nineteen was the problem.

Roses, carnations and sweet peas, small, and a note in a careful old hand. For my mother. Please don’t make it too formal. She likes things that look as though they grew together. Use your judgement.

He read it twice. He laid the roses in a straight line. Then the carnations in a straight line behind them. Then the sweet peas. He stepped back.

It looked like a guard of honour.

Xiao Pan looked at it.

“What?” said Zhao.

“Nothing, boss.”

“It isn’t right.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

Xiao Pan hesitated, then decided that a man in an apron was probably less dangerous than usual. “It looks like a flower inspection.”

Zhao looked down at it. He didn’t argue. He took it apart and tried again, the roses in a tight block, the carnations in alternating rows round them, the sweet peas round the outside like a fence. It was worse. He took that apart too.

“Boss. Can I say something?”

“Say it.”

“Don’t arrange it like you’re trying to win.”

Zhao turned his head slowly.

Xiao Pan swallowed and kept going. “Madam says flowers should look like the person. She doesn’t do everything the same height. Some up, some down. She lets them fall where they want to go. She says you can tell when someone’s forced them.”

Zhao read the note again. Things that look as though they grew together.

He put the ruler in the drawer.

This time he didn’t measure anything. He let the roses lean. He tucked the carnations in low and let the sweet peas wander through the gaps, and one rose ended up facing almost sideways and he left it. He added green until it stopped looking like something he’d built and started looking like something that had happened.

Xiao Pan leaned over the counter. “Oh.”

“What?”

“That’s actually good.”

It wasn’t even and it wasn’t neat, and it was, infuriatingly, beautiful.

“Wrap it,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The woman came for order nineteen just before noon, in a pale blue blouse, with her bag clutched in front of her. When Xiao Pan brought it out she stopped.

“Is something wrong?” said Zhao.

She put out one finger and touched a sweet pea, and then the sideways rose beside it, and her eyes filled.

“My mother had a garden like this,” she said. “She never put anything in rows. She put whatever she liked next to whatever she liked. Roses and carnations and little things I never knew the names of.” She laughed, and wiped under one eye with the side of her finger. “She always said gardens weren’t meant to be tidy. This is exactly what it looked like. Exactly.”

“I’m glad,” said Zhao.

When she’d gone Xiao Pan gave him a very small, very triumphant nod.

“Next,” said Zhao.

“Eleven-centimetre bows?”

“Of course.”

By four all forty-three were done. No cards missing, no addresses wrong, and one ribbon a fraction short, which the boss had redone himself with the ruler. Xiao Pan took a photograph of the ruler lying beside a row of finished bouquets and sent it.

Xiao Pan: Your husband survived Mother’s Day.

Elowen: Has he eaten?

Xiao Pan looked over at the counter. The boss was checking the last delivery receipt against the book with his finger.

Xiao Pan: Define eaten.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was sitting up when he got home, in a clean nightdress with her hair tied back and the thermometer beside her water.

“Thirty-eight point one,” she said.

“Better.” He put his bag down and undid his watch. “Thirty-eight point one isn’t well.”

“How was the shop?”

“Fine.”

“Did you finish?”

“Yes.”

“Did you use the ruler?”

He went still with the watch in his hand. “Who told you?”

“Xiao Pan.”

“He talks too much.”

“Eleven centimetres? Every bow?”

“It was important.”

She started laughing, and the laugh turned into coughing, and he was across the room before it had finished, a hand on her back.

“Don’t laugh.”

“You measured every bow.”

“Consistency.”

She leaned on him, still smiling, her face hot against his shirt. “Did you do nineteen?”

He was quiet.

“Oh, no,” said Elowen.

“It was difficult. Xiao Pan helped.” He looked faintly offended. “He said I’d arranged it like a negotiation.”

She laughed so hard she had to hold her ribs. He caught her hand. “Enough.”

“Did you make it look like the person?”

“I think so. She cried.”

Elowen stopped laughing. She looked at him for a while. “Then you did it right.”

“I did one without measuring.”

“I’m proud of you,” she said, and meant it, and he looked at her as if she’d handed him something heavy, and then stood up.

“Congee.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He brought it up himself. Plain rice, a little ginger, spring onion chopped very fine. He sat on the edge of the bed and picked up the spoon.

“I can feed myself,” said Elowen.

“I know.”

He scooped up a little, and blew on it, and held it out.

She looked at him. Her mother used to do that, at the old kitchen table, when she’d had a temperature: blow across the spoon twice and hold it out and wait. A small thing. She’d thought she’d never see anyone do it for her again. She opened her mouth and ate. He waited till she’d swallowed before he got the next spoonful ready, and blew on that too.

Halfway down the bowl she noticed there was a pink petal stuck to his shirt. Then another, on his shoulder. Then a bit of fern by his collar and a damp patch on his sleeve where a bucket had been. She picked one off.

“What’s this?”

“Flowers.”

“You look like you’ve been attacked by a bouquet.”

“I survived,” said Zhao.

She took hold of the front of his petal-covered shirt with both hands and pulled. He just had time to put the bowl on the bedside table before she kissed him, hot-mouthed and feverish and not at all a thank-you, her fingers twisted in the cotton, until he made a sound and put his hand flat on her back and kissed her back properly.

“You’ll catch it,” she said, when she let him breathe.

“Then you’ll have to do forty-three orders and feed me congee.”

“Stop doing my orders.”

“Somebody had to,” he said, and kissed her again, more carefully, and then picked up the bowl and made her finish it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next year she woke up on Mother’s Day with a perfectly normal temperature. She took it twice. Thirty-six point seven.

He was already awake, lying on his side watching her.

“Good morning.”

“I’m ill,” said Elowen.

“No, you’re not.”

“I might be.”

“You’re not.” He got up and started dressing. She pulled the duvet over her head, and then pushed it down again to see where he was going.

“Where are you going?”

“The shop.”

“But I’m ill.”

“You’re thirty-six point seven.”

“Maybe the thermometer’s broken.”

He put his watch on. “Then I’ll buy a new one.” He leaned over and kissed her forehead. “Stay in bed.”

“Are you doing all the orders?”

“Forty-one.”

“Only forty-one?”

“I refused two. They wanted symmetrical.”

He went. She lay there for about a minute, and then picked up her phone.

Elowen: Don’t measure the bows.

The answer came almost before she’d sent it.

Zhendong: Eleven centimetres.

Then, a few hours later:

Zhendong: Someone ordered nineteen again. Same woman. Same note.

Elowen: Did you measure it?

Zhendong: No.

Elowen: What did it look like?

Zhendong: Like the person.

She put the phone face down on her chest and lay there smiling at the ceiling. Five years ago he’d bought every flower in her shop because he hadn’t known what else to do with the woman behind the counter. Now he knew how to put a few of them together, badly, in no kind of order, well enough to give a stranger back her mother’s garden.

chapters.title: The Delivery Boy Who Saw Too Much
chapters.desc: Xiao Pan has worked at Elowen’s for five years and would like it on the record that he never wanted to see any of it. A numbered list, the cooler not included, and the best tip he ever got.
chapters.epigraph: “For looking after her. Before I knew how.”
chapters.content:
Xiao Pan had worked at the flower shop on Ferry Road for five years, and in five years he had learned a great many things.

How to tell a rose by smelling it. How to wrap a bouquet in forty seconds. How to argue with a supplier at four in the morning and win. How to carry six buckets of eucalyptus without spilling one.

He’d also learned things he’d never asked to know.

On the night of the wedding, while the guests were still drinking and the bride and groom had disappeared somewhere in the back, he sat on an upturned crate behind the cooler with his notebook on his knee and wrote a heading.

THINGS I HAVE SEEN AT THIS SHOP THAT I WILL NEVER TELL ANYONE

1. Mr. Zhao once borrowed my FLOWER POWER hoodie to go to a physics lecture.

2. He gave it back washed and ironed with a note in the pocket.

3. He was jealous of the physics lecturer. The physics lecturer had not been in a room with Madam for eight years.

4. He is very bad at stripping roses. He had five plasters on at once.

5. He has threatened people while holding a bucket.

6. He knows exactly how many lemons are on the tree at home.

7. He can tell Madam’s footsteps from the back room.

8. He has never won an argument about the dogs’ names.

9. He can tie a bow now, but only if nobody’s watching.

10. He looks at Madam as if she’s the only person in the world.

Xiao Pan looked at number ten for a while. Then he crossed it out. Too soppy.

11. He once stood in the doorway for twenty minutes because Madam was talking to a customer and he didn’t want to interrupt.

12. He buys flowers from his own wife. At full price.

13. He has been told to come out from behind the counter more times than I have been paid overtime.

14. He listens when she says no.

He looked at the list. Then he put the pen down, because there were other things, and they weren’t funny.

✦ ✦ ✦

He remembered the glass.

The Wednesday it went in, all over the shop, and the little girl Mimi under the counter with her five sunflowers and her yellow ribbon, and her mother with blood on her cheek. He remembered kneeling in front of them to check their hands. He remembered somebody saying his back was full of glass, and not believing it, because he couldn’t feel it.

Forty-one pieces. That was what the doctor took out of his back, one at a time, while his mother sat in the corridor. He’d counted the little ping of each one in the metal dish. He didn’t tell anyone that either.

Mimi had sent him a drawing a week later. Five sunflowers tied with a yellow ribbon, and underneath, in big uneven letters, THANK YOU FOR KEEPING ME SAFE. He’d pinned it up by the till. She sent another the month after, and another, and she still sent them, two years on, every few weeks. He kept every one. The first was in his locker.

He remembered the three days in March this year when the boss was gone and Madam was behind a steel door and wouldn’t come out. He’d gone to the market at four every morning with Granny Yip, because he didn’t know what else to do. She’d shown him which bunches to buy and which men to walk past, and how to tell when a flower had sat in cold storage too long by pressing its head with your thumb. He’d counted every bunch. He’d checked every invoice twice. He’d kept the cooler full and the sign on the door and the lights on, so that nobody could say the shop had shut for good.

He didn’t write any of that down.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were things from before, too, that weren’t on any list.

The way the boss used to come in every morning and sit on the stool by the window while she worked. He never went behind the counter any more. He’d read something on his phone and look up every time Madam tucked her hair behind her ear.

One morning Xiao Pan had been coming out of the back with the mop when he noticed the boss had stopped sweeping. He was standing in the middle of the floor holding the broom. He was looking at his wife.

She was at the tulips, cutting stems, frowning at them. A bit of hair had come down over her cheek and she pushed it back with her wrist because her hands were wet and went back to the tulips.

The boss didn’t move. Xiao Pan waited. Quite a long time.

“Sir?”

The boss looked at him.

“The floor.”

The boss looked down at the broom as if he’d never seen one. “Right,” he said, and swept.

Xiao Pan had decided that day there were things a person shouldn’t have to see before breakfast.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was another thing.

Every morning, before he left for the Docks, the boss came to the counter for a kiss goodbye, and he always asked first.

“Can I?”

Sometimes Madam leaned over the counter at once. Sometimes she made him wait while she finished an order. Once she’d told him he could have one after he’d carried three buckets of water through to the back, and he’d carried them. Xiao Pan had seen it so many times he didn’t notice it any more.

Except once.

The first morning the shop opened again after the glass, three weeks on, when Xiao Pan’s back was still taped up under his shirt and there were new panes in the window that didn’t look right yet. Madam was behind the counter, still pale, with the strips on her neck where the cut was healing. The boss came up to her with his coat on.

He didn’t ask.

He bent down and kissed her forehead, and then her cheek, and then her mouth, very fast, as if he were checking each one was still there. Xiao Pan had never seen him look like that. Not angry. Frightened.

Madam put her hand on his face and said something too quiet to hear. The boss shut his eyes. Then he went out.

Xiao Pan went back to sweeping. He didn’t write that one down either.

✦ ✦ ✦

He remembered Jinx coming in one afternoon last year with a toolbox, putting it on his counter and saying, “I’m building your bike.”

“My what?”

“Your bike. Your old one’s falling apart.”

“I can fix it.”

“You’ve been saying that since spring.”

She’d already ordered the parts. A week later there was a red bike outside the shop with a new engine and a frame you could have hung a door on, and Xiao Pan had nearly cried. Then she’d put a helmet in his arms.

“Wear it.”

“I always wear one.”

“Wear this one. If I hear you’ve been on it without, I’ll come and take the bike back.”

He believed her. He still wore it.

He hadn’t known she was married to Madam’s brother until four o’clock this afternoon. He’d recognised her before anyone else did, and said so out loud, and had been thinking all evening about everything he’d said in front of her in the garage about Raiden Lin being useless.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hoodie had come back three months after the lecture, folded on the counter one morning, washed, ironed, smelling of somebody else’s expensive soap. In the front pocket there was a small envelope.

Thank you for lending me your hoodie. It was useful. Zhao Zhendong.

Xiao Pan had read it twice and looked over at the window where the boss was sitting with Madam. He’d thought about showing it round. He’d put it in his locker instead, next to Mimi’s first drawing. It was, as far as he was concerned, the strangest thank-you note anyone had ever been given.

“Xiao Pan?”

He jumped. Madam was standing over him in her ivory dress with two empty glasses.

“Are you writing something?”

“No.”

She looked at the notebook. He shut it.

“Nothing important.”

“Have you seen my husband?”

He pointed with his chin. “He went in the cooler for water.”

She smiled and went. Xiao Pan opened the notebook again.

15. Madam always knows where he is.

✦ ✦ ✦

A while later the boss came out of the cooler with a petal stuck to his collar and his tie crooked, and stopped by the crate.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Good.” He looked at the notebook. “What are you writing?”

“Nothing.”

“About tonight?”

“It’s a private list.”

The boss nodded and didn’t ask again. Then he said, “Thank you,” and Xiao Pan didn’t know what he meant.

“For what?”

The boss was looking across the shop at Madam, laughing with Aurelia at the counter in the gold light with her ring on.

“For looking after her,” he said. “Before I knew how.”

For once in his life Xiao Pan couldn’t think of anything clever.

“She’s good to work for,” he said in the end. “She treats everyone properly. She pays on time.”

“I know.”

“I just did my job.”

“Still,” said the boss. “Thank you.” And he went back across the room to her.

Xiao Pan watched him go. Madam looked up when he got there, and the boss said something, and she touched his sleeve, and he bent his head down to listen to whatever she said back. Xiao Pan looked down at his list.

16. Mr. Zhao is a much better husband than he is a florist.

He thought about it. Then he added, smaller: But he’s improving.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the night, when everyone had gone, he read it all through once more. The cooler wasn’t on it. Some things belonged to the people they’d happened to.

He locked the notebook in his locker with the note and the drawing, and picked up his helmet. Through the window Madam was behind the counter and the boss was helping her gather up the leftover flowers, a bucket in one hand, listening to her talk. She reached up and took a petal out of his hair. He smiled.

Five years, and he still wasn’t used to it.

He got on the red bike. Then he remembered the best tip he’d ever had in that shop. A Tuesday in the first winter, when he’d been fighting with a delivery list he couldn’t make come out right and the boss had stood next to him at the counter for a minute, watching, and then said quietly, “You’re doing well. She trusts you,” and gone back to his stool as if he’d said nothing at all.

Xiao Pan started the engine and rode home. Behind him, the lights in the shop went off.

chapters.title: Please Tell Your Wife to Stop
chapters.desc: Chen Si rings in the middle of the night because Aurelia has been pacing the living room in her silk robe for two hours. Elowen has bought the building next door, he gave Aurelia sapphires, and somehow he’s losing.
chapters.content:
At seven minutes past two in the morning, Zhao’s phone lit up on the bedside table.

Elowen was asleep against him with one hand on his chest. He reached for the phone carefully, meaning to turn it face down. Then he saw the name.

“What?” he said, very low.

There was a pause. Then Chen Si, in the voice of a man facing a problem that couldn’t be fixed with money, a gun or a lawyer: “Please tell your wife to stop.”

Zhao shut his eyes. “It’s two in the morning.”

“I know what time it is. I’ve been awake since midnight.”

“Why?”

“Aurelia.” A breath. “She’s been walking up and down the living room in her silk dressing gown for two hours. She’s been past me so many times I’ve started counting and then stopped counting because it was frightening me. She bought the workshop in Milan.”

“What workshop?”

“The one she’s wanted for three years. The building, the benches, the studio next door. She’s expanding.”

“That’s good.”

“It’s not good. It’s a symptom.” Chen Si lowered his voice, as if Aurelia might hear him from the other room, which she almost certainly could. “Your wife bought the building next to her shop.”

Zhao looked down at the top of Elowen’s head. “Yes.”

“With her own money.”

“Yes.”

“I said I was proud of her. I said it to Aurelia. Aurelia said, and I’m quoting, ’Elowen bought a building. I bought a workshop.’ And she said it wearing the sapphires.”

“What sapphires?”

“The ones I gave her last week. A set. Rare stones. I had the setting made in Geneva. She said they were beautiful and kissed me and put them on the dressing table and went back to walking.”

Zhao thought about Aurelia Chen in silk at two in the morning, wearing a fortune round her neck and walking off something she couldn’t name. He almost smiled.

“Ah,” he said.

“Don’t ah me.”

“She doesn’t want a present.”

“She’s got everything.”

“No, she hasn’t,” said Zhao. “She wants to win something. You keep giving her things she can’t have won.”

A long silence down the line.

“I hate it when you’re right,” said Chen Si.

“Ask her what she wants.”

“I did. She said she wants to know how Elowen can buy a building and make it look like an ordinary Tuesday.” Another silence. “She also asked if I think the Milan workshop’s too small.”

“Is it?”

“Zhendong. It’s enormous.”

“Then I don’t see the problem.”

“I’m hanging up.”

“Good night.”

“Tell your wife to stop,” said Chen Si, and did.

Elowen moved against him. “Who was that?”

“Chen Si.”

“At two?”

“Aurelia’s pacing. She bought a workshop in Milan.”

Elowen opened one eye, and smiled into his shoulder. “Oh, good. She told me yesterday.”

“You knew? You didn’t tell me?”

“You were busy.”

“With what?”

“Being my husband,” said Elowen, and went back to sleep with her hand on his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

By breakfast there were three messages.

Chen Si: [a photograph of a set of sapphires on a dressing table, very blue, very alone]

Chen Si: [a photograph of a purchase agreement, in Italian, with a great many stamps]

Chen Si: She wants to know if your wife’s buying another building.

Elowen was at the other end of the table, reading supplier quotes on her tablet with toast in one hand and her tea in the other.

“Did you buy the building next door?”

“Yes.”

“With your own money?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“The owner wanted to sell, and the shop needs room.” She didn’t look up. “Storage first. Then maybe a workroom, so I can do the big hotel jobs without blocking the front.”

“That makes sense.”

“I thought so.” She turned a page. “Aurelia thinks I’m competing with her, doesn’t she.”

“Chen Si thinks so.”

“I’m not competing with Aurelia. I needed a building.” A pause. “The Milan workshop does sound lovely.”

He looked at her over his tea. “Elowen.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came up to the house that afternoon on his own, with two coffees and the face of a man entered in a race he hadn’t signed up for. He put one on Zhao’s desk in the study and sat down.

“I need advice.”

“About Aurelia.”

“Unfortunately.” He took the lid off his cup and looked into it. “I gave her the sapphires. She said thank you and put them away. Then she found the photograph Elowen sent her of that camellia on the mountain, the red one, and sat looking at it for twenty minutes.”

“It’s a better present.”

Chen Si stared at him. “It’s a photograph.”

“You gave her stones. I took Elowen to see a flower she’d wanted to see since her mother told her about it. I didn’t even let her pick it.” Zhao drank his coffee. “Aurelia can buy her own stones.”

Chen Si was quiet for some time. Then he said, “She doesn’t need me to buy her anything. She needs me to know what she wants before she has to say it. And she wants to be able to surprise me back.” He put the cup down. “She wants to win something.”

“I said that last night.”

“I know. It’s still true.” He looked out of the window, at the courtyard, at the lemon tree, at the two dogs asleep in the sun on the gravel. Then he smiled, slowly, in a way he didn’t often.

“You know what I was thinking about at three this morning? You, in Block C. The first week. You were fifteen and you had no front tooth, because the cook had caught you taking a second bun and hit you in the mouth with the ladle.”

“I didn’t take it.”

“You took it.”

“I was hungry.”

“I know you were.” Chen Si turned the cup on the desk. “You used to act as if you didn’t need anything. Food. A coat. Somewhere to sleep. You’d rather bleed than ask.” He looked round the study: the plans on the desk, her pencil in his pen pot, the photograph of the dogs that Elowen had framed and he hadn’t taken down. “And look at you. A wife who buys buildings. Two ridiculous dogs. A house full of flowers.”

“The dogs aren’t ridiculous.”

“They’re called Dumpling and Noodle.”

“They’re good dogs.”

Chen Si laughed. Then he stopped laughing and looked at him properly. “I’m proud of you, Zhendong. Not for the money. For this. For having something you don’t have to defend every minute of the day.”

Zhao didn’t say anything for a moment. Chen Si didn’t say things like that. He hadn’t said one since the room above the repair shop, with the window that wouldn’t shut.

“Thank you,” said Zhao.

“Now tell your wife to stop buying buildings.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“It’s her money.”

Chen Si laughed helplessly. “I’m losing.”

The door opened. Elowen came in with a folder under her arm.

“Chen Si. I heard about Milan. It’s wonderful.”

“She thinks you’re competing.”

“I’m not.” Elowen thought about it. Then she opened the folder and put it on the desk. “I bought the building on the other side as well.”

Silence.

Zhao looked down at it. Chen Si turned his head, very slowly.

“The other side,” he said.

“The owner wanted to sell too. It’s in Raiden’s name. He’s going to draw the renovation and run the builders for me. He says the back wall’s rotten and he’s delighted.”

“When?”

“Last week.”

Chen Si stood up. “I have to go.”

“Tell Aurelia I think the workshop’s lovely,” said Elowen.

“I will.” At the door he turned round. “Please don’t buy a third one.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

Chen Si looked at Zhao. “She’s lying.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she got into bed beside him and put her chin on his shoulder.

“Is Aurelia still upset?”

“I don’t think upset’s the word.”

“What is?”

“Competitive.”

She smiled. “I like Aurelia. She works harder than anyone I know. She should have the workshop. And the sapphires are beautiful.”

“I agree.”

“Are you worried? About the buildings?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“It’s your money.”

“Good answer,” said Elowen.

He put his book down and looked at her. “You talk in your sleep.”

“I do not.”

“You said the price of lilies had gone up twice. Last night. Quite crossly.”

She covered her face. “Oh no.”

“And you say my name.”

She looked at him between her fingers.

“Every night,” said Zhao. “Sometimes you tell me to move the buckets. Sometimes you say the roses are too short. Sometimes it’s just Zhendong. Last night you said it twice.”

“What did I say after it?”

“Nothing. Just that. Twice.” He pushed her hair back. “I like hearing it.”

She looked at him for a long moment. Then she climbed over him, a knee either side, took both his wrists and pressed them down into the pillow above his head. He let her. He was smiling.

“Don’t move.”

“Is that an order?”

“Yes.”

She kissed him slowly, very pleased with herself, and then again, and again, until his breath went uneven and he turned his hands over under hers but didn’t pull them free.

“You’re very easy to manage,” she said.

“Only by you.”

“Good.”

“Can I?” he said against her mouth, and she let go of his wrists, and he could.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Chen Si got a photograph. Aurelia, in the Milan workshop’s courtyard under a grey sky, with the sapphires on, smiling like a cat with a canary.

Aurelia: These are lucky. I went to see the port deputy director about the equipment he’s been sitting on for six weeks. He’s released it.

Chen Si rang Zhao while he was making tea.

“Your wife’s done something.”

“What?”

“Mine went into the port deputy director’s office this morning, smiled, and explained exactly why he was holding a shipment that had already cleared inspection. She knew the regulations better than he did. He signed it in front of her.” A pause. “She wore the sapphires. She says they’re lucky now. She’s going to wear them every time she negotiates.”

“Let her.”

“I will. I bought them.” A pause. “Thank you for last night. For reminding me she doesn’t need another present. She needs me to pay attention.”

Zhao looked through the door into the potting room. Elowen was at the bench with Raiden, both of them bent over a set of drawings, arguing about a wall.

“She already knows what she wants,” he said. “You just have to listen.”

“That’s rich, from a man who bought a whole flower shop instead of saying good evening.”

“It worked,” said Zhao.

“For you.”

“Yes.”

“And tell Elowen not to buy the building across the street.”

Zhao looked at his wife. She looked up, and caught him looking, and smiled, and went back to the drawings.

“I’ll ask,” he said.

“That’s not a promise.”

“No,” said Zhao, and hung up, and went to find out what she was planning to do with the wall.

chapters.title: Anniversary Math
chapters.desc: She goes looking for a pen and finds two notebooks in his drawer: every date since the night it rained, and a number in the corner of every page.
chapters.epigraph: “I thought I could at least keep the dates.”
chapters.content:
On the morning of Friday the twenty-second of March, Bao came into the shop at ten o’clock carrying a paper bag, and put it on the counter.

“From the boss.”

Elowen looked inside. Six egg tarts from the bakery on Ferry Road, still warm, the custard trembling.

“Did he say why?”

“No, madam.”

“Did he say when I’m meant to eat them?”

“No, madam.”

“Did he tell you to make sure I eat all six?”

Bao looked at a point above her head. “He said to make sure you got them before Xiao Pan did.”

From the back room Xiao Pan shouted, “I heard that.”

She offered Bao one. He refused politely and left, and she stood at the counter eating hers and looking at the calendar on the wall, and of course she knew. Four years. A steel room at the end of a corridor, and a man who’d asked first.

Elowen: Thank you for breakfast.

Zhendong: You’re welcome.

Elowen: Why six?

Zhendong: You like them.

Elowen: That isn’t an answer.

Zhendong: Happy anniversary.

She smiled at the phone.

Elowen: I love you.

Zhendong: I know.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch she rang Aurelia.

“Is it about your husband?”

“Yes.”

“Then I need a coffee first.” A pause, a cup set down. “Go.”

“Does Chen Si keep track of anniversaries?”

Silence. “Of what?”

“Dates. Things that happened.”

“Elowen. Are you telling me Zhao Zhendong remembers anniversaries?”

“I think so.”

Aurelia made a small, deeply offended sound. “That’s outrageous. Chen Si remembers the date he bought his first warehouse. He remembers the registration number of a ship he sold years ago. He remembers to the last coin what he lost in a negotiation in Rotterdam. I asked him last month when our first dinner was, and he said a Thursday.”

“Was it?”

“It was a Friday.” Aurelia sighed. “Why are you asking?”

“I was looking for a pen.”

“That sounds unrelated.”

“I think he’s been keeping notebooks.”

“Oh, I want to see those.”

“You can’t. They’re private.”

“I’ve been married to Chen Si long enough to know that a man who keeps private notebooks is either sentimental or dangerous.”

“Zhendong is both.”

“Then definitely show me,” said Aurelia, and Elowen hung up on her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found them that evening. She’d only gone into the bedroom for a pen to write a supplier’s note, and his drawer was open an inch.

His watch. A spare key. A folded handkerchief. Two plain black notebooks.

She’d seen him write in one of them at the desk late at night, more than once, and never asked. She opened it now at the front, and sat down slowly on the edge of the bed.

2 March. Rain. Seven o’clock. She was behind the counter. Roses, cutting on the angle. Blue delphinium in the bucket by the door. She asked me where her father was.

3 March. She poured tea for the man I sent to watch her.

5 March. Northgate. She brought the shipping records. She hadn’t had breakfast.

14 March. She asked me to marry her.

17 March. 9:41. She looked at the ring a long time. I thought she might change her mind.

21 March. She moved in. She brought her mother’s lemon tree. She named the dogs Dumpling and Noodle. In the corridor she said Zhendong.

22 March. 00:20. I asked. She said yes.

She read that one three times. She’d thought it was the Saturday. She’d never looked at a clock. He had.

The entries went on, a line or two each, sometimes only a word. What she’d worn. What she’d said. Which flowers she’d bought at the market and whether she’d eaten. The first time she’d fallen asleep in the car. The night she’d told him about Miles. The first morning she’d missed the market. Things she’d forgotten herself completely.

Then the mountain.

19 September. Wen estate. Rain. She said she was happy.

I’m happy.

And underneath, in the same neat hand, no crossing out, nothing pressed hard into the paper:

She did not say the other word.

There was a small number in the corner of the page. She didn’t know what it was counting. She turned over.

20 September. Road still under water. She fell asleep on my shoulder by the fire. I didn’t ask her for anything.

She sat very still on the edge of the bed. She’d known he loved her before he ever said it. She’d known he held back, sometimes, because he was afraid of asking for something she wasn’t ready to give. She hadn’t known he’d been writing down every time she came closer, and every time she didn’t come all the way. Not to hold it against her. Just so he’d have it.

Then she opened the second notebook.

It was thinner, and it had a title on the first page, in capitals.

THINGS SHE HAS SAID

I want you to stay.

I chose you.

I’m glad you’re home.

And then, from a Monday in April last year, in the shop, in the rain, on its own line: I love you.

And then again. And again. Pages of it. Each one with a date, and sometimes a word beside it. Before sleep. At the shop. In the car. While making tea. On the stairs, laughing.

The last page had a number at the top, underlined twice.

1,209.

She counted the entries on that page, because she couldn’t help it. The number was right. Of course it was right.

The door opened.

He stopped in it. He saw the notebooks open on the bed, both of them, and her with them. For a moment neither of them said anything. Then he came in and shut the door.

“You found them.”

“You counted.”

“Yes.”

“Every time?”

“Yes.”

“One thousand two hundred and nine.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He took off his watch and put it on the bedside table, and sat down beside her, and looked at his hands.

“I like knowing,” he said.

“Knowing what?”

“That you said it.” He was quiet. “When I started the first one I didn’t think you’d stay. You’d married me for your reasons, and I knew what they were, and I didn’t expect anything past the agreement. I thought I could at least keep the dates. They’d be mine.”

She put her hand over his.

“Then you stayed,” said Zhao. “And then you started saying it.”

“You don’t need proof.”

“I know.”

“You know I love you.”

“Yes.”

“Then you can stop counting.”

He considered it, honestly, the way he considered everything. “I could.”

“But you won’t.”

“No.”

She laughed, a bit wetly, and leaned over and kissed his cheek. “One.”

He turned his head. “What?”

“I love you. Two.”

His eyes went to the notebook. His hand went to the pen. She caught his wrist.

“Wait. I love you. Three.” She kissed the corner of his mouth. “Four.” His other cheek. “Five.” She put her forehead against his. “Six.”

He was smiling now, helplessly.

She kissed him properly. “Seven.”

This time she let him. He wrote the date, and seven lines under it, and then turned to the top of the page and crossed out the number and wrote the new one beside it.

1,216.

“Happy?” she said.

“Yes.”

She put her hand on his cheek. “Say yes.”

“To what?”

“To me.”

He knew what she meant. He’d said it with a fever, in this bed, with a drip in his hand. He’d still say yes. He lifted his hand to her face.

“Yes.”

She took his face in both hands and kissed him first.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later the notebooks were back in the drawer and the lamp was still on. She stood in front of him by the bed and he took his time.

He was a man who’d spent years learning that nothing he loved would stay if he grabbed at it, and he touched her now as if he’d learned it all the way down. He kissed her forehead before he took the pins out of her hair. He let her hair down a piece at a time, and combed it out over her shoulders with his fingers, and only then went to the first button at her throat. He undid them slowly, looking at her face between each one, as if every one were a question and he was waiting for the answer. She gave it to him every time. When the dress slid off her shoulders he didn’t look down at it; he looked at her, for long enough that she felt it on her skin like heat off a stove.

“The lamp,” she said.

“Leave it.”

“Leave it,” she agreed. She wanted to see him.

She pulled his shirt out of his trousers and undid it herself, faster than he’d done hers, and he laughed under his breath at the difference and let her. She put her mouth on the old burn on his shoulder and the long scar low on his side and the newer one above it, and felt him go still under her hands, and kept going. He drew her down onto the bed with him. He kissed her the way he’d kissed her that first night in the steel room, carefully at first, as if he were testing ice, until she took hold of him and he stopped being careful at all.

When he moved into her it went slowly. He wouldn’t let it go any other way, deep and unhurried, her legs wrapped round him. Every time she pulled at him he slowed down, until she was saying his name as if it were the only word she had, and he was saying hers back against her throat, against her breast, into her hair, the lamp throwing their shadows huge and joined across the ceiling. She held on to his shoulders. He held her eyes. At the end he wouldn’t look away even then.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest and his hand moving up and down her back.

“Zhendong. What happened on the twenty-second of March?”

“Twenty past twelve.”

“Before that.”

“You said Zhendong in the corridor.”

“And?”

“You named my dogs.”

“You hated the names.”

“I accepted the names.”

“After looking at me as if I’d ruined your life.”

He smiled at the ceiling.

“I’m glad you kept the dates,” she said.

“I’m glad you found them.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she lifted her head.

“One thousand two hundred and sixteen.”

“Yes.”

“That’s a lot.”

“It’s not enough.”

“I love you,” said Elowen.

He shut his eyes. “Seventeen,” he said, very quietly, and reached towards the drawer, and she caught his hand and put it back on her back where it had been.

“Tomorrow. Write it tomorrow.”

He thought about it. Then he put his other arm round her.

“Tomorrow,” said Zhao, and for once he let a number wait. She fell asleep with her hand over his heart, and he stayed awake a little longer, not counting anything at all.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Ago, Block C
chapters.desc: January, fifteen years ago. A riot in Block C, a sharpened bed slat, and Chen Si dragging him half a kilometre through the drains into the snow. Then his wife finds him awake at two.
chapters.content:
Zhao Zhendong was fifteen the winter he met Chen Si, in the laundry under Block C, where the pipes sweated and the machines shook so hard the guards shouted at them to shut up.

He was sitting on an upturned bucket trying to sew the cuff back on his only shirt with a needle he’d stolen from the mending basket. He had a split lip and a gap where his front tooth had been until Tuesday, when the cook had caught him taking a second bun and hit him in the mouth with the ladle. He couldn’t read the labels on the detergent drums. He couldn’t read much.

A new boy came in with an armful of wet sheets. Thin. A bruise along his jaw. The look of someone who’d already decided he hated the place and intended to be polite about it.

“What’s your name?”

Zhao didn’t answer.

The boy dumped the sheets. “I’m Chen Si.”

Nothing.

“Do you talk?”

“When I need to.”

Chen Si thought about that. “Good. Neither do I.” He sat on the other bucket. For a while they listened to the machines. Then he looked at the needle. “Your stitching’s terrible.”

“Can you do it?”

“Yes.”

“Then do it.”

Chen Si laughed. It was the first time Zhao had heard anyone laugh in Block C who didn’t sound frightened.

✦ ✦ ✦

A guard had left a book on a windowsill, a fat paperback about a war, with the cover gone. Chen Si read it after lights-out under his blanket with a stolen torch. Zhao watched the light move on the ceiling for three nights.

“Is it good?”

“Not really.”

“Then why read it?”

“It’s the only book in here.” Chen Si lowered it. “Can you read?”

Zhao turned over. That was answer enough.

“Come here,” said Chen Si.

“Why?”

“I’ll read it out.”

“I didn’t ask.”

“I know you didn’t.”

After the war book there was a book of stories with half the pages stuck together. Then, from somewhere, the Monkey King. Chen Si liked the Monkey King best.

“He’s always in trouble.”

“Sounds stupid.”

“He’s clever.”

“Sounds stupid and clever.”

“Exactly,” said Chen Si, and kept reading.

He’d stop and ask what Zhao thought would happen next, and Zhao always guessed the worst thing possible, and Chen Si always said he’d ruined it. One boy read and the other listened, and for an hour every night Block C was somewhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

A guard told Chen Si about his mother on a Tuesday. He came back from the office and sat on the floor by the bunk and looked at his hands. He didn’t cry.

“What?” said Zhao.

“Nothing.”

“Si.”

“My mother died.”

Zhao had never met her. He knew she wrote, sometimes, and that Chen Si kept the letters folded flat under his mattress. He knew she’d been ill and Chen Si had been waiting for a visit. He didn’t know what you said.

He looked at his own bread. Then he pushed it across the floor.

“I’m not hungry.”

“Then keep it.”

After a while Chen Si picked it up. He broke it in two and gave half back, and they ate it without saying anything. He didn’t read that night. Zhao stayed awake beside him till the lights came on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The riot started at the end of January, over cigarettes. Somebody had stolen some, somebody else got blamed, a guard shouted, a boy threw a tin bowl. Then the whole corridor was noise.

Gao had been waiting for an excuse for weeks. He was seventeen and twice the size of Chen Si, and Chen Si had corrected his arithmetic in front of three other boys and then, worse, been right. Zhao was halfway down the stairs when he saw Gao come through the crowd with his sleeve held stiff against his side and his eyes on the back of Chen Si’s neck.

The slat was out of the sleeve before Zhao reached them, a length of bed board sharpened on the floor for a fortnight. Gao drove it at Chen Si’s back. Zhao got between them, and it went into his own side instead, low, under the ribs.

For a second he didn’t feel anything. Then he did.

He got Gao’s wrist and broke it against the wall. He hit him until the slat came out of Gao’s hand, and kicked it away down the stairs, and hit him again, and again, and Gao went down on the landing and didn’t get up. Zhao could hear people shouting a long way off. He could feel his shirt getting heavy.

“Zhendong!”

Chen Si had him by the arm. “You’re bleeding.”

“I noticed.”

“Come on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They got as far as the service corridor before his legs went. Chen Si caught him. At the far end there was a drain cover nobody had lifted in years, and Chen Si got his fingers under it and heaved it aside and said, “Go.”

“You first.”

“Don’t argue with me.”

“You’re smaller.”

“Zhendong.”

Something in his voice made Zhao do it. Chen Si went in first and reached back and dragged him through by the collar.

It was cold and black and running with water, filthy, barely high enough to crawl. Every time Chen Si pulled him forward the wound tore. Zhao tried not to make a sound. Chen Si talked.

“Remember the Monkey King?”

“Unfortunately.”

“He got trapped under a mountain.”

“Because he was stupid.”

“Because the Buddha tricked him.”

“Same thing.”

“That’s not how it goes,” said Chen Si, and his voice was shaking, and he told it properly, in pieces, stopping when the drain got narrower, going back over the parts Zhao had blacked out for. The mountain. The five hundred years. The monk who let him out.

Somewhere behind them, in the black, something splashed.

Chen Si stopped. They both heard it. Breathing, wet and ragged. A boy’s voice, swearing, thick with blood. Gao had followed them into the drain.

He came out of the dark on his knees with his broken wrist held against his chest and the slat in his good hand, and he didn’t go for Zhao, who was lying in the water. He went for Chen Si.

Chen Si didn’t run. Zhao saw it in the bit of light from the grate far ahead: Chen Si’s face going completely still, the way it would go still across boardroom tables for the rest of his life. He let Gao come. He caught the slat arm under his own and turned with it, and they went down together into the channel where the water ran deepest, and Chen Si got on top.

He put both hands on the back of Gao’s head and held it under.

Gao fought. He was bigger and he fought for a long time, his good hand clawing at Chen Si’s face, his legs thrashing in the black water so it went over both of them. Chen Si didn’t let go. He knelt on Gao’s back with his whole weight and his arms locked straight and his eyes open, and he held him down, and held him, and held him, until the thrashing turned to twitching and the twitching stopped and the water went quiet round them both and ran on.

Then he held him a little longer, to be sure.

When he let go, Gao didn’t move. Chen Si crawled back to Zhao on his hands and knees and took hold of his collar again.

“Where were we,” he said. “The monk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The grate at the end was frozen into its frame. Chen Si shoved it and it didn’t move. A steam pipe ran down the wall beside it, so hot the water hissed where it dripped on it. He braced his forearm against the pipe for leverage and pushed, and the grate gave an inch, and he pushed again with his arm still on the pipe and his teeth together, and the whole thing went and they fell out into the snow.

Chen Si rolled onto his back and lay there. His sleeve was burned through. Under it the skin had gone white and shiny.

“Your arm.”

“It’s nothing.”

“It’s burned.”

“It’s the road,” said Chen Si, which made no sense, and which he would go on saying for the next fifteen years to anyone who asked, including his wife.

He got up. He got Zhao up. He dragged him half a kilometre through the back streets in the snow, not fast, not well, but without once stopping, to a red door with a sign that had lost half its letters, where a doctor lived who didn’t ask questions of people who could pay him. He looked at the two boys on his step and said, “No.”

Chen Si took a small gold pendant out of his pocket. His mother’s. He held it out.

The doctor looked at it, and at the blood in the snow, and stood aside.

He cleaned the wound and dug out the bits of slat. Chen Si held Zhao’s hands down on the table while he did it.

“Names?”

“Fong,” said Chen Si at once.

“Both?”

“Both.”

Zhao didn’t correct him.

Afterwards Chen Si sat on the floor with his arm wrapped in gauze, and Zhao looked at him from the table.

“Your pendant.”

“It’s gone.”

“Your mother—“

“Don’t,” said Chen Si.

Two days later they found a room over a bicycle-repair shop with a mattress and a kettle and a window that wouldn’t shut. Chen Si brought bread. Zhao brought two cups. That night Chen Si took out a small knife and cut the heel of his own palm and held the knife out, handle first. Zhao took it and did the same.

“If one of us has somewhere to go,” said Chen Si, “so does the other.”

“If one of us is hungry.”

“We share.”

“If one’s in trouble.”

“The other comes.”

“If one of us dies.”

“Don’t,” said Chen Si.

“Then don’t leave.”

“I won’t.”

They pressed their hands together till the blood ran down both wrists. Fifteen and sixteen, with nobody left to claim them and nobody waiting anywhere. So they did it themselves.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fifteen years later, in January, Zhao woke at two in the morning and didn’t know why.

The room was dark apart from the courtyard light round the edge of the curtain. The old scar under his ribs ached the way it did in the cold. He lay and looked at the ceiling.

“Zhendong?”

Elowen was awake, her hair loose over her shoulder.

“Nothing.”

“You’re awake. It’s two.”

“Block C,” he said, before he’d decided to.

She shifted onto her side. “Tell me.”

So he told her, in the dark. The laundry. The tooth. The war book and the Monkey King. The bread. The slat that had been meant for someone else. The drain. When he got to the steam pipe, her fingers stopped on his cheek.

“He’s never told me that.”

“He says it was the road.”

“And the boy in the drain?”

He was quiet. She waited.

“Si held him under,” said Zhao. “Till he stopped. I watched.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “Can I see?”

He pushed the sheet down. The scar ran under his ribs, pale and ragged where a back-room doctor had done his best with a sewing needle. She traced it with one finger. Then she bent her head and kissed it. Once, and again just below it, and again along the length of it, slowly, all the way to the end.

“It doesn’t hurt,” he said.

“I know.”

“It’s old.”

“I know.” She kissed it again. “Does it hurt when you remember?”

“Sometimes.”

She came back up the line of his ribs with her mouth, to his chest, his throat. He caught her hand. “Elowen.”

“What?”

“Thank you. For listening.”

“You listened to me first,” she said, and kissed him, slow, and then not slow, and pushed her fingers into his hair and pulled him down to her by it, hard enough that he laughed against her mouth.

“Careful. You’ll wake the dogs.”

“Let them complain,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards his phone lit up on the table.

Chen Si: Awake?

Zhao: Yes.

Chen Si: Old days?

Zhao looked at Elowen. She was watching him, her chin on his chest.

Zhao: Block C.

A long pause.

Chen Si: The Monkey King got out.

Zhao: Barely.

Chen Si: He had a good brother.

Zhao looked at that for a while before he answered.

Zhao: He did.

Chen Si: Go back to sleep. Your wife will kill you if you’re useless tomorrow.

He put the phone down. Elowen tucked herself against him, and he turned off the lamp, and felt her hand settle over the old scar in the dark and stay there.

chapters.title: The Ring Was Too Heavy
chapters.desc: Three weeks before the real wedding her ring vanishes from the dish by the till, and Bao is a terrible liar. Then she reads the inside.
chapters.content:
The ring disappeared on a Monday, three weeks before the wedding.

Elowen noticed just after lunch, when she reached for the little ceramic dish by the till and found it empty. She looked under the receipts. Beside the card machine. In the drawer. On the floor.

“Xiao Pan. Have you seen my ring?”

He came out of the back with a bucket, and his face did something very small.

“Which ring?”

“My wedding ring.”

“Oh,” said Xiao Pan. “No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.” He looked at the window. Then the door. Then back at her.

“Why are you looking at the door?”

“Because it’s there,” said Xiao Pan, and took his bucket into the cooler and didn’t come out.

She’d taken it off that morning to do the big hotel arrangement. She’d been taking it off a lot since spring. It had fitted perfectly for three years, and then after the shipyard, after three days of not eating behind a steel door and a month of sitting up at night with a drip on a coat hook, it had started to turn on her finger. The heavy gold, the little square green stone. It slid round so the stone was underneath. It caught on stems. So she’d been taking it off for wet work and putting it in the dish, and this morning she’d put it in the dish. She was certain.

She rang Zhao.

“What’s wrong?”

“My ring’s gone.”

A pause. “Which one?”

“Zhendong. I’ve only got one.”

“I’ll come.”

“Don’t—“

“I’ll come,” he said, and hung up.

He was there in twelve minutes. He checked the dish, the counter, the drawer and the floor under the till, and asked when she’d last seen it and who’d been in and whether anyone had touched the dish.

“It’s a ring,” said Elowen. “Not a missing person.”

“I know.”

“You look as if you’re about to close the harbour.”

“Who’s been in?”

“Xiao Pan. Two suppliers. Granny Yip, for ten minutes.”

He nodded and looked towards the back. “Bao. The shop cameras. From this morning.”

“Don’t frighten anyone.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re using the voice.”

“What voice?”

“The one that makes people confess to things they haven’t done.”

He considered that. Then he turned to Bao, who was standing in the doorway trying to look like furniture. “Please check the cameras.”

Bao looked enormously relieved. “Yes, sir.”

Zhao took her hand. His thumb went over the bare place on her finger, where the skin was paler.

“I’ll find it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came in the afternoon with a folder of sketches. Elowen had rung to ask if she’d seen the ring at the dress fitting.

“You think I stole it?”

“I didn’t say that.”

“You rang me up and asked me if I’d seen it.”

“Yes.”

“That’s an accusation, darling, in any language.” Aurelia put her folder on the counter. “And if I were going to steal something, I wouldn’t steal something that ugly.”

“It’s my wedding ring.”

“I know. That’s why I’m being polite.” She opened the folder. “I brought these. For the wedding. In case.”

A narrow gold band. A little flower setting. A pair of earrings with tiny green stones to go with the ones she already had. They were beautiful, and Elowen said so.

“Of course they are.” Aurelia looked at her bare hand. “Has he seen your finger?”

“He knows.”

“Then he’s already got a jeweller out of bed somewhere.” She shut the folder. “I’ve been married to Chen Si for four years. I know what men do when they go sentimental and have money.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she went to bed without it.

He’d been in the study with the camera footage most of the evening. “Nothing?”

“Not yet.”

“It’s all right.”

“It’s not,” he said, and turned the lamp off.

Since the armory she’d slept holding a pillow against her chest. She’d never said why, and he’d never asked. She did it now, without thinking, and was asleep almost at once.

He lay awake. After a while she moved. The pillow went, pushed off onto the floor, and her hand came across the bed, found his shirt and closed on it. Her fingers twisted into the cotton and held.

He went very still and looked down at her. She was asleep. He didn’t move. He lay there for a long time with her fist in his shirt, until his arm went dead under him, and then a while longer.

Then, very carefully, without waking her and without moving the hand that held his shirt, he reached over with his other hand and took a short piece of string out of his pocket, and wrapped it once round the bare fourth finger of her left hand, and marked it with his thumbnail.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday Bao brought noodles up to his office from the kitchen downstairs and put them on the desk and didn’t go.

“Something else?”

“No, sir.”

Bao looked at the noodles. Then the window. Then the noodles again.

“Sir. About Thursday—“

He stopped dead.

Zhao lifted his eyes. “Thursday.”

“Nothing, sir.”

“Then why did you say it?”

“I shouldn’t say, sir.” Bao looked as though he’d like the floor to open. “I’m sorry.”

Zhao looked at him for a long moment. Then, very slowly, he smiled.

“Go,” he said, and Bao went, and the man on the phone from the jeweller’s workshop on Harbour Road, who’d been listening all along on speaker under a pile of papers, said, “Thursday’s still fine, Mr. Zhao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday Elowen walked into the study and found him at the desk with a piece of string, a ruler, and a jeweller’s sizing chart.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

She looked at the string. At the chart. At him.

“Why have you got a ring-size chart?”

“Work.”

“What kind of work needs a finger measured?”

He put the string down. “Your ring was too big.”

She blinked.

“It’s been turning since April. You keep putting it in the dish.” He looked at the chart. “You’ve lost weight since spring.”

“So you measured my finger.”

“Four times.”

“Four?”

“The first time I wasn’t sure you were really asleep. The second you’d had a cold shower. The third you were holding my shirt and I couldn’t get the angle.” He paused. “The fourth was right.”

“You measured my finger while I was asleep?”

“Only the string.”

“That’s not better,” said Elowen, and started laughing. “That’s why Bao said Thursday.”

He didn’t say anything.

“You’re terrible at secrets.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You didn’t have to.” She leaned over the desk and kissed his cheek. “Don’t tell Bao I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he came to the shop at five with a small box.

He opened it. Inside was her ring. The same heavy gold, the same little square green stone, a fraction smaller.

“May I?”

She held her hand out. He slid it on. It went over the knuckle and settled at the base of her finger and stayed there, with the stone on top where it belonged.

“It fits,” she said.

“Yes.”

Then she turned her hand to the light and saw the inside of the band. Two lines, engraved very small.

9:41

7:00 p.m. Rain.

She stared at them. The minute on the registry slip, and the minute he’d come in out of the wet and stood on her mat.

“You had them put in.”

“Yes.”

“Both.”

“Both.”

“Why?”

“So you’d have them with you.” He was still holding her hand. “Now you won’t take it off.”

He didn’t say it like an order. It came out like something he’d been hoping for so long he’d stopped noticing he hoped it.

She took hold of his collar and kissed him behind the counter, long, while from the other side of the shop Aurelia, who’d come in with the table plans, made a loud and theatrical noise of disgust.

“Some of us are working.”

Elowen didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

At dinner she kept turning her hand under the table to feel it sit there. He noticed.

“You like it?”

“I love it.”

He put another piece of fish in her bowl. “Good.”

“You could have just asked me my size.”

“I wanted it to be a surprise.”

“It was.” She looked at him across the table for a moment, at the strand of hair over his forehead and the way he was pretending to be interested in the fish. Then she got up, came round the table, took him by the collar again and kissed him there in the dining room with his chopsticks still in his hand, until he put them down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning Granny Yip came in for her tulips and took one look at Elowen’s hands.

Elowen put the left one under the counter.

Granny Yip’s eyes narrowed. “Where’s your ring?”

“It’s here.”

“Don’t hide it from me.” She leaned right over the counter until her nose was nearly on the till. “STILL TOO BIG, IS IT?”

“No, Granny.”

“Then show me.”

Elowen held it out. Granny Yip took her hand in both of hers and turned it to the window and squinted.

“Ah. Better.” She turned it again. “Somebody had it taken in.”

Elowen looked past her, out of the window, where Zhao was sitting on the bench outside with a coffee, very obviously not listening.

Granny Yip followed her look and laughed out loud.

“Of course,” she said, and patted the hand twice, hard. “Keep it on this time. I’ve been watching you two since before he could carry eucalyptus. Now give me my tulips.”

Outside, Zhao lifted his coffee. Elowen lifted her left hand, and the little green stone caught the morning light, and stayed exactly where it was.

chapters.title: The Youngest Sister Sleeps Over at the Big House
chapters.desc: The heating breaks in the Walled City, so Eliana spends a weekend at the house on the hill. She takes Zhao’s security apart in thirty-eight minutes, and he has never been happier.
chapters.content:
The heating in the Walled City house broke on a Thursday night in January, and by Friday evening it was cold enough that Evangeline was wearing two cardigans, Lin Jian was shouting at the pipes, and Eliana had announced she wasn’t spending another night listening to the boiler die.

Elowen got the call while she was doing the shop’s accounts.

“Can Eliana come to you for the weekend?” said Evangeline. “Just till it’s fixed. The Wang boy next door offered her his spare room, and Baba said no.”

“Of course she can.”

There was a voice in the background. Evangeline paused, and when she came back there was something careful in her own voice, as if she were carrying a full cup. “Baba wants to know if your husband would mind.”

Elowen looked across the shop at Zhao, on the stool by the window, reading a contract.

“He won’t mind.”

“Baba says thank you.”

When she’d hung up, she said, “Eliana’s coming to stay. Baba wanted to know if you’d mind.”

Zhao put the contract down. He looked honestly puzzled. “Why would I mind? She’s your sister.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana arrived at eight with one suitcase, a laptop, three chargers, a bag of shrimp crackers and her glasses steamed up from the cold. She stood in the hall in her enormous hoodie with her brown hair coming out of its claw clip, looked round, and said, “Your house has too many cameras.”

Zhao took her suitcase. “Hello to you too.”

“Hello, Brother-in-law.”

“Your room’s upstairs. Elowen made it up.”

Eliana followed him. At the foot of the stairs she stopped and looked out through the glass at the courtyard.

“That one’s pointed too far left.”

Zhao stopped too. “Which?”

“Over the east window. It’s missing the path past the lemon tree. There’s a blind spot about two metres wide.” She walked on. “And whoever put the one in over the garage didn’t think about the reflection off the glass. At night it’ll show you the inside of your own garage door.”

He turned round and looked at her. She was already looking at the next camera.

Elowen came out of the kitchen drying her hands. “Has she started?”

“Your husband has a security problem,” said Eliana.

Zhao looked at his wife’s eighteen-year-old sister, and for the first time that evening he smiled properly.

“Show me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Thirty-eight minutes later Eliana was sitting at the kitchen island with a glass of juice and Zhao was standing opposite her with a notebook, and on the page between them, in his writing, there were five things.

The east camera, misaimed. The blind spot by the lemon tree. The garage camera’s reflection. A delay on the sensor by the side door, long enough for someone quick to get through it. And the backup line to the guardhouse, which ran through the same box as everything else, so that one cut would take the lot.

“That’s without going in the garage,” said Eliana.

“How long?”

“Thirty-eight minutes.”

He nodded slowly. “Good.”

“Good?” said Elowen.

“Very good.” He looked at Eliana. “Do the garage tomorrow.”

“I’m going to.”

“You’re encouraging her,” said Elowen.

“She’s right.”

“Thank you,” said Eliana, and drank her juice, and then held out her hand. “Wi-Fi.”

Zhao took his phone out.

“Oh,” said Elowen. “What’s the password?”

Eliana looked at her over her glasses. “You’ve lived here nearly two years and you don’t know the password?”

“I thought it was the guest one.”

“It isn’t,” said Zhao.

“You never asked,” he added, to Elowen, and told Eliana the password, and Eliana typed it, and then looked up at him with real pain.

“That’s your birthday.”

“Yes.”

“That’s terrible.”

“I know.”

“Change it,” said Eliana.

“You change it,” said Zhao, and she smiled for the first time since she’d come in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was fish, because the cook had been told there was a Lin in the house and Lins ate fish. Eliana picked at hers. Zhao watched her move a bone round the plate for a minute and then reached across and took the plate away from her.
