“It’s fine—“

“It isn’t.”

He took the whole thing apart with his chopsticks, flesh from bones, every piece checked, and put the plate back in front of her.

“Eat.”

She looked at it. Then at him. Then she ate all of it, and Elowen watched from across the table with her chin on her hand.

“You’re good with her.”

“She’s your sister.”

“That’s your answer to everything.”

“It’s a good answer,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner Eliana took her laptop into the study, and Zhao followed her with two cups of tea.

“Firewalls?” he said.

She looked up. “You know what that is?”

“Enough.”

“Sit down, then.”

When Elowen looked in at eleven, her husband and her little sister were bent over the same screen with their heads nearly touching, Eliana talking very fast about segmenting the network and Zhao listening the way he listened to Chen Si, without interrupting, asking one question every few minutes that made Eliana stop and say exactly. Neither of them noticed her. She went to bed smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after one, Eliana’s phone lit up.

She’d been sitting on the study sofa with her knees up, and she bent over it and smiled at the screen in a way Zhao had never once seen her smile at anything, and typed, and smiled again, and typed. Twenty minutes. More. Whoever it was, she’d forgotten the firewall entirely.

He knew he could find out who it was. He had a laptop on the desk that could tell him the number and the name it was registered to and the address behind the name before she’d finished her next message, and she’d never know.

He looked at her for a long moment, curled up on his sofa in her hoodie with the light from the phone on her face.

Then he opened the laptop.

It took him four minutes. He read the name. Wang Yu Chen. He read the address, which he already knew, because it was the house on the other side of the Walled City garden wall. The boy whose spare room Lin Jian had turned down the day before. The boy raised by his cousin, the detective, Song Wei Long.

He looked at the name for some time. Then he closed the window and cleared it, and pulled the firewall back up.

“Brother-in-law?” said Eliana, without looking up from her phone. “Are you listening?”

“Yes.”

“What did I just say?”

“The guest network goes on its own line. The garage doesn’t share credentials with the house.”

She blinked. “Right.” She put the phone face down on her knee. “Carry on, then.”

He didn’t ask her who she’d been talking to. He didn’t tell Elowen in the morning, or Lin Jian, or anyone. He just knew, now, and kept it, the way he kept everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she did the garage, and found a sixth thing, and by lunch she’d redrawn the guardhouse line, written new access permissions and made a list of equipment that needed throwing in the harbour. Zhao read it and rang Bao.

“Split the guardhouse box. Two separate systems. Eliana will send you how.”

There was a pause. “Miss Eliana, sir?”

“Yes.”

“Understood.”

“And change the garage code.”

Eliana looked up. “To what?”

“Your birthday backwards.”

“That’s not secure.”

“No,” said Zhao. “But you’ll never be locked out.”

She looked at him for a moment with her mouth slightly open. Then she went pink, and pushed her glasses up, and went back to her list without saying anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the evening he found her standing in the courtyard by the lemon tree, looking up at the camera on the east wall.

“I’ll have it moved tomorrow.”

“Don’t,” said Eliana.

“You said it’s a blind spot.”

“It is.” She pointed at the gravel under the tree. “That’s where you and Jiejie stand.”

He followed her finger.

“Sometimes she’s out here watering and you come out and stand next to her. You talk. Or you don’t talk, you just look at the tree.” She pushed her hands into the pocket of her hoodie. “You don’t need a camera pointed at that.”

He looked at the bit of gravel.

“Don’t fix it,” said Eliana.

“All right.”

She turned round. “Thanks for having me. And for letting me take your house apart.”

“You made it better.”

She looked at him. Then she stepped forward and hugged him round the middle, quickly and hard, with her face in his jumper.

He went still. She wasn’t a child. She was clever and stubborn and perfectly capable of taking his security apart in thirty-eight minutes and texting a boy next door till two in the morning. But she was Elowen’s little sister, and she’d come to his house because hers was cold. He put one arm round her shoulders.

“Come whenever you want,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the Walled City rang to say the boiler was fixed. Zhao carried her suitcase down to the car. He gave her a small card with the new Wi-Fi password on it, in his handwriting.

“So you don’t have to ask.”

“I chose it,” said Eliana. “I know what it is.”

“Then you’ve got it twice,” said Zhao, and she laughed and hugged him again.

When the car had gone he went and stood in the courtyard. The camera on the east wall was still pointing slightly too far left. He looked at it and didn’t do anything.

Elowen came out and put her arms round his waist from behind.

“She found five things.”

“Six.”

“In thirty-eight minutes.”

“The sixth took longer.”

“You’re proud of her.”

“Yes.”

“Did she ask you not to fix the blind spot?”

“Yes.”

“And you said yes?”

He turned round, so that they were standing exactly where Eliana had pointed. “She was right,” he said.

“About the camera?”

“About where we stand.”

Elowen looked up at him. Then she took the front of his jumper in both hands and pulled him down and kissed him, there under the lemon tree, in the two metres of his own house that nobody could see.

chapters.title: The Boss’s Wife Does the Armory’s Accounts
chapters.desc: From the private diary of Mr. Yao, Zhao’s accountant, the year the boss’s wife starts keeping the books. She finds his four-year-old mistake with a pencil, and he never quite recovers.
chapters.content:
From the private diary of Mr. Yao, senior accountant to Zhao Zhendong, the spring the boss’s wife began to read the books.

✦ ✦ ✦

Monday. The boss brought eleven ledgers into the office this morning. Eleven. I counted them twice, in case the first count was affected by the weekend.

He put them on the long table in front of Mrs. Zhao.

“The accounts,” he said.

She looked at the ledgers and then at him. “Why?”

“You said they were hard to follow.”

“I said your accountant was hard to follow.”

I was in the room. I would like that recorded.

The boss thought about her objection for a moment and then said, “Have a look,” and went to the window. I assumed she would turn a few pages, ask something polite and give them back.

Twenty minutes later she found my mistake on page twelve of the third ledger. A payment entered twice under two different codes during a very difficult quarter, four years ago, and carried forward through four sets of annual accounts since. Four auditors have been past that page. She circled it in pencil.

“Mr. Yao? I think this went in twice.”

It had. The boss came and looked at it, and at me. “Fix it.”

“Yes, sir.”

“I hope that’s all right,” said Mrs. Zhao, apologetically.

I said it was perfectly all right. I have never in my life been so humiliated by someone saying sorry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday. Mrs. Zhao sat at the long table all morning with the ledgers. She has brought her own pencil, her own ruler and a small notebook with a flower on the cover.

At about eleven the boss came in and stood behind her chair.

“Can I?”

She didn’t turn round. She closed her eyes. “Yes.”

He bent over the back of the chair and kissed her upside down.

I looked at the ceiling. When I looked down again she was smiling and he was still standing there.

“I’m working,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then go.”

He kissed the top of her head and went. I have worked for Zhao Zhendong since he had one warehouse and a borrowed van. I have watched him leave meetings because a ship was sinking and once because a man was on fire. I have never seen him leave a room because his wife told him to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday. Mrs. Zhao rang me at seventeen minutes to eleven at night about page nine.

I explained the entry. She asked three questions. I could answer two. The third needed the old file from the cabinet in the office, and I said I’d find it in the morning.

“Of course. I’m sorry to ring so late.”

I told her not to apologise. Then I heard the boss in the background.

“Elowen. Come to bed.”

“One minute.”

“It’s late. He’ll do it in the morning.”

“I know. One minute.”

There was a pause, of the kind I have learned not to imagine.

“Good night, Mr. Yao,” she said.

Then the boss’s voice, close to the phone. “Good night.” And he hung up. I was not given the chance to say good night myself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Monday. Mrs. Zhao found an unrecorded loan.

It was for a new compressor for the cooler at her shop, the first summer they were married, when the old one died in a heatwave with a whole week of roses inside it. The boss paid for it. Mrs. Zhao insisted it was a loan and wrote him a note to say so and promised to pay it back in instalments.

The note was in the boss’s desk, folded in four. She found it checking the supporting papers.

“Zhendong. This was never put in.”

He looked up from his phone. “I know.”

“Why not?”

“You paid it back.”

“I didn’t. When?”

He pointed at the note in her hand. I’ll pay you back. I promise. In her handwriting, very neat, with the date.

“That’s not paying it back,” she said.

“You paid it in other ways,” said the boss, and went back to his phone.

She looked at the note for some time and ran her thumb along the fold. It had been kept for two years. It had been kept very carefully.

“You kept it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“You wrote it,” he said, without looking up.

She was quiet. Then she put it inside her flower notebook instead of throwing it away. I examined my calculator with great attention.

✦ ✦ ✦

March. We discovered that a Mr. Lo at the north freight yard has been paid every month for six years not to open a particular container.

The boss was not pleased. I could tell from his stillness.

Mrs. Zhao read the entry twice. “Is he still being paid?”

“Yes, madam.”

“Does he know what’s in it?”

“No.”

“Does he have to touch anything?”

“No. He keeps it sealed and rings if anyone tries the door.”

She thought about it. “Then pay him on time.”

I looked at her. “Madam?”

“If that’s the arrangement, he shouldn’t have to wait for it. That’s not his fault.” She tapped the page. “But I want to know what’s in that container and who put it there, and I want to know before the next payment.”

The boss looked at her for a long moment. “Find out,” he said to me.

I made a note. I made a second note, for myself: Never assume Mrs. Zhao will leave an entry alone because it has been there for six years.

What was in the container is not for this diary. Mr. Lo was paid on time.

✦ ✦ ✦

June. Mrs. Zhao now attends some of the finance meetings. She doesn’t speak often. When she does, the room goes quiet in a way it does not go quiet for me.

This morning I was explaining a discrepancy on the warehouse account to three department heads, and she found the date on an invoice didn’t match the date on the customs declaration it was paid against. She said so. Everybody stopped.

Under the table the boss took her hand and lifted it and kissed her knuckles. She went on talking as if he hadn’t. Mr. Han from the eastern warehouses turned the colour of a brick.

I have no further comment.

✦ ✦ ✦

September. I have been keeping a separate record of the accounts since Mrs. Zhao began reading them. The unexplained discrepancies have fallen sharply. The corrections have fallen more.

The boss now asks her opinion before he signs certain transfers. She has started asking him what certain expenses are for. He answers. This is, I think, the most remarkable development of the year.

Yesterday she found a payment, three years old, to a company that no longer exists. The boss told us to look into it. She asked if it could be looked into without frightening the junior clerks who’d processed it, since they wouldn’t have known. He said yes.

I am beginning to understand why he gave her the ledgers. He didn’t need someone to count the money. He needed someone who could hear what it was saying.

✦ ✦ ✦

The spring after. The annual review was finished today. Errors in the accounts are down ninety-one per cent on last year. I checked the calculation three times.

Mrs. Zhao read the summary. She looked at the figures and then at the corrected ledgers, one after another.

“This is perfect,” she said.

I felt something I can only describe as my shoulders coming down from my ears for the first time in twelve months.

The boss, beside her, looked a great deal more pleased than the figures required. “Good work,” he said to me.

I thanked him. Then Mrs. Zhao turned to me and said, “Thank you, Mr. Yao. I know how hard you’ve worked,” and I very nearly felt better. Very nearly.

She gathered her pencils and closed the last ledger. The boss took it out of her hands before she could pick up the next one.

“Finished?”

“For today.”

“Come home.”

“I’m coming,” she said, and he held his hand out and she took it.

As they went, the flower notebook fell open on the table for a second and I saw the old compressor note tucked into the back. I’ll pay you back. I promise. The boss has the original in his desk. She has made a copy. Neither of them has ever entered it.

There are some things in that household no ledger will ever balance. I have stopped trying.

✦ ✦ ✦

Private, not for the boss. He carried her notebook down to the car, and her pencils. I asked if he wanted me to send the remaining files to the house.

He said no. Then he asked if I had eaten.

I said yes. He told me to go home.

I have worked for Zhao Zhendong for a long time. I have watched him settle disputes and break partnerships and make men twice his age change their minds without raising his voice. I have never seen him as happy as he was this afternoon when his wife told him the books were perfect.

I believe he has found someone who can tell him exactly where every number belongs. I believe he would let her correct him for the rest of his life, and thank her for it.

chapters.title: The Language of Flowers, Studied in Secret
chapters.desc: He buys her yellow roses, and she tells him what yellow means. So he buys a very old book and starts again, one stem at a time.
chapters.content:
At three o’clock one morning in March, two years after the registry, Zhao Zhendong was standing at the kitchen counter taking the thorns off a dozen yellow roses with a small knife.

He was wearing Elowen’s gardening gloves. They were too small. He’d already cut himself twice through them.

One of the night guards came past the kitchen door, stopped, and looked in.

“Sir?”

Zhao didn’t look up. “Something wrong?”

The guard looked at the roses. Then at the knife. Then at the gloves.

“No, sir.”

“Good.”

The guard went on. By four the roses were done. Zhao put them in a tall glass vase, set it on the table beside the cup she’d use for her coffee, and went back to bed.

At six she stood in the kitchen doorway in her dressing gown and looked at them.

“Zhendong?”

He came up behind her doing up his watch. “Good morning.”

“Are these for me?”

“Yes.”

She touched a petal. “They’re beautiful.” He looked pleased. Then she turned round with the vase in her hands. “Why yellow?”

He paused with the strap half through the buckle. “Because you like flowers.”

“I like lots of flowers.”

“I know.”

“Yellow roses mean jealousy,” said Elowen.

There was a silence.

“Do they?”

“In the language of flowers. Some people say friendship, now. My mother always said jealousy.” She was trying not to smile and failing. “Are you jealous?”

“No.”

She waited.

“Occasionally.”

“Of whom?”

He finished doing up the watch.

“Miles?” said Elowen.

“I don’t see why we’re talking about him at six in the morning.”

“Still?”

“I never said I’d stopped.”

She put the vase down and kissed his cheek. “Poor Zhendong.”

“Don’t pity me.”

“I wouldn’t dare,” she said, and went to make the coffee, and he stood looking at a dozen roses that had said something he hadn’t meant, and decided he needed to learn the language.

✦ ✦ ✦

The book came the next week in a wooden box from a dealer who didn’t usually sell to people who couldn’t pronounce the author’s name. The Language of Flowers, London, 1884, with little coloured pictures of girls in bonnets and the meanings of several hundred flowers, one to a line, in a typeface like a wedding invitation.

He read it at night after she’d fallen asleep. He read it in the car between meetings. He found out that flowers had an unreasonable number of meanings, and that some of them contradicted each other, and that a good few seemed to have been invented by people who badly wanted to say something and would do anything rather than say it.

He bought a notebook and started writing things down.

Rose, yellow. Decrease of love. Jealousy. (She was right.)

Larkspur. Lightness. Levity. He stopped on that one for a while. Larkspur was a delphinium. He thought of a blue floret on the back seat of a car on a wet Monday night, in a flat case beside his wallet. Wrong, he wrote next to it.

Rosemary. Remembrance.

Quince. Temptation.

Honeysuckle. Generous and devoted affection.

Ranunculus. You are radiant with charms. He underlined that. He’d heard it before, in her voice, in a different form, on a night when she’d told him about her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it on a Saturday afternoon, by accident. She’d gone down to his old room at the end of the downstairs corridor, the one he’d slept in for the first month while she slept upstairs behind her underlined clause, looking for a box of her own winter things, and the mattress on the old bed was lumpy in a way mattresses weren’t.

The book was under it, with the notebook inside.

She sat on the bed and turned the pages. The early ones had a few neat lines in pencil. The later ones were covered. Dates. Little notes in his small hand. Flowers she’d mentioned once in passing and forgotten mentioning.

Camellia had a box round it. Not underlined. Boxed, with a ruler, four perfect straight lines. Beside it he’d written: She wanted to see where it grew. She didn’t want to pick it.

She smiled at that.

On the next page: Ranunculus. Radiant with charms. Someone thinks you are lovely.

She stopped smiling. She knew that one. She closed the book carefully and put it back under the mattress exactly the way she’d found it, and went upstairs with her winter box, and didn’t say a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday there was a stem of rosemary in a narrow glass by her coffee. No note.

On Tuesday, a sprig of flowering quince.

On Wednesday, a single blue violet.

On Thursday, a white one.

By the second week she’d stopped asking and started coming down the stairs a little faster. Every market morning, before she left the house in the dark, there’d be one stem by the coffee cup in its own glass. Sometimes something from the shop. Sometimes something from the courtyard. Once a scrap of a yellow wildflower that he’d apparently made the gardener find out the name of, because the gardener told her, red-faced, at the gate. He never explained a single one. She never asked. The glasses started to collect along the kitchen windowsills, and then the sitting-room ones.

✦ ✦ ✦

In April he cut honeysuckle off an old man’s wall.

He’d seen it from the car on the way back from the Docks, a whole wall of it spilling over a little house at the bottom of the hill, and he’d made Bao stop. He got out with a pair of secateurs from the boot. The old man who owned the wall was standing at his gate in his vest, smoking, watching.

“You could have asked,” said the old man.

“I did ask.”

“You asked if you could take it. You didn’t ask if you should.”

Zhao looked at the stems in his hand. “Should I?”

The old man shrugged. “Depends who it’s for.”

Zhao put the honeysuckle on the back seat. The old man watched him do it.

“Did it work?” he said.

Zhao stopped. “Did what work?”

“The flowers. Whatever you’re doing with them. Is it working?”

Zhao looked at him for a moment. Then, to Bao’s visible alarm, he smiled.

“I think so.”

“Then take more next time,” said the old man, and went back inside.

She found it that evening in a glass by the kitchen window, and knew it at once.

“Where did you get this?”

“An old man’s wall.”

“Did you ask him?”

“Yes. He said take more.”

“What does it mean?”

He was taking his jacket off. “Devotion.”

“You know that one.”

“I’ve been studying.”

“I noticed,” said Elowen. “Your book’s very interesting.”

He stopped with one arm out of his sleeve.

“I found it.”

“You weren’t supposed to.”

“I didn’t know it was a secret.”

“It wasn’t.”

“Then why was it under your old mattress?”

He had no answer to that at all. She laughed and kissed his cheek and said, “Keep studying,” and went to see to the rice.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ranunculus came on a Tuesday in May.

Pale pink, layered like a tiny rose, in its own glass beside her coffee. She came down the stairs and saw it and stopped on the bottom step, and the kitchen went away.

She was seven. She was at the old table in the Walled City in her school uniform, and her mother was putting a flower down beside her bowl. Every Tuesday, for no reason. A daisy. A small rose. A ranunculus from the market when they had them. And when Elowen asked why, it was always the same answer, over the top of the teapot.

Because someone thinks you’re lovely.

She picked it up. Zhao was standing in the doorway to the courtyard.

“You remembered,” she said.

“You told me once.”

“I didn’t think you’d remember.”

“I remember most things you tell me.”

She looked at the ranunculus. “My mother did this. Every Tuesday.”

“I know.”

“She said someone thought I was lovely.”

He came across the kitchen and touched her cheek with one finger, under her eye, where it had gone wet.

“Then she was right.”

She couldn’t speak for a moment. Then she put the flower down very carefully on the table, took a handful of his jumper and pulled him in, and kissed him. He smiled against her mouth.

“Good morning.”

“It’s nearly seven.”

“Good morning,” he said again, and she kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she came down with the book and put it on the counter beside him and opened it.

“Explain this.”

He looked. “Honeysuckle?”

“No. This.” She put her finger on the ranunculus. He read it.

“Radiant with charms.”

“And?”

“Someone thinks you’re lovely.”

“You knew the exact words.”

“Yes.”

She closed the book and took hold of his jumper again.

“Tell me to stop,” said Elowen.

His face changed. “Elowen.”

“Tell me.”

He looked at her eyes for a long moment. “Stop?” he said, very quietly, as if it were a question.

“Don’t you dare,” said Elowen, and pulled him down.

He backed her into the counter with one hand at her waist and the other flat on the worktop beside her, and kissed her until the rice boiled over on the stove behind them and neither of them did anything about it. When she finally broke away she was laughing.

“Is that in the book?”

“No.”

“What does the book say?”

He pushed a strand of hair behind her ear. “I haven’t found that page yet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Saturday Raiden came up to the house to look at a switch in the glass room that kept tripping, and stopped dead in the kitchen.

Every windowsill was full of glasses. Rosemary, violets, quince, roses, honeysuckle, a dozen things he couldn’t name.

“What happened?”

Zhao was chopping spring onions. “Flowers.”

“I can see that.”

“Zhendong’s been learning the language of flowers,” said Elowen, coming in with another glass.

Raiden looked at his brother-in-law. Then at the windowsills. Then back. “Why?”

“Because I wanted to,” said Zhao, and kept chopping.

Raiden took a tape measure out of his pocket. “You’re out of room. I’ll build you a shelf.” He measured the wall under the east window. “It wants a lip so they don’t slide off, and a drip tray. And it goes low enough she can reach it without climbing on a chair.” He looked at Zhao. “Don’t put anything heavy on it.”

“I won’t.”

At the door he turned round. “What’s the honeysuckle?”

“Devotion,” said Zhao, without looking up.

Raiden nodded. “Good,” he said, and went.

The shelf went up on Monday, right across the east windows, with a narrow lip and a tray underneath. Elowen put the glasses on it herself, with the ranunculus in the middle. Zhao stood beside her holding the last one, a sprig of rosemary.

“Where does this go?”

“Next to the ranunculus.”

He put it there. She turned round.

“You’ve been studying all spring.”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what my favourite flower is?”

He thought about it. “Middlemist’s Red.”

“That’s not what I meant.” She took his hand and kissed his knuckles. “My favourite’s the one you bring me.”

For once he didn’t have an answer.

“Though I wouldn’t mind fewer yellow roses,” said Elowen.

On the windowsill, beside her coffee cup, there was already a stem for the morning. No note. He’d learned by then that some things didn’t need one.

chapters.title: Valentine’s Day in a Flower Shop
chapters.desc: Nine hundred roses, one till, and an arms dealer saying “Next.” The customers have never been so polite.
chapters.content:
By six o’clock on the morning of Valentine’s Day, Elowen had counted nine hundred roses. By a quarter past she’d lost count and started again.

“Three hundred and eleven orders,” said Xiao Pan, reading off the clipboard as if it were his own death certificate. “Nine hundred roses. And the walk-ins.”

“Good,” said Elowen, and tied another ribbon.

“Madam. We’re going to die.”

“Not till tonight.”

On the other side of the counter Zhao put down a crate of red roses. “Where do you want these?”

“Worktable. Not next to the white.”

He was wearing her pale green apron. The same one he’d worn the first spring, when he’d tried to strip a rose and bled on half a bucket of them; it had gone soft with washing and the pocket had never sat straight. Xiao Pan had once suggested getting a new one. Zhao had looked at him and Xiao Pan had never suggested it again.

“When you’ve done those,” said Elowen, “I need someone on the till.”

“I’ll do it.”

Xiao Pan looked up.

“Do you know how it works?” said Elowen.

“Yes.”

“Cash and card?”

“Yes.”

“Change?”

He gave her a look. “I’ll manage.”

“Then you’re promoted,” she said, and handed him the till key, and Xiao Pan watched it go from her hand to his with the face of a man watching someone pass a lit match over a petrol tank.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao took up his position behind the till. He looked at the queue. The queue looked at him.

Then the first man stepped forward. “Good morning, Mr. Zhao.”

“Good morning.”

“Two dozen red, please.”

“Certainly.”

The man paid at once. He didn’t ask for a discount. He didn’t ask if they could be cheaper by the dozen. He took his receipt in both hands, said thank you twice, and left.

“Next,” said Zhao.

By eight the shop had an atmosphere Elowen had never felt in it before on Valentine’s Day. Everyone was polite. Everyone said please and thank you. Nobody complained about the price. A man who’d once argued with her for a quarter of an hour over a delivery fee paid in full without blinking. A woman who’d once accused Xiao Pan of stealing three stems apologised to him for holding the queue up.

Elowen leaned over. “Why is everyone so polite?”

Zhao was squaring a stack of notes in the drawer. “I don’t know.”

“They’re frightened,” Xiao Pan whispered from the bench.

“Of what?”

Xiao Pan looked at the till. It was the winter after the Red Notice. The boss’s face had been in every newspaper in the city all last spring, and here he was in a pale green apron taking their money.

“Zhendong,” said Elowen. “Smile.”

He smiled. It was a perfectly pleasant smile. The customer in front of him said thank you three times very fast and practically ran out of the door.

“That was worse,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past ten a man in a good coat came to the counter and didn’t look at the till. He looked at Elowen.

“You look lovely today, Miss Lin.”

“Thank you. What can I get you?”

“I was wondering if I might have your number.”

“I’m married.”

“I don’t mind,” said the man, smiling.

Zhao stopped counting. He didn’t say anything. He reached out and took the man’s card off the reader, where he’d left it after paying for his roses, and turned it over, and read the name on it aloud.

Then he read the man’s address. The street, the building, the floor, the colour of the door. He said the name of the man’s mother, who lived with him, and the name of the man’s wife, who did not, and the name of the bar on the corner of his street where the man went on Thursdays. He said it all in the same pleasant, unhurried voice he used for certainly, without looking up from the card, as if it were printed there.

The man had gone the colour of the white roses.

Zhao held the card out between two fingers. The man took it, very carefully, so their fingers didn’t touch.

“Your roses,” said Zhao, and nodded at them on the counter.

The man left without them.

The queue had gone absolutely silent. Xiao Pan had a rose in each hand and had forgotten what either of them was for.

Elowen looked at her husband. He’d gone back to counting the notes, square and neat, as if he’d done nothing at all. She knew perfectly well that he’d had the man’s whole life up on his phone under the counter before the man had finished saying Miss Lin, and that if she hadn’t been standing there something worse would have been said, somewhere else, later.

She also knew she’d have to talk to him about it tonight.

She turned to the queue, tucked her hair back with her left hand so the ring caught the light, and said clearly, for the benefit of the whole shop, “I’m married. To him.” Then, to the next customer: “Next.”

Zhao didn’t look up. But the corner of his mouth went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon she finally tried to eat. She had a bowl of noodles balanced at the end of the worktable and kept putting her chopsticks down every time somebody asked her something. Zhao watched her do it four times. Then he came out from behind the till.

“Eat.”

“I am.”

“You’ve had three mouthfuls.”

“Four.”

He took the chopsticks out of her hand, picked up some noodles and held them in front of her mouth.

“What are you doing?”

“Eat.”

“People are watching.”

“Then eat quickly.”

She laughed and ate off his chopsticks. A customer waiting for a bouquet became deeply interested in the ceiling. He fed her another mouthful. She stole the chopsticks back and fed him one, and he ate it without a word, standing at her bench in her apron in front of twenty people.

“I’m going to pretend I didn’t see that,” said Xiao Pan.

“Good,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came in at a quarter past one in a camel coat, holding a coffee, looking much too relaxed for a man whose brother was working a till on Valentine’s Day. He looked at the queue. Then at the till. Then at the apron.

“Oh,” he said.

“Don’t,” said Zhao.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Back of the queue.”

“I’m here to buy flowers.”

“Then get in the queue.”

Chen Si looked at Elowen. “Your husband’s very unfriendly.”

“He’s working.”

Chen Si went to the back of the queue. It moved fast. When he got to the front Zhao looked at him without any expression whatsoever.

“Forty roses,” said Chen Si. “Red.”

“Delivery?”

“I’ll take them. Do I get a discount? I’m your brother.”

“Pay,” said Zhao.

“Marriage has made you cruel.”

“Next.”

“I’m still here.”

“Your order’s finished.” Zhao put forty red roses in his arms. Chen Si looked at the apron one last time.

“Does Aurelia know you’ve become a florist?”

“Get out,” said Zhao, and Chen Si laughed all the way to the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three a girl of about ten in a school pinafore came to the counter with a handful of coins and stood looking at the roses in the display.

“Hello,” said Zhao.

“Hello.”

“What would you like?”

“One rose.” She opened her hand. It wasn’t enough for anything in the display, and she seemed to know it. “It’s for my teacher. She helped me when I was ill.”

Zhao looked at the coins. Then he reached under the counter and brought out a single red rose he’d done himself at five that morning, every thorn off, the stem cut on the angle, the outer petal peeled away so it opened perfectly. He looked at it once more, wrapped it in brown paper and tied a small bow round it.

“Be careful with it.”

She held the coins out. He took them, every one, and put them in the till.

“Next year,” he said, “bring her another.”

She went out holding it against her chest with both hands. Elowen had watched the whole thing from the worktable. When the door shut she came round and kissed his cheek.

“What was that for?”

“Nothing.”

He went back to the till. His ears had gone faintly red.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six the last delivery had gone and the last order had been collected. Zhao had been on the till for nearly ten hours and hadn’t made one mistake. He’d also frightened at least twenty people into paying full price, and one into leaving the country, or at least the street.

Elowen counted the drawer. “Perfect.”

“Good.” He took the apron off.

“Your feet hurt.”

“How do you know?”

“You’ve been standing since five.”

He looked at her for a moment. Then he reached under the counter again and brought out one last rose.

It was crooked. The stem bent near the top. The head was lopsided, one side smaller than the other, a bruise on the outer petal. It was, quite honestly, the worst rose in the shop.

“For you,” he said.

“Why that one?”

“I liked it.”

She looked at it. Out of nine hundred, he’d kept back the one nobody would have bought. For her. She opened the till and lifted the tray and put it underneath, in the little space where she kept things she didn’t want to lose.

“I’m keeping it.”

“I thought you might.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After closing she sat on the counter with the lights down and the whole shop still smelling of roses. He was putting the last of the wrapping paper away.

“Come here.”

“Why?”

“Come here.”

He came. She hooked her fingers in both straps of the apron, which he’d put back on to sweep, and pulled him in between her knees.

“Mrs. Zhao.”

“Mr. Zhao.”

“You’re supposed to be going home.”

“I am. Closer.”

He leaned down and she kissed him, and then again, slower, her hands still on the straps, until he put his on her waist and stopped smiling and kissed her back properly.

“About the man with the card,” she said, against his mouth.

“Yes.”

“Don’t do that in my shop again.”

“He asked for your number.”

“And I said no. I can say no on my own.” She looked at him. “Next time let me say it first.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “First,” he said. It wasn’t a promise not to do it at all, and they both knew it, and she let it go, because she’d said to him in front of twenty people, and meant it.

“Happy Valentine’s Day,” he said.

“Happy Valentine’s Day.”

He looked down at the apron. “Do I have to wear this again tomorrow?”

“Only if you want to.”

“I’ll wear it.”

“Why?”

“Because you gave it to me,” said Zhao, and she pulled him down by the straps and kissed him again, while under the till tray the crooked rose waited for her to come back in the morning.
